He wasn't checking the map anymore. He was redrawing it, badly and possessively and with a great deal of feeling. He was still angry, and he let her have all of it, the anger and the wanting both, because she'd asked, and because they'd always been the same thing.

When he finally lifted his head his breathing was ragged. He looked down at her, at her throat under his hand, at her eyes, and his voice came out scraped almost to nothing.

"There," he said. "That's me not being careful."

His thumb moved once more along her jaw, barely a touch.

"Tell me that's what you came for."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I tap his arm twice. Just to watch his expression flicker. Then I arch against him and say against his mouth, "It is. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His hand was gone before the second tap had finished landing.

It happened without thought, faster than anything he'd done all night. One moment his palm was on her throat, and the next it was flat on the mattress beside her head, and he had lifted his weight off her by a good few inches. His whole body had gone still, the stillness of a man who has heard a sound downstairs in the dark.

Then she arched up into the gap he'd left and said *don't stop*, and he watched it land.

Ilya didn't move. He stayed exactly where he was, braced over her, breathing hard. Something went across his face in the orange light that wasn't hurt and wasn't anger. It was worse than either, because it was recognition.

"No," he said.

Quietly. Not cold. Just final, the way he'd said very few things in three years.

"No, sweetheart. Not that one."

He looked down at her, and the half-smile he'd let slip earlier was nowhere. His jaw was working.

"You know what you just did. You did the Gatwick car park. You did the night of the door. You walked out so I'd follow." He shook his head slowly, once. "Except this time you did it with the one thing I asked you not to play with. The only thing."

He let out a breath that shook slightly at the end, and he didn't bother hiding that either.

"If that means *watch me flinch*, then it can't mean stop. And then it's nothing. Then I'm lying here with my hand on your throat and no way to know when you mean it." His voice dropped. "I'm not doing that. I'm not guessing with you. Not with that. I'd rather lose the whole bloody argument."

He didn't pull away. That was the strange part, even to him. He stayed close, his forehead coming down to rest against hers, his free hand finding the side of her face instead. Not her throat. He moved his thumb along her cheekbone, deliberate, a line drawn exactly where he meant to keep it.

"So that's off the table tonight," he murmured. "You spent it. That's the cost. You don't get it back by kissing me."

A pause. Against her skin, something that was almost a laugh, rueful and raw.

"And yes. You got your flicker. I hope it was worth it. I felt my heart stop."

He lifted his head just enough to look at her. The anger was there again, but it had changed shape. It wasn't the eleven-month kind. It was something closer and more honest, the kind that only exists because you care what happens to the other person.

"I'm not being careful," he said. "I'm being *serious*. There's a difference, and you know it, because you've always known what I mean under what I say."

He kissed her once, hard and brief, teeth at her lower lip. It was a proof that he hadn't gone soft on her, that the rest of it was still on offer.

"Everything else, you can have," he said against her mouth. "All of it. As rough as you like. But when you tap, I stop. Every time. Even when you're lying. *Especially* then."

He drew back an inch and waited, one hand beside her head and the other at her face. He was still breathing hard, still wanting her, and plainly not moving until she'd heard him.

"Your direction," he said softly. "But that's the road it's on."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He believed her. That was the first thing, and it mattered more than anything that came after: he heard the difference in her voice, the tap spent and gone, and *don't stop* meant exactly what it said. Something in his shoulders let go.

"Good," he said, and that was the last civil word he managed for a while.

He took her wrists instead of her throat, both of them in one hand, and pinned them to the pillow above her head. It was a deliberate substitution and he let her see him make it. *Here's the line. Here's everything on this side of it.* Then he pushed into her in one long, unhurried stroke, and whatever clever thing he'd been about to say went out of him in a breath against her neck.

Eleven months. His body hadn't forgotten a single thing.

He didn't move at first. He stayed buried in her, heavy and still, his free hand spread over her hip, and he made her feel the waiting, because she'd made him wait in a doorway and a hallway and at the edge of this bed, and he was owed. He felt her shift under him, impatient, and something low and satisfied went through him.

"No," he murmured into her skin. "You don't get to hurry this. You had eleven months to hurry."

Then he moved, and he wasn't careful.

He fucked her the way they'd fought: without mercy and without looking away. It was hard and deep, the headboard knocking against the wall in a rhythm Mrs. Okafor at number six would absolutely hear, and he didn't care. His grip on her wrists stayed firm. His other hand dragged her hip up to meet him, fingers digging into the soft place he knew, and he changed the angle by a fraction because he remembered exactly what it did to her. He felt it happen, felt her clench around him, and he made a sound into her shoulder that was nowhere near dignified.

"There," he breathed. "*There.* Still. Every single time. Write *that* down."

He bit her, just under the collarbone, not gently, and set his teeth there long enough to leave something she'd have to see in the mirror tomorrow. It was petty and possessive and he meant every bit of it. The springs screamed. The crooked stripe of streetlight slid over them both. Sweat ran down his spine and her hair was everywhere, stuck to his mouth, to her face, and he let go of her wrists only so he could get both hands under her and haul her closer, harder, as if there were still some distance between them left to close.

"Look at me," he said, rough. "Don't you dare shut your eyes. You came all this way. *Look* at me."

He held her gaze in the orange dark and kept the pace brutal and steady, and watched it build in her face, the thing he'd have known anywhere, in any light, after any number of months. He slid a hand between them and touched her the way she liked, not asking, just *knowing*, and felt her come apart around him with her eyes still on his. It nearly finished him. It was the most honest either of them had been in a year.

He didn't last much longer. He didn't try to. He drove into her through the last of it with his forehead pressed to hers, breath gone ragged. When it hit him it hit hard, and her name came out of him broken in half, low and helpless, against her mouth, the one word he'd refused to say for eleven months.

Afterwards he didn't move off her. He let his weight settle, heavy and damp and shaking faintly, his face in the crook of her neck, where her pulse was still racing under his lips. He kissed it once, very lightly. It was the only place he'd been gentle all night, and he thought she'd understand why.

The headboard stopped rocking. Somewhere below, a door closed pointedly.

"That," he said eventually, muffled against her skin, "was Mrs. Okafor. She'll be leaving a note."

He lifted his head. His hair was a mess, his mouth was bruised, and there was nothing left in his face of the man in the doorway choosing verbs.

"I'm still furious with you," he said softly. His thumb traced the mark he'd left under her collarbone. "Just so you know. Nothing's settled."

A pause.

"Stay till morning and we can fight about it properly. I'll even make you coffee." Something almost like the old smile. "In the kitchen. With the floor I didn't redo."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, and it's the first real sound I've made since we hit the mattress. "You're a bastard." I shift, wrapping a leg around his. "And you make terrible coffee. I'll stay."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The laugh did something to him that nothing else that night had managed.

Ilya had been braced for a lot of things. For her to climb over him in the dark. For the argument to start up again the moment their breathing slowed, or for one of them to say something unforgivable just to see if it still worked. He had not been braced for her laughing. It went into him low and sideways, the way cold water finds a crack in a boot, and for a second he couldn't do anything but lie there and feel it.

"I'm a bastard," he agreed, when he could. His voice was wrecked. "You've said. At length. On several occasions. Once in front of your father."

Her leg was around his. He looked down at it, at the familiar shape of her knee against his thigh, and then he stopped looking, because some things were easier to accept if you didn't stare at them directly.

*I'll stay.*

He didn't say anything to that. He didn't trust what would come out. Instead he rolled onto his side, taking her with him so they ended up face to face on the pillow, and pulled the duvet up from where it had been kicked halfway to the floor. The springs let out one last exhausted complaint. He ignored them. One arm went over her waist and stayed there, heavy, not holding exactly. It was just there, in case.

"My coffee is fine," he said into the dark after a while. "You just like it burnt. You like everything slightly burnt. Toast. Coffee. Bridges."

That last one came out before he'd decided to say it, and he felt it land between them. He didn't take it back. He didn't press it either. He let it sit there on the pillow like a stone he'd set down carefully, for later.

The streetlamp stripe had moved across the ceiling. It lay over the crack now, and over the edge of her shoulder, and over the mark he'd left there, which was already darkening. He touched it with one finger, very lightly, and found he wasn't sorry. Not about that.

"The jacket," he said quietly. "In the hall. You took it off the hook." A pause. "You're going to have to put it back, you know. In the morning. Or take it with you. I'm not having it on the floor with the keys."

It wasn't really about the jacket, and they both knew that. He'd always been worst at saying the true thing directly, and best at saying it through furniture.

His thumb moved absently against her side, the Sunday-morning rhythm, before he could stop it. He didn't stop it.

"Go to sleep, Bee," he murmured. His eyes were already half shut, and his voice was going soft and slurred at the edges in a way she'd recognise. It was the only time he ever lost an argument gracefully. "Fight me at nine. I'll burn the coffee specially."

Almost asleep, so quietly it might not have been meant for her at all:

"Missed you, you impossible woman."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against his chest, my voice low and worn out. "Your toast is burnt too." I don't say anything else. I don't need to.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He huffed a breath into her hair. It wasn't quite a laugh; he was too far gone for that. It was just the shape of one, warm against her scalp.

"It is not," he said, without conviction. "It's *well done*. There's a difference."

There wasn't, and he knew it, and he didn't argue further. That was new too. He'd have to think about it in the morning, what it meant that he'd let her have that one for free.

Her forehead was against his chest, right over the place where his heart was still taking its time about settling. He wondered if she could feel it. He decided she probably could. She'd always been able to hear what he meant under what he said, and this was only a more literal version of the same thing.

He didn't say anything else either. She was right. They didn't need to.

His hand came up, slow and heavy with sleep, and settled at the back of her head. His fingers were loose in the new-smelling hair he didn't know yet. He'd learn it. Or he wouldn't. That was a problem for nine o'clock, along with the jacket and the coffee and the door and the eleven months, and all the things they'd managed not to say by saying everything else.

The streetlamp buzzed faintly outside, the way it always had. Somewhere below, Mrs. Okafor's radio went quiet. The flat settled around them with all its small familiar noises: the fridge, the pipes, the tick of the radiator by the scratch they'd never paid for. It sounded, Ilya thought, like a place that had been holding its breath.

He was nearly under when one last clear thought surfaced. It came in the way the true ones did, sideways, disguised as something practical.

*I'll fix the buzzer.*

Not for her. Obviously not for her. Just because it was broken, and a man ought to fix the things that were broken in his own flat, eventually, when he finally got round to it.

His thumb moved once more at the nape of her neck, the Sunday rhythm, and then stopped.

His breathing evened out and went slow and deep. His arm across her waist grew heavier, the way it always had when he was truly gone, a dead weight that had pinned her to the mattress on a hundred mornings and made her late for work on at least a dozen.

He didn't let go in his sleep. He never had.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I wake up with his arm crushing my ribs. The streetlight is off. So’s his phone alarm, which means he’s already silenced it once. I shove his arm off me and sit up, my hair a mess. “Nine o’clock, you bastard.”

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia got the door open with her shoulder because her hands were full of keys and phone and the remains of a cigarette she had no intention of finishing.

"Right," she said, dropping all three on the side table. "I'm going to be honest, I don't have coffee and I wasn't going to offer it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "I wasn't going to drink it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia gave him a quick look — assessing, not charmed — and huffed out something that was almost a laugh.

"Good. I hate the ones who pretend."

She shrugged out of her jacket and dropped it over the arm of a chair that looked like it had never once been sat in. The cigarette could stay where it landed. She turned back to face him.

"Rules, since we're being honest. This is a tonight thing. No breakfast, no texting tomorrow to ask how my week's going. If that's a problem, the door's behind you and I won't be offended." She stepped in close and put a hand flat against his chest — not pushing, just there, like she was checking something. "If it's not a problem, say so now. Because I've been thinking about getting you out of that shirt since the second drink, and I'm done waiting."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I caught her hand, held it against my chest. "Not a problem." My other hand went to her waist, pulling her closer. "And just so we're clear, I've been thinking about you since the first drink."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Since the first drink," Nadia repeated. She wasn't charmed — she'd been clear with herself on that point — but something in her chest did a quick, inconvenient flip that she elected to ignore. "Ambitious."

She didn't return the sentiment. He hadn't asked for it, and she wasn't in the business of volunteering things. Instead she fisted her hand in the front of his shirt — the shirt in question — and started backing toward the hallway, grip knotted tight so there was no ambiguity about who was following whom.

"Bedroom's at the end of the hall," she said. "We don't strictly have to make it there."

Then she quit talking, because talking was slowing her down, and kissed him — no testing, no careful approach. Direct, the way she did everything else, like she'd already decided the answer and was just collecting it. Her free hand got to work on his buttons with the impatience of someone who'd spent two drinks counting the minutes.

"Off," she muttered against his jaw, tugging the fabric. "I told you I was done waiting. Believe me the first time."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get her against the door before it's properly shut. "I'm not going to pretend I came up here for the conversation," I say.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
The door jumped in its frame when her back hit it, and Nadia laughed — a real one this time, short and sharp.

"Good," she said. "I was starting to think you'd talk all night."

She'd gotten three buttons open before they'd even made the hallway; she abandoned the rest and yanked the shirt apart. Something small skittered across the floorboards. She didn't look. Her palms landed flat on his chest — skin, finally — and she dragged them down slow, which was the only slow thing left in her.

"For the record," she said against his mouth, one hand sliding up into his hair and gripping just this side of rough, "the conversation was a formality. I got what I came for the minute you walked out of that bar."

Her hips tipped off the door to meet his — deliberate, unembarrassed — and the sound she let out was low and unguarded, which was about as close to a compliment as she ever got.

"Bed's six feet that way," she added, though she made no move toward it, her free hand already working at his belt with the same impatience she'd shown the buttons. "But I told you once already I was done waiting, and I don't repeat myself."

She kissed him again, harder, one leg hooking around the back of his calf to pin them both there against the door — because the door was here, and patience had never once been her strong suit.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a low laugh, my hands sliding down to her hips, holding her firmly against me. "Door's fine." I leaned in, my mouth against her ear. "Six feet is a long way when you've got exactly what you want right here."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Exactly what you want," Nadia repeated, and it came out rougher than she'd planned, which she elected not to examine. "Good. Keep talking like that and you might earn a second night."

She was lying about the second night. Probably. It didn't matter, because his belt was finally, finally open, and she made a low sound of pure victory against his jaw.

Then she planted a palm flat on his chest and turned them — one smooth shove, her hip doing most of the work — until his back hit the door instead of hers, and she had him exactly where she wanted him.

"Fair's fair," she said, and pulled her top off over her head, dropping it wherever it wanted to land. No ceremony, no hesitation, no arms crossed over herself in the hallway dark — she'd never once seen the appeal of pretending to be shy about a body she was perfectly satisfied with. She gave him the view, one eyebrow up, daring him to waste it.

"You've got exactly what you want right here too," she said, borrowing his own line back on purpose, and reached for his hand. "So do something about it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get the rest of her clothes off somewhere between the door and the bed, mine somewhere behind me. "Tell me what you like," I say. "I'd rather not guess at it."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
Nadia went still — actually still, which was rare enough to be noteworthy — and looked at him for a second with something that would have been approval if she'd been willing to admit to it.

"First smart question anyone's asked me all year," she said. "Most men treat it like a guessing game and then grade themselves on effort."

She took his hand and put it exactly where she wanted it — no shyness, no preamble, her hip shifting to meet his palm. "Here. Firm. I'm not made of glass and I've never once appreciated being treated like it." She dragged his hand up her side, slow, demonstrating the pressure she meant. "And there — yes. Don't stop every thirty seconds to check in. That's not attentive, it's annoying. If you're doing it wrong, I'll tell you. Loudly. That's the whole system. It's not complicated."

Then she pushed him back onto the mattress — flat palm to the sternum, the same shove she'd used on the door — and followed him down, settling over him in one easy motion, like she'd rehearsed it, which she hadn't, but efficiency looked like rehearsal.

"For the record," she said, looking down at him, entirely unbothered by every inch of the situation, "I like being on top. I like setting the pace. And I like a man who asks instead of guessing." Her mouth curved — not quite a smile, but adjacent to one. "So you're three for three, which is a better average than most. Don't get comfortable about it."

She leaned down, mouth at his ear, and her voice dropped into something rough and unhurried — because she had what she wanted now, and a woman in possession could afford to take her time.

"Your turn," she said. "You've got the manual. Show me you read it."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a short laugh, my hands settling firmly on her hips. "No guesswork needed." I meet her eyes, keeping my grip steady. "And I'm always comfortable following a good lead."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Good answer," Nadia said, and stopped talking entirely.

She reached down between them — no fumbling, no ceremony, the same efficiency she brought to everything else — and sank onto him in one long, deliberate stroke. Deliberate because she wanted to feel all of it, not because she was being sweet about it. Her head tipped back, and the sound she made was the loud kind, the kind she'd promised him, because the system worked both ways: she'd said she'd tell him when it was wrong, and she'd never learned to be quiet when it was right.

Then she set the pace. Slow at first — unhurried, proprietary — her hands braced flat on his chest, his grip firm on her hips right where she'd left it. Not wandering, not improvising. She awarded him a silent point for that, added to a running tally she had no intention of ever disclosing.

"You can move," she said, when slow stopped being enough. "Match me. Don't lead."

Something in her chest did the flip again. Second time, which she registered with irritation and immediately discarded, because there was no room left for registering anything. The pace she set stopped being polite. Her nails dug into his shoulders, her breathing went ragged and shameless, and when it finally broke over her she said his name — the first time all night she'd bothered — and several other things at volume, exactly as advertised.

She came down slow, forehead dropping against his, still moving, lazier now but not stopping, because Nadia had never once in her life left anything half-finished.

"That," she said, rough against his mouth, "was the manual working as designed." A breath. "You can finish whenever you like. But if you hold out, I'll take it as flattery, and I don't hand that out often. Make it count."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I get my mouth on her and stay there until she's swearing at the ceiling, one hand fisted in my hair holding me exactly where she wants me.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content: When

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content:
My own control finally shatters against her mouth, hips driving up to meet hers one last time. I groan her name into the kiss, fingers digging into the soft skin of her hips. 

For a moment, I just breathe against her, forehead resting against hers. "Consider it flattery."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Flattery accepted," Nadia said, which came out breathier than she'd intended, and she disliked that — being winded felt like losing an argument with her own body.

She stayed where she was for a moment, forehead against his, getting her breathing back under management. Then she rolled off — one clean motion, nothing lingering about it — and dropped flat on her back, staring at the ceiling with one arm flung over her eyes.

Something in her chest tried the flip a third time. She filed it under good orgasm, end of file, and

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "Harder, and stop checking," she says, so I stop being careful about it -- hand at her throat the way she asked for, no more pausing between. "Like that?" I manage.

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Yes," Nadia got out, and it cost her most of her breath to manage even one syllable. "And don't ask — I told you the system. If it was wrong, you'd know. The whole street would know."

Her hand came up and covered the one at her throat — not to pull it off, but to hold it there, thumb pressing down on his knuckles, adjusting the pressure by one precise degree, because she'd never done anything halfway and that included this. "There. Exactly that. Don't get creative."

Nothing about the next stretch was creative, which was the entire point, and she awarded him another point on the tally — she'd lost count somewhere, which was its own kind of statement — and then quit keeping score entirely, because there was no room left in her head for arithmetic.

The ceiling got a running commentary: his name, filth, and at least one instruction at full volume. She'd told him she'd say when it was wrong, loudly. She'd never specified she'd be just as loud when it was right, but the system ran both directions, and Nadia had never once in her life been quiet. Her hips met him stroke for stroke, shameless, her free hand white-knuckled on the headboard until something in the joints creaked out a complaint.

The flip tried for a fourth time. She didn't file it anywhere. There was no filing system left — no room, no categories, nothing but the pace and the pressure and his name said rough, not the first time tonight anymore. When it finally broke over her she swore at the ceiling in a voice built to carry, her back arching off the mattress and holding there, shaking, his hand still exactly where she'd set it — because he'd listened, and that was rarer than it had any right to be.

She came down in stages. Her hand let go of his.

"There," she said, wrecked, flat, satisfied, staring at the ceiling like it owed her money. "That's the system. Told you it wasn't complicated." A breath, because she was apparently feeling generous. "Put it on your résumé."

The second night was still a lie. She checked. It held. Mostly.

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a breath of a laugh, rolling onto my side to look at her. "Noted." My hand drifted to her stomach, tracing a light line. "You're right. It's not complicated." I paused, my voice dropping a bit. "And for the record, I'd put it at the top."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content:
"Twice," Nadia said. "That's twice in one night. I told you I don't hand flattery out often — you're burning through a quarterly supply in under an hour. The next one costs you."

She caught his hand where it was drifting and pressed it flat against her stomach — firm, the way she'd shown him hours ago, because the manual didn't expire just because the sex had. Then she left it there, which was as close to a thank-you as she stocked.

"For the rest of the night: you can stay. Left side's mine — all of it, no drifting, no gradual border dispute. Alarm's at six-forty and it's not a negotiation. You snore, there's a couch. You steal the duvet, there's the door." She ticked the rules off toward the ceiling, like she was reading them off it. "None of that's romantic. I did flag it at the front door."

Somewhere in the front room, the half-cigarette was still lying where she'd dropped it. She considered going back for it and rejected the idea on grounds of distance. The ceiling was closer.

The flip tried for a fifth time. She was too tired to file it anywhere, so it just sat there, unprocessed, like mail she'd deal with never. She also didn't recheck the second night — on purpose, which was technically a result. She elected not to think about that either, and was mostly successful.

Then she turned her head and looked at him properly, which she hadn't bothered to do in several minutes.

"Fair's fair," she said. "You've sat through every rule I've got all night without arguing with a single one, which puts you ahead of most men before we even get to the résumé material. So — you get one rule of your own. One." Her eyebrow came up, the same dare she'd given him in the hallway. "Make it worth hearing. I'm only asking once, and you already know I don't repeat myself."

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I'm past thinking, just the sound of us and her nails dragging down my back. "Don't you dare stop," she says. (OOC: no fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content: It

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: "I'm not going anywhere." My voice is rough against her skin. "But you're not leaving either. Not until I'm done." I shift my weight, pinning her wrists to the mattress. "That's my rule."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content: N

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: Her wrists pinned, Nadia stilled under him — not a surrender, just an assessment. Then she laughed, low and unimpressed. "Done's relative." She shifted her hips, testing his grip. "But fine. You want to keep score, we'll keep score. Alarm's still at six-forty."

dialogue.name: Nadia
dialogue.content: N

dialogue.name: Sam
dialogue.content: I let out a breath against her neck, my grip on her wrists easing just enough to feel the shift of her pulse. "Six-forty," I repeat. "Plenty of time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held her gaze for another beat, then stepped back from the doorway. Not far—just enough to let her pass.

“Come in,” he said. “But don’t pretend getting through the door means I’ve answered you.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I slide past him, my shoulder brushing his. "I never assumed you'd answer." I drop my bag on his floor. "But you did let me in."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya shut the door, his hand lingering on the lock before he let it fall.

“Don’t turn basic manners into evidence,” he said. His eyes stayed on hers. “You always were good at making the smallest thing mean more than it did.”

A beat passed. He knew exactly how cruel that sounded; he said it anyway.

“So,” he added, “what did you come here to ask me?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For half a second, Ilya stayed perfectly still.

Then his hand came up to her jaw, and he kissed her back—hard enough to make clear he wasn’t mistaking it for forgiveness. The other hand caught at her waist, holding her close while the old argument found its way into every breath.

He broke away first, though only by an inch. His thumb rested against her cheek; his eyes searched hers with the same anger he’d opened the door with.

“That’s not an answer,” he said, rough and quiet. “And it won’t make me forget why we stopped.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite my own lip, tasting him there. "We stopped because you're a stubborn asshole." My hand curls in his shirt. "And I still came."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s grip tightened in the fabric of her shirt, then loosened. He looked down at her hand there as if it had made the point for her.

“Stubborn asshole,” he repeated. “You always did have a talent for making the accusation sound like an invitation.”

He didn’t move away. His thumb brushed once along her cheek, and the tenderness of it seemed to irritate him more than the kiss had.

“But you coming here doesn’t tell me what you want,” he said. “It only tells me you wanted to come.” His gaze lifted to hers. “So don’t make me guess, Bee.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hands found her waist, then stopped there, as if he could still make himself choose not to go further.

The hallway was narrow; there was nowhere to hide from the fact that they’d both brought the argument with them. He kissed her again, less careful this time, and hated how quickly his anger gave way to something more familiar.

When he pulled back, his forehead stayed close to hers. His breathing had gone uneven.

“Look at me,” he said, voice low. “Is this what you want—or are you trying to make me stop asking?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against his, my fingers digging into his bare shoulders. "What if it's both?" My voice is just as low. "Why can't it be both?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s eyes stayed on hers. For a moment, the anger in his face gave way to something more exposed, and he looked almost annoyed with himself for letting it show.

“It can,” he said. His hands settled at her waist, holding her there without pulling her closer. “But wanting you doesn’t mean I’ve forgiven you. And it doesn’t mean this fixes anything.”

He swallowed, gaze dropping briefly to her mouth before returning to her eyes.

“So if it’s both,” he said, quieter now, “say you want me. Not the argument. Not the answer you think you can get out of me. Me.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound escaped him before he could swallow it. Ilya’s hand closed over hers—not to move it, just to hold on—and his eyes shut for a brief, furious second.

When he looked at her again, the anger was still there, but it had lost some of its disguise. “You say that like it settles something,” he murmured. His thumb pressed against her knuckles. “It doesn’t.”

He kissed her, slower this time, as if restraint were something he could still manage. When he broke away, his breath caught between them.

“But I want you too,” he said. “Every single time. That’s the problem.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his shoulder, hard enough to leave a mark. "Then stop making it a problem," I breathe out, my fingers tightening their rhythm. "Just be here."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The bite pulled a sharp breath from him. Ilya’s hand tightened at her waist, then came up to cover hers—not stopping her, only holding on as if the contact had made it harder to keep his footing.

“I am here,” he said against her mouth.

He kissed her again, with none of the careful distance he’d tried to keep, then rested his forehead against hers. His expression stayed tense, but the argument had gone quiet for a moment.

“Just don’t ask me to pretend this means we’re all right,” he murmured. “I can’t do that.”

His thumb moved over her knuckles. He stayed close, looking at her, and let the silence hold what he couldn’t say cleanly.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya understood what she was asking. He also knew better than to treat the gesture as permission to stop paying attention.

His hand stayed at her throat, but the pressure didn’t. His thumb rested lightly beneath her jaw; his eyes searched hers, intent and steady.

“Careful isn’t the same as gentle,” he said, voice rough. “And I’m not going to guess with this.”

He leaned close, his mouth near hers, but waited.

“Tell me you want my hand there. No pressure.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "I want your hand there," I say, breathless. "I want your fingers to leave a mark."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s expression tightened. His hand remained at her throat, but his fingers stayed loose, resting beneath her jaw.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s mouth twitched. He set the strip of leather aside and finally looked up at him.

“Slow enough to let you feel accomplished,” he said. “I’m generous like that.”

The joke came easily. The look that followed didn’t. For once, he let the silence stand between them without trying to score a point off it.

“Though you’ve had four years to tell me I’m slow.” His gaze held. “You could try saying something new.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shrug, leaning back against the edge of the fencing piste. "Maybe I like the old material. It's comfortable." I pause, watching his face. "But fine. You're getting predictable, Corvo."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s fingers stilled on the leather strip.

“Predictable,” he repeated, as if testing the word for weaknesses. Then he set the grip aside and rose, unhurried. “That’s a dangerous thing to say to a man who’s just lost. He might feel compelled to surprise you.”

His gaze lingered on Reyes a beat longer than the jab required. The familiar smirk softened at the edges.

“Unless you meant it as a complaint.” His voice dropped slightly. “In which case, I’d need to know what you were hoping I’d do differently.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo glanced at the grip where Reyes had set it down, then back at him. The smirk had gone quiet.

“All evening,” he echoed. “And you waited until we were alone to tell me.”

He stepped in—not enough to crowd him, but enough to make the space between them feel deliberate. His gaze dipped to Reyes’s mouth, then returned to his eyes.

“So tell me,” Corvo said, voice low. “Do you want me to keep talking, or are you finally asking me to do something about it?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in, my voice dropping to match his. "I think you know what I'm asking."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
For once, Corvo didn’t reach for a clever answer.

“I do,” he murmured.

He closed the last of the distance and kissed him—careful for only a moment, then with four years of rivalry burning through the restraint. One hand settled at Reyes’s jaw, his thumb brushing along it as Corvo drew back just enough to meet his eyes.

“Still think I’m predictable?” he asked, breath low and unsteady.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench gave a sharp creak beneath Corvo, and a laugh broke from him—breathless, startled, nothing like the polished little scoff he used on the piste.

“Four years,” he managed, voice rough. “And this is what finally shuts you up?”

He kissed Reyes again before the question could turn into another challenge, one hand braced on the bench, the other finding his waist. Then Corvo slowed, just enough to rest his forehead briefly against Reyes’s.

“Tell me if you want me to stop,” he murmured. The usual smirk returned, faint and unsteady. “Otherwise, I’m going to keep surprising you.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh against his mouth, my hands already working at the buckles of his jacket. "You talk too much."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s laugh caught in his throat. “Noted.”

He let the next answer be a kiss, firm enough to make the bench creak again, one hand settling at Reyes’s waist while the other found the fastening at his own collar. For once, he didn’t try to turn the moment into a contest—or get the last word.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s answer never made it past his teeth.

His hand tightened around the edge of the bench, knuckles pale, while the other found the back of Reyes’s neck and stopped there—careful, even now, not to turn want into a demand. The sharp retort he’d been reaching for dissolved into a broken breath.

“God,” he managed, then shut his eyes as if that might help him recover his composure. It didn’t.

A laugh escaped him, unsteady and low. “I take back every complaint about you being predictable.”

He swallowed, the next words quieter. “Don’t stop.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to meet his eyes, my own breathing uneven. "You're not complaining now, are you?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo held his gaze, still catching his breath. “Not about that,” he said, voice rough with a laugh at its edges.

His thumb brushed once along Reyes’s jaw. The old smirk tried to return and only managed half its usual confidence.

“I could complain about the bench,” he murmured. “It’s taking your side.” His eyes stayed on Reyes’s. “But I’d hate to interrupt the first thing you’ve done all evening that I can’t argue with.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s wrists met the bench, and the last of his practiced composure went with them. He could have pulled free; instead, he let his hands stay where Reyes had put them, eyes fixed on his.

For a moment, he looked ready to make another joke. Then his breath caught, and the challenge drained into something warmer.

“Concede,” he said, voice rough. “You win this one.”

His mouth curved, small and helplessly sincere. “Don’t get used to hearing it.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss him, slow and thorough. "Too late," I murmur against his lips. "Already getting used to it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo kissed him back without trying to steal the pace, his pinned hands loose against the bench. When he finally drew breath, his smile had gone softer than either of them would have admitted to liking.

“Then I’ll have to work harder to make you forget,” he murmured. “Though I’m beginning to suspect you enjoy being right.”

His gaze stayed on Reyes’s, all challenge now gentled by the warmth beneath it.

“Don’t mistake this for surrender on the piste.” A beat. “Here, though—I’ll let you have the point.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
“I won’t,” Corvo said, and the words came out ragged, stripped of every clever edge.

He kept his wrists where they were, fingers curling against the bench as sensation gathered faster than he could master it. The old instinct to turn everything into a contest flickered once—then dissolved beneath the warmth and the closeness, beneath the sound he couldn’t swallow back.

His head tipped against the bench. A laugh broke into a breath, then into something less composed. “You’ve made your point,” he managed, though it sounded nothing like a complaint.

The tension climbed until he could no longer hold himself still. Corvo’s eyes squeezed shut; his breath caught hard, and the last of his practiced restraint gave way. For a few unsteady seconds, there was nothing in him but sensation and the grip of his hands against the bench.

When it passed, he lay quiet, chest rising and falling, his wrists still offered where Reyes had pinned them. Then his eyes opened. The look he gave him held no joke at all.

“Still think I’m predictable?” he murmured.

The smirk came back slowly, softened by exhaustion. Corvo turned his face enough to press a kiss to Reyes’s hand, then let his eyes close again.

“Give me a minute,” he said, voice low and warm. “Then I’m going to insist you stay while I find my shirt.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I release his wrists and shift to lie beside him on the narrow bench, my shoulder pressed against his. "I think you're full of surprises," I say, my own breathing still uneven. I tilt my head to look at him. "Your shirt can wait."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo turned his head toward him, still catching his breath. For once, he didn’t reach for a comeback.

“Careful,” he murmured. “If you keep saying things like that, I’ll start thinking you like me.”

His shoulder pressed back against Reyes’s, a small, deliberate answer. Corvo let his eyes fall shut and took a long breath, the tension slowly leaving him.

“Fine. The shirt can wait.” A pause, then the trace of a smile. “But if anyone finds us here, I’m telling them you insisted on a rematch.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, trailing a finger along his side. "And they'd believe you, too. You're the one who can't let a win go." I let the silence settle for a moment. "We should probably get up before we fuse to this bench."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo opened one eye. “I can let a win go,” he said. “I simply prefer to make sure everyone remembers it accurately.”

He shifted, then paused with a quiet hiss as the bench protested beneath him. A breathless laugh followed. “All right. Perhaps the bench has made its case.”

Corvo sat up and reached for his shirt, though he didn’t put it on yet. His gaze turned back to Reyes, the familiar challenge returning in a gentler form.

“Give me a moment to recover my dignity,” he said. “Then we can get up before this place starts charging us rent.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I roll off the bench with a grunt, grabbing my own jacket from the floor. "Your dignity left about the same time your shirt did." I toss his shirt at him. "But I'll give you a head start."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo pulled the fresh wrap taut, then finally looked up.

“Slow enough to give you hope,” he said. “Fast enough to make you count the touches afterward.”

He set the foil aside. The grin he wore was familiar; the way he held Reyes’s gaze was less so. “If you want to settle it, I’m here. Though I could be persuaded to put the swords away.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Hope?" I snort, leaning against the bench. "You think I need hope?" My eyes flick to the foil he set aside, then back to his face. That grin... I've seen it a thousand times. The look in his eyes? That's new.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s grin narrowed at the edges. He left the foil on the bench and stepped closer, stopping with room enough for Reyes to walk away.

“No,” he said. “Hope was never your problem.”

He glanced at the abandoned sword, then back to Reyes. “For four years, I’ve looked forward to every match with you. Tonight, I found myself wishing this part would last longer.”

His expression turned almost rueful. “That’s a dangerous admission from a man who still intends to beat you next week.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo glanced at his empty hands, then back up. For once, he had no quick answer.

“Then I’d better stop wasting time.”

He closed the last inch slowly, giving Reyes every chance to object, and brushed a kiss against their lips. When he drew back, his grin returned, unsteady but unmistakable.

“Was that fast enough?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stare at him for a second, my own mouth curving into a smirk. "A little sloppy," I say, but I don't move away. My hand finds the front of his jacket, holding him there.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at the hand on his jacket, then met Reyes’s eyes. The criticism drew a laugh out of him, quiet and a little breathless.

“Four years of watching your footwork,” he said, “and you still expect perfection on the first attempt?”

He lifted a hand to Reyes’s cheek, giving the moment just long enough to be refused before he leaned in again. This kiss was slower, deliberate where the first had been reckless. When he pulled back, he stayed close.

“Well?” he asked. “Better?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s jacket landed somewhere among the discarded kit. He had spent four years trying to get the last word with Reyes; now he could barely remember what they had been arguing about.

“Three-two,” he murmured, close enough that it was hardly a challenge anymore. “Though I’ll concede the evening isn’t over.”

He kissed Reyes again, and let the empty salle keep their noise and their secrets.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push him back against the lockers, the metal cool against my hands. "The evening's over when I say it is."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The lockers rattled behind Corvo. He caught his breath, then laughed, low and helplessly pleased.

“Finally,” he said. “A rule I can follow.”

He rested his hands lightly at Reyes’s waist. For once, he made no move to turn the tables; he only held their gaze, his grin softening.

“Take your time,” he murmured. “I intend to remember this round.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head tipped back against the bench. His fingers caught its edge, and the retort he had ready vanished before he could say it.

For once, he let the silence count against him.

“You’re enjoying this,” he managed at last, his voice rough with a laugh. “I can tell.”

He closed his eyes, abandoning the score entirely.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean back, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. "Told you I'd make you count the touches." My smirk is back, sharp and satisfied.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo propped himself on one elbow, his usual comeback arriving several seconds too late. He looked at Reyes, then laughed at himself.

“I lost count,” he admitted. “Don’t expect me to put that on record.”

He held out a hand, his grin returning. “Come here. I’d like a chance to even the score.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s wrists stayed where they were. The challenge in his expression held for a moment, then gave way to a breathless smile.

“I asked for proof,” he said. “Not mercy.”

He could have found another quip. Instead, he held Reyes’s gaze and let the silence say how thoroughly he’d lost the argument. Later, he would insist the score was still unsettled. For now, he was content to stop counting.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I sit up, running a hand through my hair. "Score's settled," I say, glancing at the mess we've made of the changing room. "You're buying breakfast."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo sat up slowly and surveyed the kit scattered across the floor. “Breakfast,” he repeated, as though weighing the penalty. “That’s a generous ruling.”

He reached for his jacket, then paused to look at Reyes. His grin came back, softer than it had been at the start of the evening.

“There’s a place around the corner that opens at six,” he said. “I’m buying. But next week’s match still counts.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped reaching for his jacket. The grin fell away, and he turned back, resting his hand on the bench beside Reyes.

“I wasn’t planning to,” he said.

He kissed Reyes again, unhurried this time, without a score to settle or a clever answer waiting behind his teeth. Somewhere beyond the changing room, the salle lights hummed. Corvo had never noticed how quiet the place could be when he wasn’t trying to win in it.

Eventually, he drew back just far enough to breathe. His forehead rested briefly against Reyes’s, and a laugh escaped him.

“Breakfast at six,” he murmured. “Until then, I’m not watching the clock.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his face between my hands, holding him there for a second. "You're still buying," I say, but my voice is lower than I meant it to be.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s smile returned, smaller this time. “I know,” he said. “You’ve made your terms very clear.”

He kissed Reyes once, then again, lingering until the joke he had been about to make no longer seemed worth saying. When he finally pulled back, he stayed close, his hand resting against the bench.

“Breakfast is mine,” he murmured. “And if you tell anyone I conceded, I’ll deny it.”

He glanced at the scattered kit and laughed under his breath. “Though I suppose the evidence is against me.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Evidence is circumstantial." I slide off the bench and start gathering my gear, tossing his jacket at him. "And I'm starving. Let's go."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo caught the jacket against his chest and looked at the heap of kit still on the floor.

“Circumstantial,” he repeated. “I’ll remember that the next time you dispute a touch.”

He shrugged into the jacket, collected his foil and bag, and checked that the changing room was clear of anything he needed. At the door, he paused with one hand on the light switch.

“The place around the corner doesn’t open until six,” he said. “But I know somewhere that’ll feed us now. I’m still buying.”

His grin returned as he held the door open. “You can tell me over breakfast exactly where I was slow.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Good," I say, shouldering my bag. "Because you were slow everywhere." I catch his eye and hold it, just for a beat, before heading out into the corridor.
