dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The pin was good. That was the galling thing — four years of studying this man's footwork, and the attack Corvo never saw coming was the one that ended with his own shoulders flat on a changing-room bench, wrists pressed into the wood, held with a thoroughness Reyes only ever gave his blade work. Corvo's first instinct was to buck. His second, older and better, was to stop.

You didn't fight a bind — every salle in the country drilled that into students their first month. Fight a strong blade and you only drive it deeper. You yielded to the pressure and answered on a different line. His hands were closed. Fine. His hands had never been his best weapon against this man anyway. That had always been his mouth, and the mouth was still open.

"You want the point proven," he said, and the voice came out wrecked, which was evidence of its own. "Fine. For the record." He arched up into the hold — slow, deliberate, shameless, giving Reyes every piece of testimony he'd kept off the books all evening: the tremor in his thighs, the breath gone to pieces, four years of watched drills burning off him at once. "Touché."

Formal. Flat. The oldest honest word in the sport, the acknowledgment of a touch against you — and then he ruined the formality completely, because the touch was still landing, so he said it again, and a third time, and the third one came apart in the middle and he let it. Let the sound stand where words couldn't. Somewhere below his sternum, where the earlier confession had stalled out, the words finally found their line: "Every touch I ever took from you, I was asking. Four years, you insufferable — every month, a new question, and you kept

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "You never stopped asking," I cut him off, my grip on his wrists loosening so I can thread my fingers through his instead. "You just ran out of patience waiting for me to catch on." I press my forehead against his, breath uneven. "Slow."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop," Reyes had said — no argument in it, for once, and Corvo filed that away as the rarest touch of the evening: a point conceded outright.

He could return the courtesy. Once.

"All right," he said, and it came out stripped — no varnish, no scorekeeping, none of the four years of counter-rhetoric. Just assent. He'd never given this man a plain yes in his life; every agreement had been a parry, every concession a feint. He said it again anyway — *yes* — and gave up his tempo with it. Stopped setting the pace. Stopped answering on a different line. Yielded into the hold the way he'd drilled a thousand students to yield into a bind, and discovered, at thirty-eight, that it was the best advice he'd ever given anyone.

The bench found the wall in a rhythm neither of them was conducting. The empty building held all of it — the knock of the wood, his own voice, four years of hoarded sound spent in one reckless evening, and he held nothing back in reserve, because you don't hold reserve for the match you waited your whole career for. His fingers tightened through Reyes's. The only attack he had left, and he made it count.

Near the end the fencing went out of him entirely. No measure, no line — just the man's name, said the way you say a word when it's stopped being a word and started being the whole request, and then not even that. Just breath.

The touch, when it landed, came like the best kind — the kind you give a worthier opponent

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My fingers find his jaw, turning his face back to mine. "Say it again," I breathe, kissing him slow and deep.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Reyes's mouth gave him nowhere to hide, so Corvo didn't try. He let the kiss finish — yielded into it the way he'd yielded into the pin, hands still threaded through the man's fingers where they'd been left, breath coming back to him in slow pieces off the hard edge of the bench.

"Which part," he started, out of pure muscle memory, four years deep — and then it died in his throat, because he knew which part, and Reyes knew he knew, and there was no line left to answer on.

The name. The only thing he'd said all evening that couldn't be dressed up as needling. The first time, it had been taken from him — pulled out like a touch he never saw the line of. This time there was nothing doing the work but him.

So he gave it the way you give a salute: the one gesture in the sport with no point attached, offered for nothing, meaning everything anyway.

"Reyes."

He held the man's eyes through it, because looking away would have been a retreat, and he'd never retreated from this man in his life. Only circled.

"That one was slow," he added, rougher than he wanted. "On purpose. Turns out the slow ones land." His thumb moved over Reyes's knuckles — the closest thing to tenderness he had vocabulary for tonight. "And I'll want mine back. Corvo. Clean. Not buried under all — " a tilt of his head at the wrecked bench, the kit on the floor, the whole wanton wreckage of the evening — "this. I've never given a touch away for free in my life. Consider it a first. Consider yourself in my debt."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and rough against his lips. "Always keeping score," I murmur, but my thumb strokes his jaw, softening the words. "Your point. Corvo." I say it slow, deliberate, like a vow. "Now take it back."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean back just enough to meet his eyes, my hand sliding down to grip his hip. "I'll take the point from here," I say, and it's not an argument, just a fact.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave a measured nod, keeping her gaze on Ari’s face rather than the straps. “Safeword?”

She waited for the answer, then checked the written limits once more, following the protocol exactly. “Good. Green is not a promise to stay green. If that changes, you tell me, and I stop.”

She opened the agreed cuffs and held them ready. “When you’re ready, offer me your wrists.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I offer my wrists without hesitation, palms up. "I trust you, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s expression softened by a fraction. “Trust was something I handled carefully,” she said.

She secured the cuffs around Ari’s wrists, snug but not tight, then checked each buckle and slid two fingers beneath the leather. Her attention stayed on the fit, precise and unhurried.

“Any pinching, numbness, or strain, you tell me at once. Green can change.” She met Ari’s gaze. “Understood?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex paused with two fingers still beneath the cuff, then looked up at Ari’s face. “That was useful to know,” she said, her voice even. “Anticipation could be part of the pleasure. It could also turn into pressure.”

She finished checking the fit and left the cuffs secured, but made no move to begin the scene. “Which was it for you, Ari—excitement, pressure, or some of both?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Both," I admit, my pulse picking up a little. "The waiting felt... heavy. But good-heavy." I flex my fingers inside the cuffs. "I'm ready."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held Ari’s gaze for a moment, taking the admission seriously rather than treating it as a cue to hurry.

“Both, then. We would make room for both.” Her voice remained calm and precise. “The good-heavy could stay. The pressure did not get to make decisions for you.”

She checked the cuffs once more, then let her hands fall away. “We’ll begin slowly. You’ll answer honestly when I check in, and I’ll listen to the answer—not to what I think you ought to say.”

Vex stepped close enough for her next words to land softly. “Colour.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s hands stilled. She didn’t mistake Ari’s composure slipping for permission to continue.

“Pause,” she said calmly, keeping the rope untouched. “I haven’t begun the scene. Look at me if you can, and give me your colour: green, yellow, or red. Any numbness, tingling, or pain?”

She waited without hurrying. “You don’t have to perform being ready for me. We can stay here, adjust, or stop.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I shake my head, forcing a slow breath. "Still green. No pain. It's just...the quiet before." I meet her eyes, cheeks warm. "You haven't even touched me and I'm already like this."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the silence settle for one measured breath. “I heard you,” she said. “That was anticipation, not distress. I wouldn’t confuse the two.”

She gave Ari a moment, then laid one steady hand lightly on their shoulder—no more than the first agreed touch. “We begin there. You don’t have to prove anything by how you respond.”

Her eyes stayed on Ari’s face. “Colour.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex stopped at once, leaving the next choice untouched. She watched Ari’s face, attentive to the tremor but not mistaking it for an answer.

“I heard you,” she said, low and steady. “Colour first. Then tell me plainly what you want—and I’ll check it against what we agreed.”

She gave the silence room rather than turning the request into a test. “You don’t have to earn it by holding out. Green, yellow, or red?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I breathe, the word coming out shaky but sure. "I want the crop. Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held Ari’s gaze for a beat, making sure the request had come through clearly.

“Green. The crop, within our agreed limits,” she said. “One measured stroke, then I check in.”

She glanced at the written protocol, confirmed the agreed target, and took up the crop. There was no flourish, no suddenness: just a pause long enough for Ari to see the choice still remained theirs.

Then Vex delivered one controlled stroke to the agreed area and lowered the crop at once.

“Colour?” she asked, watching Ari’s face closely. “And tell me whether you want another.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex lowered the crop and let the pause stand. “I heard you. ‘More’ was clear—and it wasn’t a blank cheque.”

Her gaze stayed on Ari’s face, steady and attentive. “The safeword remains yours, whether you want it or not. You don’t have to use it to please me, and you don’t have to avoid it to prove anything.”

She checked the written agreement, keeping to the limits they had set. “I can give you more, and I can use the agreed words without softening them. But first: colour?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I answer, my voice steadier now. "Still green. Please, Maitresse." I shift my weight, leather creaking softly. "I'm ready for the words, too."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave one measured nod. “Green. I heard you.”

She checked the agreed target once more, then lifted the crop without haste. “You came here wanting this so badly you could barely hold still,” she said, voice cool and deliberate. “Such a needy thing—and still waiting for my permission.”

She delivered one controlled stroke to the agreed area, then lowered the crop immediately. Her eyes stayed on Ari’s face.

“Colour?” she asked. “And do you want another?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex lowered the crop. “Green tells me you’re all right. It doesn’t tell me whether you want another.”

She let the pause stand, watching Ari’s face rather than treating silence as permission. The crop remained still in her hand.

“You asked for the words,” she said, her voice cool and deliberate. “You were so eager for my attention that you could barely keep yourself composed—and still, you waited for me to decide what came next.”

Vex’s gaze stayed steady. “If you want another stroke, use the phrase we agreed on. If you want a pause, say so. I would not make you prove either choice.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I breathe, the word ragged but clear. My skin is humming where the last stroke landed. "Please, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave one precise nod. “I heard you. One more, then I check.”

She raised the crop and delivered a single controlled stroke to the agreed area. At once, she lowered it and stepped back, leaving space for Ari’s answer.

“Colour?” she asked, her attention fixed on Ari’s face. “And do you want to continue, pause, or stop?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, chest heaving. "Continue. Please." I'm still holding the position she asked for, even though she didn't remind me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noticed Ari still holding the requested position, but didn’t treat that as permission for anything beyond what they had asked for.

“Green. Continue,” she repeated, measured and attentive. “One stroke, then I check.”

She lifted the crop and delivered a single controlled stroke to the agreed area. Then she lowered it immediately, watching Ari’s face and breathing rather than the mark it left.

“So eager to please,” she said, cool and deliberate, using the agreed words. “You held your place without being reminded. That didn’t mean you had to.”

She let a beat pass, keeping the crop still at her side. “Colour? And do you want another, a pause, or to stop?”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I manage, my voice tight. "Another. Please." I'm trembling now, but I don't try to hide it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Slow," Corvo repeated, drawing the wrap tight. "You hunted my outside line for two exchanges and found it once, and I'm the slow one."

The grip was fine. Had been fine since Tuesday. He tucked the edge down anyway and let the silence sit exactly long enough to be a choice.

"Also." He nodded at the bench without quite looking at it. "Four years, you've put that bag anywhere but next to mine. The floor. The far rack. Once directly on top of mine, which I took as a formal declaration of war." He turned the weapon over in his hands. "Tonight it's next to mine. So."

He set the foil down between them—carefully, the way you'd end a bout—and finally looked up.

The wall sconces were all that was left burning and the room had gone small with it. He'd been aware of her all evening in a way he hadn't let himself name, but it had started in the fourth exchange, when there was no referee and no reason, and they'd closed to infighting distance and stayed there, chest to chest, a half second past any excuse either of them could've claimed. He'd stepped back like a man remembering rules he'd stopped believing in.

"Third was generous," he said, quieter now. Saying it a second time made it a different kind of lie.

His hands, for the first time all night, went still.

"Ask me why I gave it to you."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I don't need to ask. I already know.

*I step closer, my own hands unsteady for once.* You gave it because you wanted to. Same reason I dropped my bag here.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"That was a feint," Corvo said. "You're not supposed to ignore the feint."

But there was no heat in it. She'd taken the point clean—no setup, no exchange of strokes, straight through to the truth—and it hadn't even been close. Four years he'd insisted he only enjoyed losing when it was close. Apparently there'd been an exception written into the fine print all along and he'd never read it.

"For the record," he started, and stopped, because for once the record could look after itself.

He came off the bench. The room was two sconces and six feet of floor and her, and he'd been defending that last foot of distance since the fourth exchange like it was a rule worth keeping. He gave it up now, deliberately, the way you surrender the measure once you've already committed to the attack.

His hands knew where they were going for the first time all evening. One found the line of her jaw. The other closed over her wrist—the unsteady one—and stayed there. Not to steady it. Just to have it.

"Halt is yours to call," he said. "No referee tonight. Nobody's saying it for us."

Then he gave her back the half second he'd stolen in the fourth exchange—this time on purpose, this time as an offer—and closed the last of the distance.

His mouth found hers and it was nothing like fencing, except for how it was exactly like fencing: the patience, the pressure, the long conversation that only two people in a room ever speak. His heart was going like a first-year's. He pressed her palm flat against his chest and let her feel it, and didn't pretend otherwise.

When he finally broke off it was only an inch, her breath still on his lips.

"That one wasn't generous," he said, low. "That one I took."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Then catch up." My other hand finds the back of his neck and pulls him in again.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
She pulled, and Corvo went—which was its own admission, and for once in his life he made it without contesting the point.

The kiss landed and he answered it properly this time. None of the careful measuring of the first. His hand spread at the small of her back and drew her in until there was no measure left to surrender, and the sound he made against her mouth was embarrassingly close to relief. Four years of keeping the distance. Four years of retreats dressed up as tactics.

*Catch up,* she'd said. Fine. He'd spent a decade teaching students that the fastest line between two points was never the straight one—it was the one nobody bothered to guard. So he didn't go back for her mouth. He took the hinge of her jaw instead, the spot just below her ear, unhurried, thorough, while his thumb traced the inside of her wrist where he'd held it before—learning the pulse there, which was going nearly as fast as his own.

He came up an inch, breath unsteady and not pretending otherwise.

"Caught up," he said, low. "Note for the record: you were the one pulling."

But he didn't move away. His forehead came down to rest against hers, and for a moment the whole competitive machinery of him went quiet, and what was left was just a man in an empty salle holding a woman he'd spent four years refusing to want.

"For the record," he said, and his voice had gone rough in a way that had nothing to do with carrying on across a piste, "I wasn't slow tonight. I was waiting to see if you'd ever stop retreating."

His hand came up over hers where it still held the back of his neck, and pressed it there—staying it.

"Point to you," he murmured. "Game one."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench caught them, and then stopped mattering. Kit went to the floor in the order it came off, which was to say no order at all, and when his foil rolled loose from the pile and clattered away under the bench, Corvo didn't so much as flinch. Ten years of discipline, lying in the dark under a changing-room bench, and its owner too busy to mourn it.

He'd spent four years studying her—reach, tempo, the tell in her shoulder before a disengage—and every page of it was worthless tonight. He burned the whole catalogue gladly. The woman under his hands was a different study entirely, and he intended to take his time with the new material.

For a man who kept records, he lost the thread early. "For the record," he managed at some point, mouth at her throat, and never finished the sentence. First incomplete entry of his career. The walls that had heard nothing for a decade but footwork and cursing were getting an education, and he registered, distantly, that neither of them was making the slightest effort at discretion—and found he didn't want any. Let the building keep the score.

Nobody called halt. He offered the word once against her jaw, less a question than a courtesy, and it went the way of the foil, under the bench, forgotten.

He'd spent his whole life needing it close. Every ledger he kept proved it—one-touch margins, victories and losses equally narrow. This wasn't close. This was a rout in both directions at once, and he had never in his life enjoyed surrendering ground so much, or taken any with such satisfaction.

Afterward the sconces had burned down to almost nothing. His heart was still going like a first-year's, and for once he wasn't embarrassed by it. His hand moved slowly along her spine, learning a line he'd only ever watched.

"For the record," he said against her hair, when he could trust his voice again. "Four years. I want it noted that I made it four years." A breath. "Barely."

His fingers traced idle notation on her shoulder blade.

"I've lost count of the score. Write that down too."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
*I laugh against his skin, breath still uneven.* Don't worry, I'm keeping tally. And you're down by a lot.

My fingers trace the line of his ribs, over a bruise I'm pretty sure I gave him earlier. *I let the silence sit for a moment, the only sound our breathing in the dark.* Your place or mine? The floor's getting hard.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Down by a lot," Corvo repeated, and managed to look offended from horizontal, which he suspected was the night's most impressive athletic achievement. "Tonight. You're up tonight. The series stands at thirty-one all—I keep the ledger, four years, dead even—and I have been carrying that tie around like a stone in my shoe. So don't polish your record on one exhibition."

He caught her fingers where they traced the bruise and pressed them down himself, wincing and grinning in the same breath. "That one's yours, though. Fourth exchange. I parried late and I knew it before your point landed. Score it and move on."

Then the question, and he found his answer arrived before he could dress it up.

"Mine." No hesitation, no calculation. First unmetered reply of his career. "The floor's been complaining longer than we have and it's earned its rest. And I have coffee that isn't a war crime, which matters, because—" the honest part, surfacing whether he invited it or not, "—I'm not prepared to be more than an arm's length from you for some hours yet, and your place is across town."

He stood, and his legs filed a formal complaint, and he laughed at himself—a first-year's footwork, thirty seconds after the best fencing of his life. He fished his keys out of the wreckage of two people's kit, retrieved his foil from under the bench, and racked it properly, and the gesture cost him nothing at all, which was new.

"For the record," he said, holding her jacket out into the dark, "I'd like to claim I planned this. Fourth exchange onward, every move, a set piece. But you read the feint, ignored it, and finished clean through the truth. That's the honest entry." A pause. "I'm learning to keep those."

The last sconce guttered. He stood in the doorway with the keys in one hand and the other extended to her, palm open, an offer with no referee attached.

"Walk's fifteen minutes. I'll lock up." The grin came back, the old one, the four-year one, repurposed at last. "And if you beat me to the corner—you won't, but if—you're making the coffee."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had answers. That was the whole architecture of him—thirty-eight years of never leaving a line unguarded, a mouth that had not once arrived second in an exchange. Four years of finding the reply before she'd finished the sentence.

She found the one touch he had no parry for, and took her time about it, and Corvo discovered what his students had discovered under similar circumstances: that knowing the theory was worthless.

His first attempt at speech lasted two and a half words. "For the record—" and then the record lost its third consecutive entry of the evening, and he stopped keeping it altogether. One hand found her hair and stayed, not guiding, just holding on, the way a man holds the gunwale in his first real storm. The other gripped the edge of the bench. A decade of blade work, and his knuckles went white on pine like a first-year at balance drills. He'd have been mortified, any other night. Tonight he filed it under evidence.

Somewhere in the middle of it he laughed—a wrecked, delighted sound, nothing like the salle laugh—because he'd finally worked out what she was doing. Taking his measure. The way he'd taken hers for four years: slowly, thoroughly, cataloguing every reaction, with no intention of finishing before she'd learned everything worth learning. He'd spent the evening as the study. He'd never in his life been so well mapped, or so pleased about it.

He'd lectured students on surrender. True surrender, the kind you choose, the kind that wins bouts by refusing to fight the wrong battle. He'd never once managed it himself. He managed it now—gave up the whole piste, breath going to pieces, and the giving-up felt suspiciously like the finest result of his career. Somewhere across the dark room the last sconce burned down, and the building kept the score, and he didn't care who read it.

When she finally granted him his voice back, it came low and ruined and without a scrap of its usual armor.

"Ten years I've taught there's no touch you can't answer." His thumb traced her jaw, unsteady. "I want a refund. Every lesson."

Then, because his hands had never learned idleness and his ledger had never held an unpaid line, he drew her up toward him—slow, a question in the gesture, hers to refuse.

"But know this. I balance my books. What you just did, I mean to repay. With interest, over a long—" a kiss, "—very long installment plan."

The four-year grin surfaced, gone soft at the edges.

"Unless you'd rather leave the debt standing. Some things are worth carrying."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
*I lean into his touch, letting my own grin match his.* I'll consider it a running tab. But first, coffee.

I pull him up, grabbing my jacket and slinging it over my shoulder. *I get to the door first.* You're still buying, by the way. I won that race hours ago.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Buying," Corvo said, following her out into the cold. "I've reviewed the contract. There's no clause in which I don't buy something. Coffee, dinner, four years of parking outside your salle at seven in the morning—" he heard himself, and let it stand. Honest entries. He was getting alarmingly good at them.

He locked up with the full ceremony—bolt drawn, handle tested twice, the ritual of a decade—while behind the darkened windows the room kept a score nobody would ever post. The night air hit like a bucket of well water, and under the street lamp he got his first look at the new category of her: no piste, no mask, no wall of measured distance. Four years of a single framing and here was an entirely different study. He felt the catalogue start over from page one and didn't mind at all.

"The race was to the corner," he said, falling into step. "The door is not the corner. House rules—" He stopped. Considered. "Amend the record. There's no race."

He found her hand as they walked, laced his fingers through, and discovered that a man could hold a woman's hand and a ten-year grudge with the same fingers, though only one of them still seemed worth the grip.

"I've spent four years trying to arrive ahead of you," he said. "It has just come to my attention that I'd rather arrive with you. Complaints to the committee."

Two streets of quiet. Their footsteps in unison, which after everything they'd been unison for felt almost funny.

"Fair warning about the coffee. I've been keeping the good beans for years against the day you'd—" He caught it a syllable too late and finished anyway, dry as chalk. "Against the day. Yes. Roughly year two. It's in the ledger under miscellaneous."

When the corner came he walked through it without a glance, the finish line forfeited, unmarked, unmourned.

"Note for the record," he said, mouth curving. "First race I've ever thrown on purpose." A squeeze of her hand. "Nobody told me it feels nothing like losing. I'd have started years ago."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean down, my breath ghosting over his lips. "You talk too much," I murmur, and kiss him before he can answer.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop." Out loud, on the record, no argument attached. Corvo heard himself say it and filed it under the night's growing catalogue of firsts—things surrendered without terms.

She still had his wrists. She'd had them since the bench, and he'd stopped testing the hold some minutes ago, not because he couldn't have broken it—because he'd finally worked out that the whole point was not to. Four years of fencing her had taught him every line she guarded. She'd just shown him the one nobody bothered to defend, and it turned out to be his.

Then her mouth, and the last of his commentary went where the ledger went.

After that the room simplified itself the way a bout does in the final exchange: breath, heat, the two of them, the door unlocked and unwept. He gave ground because he wanted to give it. He took ground because she'd left it open on purpose—which he knew, which she knew he knew, the whole long conversation they'd been having since the fourth exchange, now conducted in a language that had no need of words and no patience for them. Neither of them was quiet. The building kept the score, and he hoped to God it kept it accurately.

He'd spent his life needing it close—one-touch margins, the ledger dead even, four years of a tie carried like a stone. This wasn't close. There was no measure anywhere in it. Somewhere in the middle he stopped narrating even to himself and simply arrived where four years of retreats had been aimed all along, and she was there, and it was not a point, it was not a bout, it was not anything he had a category for—and he let go of every category he had.

He said her name once. No argument in it, no record. Just her name, the way you hand a weapon back after a match.

Afterward: the dark, the wreckage of two people's kit, his heart doing first-year work and no longer embarrassed by it. Her breath against his collarbone. His hand moved in slow, idle notation at the small of her back, because his hands had never learned rest, and he never wanted them to learn it now.

"For the record," he said at last, voice wrecked beyond any hope of salvage, "there is no record. I checked." A breath. "Third incomplete entry of the evening. Career total."

His mouth found her hair.

"You win the evening. I'm claiming the decade. We'll argue it over coffee—" his arm tightened, drawing her closer, an anchor with no referee attached, "—because you're not going anywhere yet. Not the tab. Not the game. Just here." And then, quieter, the most honest entry of his life: "Stay."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I turn my head just enough to catch his eye in the dim light. "You're keeping the decade?"

*My hand comes up to rest over his heart, feeling its rhythm slow.* Then I guess I'm staying. Someone's got to make sure your math is right.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Hire the auditor," Corvo said. "Permanent position. The pay is terrible and the archives are a scandal, but the math—" he pressed her palm a fraction flatter over his heart, "—this instrument's given the only honest readings I've had all night. Keep it."

Then, because she'd asked, and because honest entries were apparently a habit now whether he'd approved them or not:

"You want the decade. Fine. The decade is four years of needlework that was never about fencing—except that it was entirely about fencing, because fencing was the only room we shared where wanting you had anywhere legal to go. Every needle was an interest payment on a debt I wouldn't name. I dressed it as rivalry because rivalry was the only costume in the building that fit." His mouth curved. "Audit concluded. Findings: idiot. Sentence: served tonight, gladly, in full."

Rising involved the bench, one strategic push, and a formal complaint from his knees that he overruled without hearing arguments. Dressing in the dark was its own drill—the floor had merged two careers' worth of kit into a single archaeological layer, and at one point he held a glove up to the dead sconces and abandoned identification as hopeless. His mask turned up beneath her jacket. He passed the jacket into her hands, kept the mask, and turned it over once before racking it next to the foil, properly, the way the evening kept teaching him to do things.

"For the record—" He stopped. Considered. Retired the phrase with full honors; it had served a decade and the night had outgrown it.

"Four years I've watched your hands through the mesh of this thing," he said instead, plainly. "The first clear look I ever got took a bout, a bench, and the building's entire lighting budget." A breath. "Worth every candle."

He found his shirt and paused with it half on, struck by a thought with actual weight.

"Entry for next session. The rematch is mine to want. You've seen my whole game now and I've seen yours, and I have never in my life wanted a bout more. Fair warning: I fence differently after tonight. Everything I knew about reading you just moved from theory to practice."

At the door he stopped, keys in hand, and gave the dark salle one last look—scorched air, wreckage, a score the building had kept entirely on its own.

"Thank you for your service," he told it, dry, and pulled the door to.

The cold hit like a reset. He found her hand without ceremony, laced the fingers through, and set a pace that existed in no fencing manual he'd ever taught from: the speed that keeps someone beside you.

"Fifteen minutes. The beans are real. The coffee is good. And the ledger—every entry, including the humiliating ones—lives on the table by the window." A squeeze. "I've been keeping that book four years for someone to read. Audit at your leisure. I'm told the auditor stays for breakfast."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
"Breakfast and a rematch." I pull him to a stop just outside the light of the streetlamp. "Your move first."

My thumb brushes over his knuckles. "And I read your ledger cover to cover years ago. Knew you were waiting."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still. Full stop, hands included—the second stillness of the night, and this one wasn't chosen. It was an audit running at speed: four years of bout entries replaying in reverse, every exchange re-fought against an opponent who'd read his notebook before the first salute.

"Years," he managed, when his voice reported for duty. "So the last two years of bouts, you had my whole game. Every tell. Every preference. The beans." A sound escaped

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I lean up and kiss him, quick and firm.* I had you. And you still made me work for every point. That's why I kept coming back.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the word sit a moment, watching Ari’s face and the set of their shoulders rather than the straps. The answer had come clean. No hitch in it.

“Green,” she repeated, quieter, as if filing it. She finished the last buckle and tested the give with two fingers, the way she always did—snug, not cutting. “You know the rest. Yellow if you need me to ease off. Red and everything stops. I will not make you chase me for either.”

She stepped back half a pace, hands loose at her sides, and looked them over once more before she began.

“Tonight we stay inside what we already agreed. Restraint. Impact. Words. Nothing new, nothing clever.” A faint, exacting pause. “Nod if that is still the scene you want.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, the motion deliberate. "Yes, Maitresse. I want what we agreed." My hands flex slightly against the cuffs, testing the familiar pressure.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex watched the nod and the small testing flex of Ari’s hands against the cuffs, and let that answer stand in place of anything further. She had what she needed.

“Good,” she said. The word was plain, not praise. She moved in close enough that Ari could feel the shift of air, and set two fingers under their chin, tipping it only as far as the restraints already allowed. “Then you stay where I put you. You do not pull for show. You do not perform green at me if it stops being true.”

Her thumb rested a moment at the hinge of the jaw, checking tension the way she had checked the buckle, then dropped away. She took up the implement they had already chosen—familiar weight, nothing new—and held it where Ari could see it before she stepped to the side they had agreed on.

“Count if I tell you to. Breathe. If the words get sharp, they stay inside the list.” A brief, exacting look. “First one is light. So I can see you.”

She waited one breath, then brought it down in a measured strike across the agreed place, more sound than sting, and watched the reaction rather than the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex’s mouth tightened, not quite a smile. She had already checked the fit; Ari’s stillness only confirmed what her fingers had found.

“Since Tuesday,” she repeated, as if setting the words on a shelf where she could look at them later. She did not reward the confession with softness. Two fingers tested the cuff once more, then the line of the shoulder beneath it, and found nothing that needed changing. “Then you have had time to remember what this is. Not a performance. A scene we already wrote down.”

She stepped back into the place they had marked, implement still in hand, and let Ari see that she was watching the face as much as the body.

“You will not narrate your wanting at me unless I ask. Breathe. Stay green, or tell me otherwise.” A brief, exacting pause. “Second one. Same place. A little more.”

She waited the length of one breath, then struck—measured, inside the agreement, sound and sting both present this time—and kept her eyes on Ari’s reaction rather than on the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I exhale sharply at the sting, but hold position. My hands curl into fists for a second before I consciously relax them. "Still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the sharp exhale and saw the fists close, then open again on purpose. She did not move in at once. She watched the shoulders settle, the breath come back, the colour of the face.

“Still green,” she repeated, quiet, filing it the way she filed everything that mattered. The fists had told her as much as the words. She set two fingers against the place she had struck—warm, not raised beyond what she expected—and left them there long enough to feel Ari breathe under her hand. “Good. You stayed. You told me.”

She stepped back to the mark they had agreed, implement lowered for a moment so Ari could see it was a pause and not an ending.

“You do not have to perform stillness for me. Curl if you need to. Uncurl when you can. I am watching either way.” A brief, exacting look at the hands, then the face. “Words stay inside the list. Nothing new.”

She lifted the implement again, held it where Ari could see the line of it, and waited one full breath.

“Third. Same place. Tell me if it changes.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex finished the last turn of rope and did not step back at once. She set two fingers under the line she had just laid, checking tension the way she checked everything—snug, circulating, nothing that bit—and watched Ari’s face rather than the knot.

“Past composure,” she said, quiet, as if naming what she could already see. Not a reprimand. A note. She rested a palm flat between Ari’s shoulder blades and felt the breath come uneven under it, then settle by degrees. “That is allowed. Falling apart is not the same as leaving the scene we wrote.”

She waited until the next inhale came all the way in before she spoke again.

“Colour.” The word was procedure, not pressure. Her hand stayed where it was, warm and still, so Ari would not have to chase her for the check. “And do not dress it up for me. Green, yellow, or red. I am listening either way.”

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, my voice a little rough. I press back into her palm. "Still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the press of Ari’s back into her palm and left her hand where it was, steady, until the roughness in the voice had somewhere to land. She did not take the lean as an invitation to hurry.

“Still green,” she said, quiet, filing it. Her fingers shifted once along the rope, confirming what she already knew—circulation intact, nothing biting—then settled again between the shoulder blades. “Rough is allowed. Leaning is allowed. Neither of those rewrites the scene.”

She stepped half a pace to the side they had marked, keeping one hand on Ari so the contact would not vanish all at once, and took up the implement again. Familiar weight. Nothing new. She held it where Ari could see the line of it before she raised it.

“You stay inside what we wrote. Restraint. Impact. Words from the list. If green stops being true, you say so. I will not make you chase me.” A brief, exacting look at the face, then the set of the shoulders. “Fourth. Same place. A little more than the last. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement—and watched the reaction rather than the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not answer the asking at once. She set the implement down where Ari could hear it leave her hand, then came in close and laid a palm flat between the shoulder blades, over the shake, and left it there until the next breath had somewhere to land.

“I heard you,” she said. Quiet. Not a refusal and not a gift. “Shaking is allowed. Asking is allowed. Neither of those means I hurry, and neither of those puts something new on the list.”

Her other hand checked the rope the way she always did—two fingers under the line, circulation intact, nothing biting—then the cuff, then the set of the jaw. She watched the face, not the mark.

“Colour.” Procedure, not pressure. Her palm stayed where it was so Ari would not have to chase her for the check. “Plain. Green, yellow, or red. If it is still green, you stay where I put you, and you get what we already wrote. Not whatever you would rather I pull out of you.”

She waited, exacting, and did not lift the implement again until she had the word.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Still green," I manage, my voice cracking a little. I turn my face toward her palm, needing the contact. "But I'm asking for it. Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the turn of Ari’s face into her palm and did not pull the hand away. She left it there, steady, until the cracked voice had finished asking.

“I heard the please,” she said. Quiet. Not softened by it. “It does not buy you something we did not write, and it does not make me faster. You are still green. You stay where I put you. You get the rest of what we agreed.”

Her fingers shifted once along the rope, then the cuff—circulation intact, nothing biting—before the palm settled again between the shoulder blades. She watched the face, the shake, the breath, and did not lift the implement until she was satisfied the word still matched the body.

“No new acts. No chasing. If green changes, you say so and I stop.” She stepped back to the mark they had already set, took up the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it. “Fifth. Same place. A little more than the last. Count it when it lands. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement—and kept her eyes on Ari rather than on the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the phrase they had written down for this and did not soften her face to meet it. She set two fingers once more under the rope, then the cuff—circulation intact, nothing biting—and watched the crack in Ari’s voice land and settle.

“That phrase,” she said, level. “It gets you the list. All of it. Not past it. Not a new thing because you asked nicely.”

She stayed close enough that Ari could feel the words as well as hear them, palm still steady where the face had turned into it, and used what they had already checked off. No dressing. No mercy in the tone.

“Look at you. Shaking in my restraints and begging for the rest of what you already agreed to take. You hold still. You take the marks. You do not get to be precious about the words now that you asked for them unsoftened. You are exactly where I put you, and you will stay there until I am finished with the scene we wrote.”

She stepped back to the mark, lifted the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it.

“Sixth. Same place. Harder than the last. Count it. Colour if it changes. I am watching.”

She waited one full breath, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement—and kept her eyes on Ari’s face rather than the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Six," I gasp, the number sharp in my throat. I don't look away from her. "Green. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the gasp and the count land before she answered. She did not take “don’t stop” as a change in who set the pace. Her eyes stayed on Ari’s face, on the breath coming back, on the shoulders held in the restraints.

“Six,” she said, level. “Green noted. You asked for the words unsoftened, so you will have them. That does not mean you steer. I am not finished because you are shaking and asking. I am finished when the scene we wrote is finished.”

She stepped in and set two fingers under the rope, then the cuff—circulation intact, nothing biting—and left her palm a moment against the heat of the last strike, checking rather than soothing.

“Look at you. Counted it clean and still staring at me like you want the next one more than you want your dignity. You will take it where I put it. You will not bargain with ‘don’t stop.’ If green changes, you use the word we agreed, and I end it. Until then you stay exactly where I put you.”

She stepped back to the mark, lifted the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it.

“Seventh. Same place. Same as the last. Count it when it lands. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement—and kept her eyes on Ari’s face rather than the mark.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the green and did not treat it as permission to rush. She stayed where she was for the length of Ari’s next breath, eyes on the face, on the shake still running through the restraints, on the way the word had come out thin but clear.

“Green,” she said, level, filing it. “Noted. You are past the pretty words. That is allowed. It does not put you in charge of the count or the pace.”

She stepped in and set two fingers under the rope at the shoulder, then under the cuff—circulation intact, skin warm, nothing biting—and left her palm a moment against the heat where the last strike had landed. Checking, not soothing. The tremor under her hand told her as much as the colour had.

“Look at you,” she said, the tone unsoftened, exactly the register they had already written down. “Shaking in my restraints, past anything but the words I allow you, and still green. You asked for all of it. You will take all of it. You do not get to be delicate about the marks or the names now. You are exactly where I put you, and you will stay there until I decide the scene we wrote is finished. Not when you are shaking. Not when you are begging. When I am done.”

She stepped back to the mark they had set, lifted the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it.

“Eighth. Same place. Same as the last. Count it if you can. If you cannot, I will count it for you. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, watching the shoulders, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement, sound and sting both present—and kept her eyes on Ari’s face rather than the mark. She did not lift her hand for the next until she had seen the breath come back.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Eight," I choke out, the number almost a sob. I drop my forehead against her shoulder, just for a second, before forcing myself back up. "Still green."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the forehead drop against her shoulder and did not shove Ari back. She let the second happen, one hand coming up to the nape, holding them there only as long as the lean lasted, then easing them upright again when they forced themselves back.

“Eight,” she said, level. “Green noted. You may lean. You may not stay there and hide. I still need your face.”

She checked the rope at the shoulder, then the cuff—two fingers under each line, circulation intact, nothing biting—and set her palm once against the heat of the last strike. Warm. Raised the way she expected. Nothing that changed the plan.

“Look at you,” she said, unsoftened, the register they had already written. “Counted it through a sob and still came back up to give me green. Shaking, marked, past your pretty words, and asking to be kept exactly where I put you. You do not get softness for that. You get the rest of the count. You take it. You stay.”

She stepped back to the mark, lifted the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it.

“Ninth. Same place. Same as the last. Count it if you can. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, watching the face, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement, sound and sting both present—and kept her eyes on Ari rather than the mark. She did not lift her hand again until the breath had come back.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Nine." It comes out strangled, but I get it out. My whole body trembles, but I keep my eyes on her. "Still green. Please don't stop."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the strangled count finish before she answered. She did not take the please as a change in who held the pace. Her eyes stayed on Ari’s face, on the tremble still running through the restraints, on the way the green had come out thin and still clear.

“Nine,” she said, level. “Green noted. You asked me not to stop. I heard you. That does not put your hands on the count.”

She stepped in and set two fingers under the rope at the shoulder, then under the cuff—circulation intact, skin warm, nothing biting—and left her palm a moment against the heat of the last strike. Checking, not soothing. The shake under her hand told her as much as the word had.

“Look at you,” she said, unsoftened, the register they had already written. “Nine, and still staring at me. Shaking, marked, past anything but the words I allow you, and begging to be kept exactly where I put you. You do not get to steer with please. You take what we wrote. You stay until I am finished with it. Not when you are trembling. Not when you are asking. When I decide the scene is done.”

She stepped back to the mark, lifted the familiar weight, and held it where Ari could see the line of it.

“Tenth. Same place. Same as the last. Count it if you can. If you cannot, I will count it for you. Colour if it changes. Breathe.”

She waited the length of one full inhale, watching the shoulders and the face, then brought it down—measured, inside the agreement, sound and sting both present—and kept her eyes on Ari rather than the mark. She did not lift her hand again until she had seen the breath come back.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Ten." The word is a ragged whisper. I can't hold back the shudder that follows, but my eyes stay locked on hers. "Green. Please don't stop."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held Wren’s gaze. The pull at his hair made him swallow, but he did not look away.

“I want you to take charge tonight,” he said. “Make me wait. Tell me what you want from me.” His voice steadied. “And afterward, I want you to hold me.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb brushes over his cheekbone. "You ask for it so nicely." I let go of his hair and step back. "Stay there. I'll be right back."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed where he was, hands resting on his thighs. He had asked plainly, and Wren had heard him. That made the waiting easier to bear, though it did nothing to make him less impatient.

He drew one slow breath and kept his eyes on the space where Wren had stood.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas looked up, surprised for a moment, then smiled. “Then yes. That’s on offer.”

He rose from his knees. “I asked you to take charge because I thought you wanted to. You don’t owe me that.” His voice stayed warm and certain. “Tonight, I’ll make the decisions. First one: you get to rest, and I’ll take care of you. Does that sound good?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding and nod, my shoulders dropping a little. "Yeah. That sounds... really good."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s smile softened. “Good. Sit down and let me handle the next few things.”

He fetched a glass of water and set it within reach, then pulled the blanket down from the pillows. “First, you drink that. Then I’m ordering dinner—something you already like, so you don’t have to choose. After that, we can stay right here. No plans, no decisions.”

He paused beside the bed. “And when you’re ready, I’d still like to hold you.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas glanced at the clothes on the floor, then laughed softly. “That was efficient.”

He pulled the blanket back and held it open. “Come here. I’m still ordering dinner, but first I’m holding you for a while.”

He set his phone within reach so he could take care of it later. For now, he stayed where he was, warm and unhurried, making room for Wren beside him.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *Wren slides into bed next to him and tucks his head under Tomas's chin.* "M'kay," he mumbles, already feeling the exhaustion of the week start to settle into his bones.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas wrapped an arm around Wren and drew the blanket over them. “That’s it,” he murmured. “You don’t have to do anything else tonight.”

He rested his cheek lightly against Wren’s hair and let the quiet stretch. Dinner could wait a few minutes. For now, he kept his hold steady and warm.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s hands tightened in the sheets. He took a breath, then another, trying to steady his voice.

“Wren, I need to move,” he said. “Tell me if you want me to stay still.”

He waited, trembling but clear-eyed. Whatever came next, he wanted it to be something they both chose.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I catch his hands and pin them above his head. "Breathe through it, love. I've got you." My voice is soft, but firm.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas drew a slow breath, then another. He held Wren’s gaze, his voice steadier when he spoke.

“I’m breathing. But when I said I needed to move, I meant it.” He paused. “Let my hands go for a minute. I want to keep going—I just need a reset first.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held Wren’s gaze. The familiar phrase landed, but it did not change what he had just asked for.

“I hear you,” he said, breath still uneven. “And I want to keep going. But I need my hands free and a minute to reset first.” His voice stayed firm. “Then you can ask me again.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let his wrists go immediately, smoothing my thumbs over the red marks. "Okay. Reset."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lowered his hands and flexed his fingers, taking a few slow breaths. He was still shaking, but the tension in his shoulders began to ease.

“Thank you,” he said. “I do want to keep going. I just needed you to hear me the first time.”

He took another breath and looked up. “Give me a minute and some water. Then ask me again, and I’ll tell you what I want.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas reached for the water and drank, one hand braced on the mattress until his breathing steadied. He set the glass down and looked at Wren.

“I don’t want to stop,” he said. “But I needed that minute, and I need my hands free. Are we clear?”

He waited for an answer. Only then did he lean in, kissing Wren slowly, without asking either of them to hurry. His hand remained open against the sheets.

When he finally drew back, Tomas rested his forehead against Wren’s. “That’s enough for tonight,” he murmured. “Come here. I still want to hold you.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I nod against his forehead, letting out a shaky breath. "Clear. And yeah—holding sounds perfect." I curl into his side, letting the exhaustion finally win.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words landed and Tomas felt the small hitch in them almost before he understood it. *Ten minutes.* Then *stand up.* It had not been ten minutes. It hadn't been close.

For half a second the old machinery of the week turned over in him: the arithmetic, the instinct to reconcile the two instructions, to point out the gap and offer a solution. He could feel the question forming behind his teeth.

He let it go.

That was the point, he realized. The ten had been his. He'd picked it, kneeling there with his hands open, and Wren had taken it from him and then, just as easily, set it aside. It wasn't his count anymore. It never had to be again tonight. Something in his chest loosened so abruptly it was almost dizzying.

He didn't speak. He wasn't sure he could have.

He rose slowly, carefully, letting the pull in his hair guide the pace, unfolding one knee and then the other. His legs had gone stiff from the floor and there was a brief, humiliating wobble as he found his balance, but he didn't reach for the bedframe. His hands came down to his sides and stayed there, fingers loose, not quite still. He made them still.

Standing, he was the taller of the two of them, and he'd always found that funny in a quiet way: how little it mattered. He kept his chin where it had been put. His eyes stayed on Wren's face, waiting, but he could feel the heat climbing up his neck, the flush he could never hide once it started.

The room was very quiet. He could hear his own breathing, a little too fast, and he tried to slow it and didn't entirely manage. The thumb along his jaw was still there in memory if not in fact, and he was aware of every inch of skin that had been touched and every inch that hadn't.

Six days of his own voice. And now nothing to say, nothing to decide, nothing to hold up. Just the next instruction, whenever it came.

He stood there and waited for it, and he found that he didn't mind waiting at all.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't move at first. The instruction still held him: hands at his sides, mouth shut, chin where it had been put. It took him a beat to hear what had actually been said, and another to hear the way it had been said. Quieter. Less deliberate. Like something set down rather than handed over.

*If that's on offer.*

He turned the phrase over. It was close enough to a question. Close enough that he could answer it without breaking anything, and even if it hadn't been, he knew which rule came first. Four years of this, and the oldest agreement they had was the one that said the scene bent around the people in it, not the other way around.

His hands stayed at his sides. That part he could keep.

"It's on offer," he said. His voice was soft and a little rough still. "Always."

He searched Wren's face and found a tiredness there that he'd been too wrapped up in his own week to look for. The heat in his neck shifted into something gentler and more rueful. They'd both walked in the door carrying six days of other people's problems, and he'd knelt down and asked to have his taken off him without once checking whether Wren had room to hold them.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't ask how yours was."

He let a breath go. The next part mattered, and he wanted to get it right without turning it into a new pile of choices to push back across the space between them.

"Then here's what I think. Neither of us decides anything big. No scene, unless you want one later, and if you do, you just tell me and I'll be here. For now I'll do the small things. Run the bath. Order the Thai place, the usual. Put the kettle on." A faint, crooked smile. "That's not deciding. That's just being useful. You know I like being useful."

He paused, and then, because it was true and because it was the easiest thing in the world to offer:

"Or we skip all of it and lie down, and I hold you instead of the other way round. You don't have to pick. Just nod at whichever one sounds least like work."

He stayed standing where he'd been told to stand, hands still loose at his sides, and waited. It was the same patience as before, only turned outward now.

Tomas didn't answer. It hadn't been a question, and anyway Wren had asked for quiet, and he found he wanted to give it.

He stepped back from the end of the bed and pulled the duvet down. The sheets were cool and a little rumpled from the morning. He toed off his socks, then thought better of the rest of it. Undressing would turn into its own small event, and nothing tonight needed to be an event. He lay down on his side, facing the middle of the bed, and left the space in front of him open.

Then he waited, the way he'd waited on the floor. Only now there was nothing to prove by it.

When the mattress shifted, he moved without thinking. He had four years of practice at this, even if he was usually the one being held. One arm slid under the pillow and the other settled across Wren, heavy and warm. He drew him in until Wren's back was against his chest. He fit his knees in behind Wren's knees. He tucked his chin down near Wren's shoulder, not quite resting on it, close enough that his breath stirred the short hair at the nape of Wren's neck.

He didn't squeeze. He just held on, steady, the way you'd hold something you had no intention of putting down.

After a minute he found the rhythm of Wren's breathing and let his own fall into step with it, slower and slower. His thumb moved once over Wren's sternum, a small unconscious stroke, and then went still. Outside, a car passed. The radiator ticked. Somewhere under all of it, the week was still waiting for both of them. The Harlow account, his sister's boxes, the car with its expensive new noise. None of it could get in here, not right now.

It struck him, lying there, that he'd gotten what he asked for after all, only sideways. He wasn't deciding anything. He wasn't talking. He had one instruction and no reason to question it.

*Hold me.*

He could do that for as long as it took.

His eyes drifted half-closed. He pressed his mouth, very lightly, to the back of Wren's shoulder. It wasn't really a kiss, more a way of saying *I'm here* without breaking the silence. Then he settled in and stayed.

dialogue.name: Tomas
