Tomas wasn't sure afterward which of them had moved first. It didn't seem to matter. One moment he was lying there with his mouth against Wren's shoulder, and the next his shirt was somewhere on the floor and the rest had followed. There was a brief tangle of elbows and a sleeve that wouldn't let go of his wrist. Then there was just skin, and the duvet half-kicked off, and the cool air of the room on his back.

He almost laughed. It came out as a breath against Wren's neck, warm and a little unsteady. *Be quiet with me for a while.* He could still do that. Nothing about this needed words.

He pulled Wren back in, the same way as before. Chest to back, knees fitted behind knees, one arm across him. But the sameness was the point. It was the same hold, with nothing between them now, and the difference ran through him like current. He could feel Wren's heartbeat under his palm. He could feel his own, faster, knocking against Wren's spine.

He didn't hurry. That was the thing he noticed about himself, distantly: no urgency, no plan, none of the week's clock ticking in the back of his head. He let his hand move slowly down from Wren's sternum to his stomach and rest there, fingers spread, just to feel him breathe. He pressed his mouth to the curve where neck met shoulder, properly this time, and stayed there longer than he needed to.

It wasn't a scene. There were no instructions to hold to and no count to keep. It was just the two of them, tired and warm and wanting each other, the way they'd been long before either of them had a word for anything else they did together. Tomas had always loved that this was still here underneath it all. Plain and easy and theirs.

His thumb traced a slow line along Wren's hip bone, and he felt his own breath catch at the heat of it. Then he paused there. It wasn't hesitation, exactly. It was a question asked the only way that didn't break the quiet: stillness, a little space, his hand resting where it was and going no further until he felt an answer.

He waited, cheek against Wren's hair, and let himself want.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean back into him, pressing my hips against his. My hand finds his wrist, guides his hand lower. "Yes."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word went through him like warmth through cold hands.

Tomas let himself be guided. He didn't take over, didn't rush past where Wren's grip was leading, just followed the pressure on his wrist until his hand was where Wren wanted it. He closed his fingers slowly, and the small sound he made against Wren's neck wasn't anything he'd planned.

For a moment he just held him like that, learning the heat and weight of him all over again, the way he did every time as if four years hadn't taught him a thing. Then he began to move, unhurried, matching the slow roll of Wren's hips back against his own. He could feel his own arousal pressed hard and aching against the small of Wren's back, and he let it stay there without asking anything of it. This wasn't about him. Or it was, but only in the way that giving something was ever about the giver.

He kept his mouth at Wren's shoulder. Sometimes he kissed there. Sometimes he just breathed, open-mouthed and a little ragged, and let Wren feel what this was doing to him. His other arm, still pinned under the pillow, curled up across Wren's chest and held on.

He paid attention. That was the one thing he let himself do deliberately. He listened to the catch in Wren's breathing, felt where the tension gathered and where it gave, and adjusted without thinking about adjusting. Slower when Wren pressed back harder. A little firmer when the hand on his wrist tightened. He wasn't deciding anything. He was just listening with his whole body, the way he'd been trained to by years of wanting to get this right.

Somewhere in it he stopped keeping track of time entirely. There was no count. There was the rhythm of his hand, and the heat between them, and the damp press of skin where they were fitted together, and the steady, quiet fact of being wanted back.

He pressed his forehead to the nape of Wren's neck and shut his eyes.

"I've got you," he breathed. It was barely a sound, more shape than voice, the only words he'd let himself have. Then he went quiet again and kept going, patient and steady, holding Wren close enough that there was nowhere to go but into it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had stopped trying to hold still some time ago and started simply trying not to move, which turned out to be a different thing entirely.

He was on his back now. He couldn't have said exactly when that had happened either, only that at some point the shape of the night had turned over, the way it sometimes did between them, without a word spoken. He had felt it happen. He had felt the old quiet settle back over him, familiar as a hand on the back of his neck. Nobody had told him he could move. So he hadn't.

His hands were fisted in the sheet on either side of him. He had put them there because they needed to be somewhere, and the sheet was the only thing within reach that wasn't Wren. His knuckles ached with it. His thighs were trembling in long, uneven waves he couldn't stop, and his stomach kept jumping under his own breath, and every so often his heel dug into the mattress before he caught it and made it go flat again.

It was the not-moving that undid him. It always was. Anything else he could have ridden out. But the instruction sat underneath everything like a floor, and every time his body tried to arch or reach or chase, he felt himself bump up against it and stop. The stopping went straight through him, worse and better than anything else.

His breath was coming in short, broken pulls through his nose. He had his jaw clenched so hard his teeth hurt, because *be quiet with me* was still true, and a sound was building in his chest that he didn't trust himself to let out. What escaped anyway was small and wrecked, half a breath and half something else. He hated how much it gave away. He didn't hate it at all.

He was so close he could feel it as a kind of pressure behind his eyes. And he wasn't going to go over. Not without being told. The certainty of that was the only solid thing left in him.

He opened his eyes. The ceiling swam. He tipped his chin down just far enough to look. It wasn't moving, exactly. It was the smallest thing he could do and still find Wren's face. His own face was flushed all the way down his chest. He knew it. He could feel the heat of it, and the wet at the corners of his eyes, and the way his mouth had gone soft and open despite himself.

He didn't ask. He didn't speak. He just looked, shaking, hands knotted in the sheet, every muscle strung tight and held, and let his eyes say *please* for him.

Then he waited to be told.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I watch him come apart for another moment, just to see it, then lean down to murmur in his ear. "Now. Let go." My hand wraps around him, finishing what my mouth started.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word reached him before the touch did, and then both at once, and there was no space left between them.

*Now.*

Tomas went over like something cut loose. His back came up off the mattress in one long, helpless arc, and for the first time in what felt like hours his body did what it wanted without bumping into anything. There was no floor under him anymore. It had been taken away on purpose, and he fell. The sound he'd been holding in his chest broke out of him all at once, raw and low and nothing like quiet. He didn't try to stop it. He hadn't been told to.

His hands tore loose from the sheet. One found Wren's shoulder and clung. The other just shook in the air for a moment, as if it didn't know where it was allowed to go, and then fell back against the mattress, open. The shudders ran through him in waves that didn't seem to end so much as get further apart. Each one pulled a small, ragged breath out of him. His heel dragged against the sheet and this time he let it.

When it finally let go of him, it let go all at once. He sank back into the bed like something poured. His chest heaved. His thighs were still trembling, fine and uneven, little aftershocks he had no say over. The wet at the corners of his eyes had spilled over at some point, and he felt it cool along his temples toward his hair and didn't care.

For a while he couldn't have said anything if he'd been asked. The room came back in pieces: the tick of the radiator, the cool air on his damp skin, the weight of Wren close, the warmth of breath near his ear where the word had been. His hand was still fisted in Wren's shoulder. He made it loosen, slowly, until it was just resting there, palm flat. He needed to feel that someone was still there.

"Oh," he said at last. It came out cracked and barely voiced, more exhale than word. A breathless, wet little laugh followed it, surprised out of him. "Oh, *God.*"

He turned his face toward Wren without lifting his head. It was all he could manage. His eyes were heavy-lidded and unfocused, and whatever the week had done to him, it was gone from his face entirely. There was only something scraped clean and open and a little dazed.

"Thank you," he whispered. He meant it the way he always did, all the way down.

Then, more quietly, because four years had taught him to say it even when he didn't strictly need to, and because tonight they had both come in the door running on empty:

"Come here. Please. I want—" His breath hitched. He swallowed and tried again, and his fingers pressed gently at Wren's shoulder, asking without pulling. "I want to hold you, and I want you to hold me back. Both. If you're not too tired."

He lay there wrecked and shaking and waited, the way he'd waited all night. Only now he was reaching.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The phrase landed and Tomas knew it before he'd finished hearing it. Four years of it. It had never once been said lightly.

Something in him turned over, the way the night had turned over earlier, only faster this time. The drift went out of his limbs. He was still wrung out, still trembling faintly at the edges, but that didn't matter. Being spent wasn't the same as being empty. There was plenty left in him for this.

"I know you would," he said. His voice was still wrecked, but it had found a floor again. "I know."

He moved.

He rolled them without ceremony, one arm hooked under Wren's back, and brought him down onto the mattress hard enough that the headboard knocked the wall. He didn't apologize for it. He caught both of Wren's wrists in one hand and pressed them into the pillow above his head. His grip was firm. It wasn't cruel, but it wasn't asking either. Then he put his weight down, all of it, chest to chest. He wanted Wren to feel exactly how much of him there was and exactly how little room he'd been left.

His free hand went into Wren's hair and closed. He tipped Wren's head back the way his own had been tipped at the end of the bed an hour ago, and held it there. He looked down at him. He let Wren see the difference in his face: the softness gone, the attention sharpened to a point.

"You asked," Tomas said, low, right against his mouth. "So you're going to take it."

He kissed him. There was nothing gentle in it. It was all teeth and pressure, and he bit down on Wren's lower lip until he felt the breath hitch under him. Then he dragged his mouth down the line of Wren's jaw to his throat. He found the place under the ear he knew by heart and set his teeth there. He bit hard. He held it long enough to leave a mark he'd be looking at tomorrow, and felt Wren arch under the weight pinning him flat.

Then he let go of his hair and reached down between them, and he wasn't slow about it. His hand closed around him tight and rough. The pace he set was nothing like the patient one from before. It was meant to overwhelm, not to soothe. With his other hand he kept Wren's wrists shoved into the pillow, and he felt the pull against his grip and didn't give an inch.

"Don't," he breathed into Wren's ear, when he felt him try to twist. "You don't get to move. You don't get to set the pace." His teeth grazed the shell of Wren's ear. "You wanted me to decide what hard means. I'm deciding."

He was watching the whole time. Even now, even like this, some steady part of him stayed on watch. He tracked every breath and every sound, the way Wren's body pulled against him, and he held all of it up against four years of knowing what Wren's *yes* felt like. He'd hear the word if it came. He'd hear it faster than Wren could finish saying it.

Until then, he didn't ease up at all.

---

*(Out of character: I read this as Wren asking Tomas to be rough with him, a switch from how the evening started, and wrote Tomas taking charge. If you meant that line for Tomas, asking Wren for more, tell me and I'll redo it.)*

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I buck against his grip, a sharp, desperate movement, my breath catching in a choked-off sound. My hips stutter against his hand, the friction almost too much. "Tomas—" I gasp his name, half plea, half curse.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
His name went through him like a hook.

Tomas felt the buck hit his grip and held. His fingers stayed locked around Wren's wrists and didn't give. He felt the stutter of Wren's hips against his palm and heard the choked-off edge in the gasp, and some part of him that never fully went under caught it, weighed it, and filed it. *Not the word.* It was his name, which was a different thing entirely. Four years had taught him the difference between Wren fighting the edge and Wren hitting a wall. This sounded like the edge.

But *almost too much* was a place worth being sure about.

So he didn't stop, and he didn't ease off either. He changed the grip instead. He went slower for a few strokes, and harder, a deliberate drag that gave nothing back, and he pressed his forehead down against Wren's temple so that when he spoke, there was no distance for it to cross.

"Color," he said. It wasn't a question, not quite. It was low and flat and certain, the way you'd ask someone to hand you something you knew they were holding.

His hand kept moving, slow and punishing, so the check didn't become a rest. His weight stayed where it was, heavy across Wren's chest. The grip on Wren's wrists didn't loosen by a hair. Only his eyes changed. He lifted his head just far enough to look down into Wren's face, and he watched it the way he'd watched it all night: every flicker, every breath, the set of the mouth, the wet at the lashes if there was any.

"Tell me," he murmured, "and I'll give you the rest of it."

His thumb dragged once, cruelly, just under the head, and he felt the answering jolt all the way through Wren's body and into his own. His breath shook. He was wrung out and aching and more awake than he'd been in six days, and every inch of him was pointed at the person under him.

He held there, pinning him, working him slow and rough and relentless, and waited for the answer.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop.*

It wasn't a color. But Tomas had asked for an answer, and he knew what this one sounded like: not a wall, not a wince, just someone past the point of words and still reaching for more. He'd heard Wren say *red* before, years ago, once, and it had sounded nothing like this. This was green with the edges burned off.

"Good," he breathed. "Then you're going to take all of it."

He didn't stop.

He let go of the slow drag and went back to the rough, relentless pace. It was faster now, his grip tight and slick and unforgiving, and he twisted on every upstroke the way he knew undid Wren fastest. The hand on Wren's wrists bore down harder. He shifted his weight so his hips pinned Wren's thigh flat to the mattress and there was nowhere left to buck *to*. Wren could strain, and Tomas felt him straining, but the strain went nowhere. It all came back into Tomas's hand.

He put his mouth at Wren's ear and kept it there.

"That's it," he said, low and unsteady, because he wasn't much better off either. "That's it. You don't get to hold it back. Not from me."

He felt it building under him. The breath went short and ragged. The muscles of Wren's stomach jumped against his forearm. The wrists under his hand stopped pulling and just shook. Tomas knew this part the way he knew his own heartbeat. He knew the moment it tipped from *almost too much* into *inevitable*, and he knew that the kind thing now was not mercy. It was to hold on harder.

So he did. He set his teeth in the mark he'd already left under Wren's ear and bit down again. He worked him hard and fast straight through the moment of it. He didn't slow when Wren's whole body went taut and arched up against his weight. He didn't slow when he felt the first pulse of it spill hot over his knuckles and onto both their stomachs. He stroked him through every shudder, firm and steady. His forehead was pressed to Wren's temple, and he took every sound Wren made right into his own skin. Only when the shaking changed, when the tension broke and started turning into oversensitive flinches, did he ease off. First the pace, then the pressure. Then he stopped, and just held him, cupped and still, while the last aftershocks worked their way out.

He let go of Wren's wrists.

He did it slowly, sliding his fingers down so that the release was a touch too. He brought Wren's arms down one at a time and pressed a kiss to the inside of each wrist, right where his grip had been. Then he let his weight off, not all at once but carefully, rolling half onto his side so Wren could breathe. He kept one leg hooked over Wren's and one arm across his chest. He was still there. Just not pinning him anymore.

"Hey," he murmured. The edge was gone from his voice. It had gone soft again, and hoarse, and a little wondering. "Hey. I've got you. You're okay."

His thumb moved in slow circles over Wren's sternum, the same place it had rested an hour and a lifetime ago. He looked down at him, at the flush, the marks, the wet lashes if there were any, and his chest ached with something that had nothing to do with the night's exertion.

"You did so well," he whispered, and kissed his temple. "So well."

After a minute he reached over the edge of the bed without really letting go and found his discarded shirt by feel. He wiped them both down with it, clumsy and gentle, and tossed it back to the floor. Then he dragged the duvet up over the two of them and tucked it in around Wren's shoulder. He settled in close, chest to side, his mouth near Wren's ear again, where the bruise was starting to darken.

"Water in a minute," he said. "And that bath, if you want it. And the Thai place, if either of us can stand up." A tired, crooked breath of a laugh. "No decisions. I'll just do it."

Then he went quiet. He held on and waited, warm and wrung out and entirely present, for whatever Wren needed next.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My breath comes back slowly, uneven. I turn my face into his shoulder, letting the warmth ground me. My hand lifts, shaky, to rest over his on my chest. "Later," I murmur. "Stay like this."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Stay like this.*

Tomas didn't answer. He didn't need to. The water and the bath and the Thai place slid quietly off the list, and he let them go without a flicker of regret. *Later* was a decision, and it wasn't his, and that was exactly how he wanted it.

He turned his hand under Wren's so their palms met and laced their fingers together over Wren's sternum. He held on, not tight, just there.

Wren's face was warm against his shoulder. Tomas shifted the smallest amount, barely a movement at all, so the curve of his neck made a better place to rest. Then he went still. He brought his other hand up, unhurried, and settled it at the back of Wren's head. He wasn't gripping this time, only cupping. His fingers slid into the damp hair at the nape and stroked once, slowly, the way you'd smooth down something that had been ruffled.

His own body was starting to catch up with him. The ache in his thighs, the tenderness in his wrists from the sheet, the heavy, sandbagged feeling in every limb. He noticed it all distantly, with a kind of fond disinterest. None of it needed doing anything about. He had been used hard and then he had used, and now there was only this, and it was the part he'd wanted most.

He pressed his lips to Wren's hair and left them there.

The radiator ticked. A pipe knocked somewhere in the wall. The duvet was warm and a little too heavy, and he didn't move to adjust it. The sweat was cooling on his back where the cover didn't quite reach, and he didn't move for that either. He kept stroking Wren's hair in slow, even passes. Once his thumb found the edge of the bruise under Wren's ear, and he went lighter there without thinking, barely a touch, just enough to say *I know that's there. I put it there. I've got it.*

It occurred to him that he should probably say something. Check in again, make sure. The old reflex from the week stirred, looking for a job.

He weighed it and decided against it. Wren had asked for quiet, and then for this. If something was wrong, Wren would say. Tomas trusted that the same way he'd trusted it at the end of the bed, kneeling with his hands open. Trust went both ways, or it didn't really work.

So instead he just breathed, slow and deep, and let his chest rise and fall under Wren's cheek. He let that be the thing he offered: something steady to lean against, and a rhythm to follow if Wren wanted one.

His eyes drifted closed. Not asleep, not yet. He stayed right at the edge of it, warm and heavy and entirely awake to the weight in his arms.

"Not going anywhere," he murmured into Wren's hair, so low it was almost only breath.

Then he went quiet again, and stayed.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, shaky breath, the last of the tension leaving me. My fingers tighten around his, just a little. "Thank you," I whisper against his skin. "For all of it."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The words were barely there, warm against his skin. Tomas felt them more than heard them. They landed somewhere under his collarbone and stayed.

He didn't answer right away. He let the fingers tightening around his own say what they were saying, and he tightened back the same small amount. It was an echo, not an escalation.

*For all of it.*

He thought about the floor at the end of the bed, his hands open on his thighs, the ten minutes he'd decided on and never got to finish. He thought about the moment the night had turned over and handed him something he hadn't asked for. It had turned out to be exactly the thing he needed: someone to hold, and then someone to take apart, and then someone to hold again. He'd walked in wanting to put everything down. He had, in the end. It just hadn't looked the way he'd pictured it.

"You don't have to thank me," he murmured into Wren's hair. Then, because that wasn't quite true, and they'd never been in the habit of saying things that weren't quite true to each other: "But I'll take it."

A breath went out of him, almost a laugh, soft and tired.

"Thank you, too. I came in here wanting you to carry my week for me." His thumb moved once over the back of Wren's hand, slow. "And you did. You just did it by letting me carry yours for a bit." He paused and felt for the rest of it. "I think that's the version I needed. I didn't know that at the start."

He pressed his mouth to Wren's hair again and kept it there a moment longer than he meant to.

The hand at the back of Wren's head kept up its slow passes, unhurried, smoothing. He was aware of the bruise under Wren's ear, of the wrists he'd held down, of the tenderness he'd have to check on properly once the lights were on and they were both upright. That was for later. Later was Wren's word, and he'd keep to it.

"We're okay," he said quietly. It wasn't a question. It was just a thing he wanted in the room. "Both of us. We're okay."

He shifted a little lower on the pillow so Wren wouldn't have to hold his head at an angle, and drew the duvet up the last few inches to cover the cooling skin of his own back. It was the first thing he'd done for himself all night. It felt fine, and small, and allowed.

Then he let his breathing slow again and fall back into step with the one against his chest.

"Sleep if you want," he whispered. "I'll wake you when the food's here. Or I won't, and we'll have cold noodles at midnight." The crooked smile was audible even at that volume. "No decisions. Remember?"

He closed his eyes and held on.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I huff a soft, breathless laugh against his skin. "Cold noodles," I murmur, already half-gone. My fingers go slack in his. "Perfect."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held still under Wren's hand, throat bared, and met their eyes without flinching.

"I want you to use me," he said, plain and even. "However you want. I waited because I wanted you to make me ask out loud." His mouth tipped, not quite a smile. "So. I'm asking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I run my thumb over the line of his jaw, studying his expression. "That's a dangerous thing to give someone."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's gaze stayed steady under Wren's thumb, the line of his jaw gone a little taut where the touch caught it.

"I know," he said. "That's why I waited to say it to you." He didn't pull against the hand in his hair, only tipped his chin the last fraction so the words landed clean. "Limits are the same as always. Safeword if I need it. Aftercare after. Everything in between—" a breath, not quite a laugh, "—is yours, if you want it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went still under Wren's hand, the ask landing somewhere he hadn't braced for and didn't bother to hide.

"It's on offer," he said, even. "If you mean you want me deciding, and you don't want to steer it." He didn't pull free. His eyes stayed on Wren's, checking once, not asking twice. "Same rules. You say if it stops being what you want. Until then—" a breath, the corner of his mouth gone steady rather than soft, "—I'll take the few hours. Come up here."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I shift on the bed, making space beside me. "Come up here then." My hand stays in his hair, guiding him up. "You decide what happens next."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas rose under the guiding hand, the grip in his hair easing only enough to let him stand. He settled onto the bed beside Wren, weight angled in, one knee braced so he could turn and face them fully.

"Lie back," he said, quiet. His hand came up to Wren's wrist and redirected it from his hair to the mattress, not gripping hard. "Hands stay there unless I move them. You've had a week of deciding. You don't get to start now."

He held Wren's eyes for the beat it took to check this was still wanted, then leaned in until his breath caught the line of their throat. "Tell me if that changes. Otherwise I'm going to take my time with you."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas didn't rush the minute. He used it.

His hands were sure where they mapped Wren's shoulders and the line of their ribs, stripping what was left between them and letting it fall off the edge of the bed. When they were both bare he sat back on his heels for one breath, looking, the way he looked when he intended to remember something. Then he came down over Wren, weight braced on one forearm, the other hand settling flat at the center of their chest—not pinning, just there, warm and steady.

"Good," he said, low. "Stay like that."

He kissed them once, unhurried, and then again lower, at the hinge of the jaw, the hollow of the throat, the place just under the collarbone where their pulse jumped. He didn't ask what they wanted. He listened with his mouth and his hands, following the hitch of breath, the way Wren's body answered when he dragged his teeth lightly and then soothed it with his tongue. His palm slid down, slow, over stomach and hip, and settled between their thighs with the same unhurried certainty he'd used to put their hand on the mattress.

"I've got you," he murmured against their skin, and meant the next few hours, not only this. "You don't have to do anything but feel it. If you need me to stop, you know how. Until then—" his fingers moved, deliberate, learning them again in the dark of the room, "—this is mine to decide."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: A sharp inhale escapes me as his fingers move. My knuckles press into the mattress. "Yours," I agree, the word thin and breathless.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas felt the word more than he heard it—thin, given up, landing against his mouth where it rested at the hollow of Wren's throat. He didn't answer it. He let it stand.

His fingers didn't hurry. They moved in a slow, even stroke, learning the shape of the sound Wren had just made and then drawing it out again, a little firmer, a little deeper, until the knuckles pressed into the mattress told him exactly where the edge of it was. He kissed the jump of pulse under his mouth and stayed there, breathing against warm skin, one hand braced beside Wren's head so none of his weight asked them to hold anything up.

"That's it," he said, quiet, not praise so much as confirmation. His thumb circled, unhurried, and he watched the way Wren's breath broke around it. "You don't reach for me. You don't help. You stay right where I put you."

He shifted lower, mouth tracing the line of the sternum, the soft give of the stomach, taking his time because the hours were his to spend and he intended to spend them. When he settled between Wren's thighs he didn't rush the first touch of his mouth either. He breathed there first, warm, and then set his tongue to them in one long, deliberate stroke, the same pace as his fingers, listening for the next inhale like it was the only instruction he needed.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stayed where he had been put, shaking and not reaching, the aftershocks still running through him in tight, helpless waves. His hands stayed fisted in the sheet. He didn't lift his hips. He didn't ask.

His breath came rough against the mattress, mouth open, eyes shut. When he could shape words, they were thin and even, the same voice he used when he meant them.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lifted his head under the tug, eyes finding Wren's and staying there. The permission hit harder than the pull. For a second he didn't spend it—just breathed, shaking still running through his arms, hands uncurling from the sheet one finger at a time.

"Thank you," he said, rough and even.

Then he moved. He came up on his elbows and closed the distance, mouth finding Wren's without asking, the kiss open and a little unsteady from how long he'd held still. One hand slid into their hair, not to guide so much as to hold on. The other braced beside their shoulder as he shifted his weight over them, hips settling in, the first real press of his body against theirs pulled straight out of the shaking he hadn't been allowed to spend.

He broke the kiss only far enough to speak against their mouth.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the word and the phrase that came after it without softening either one. He knew the shape of that ask; they had used it enough that he didn't need it translated.

He shifted his weight, one hand closing hard at Wren's hip to hold them where he wanted them, the other braced beside their head. dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:

His hand left their hip only long enough to catch their wrist and pin it to the mattress beside their head, not cruel, just sure. The other stayed braced so his weight never asked them to hold him up.

"You don't have to think," he murmured, mouth dragging along their jaw, teeth catching once at the hinge before he soothed it. "I've got the rest. You feel it. You tell me if it changes."

He didn't slow. He kept the rhythm they'd asked for, hips snapping, grip firm, every stroke deliberate, and listened for the next sound they made like it was the only thing in the room that mattered.

He let his eyes close for a second under their hand, then opened them again so he could see their face. The grip at their hip loosened only enough that it stopped being a hold and became a rest, palm warm against skin.

dialogue.name: Wren

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the words land and didn't deflect them. His eyes stayed on Wren's, the line of his jaw steady under their thumb, breath still coming a little uneven against their mouth.

"Good," he said, quiet, rough at the edges. Not agreement so much as receipt. "I wanted it to be."

He didn't move. The hand at their hip stayed a rest, warm and still, and the arm braced beside their head held his weight so none of it asked anything of them. A last tremor ran through his shoulder and eased. He turned his face the smallest fraction into their palm, not pulling free, just there.

"I'm staying," he said. "You don't have to let go until you want to."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex allowed herself a small nod — the only reward the word *green* ever earned, and all it needed. "Good."

She crossed to the cabinet and laid out the evening's implements on the linen cloth, one by one, in the order she intended to use them: the soft leather cuffs first, then the braided flogger, then — at the far end, deliberately apart from the rest — the wooden paddle she knew he both dreaded and counted the hours toward. She let him watch her do it. The arranging was part of the scene. The waiting was part of the scene.

"Reminders," she said, straightening. "Amber slows us down. Red ends everything, no questions, no consequences, no aftercare withheld. You know this. I say it anyway, because ritual is not redundancy — ritual is the frame that holds the picture." Her eyes moved over him slowly, cataloguing, unhurried. She had learned in two years that being looked at this way did more to him than the flogger ever would.

"And tonight," she continued, "you will address me as Maitresse, you will not speak unless spoken to, and you will hold position until released. If your hands tremble, they tremble. I will decide whether that is a failure or a compliment." A pause, thin and deliberate. "It will be a compliment."

She stepped close — close enough that he could feel the warmth of her, not close enough to touch — and lifted her chin a fraction, studying his face the way she studied her instruments before a scene.

"Now. Undress. Fold everything neatly on the chair." Her voice dropped, cool and precise. "And when you're finished, kneel at the bench and tell me what you are to me tonight."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, feeling the familiar flutter in my chest as I begin to undress, folding each piece with deliberate care. I kneel at the bench, my head bowed slightly. "I am yours to command, Maitresse. Yours to shape."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the words settle into the room the way she let all his answers settle — tested for weight, then kept.

"Yours to shape," she echoed. "Yes. And I take excellent care of what is mine."

She moved behind him, and for a long moment she only looked: the line of his spine, the discipline of his knees against the wood, the small involuntary catch in his shoulders that told her the anticipation was already doing half her work. She catalogued it all without comment. There would be time.

"Hands behind you."

She buckled the leather cuffs with the same unhurried precision she had shown the implements — snug, then a finger's width checked beneath each strap, then snug again. She turned his wrists gently inside the restraint and watched the blood return to the skin, watched his breathing rather than his face, because breathing lied less. Satisfied, she drew him upright and guided him to the bench, bending him over it with a hand flat between his shoulder blades, arranging him the way she arranged everything in this room.

The flogger's falls whispered across him first — shoulders, back, the backs of his thighs — so he would learn their weight before they ever landed. She let the leather drag. She let him flinch at nothing.

"We begin slow," she said. "I want your attention before I want your endurance. Six, to start. You will count them for me."

The first stroke fell — measured, more thud than sting, a statement of intent rather than a punishment. She stood still in the quiet that followed it, one hand resting lightly on the small of his back.

"Count, Ari."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex went very still.

Not the stillness of surprise — she was rarely surprised — but the stillness of a woman setting down one instrument to pick up another.

"Tuesday," she said, tasting the word. "That would explain dinner on Wednesday. You passed the salt twice and looked straight through me both times. I had wondered."

She let the observation land and did not soften it. Her hand stayed flat on the small of his back, a fixed point of warmth, while her voice did all the work.

"You were given two instructions, and you have failed both in a single sentence. You did not count. And you spoke unbidden." A pause, measured out as precisely as the strokes would be. "The wanting, I will keep. Four days of it is a compliment, and I told you I would decide which of your lapses were which."

She straightened, and the hand lifted away.

"But the count is not yours to drop, Ari. The count is how I know where you are when your mouth cannot tell me. Lose the count, lose the frame. We do not lose the frame in this room."

She stepped back and gathered the falls of the flogger over her forearm, unhurried, resettling her grip the way she resettled everything.

"So. The stroke you received without counting will be counted now — one. And once more, for the losing of it — two. Then we begin the six again, cleanly, because I do not accept sloppy arithmetic in place of the real thing. You will have earned every stroke you get tonight. That is rather the point of you."

The leather fell again — same weight, same placement across his shoulders, the counted version of what he'd already taken. She had ruled his eagerness a compliment. The arithmetic would simply have to be honest.

"One, Ari. Say it properly."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold my breath for a beat, then let it out. "One, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"There." Vex let the single word carry all the approval she intended to spend — a word, and no more, because properly done was worth exactly this and he should learn the exchange rate. "That is how the frame sounds when it holds."

She let him stand inside the count a moment. A number was not merely a number in this room; it was a place to put his weight, and she wanted him to feel the ground under it before she asked him to keep moving.

Her palm settled again between his shoulder blades — the fixed point, warm, unhurried — while her other hand gathered the falls and let them whisper over his flank, texture before intent, the way she always gave it.

"For the record," she said, "you will notice the penalty is not heavier. A punishment that outruns its reason is only cruelty with better posture, and I don't traffic in that. The penalty is simply that it is owed. Everything else stays honest. Arithmetic included."

The leather fell — same weight, same line across his shoulders, the count kept clean.

"Two, Ari."

While it settled into him, she watched his hands where they were folded in the cuffs behind him. Not his face; faces learned to flatter long before hands did, and she had spent two years learning his dialect of breath and knuckle and skin. Steady. Warm. Exactly where she wanted him, and nowhere near where she intended to leave him by the end of the linen cloth's inventory.

"Count," she said, mild as anything — which from her was the warning. "Then the six begin again, at three. And hold your tongue after it, unless I ask. The four days of wanting you confessed to — I am keeping those. I will collect them later, when you're soft enough to feel the full weight of what you've been carrying since Tuesday."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex finished the last knot before she answered him — rope deserved an unhurried hand, and so, frankly, did he. She laid her palm flat against the woven line across his back, feeling the give of it, the honesty of good tension, and checked the circulation at his wrists with two fingers, reading his pulse the way she read everything in this room: for truth rather than performance.

"You spoke again," she said. "After being told to hold your tongue. Twice tonight your mouth has run ahead of its instructions, and I begin to think the wanting has loosened something in it."

She moved around him slowly, the way she moved around furniture she was considering repositioning.

"But I know what that joke was. You reach for humor the way other men reach for a handrail — when the ground is moving and you would rather no one notice. Two years, Ari. I read your dialect. You were not being impertinent. You were falling, and dressing it as wit so it would look intentional." A pause, weighed out. "I will allow it. This once. Not because it was permitted — it was not — but because it told me more than a count would have. Silence next. I am collecting it, along with the four days. You are very nearly soft enough for me to gather all of it at once."

Her hand gathered his hair, not pulling — anchoring. The fixed point.

"As for what you would have to explain to anyone — give it an hour. You have seen two items leave the linen cloth. The third has not been touched, and you have been counting toward it since the door closed. Sleeves exist. So does Tuesday; you will wear some of it under your shirt tomorrow, and you will think of me."

She withdrew to the foot of the bench, where her shadow fell across him first.

"Now. You have told me you are past composure, and I do not take a man's word for his own condition — I take his colour." The pause was thin, deliberate. "You have leave to speak. One word's worth. Colour, Ari."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My breath hitches. The rope is still new against my skin. "Green, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the hitch and banked it — that small catch in his breath, the body confessing what the voice had kept steady. Green, properly given. She rewarded it the only way that meant anything in this room.

"Noted," she said. "And spent. Colour is currency here, Ari. You have just paid for the next hour, and I intend to give you your money's worth."

The flogger resumed — no longer the measured introductions, but the real work now, a slow-building rhythm across his shoulders and thighs, each fall landing a fraction heavier than the last. She watched his breathing rather than his face and waited for the change she knew was coming: the moment the caught breath burned off and something even and distant replaced it. When it came, she spoke into it, quiet, the way one speaks into a church.

"There. That is where you live when you stop performing. I told you once you reach for handrails. Look around you, Ari. There are no handrails in this room." A stroke, unhurried. "There is only me. You may fall as far as you like."

She paused when she saw his fingers curl open behind him — slack, honest — and pressed her thumb into his palm until his hand closed around it. The oldest question and answer between them. His grip answered. She allowed herself one breath of something that was almost tenderness, then put it away where she kept everything else.

"You are exactly where I want you. Which is why we will not waste it."

She crossed to the linen cloth and lifted the last item. She did not use it. She laid the paddle across his back, between the woven lines of rope — cool wood, full weight, resting on him like a verdict he could feel coming.

"You have counted toward this since Tuesday. I know. I let you." Her hand settled over the wood, pinning it in place. "But hear me: I do not take what is not offered, even what is mine. That is the difference between keeping a man and merely handling him."

She bent close, her mouth near his ear.

"Ask me for it. Properly. You have leave to speak for exactly as many words as it takes."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm shaking now, my forehead pressed to the cool bench. The words come out rough, scraped raw from wanting. "Please, Maitresse. Please use it. I need to feel it."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex did not answer at once. She stood with the request the way she stood with everything he gave her — weighed it first, for accuracy's sake.

*Please. Please use it. I need to feel it.*

No wit laid over it. No handrail. He had asked her in plain words, and plain words from this man were rarer than obedience and worth considerably more.

"Offer

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the word finish falling before she moved — *more*, the phrase they had agreed would open the last door in this room, spoken with his safeword loose in his mouth and deliberately unused. She noted that too. It was, in its way, the most honest thing he'd said all evening, and he had said it with his forehead against the bench.

"More. So be it." She straightened. "The word is given, and I will not ask again tonight. Red stays yours — it always stays yours, even now. Between here and red, I keep what you have offered, and you have just offered me the whole of it."

She lifted the paddle from his back, letting him feel the absence of its weight first. The loss would do half the work.

"Then hear what I do not say at dinner." Her voice did not rise. That was the trick of it — the worst things she said arrived in the same register as her mildest instructions, and his body had learned to flinch at the tone before the meaning landed. "You sat across from me on Wednesday with your collar buttoned and your hands steady, and no one at that table knew you were counting days toward a bench. That man is the performance. This — the man on the wood, cuffed, begging in plain words — this is the true inventory. You begged tonight, Ari. Unmade to do it. I have wanted that particular honesty out of you for some time, and now that I hold it, I intend to spend it."

The first stroke landed where the flogger had prepared the ground — heavier by a full measure, wood rather than leather, a sound like a door closing. She kept her palm flat on his back through it, reading him through her own hand.

"The paddle keeps its own count. Clean arithmetic, always."

The second fell to the same line, unhurried, exact.

"You are not a man who endures. Resilience is for your dinners and your letters. In this room you are an instrument I have spent two years learning to play, and every stroke is proof that I learned correctly. Tomorrow you will sit in some meeting feeling exactly where I have written on you, and you will be composed, and it will be the biggest lie you tell all day."

She set the wood against him once more — resting, not striking — and let him count toward it the way he had counted toward all of it since Tuesday.

"Three, Ari. Say it as though you are grateful." A pause, thin and deliberate. "You are."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Three," I say, and my voice is ragged. "I'm grateful, Maitresse." I'm breathing hard against the wood.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the ragged edge of it and did not soothe it. Soothing was for after; the middle of a scene belonged to her, and she meant to keep it.

"Gratitude," she said. "From a man who buttons his collar at dinner. If your colleagues could hear you now, they would not recognize you — which is rather the point. They have never met you, Ari. I have."

The fourth stroke fell lower than the third, across the tops of his thighs where the flogger had laid its groundwork, and she felt it arrive through her palm still resting between his shoulders — the flinch traveling up his spine like a word being underlined.

"Four, Ari."

She gave him a moment, and read him while she did. Breath even and far away. Fingers slack in the cuffs. And the shaking — the shaking had changed its nature entirely. It was no longer effort. It was arrival. Two years had taught her the difference, and here it was, on schedule, directly under her hand. His body had already answered the colour question; she simply had better access to it than he did.

"There it is," she said quietly. "Do you feel it? That is not fear. That is the thing you drove here for — the performance ending. I told you there were no handrails."

The fifth she gave him without commentary. Some strokes were speeches. Some were simply gifts. "Five."

The sixth she announced first, because endings deserved to be known while they were still coming.

"Last of the wood tonight. I ration what is precious, and I want you hungry for it again before the marks have faded. You may dread that. You may also count toward it — I know you will." The stroke landed full and unhurried, a door closing. "Six, Ari. You will give me four, five, and six together, and then the wood goes back to the cloth."

She set it down deliberately, letting him hear it land on the linen — the small sound of an appetite banked, not spent. Then her hand gathered his hair again. The anchor. The fixed point.

"And now I collect. You were told I would." Her voice stayed in its mildest register, which from her was always the dangerous one. "Four days, Ari, and you have leave to speak for exactly as long as it takes. Tell me what Wednesday was. Not the dinner — the inside of it. I watched you pass the salt twice with perfectly steady hands. I want to know what those hands were doing under the table."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex received the word and weighed it, and found it was not the answer she had asked for — and was, on inspection, better.

"Green," she repeated. "I asked you for Wednesday, and you gave me your colour instead. From most men I would call that evasion." She let the pause sit. "From you, in this state, it is the shortest true sentence you have left. So I will rule on it, as I rule on everything: the colour I accept. The confession I keep as a debt. A debt is not waived because the debtor is broke — only postponed. Words will come back to you. They always do. I will be waiting."

Then she brought him down.

The flogger returned once more, but stripped of intent — the falls passing over him with barely any weight at all, the way one lays down something sleeping. Shoulders. Back. The marked tops of his thighs, gently, so he would hear the difference between the evening and its ending. Her voice stayed with it, even and unhurried.

"Coming up is done as carefully as going down. Anything less is merely violence at a slower tempo, and we do not do that here. The frame holds to the last knot."

She unbound him in the reverse order of his making. The rope came off slowly, knot by knot, her fingers patient with her own work, each line leaving a pale seam across the red that she would inventory later. The cuffs last — buckle, then strap, then her thumbs circling his wrists until the blood came fully back, watching the skin the way she watched his breathing: for truth. When she pressed her thumb into his palm, the old question, the grip closed around it. The oldest answer. She nodded once, to herself.

"The bench is finished with you. So is the wood; you heard where I put it. Six of the one, leather over the top of the other, and every stroke earned and counted. Tomorrow you will find them in a mirror before your meeting and you will know they were earned, which is not the same as saying sorry for them. It is better."

She eased him up from the bench and down again — the floor, the blanket from the cabinet that existed for exactly this and no other purpose, the water pressed into his hands and waited over until he drank. Then she settled beside him, her hand finding his hair, and permitted herself the thing she had put away earlier in the evening. She did not call it tenderness aloud. She never did. She simply let it be obvious, which for her was the same confession.

"Your hands trembled at the start of the evening," she said. "I ruled it a compliment then. I stand by the ruling — look at what they were trembling toward."

She waited until his breathing found its floor. Then, mild as anything, which from her was always the register that mattered:

"Now. Wednesday. The hands under the table. You have leave to speak for as long as it takes, and I will wait for every word. And Ari — I already know the shape of it. I want it said anyway. Some things are only real once they are spoken aloud to the person who kept them safe."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My hands were still in my lap. They were fists. I kept thinking if you could see them, you'd know everything. "I was counting the hours," I say, my voice quiet. "Every time you spoke, I heard the way you say my name in here."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I lean into her hand in my hair, my eyes closed. "And I was thinking about the paddle. Where you'd put it, when you'd use it. It made the dinner feel like a game only we knew."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the confession finish before she ruled on it — she had learned that his best sentences deserved the same unhurried receipt as his worst.

"A game only we knew," she repeated, tasting it. "Nearly right. Amend it thus: a game has an audience, and a scoreboard, and a loser. Wednesday had none of those. It had a room inside a room, and only the two of us held the key. You sat in the outer one all evening — buttoned, steady, passing salt — while the inner one sat under your tongue." Her thumb traced a slow line behind his ear. "That is not a game, Ari. That is the truest architecture of us. I am keeping the phrase anyway. You will not always be able to say it that well."

She reached for the folded cloth on the cabinet — cool water, wrung nearly dry — and began the inventory she had promised the rope seams earlier. Shoulders first, unhurried, reading the skin under her hand the way she read everything in this room.

"The flogger's account," she reported. "Warmth, and nothing that will outlast Thursday. It will ache sweetly when you reach for your glass at dinner and not one moment before." The cloth moved lower, gentler where the ground was tender. "The wood's six, here. These will write on you for days. Sit in your meeting. Cross your legs. Compose your face while your body tells the truth. That is our second game — the one only you and I know, and the one you lose on purpose every time."

She set the cloth aside and settled back against him, her hand returning to his hair, the fixed point reestablished.

"The debt of words is paid, incidentally. Fists, and hours, and my name in your head — entered in full. And since accounts balance in this room or not at all: you were not the only one counting. I laid the linen cloth at seven. The scene began at nine. I do not keep even score. I keep honest score."

The pause she took then was longer than her usual ones, and deliberate even in its deliberateness.
