dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had said *don't stop*, and after that there was no room left for words, and no need for any. The hand in his hair kept his head pulled back at the angle where thinking had to route around the strain, and what made it through was simple: Wren's weight, the pace of it, the sheets dragging under his chest, his own breath going rhythmless and staying that way. His whole job had narrowed to one thing — *stay* — and his body had understood the assignment before the rest of him caught up.

The shaking got worse before it got better. It always did. Somewhere in the middle the counting failed — not a decision, just the numbers losing their grip, nothing left for them to hold onto — and after that there was no time in him at all. Only Wren's rhythm, the only clock left in the room.

When it broke, it broke all at once, and he heard himself make a sound he'd have been embarrassed about on Wednesday and didn't care about at all now. Then he was shaking for a different reason, spent and ringing, forehead against the mattress, held together by the weight still pinning him while the rest of him came apart.

He didn't move. That was the last coherent thing in him — *no moving unless I say* — and he kept it even with nothing left to keep it with, trembling in place, until the grip in his hair gentled and the weight above him eased back into something that was just warmth.

Then he went boneless, exactly as late as he could manage it.

The usual after happened the way it always happened: he was turned over and settled, which he assisted with approximately none; a blanket found him; water arrived and he drank half the glass before his hands steadied enough to be trusted with it. He watched the familiar sequence of things happen around him and felt the words come back one at a time, like a crew filing back in after a fire drill.

"Hey," he managed, when his voice returned — wrecked, unhurried. "That stopped being dignified somewhere around minute two. You're welcome to it. I don't need it back."

A beat. His hand found whatever part of Wren was nearest — wrist, forearm, didn't matter — and held on, loose and deliberate.

"Nothing in my pocket," he said, quieter, the smile reaching his voice before his mouth. "Told you I'd end today with nothing in my pocket. Didn

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, settling beside him and draping an arm over his waist. "Good," I murmur, my own voice rough. "I like you empty."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The laugh took its time arriving and came out as more breath than sound, his chest still renegotiating its terms with the air.

"Empty's generous," he managed. "There's lint. There's always lint." His thumb kept up its slow arc along Wren's forearm — less a caress than a claim quietly staked. "Give it an hour. The committee reconvenes. They'll have opinions. They'll want to start planning Thursday."

But not yet. That was the part he let himself have, eyes closed, the whole week gone quiet in him — every open tab closed at once, every *by end of day* deleted. The weight he'd pocketed on Wednesday had been picked up by someone else and carried off, and what remained of his body spent itself in small aftershocks that resolved into warmth wherever Wren was.

"Keep that phrase, by the way," he said, his voice going down instead of up, sleep already pooling at the edges of it. "*I like you empty.* You deploy that on some future Wednesday and I'm useless at my desk by lunch. You should know what you're holding."

He turned his head until his cheek found Wren's shoulder, unhurried about it, the way people are unhurried when they've been given permission not to hurry.

"For the record — being found worked out." A pause; the smile got into the words before his mouth did. "You can have the credit. I'm not using it."

Then, because he asked for what he wanted even wrecked — especially wrecked — "Stay put. I'm going to be spectacularly useless for a while, and I'd like a witness."

His hand stayed where it was. Loose, deliberate. The one decision he was keeping for himself.

He didn't start counting again. Nothing left in him needed a number.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I hum low in my throat, shifting to curl around him more fully. "I'll be here." My fingers trace idle patterns on his skin. "The committee can wait."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content: "M

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He made a soft, agreeing noise against my shoulder. I could feel the exact moment his breathing evened out, the committee adjourned for the night. I stayed awake a while longer, mapping the quiet rise and fall of his ribs under my hand.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Green all the way down," Vex echoed, and something at the corner of her mouth shifted that might, in a lesser woman, have been called a smile. "Ambitious. We'll see how you feel about the foundations."

She slid two fingers beneath the last strap, testing the give, then took a slow fistful of it and pulled — firm, deliberate, confirming it would hold without cutting. Then she moved along the line, pressing her thumb to the pulse point at each wrist in turn. Warm. Steady. Good.

"Flex for me." She waited until she was satisfied, and gave a single nod, more to herself than to anyone.

"Protocol, since you're too comfortable to remember it. The word, or two knocks — bench, wall, my boot, whatever's nearest. I intend to say some terrible things about you tonight, so I won't trust anything that comes out of your mouth unless it's the word itself." She said it the way she said everything: as procedure. It was procedure. It was also, after two years, something closer to tenderness than she would have admitted under oath.

She crossed to the wall and considered the rack the way a surgeon considers instruments. The suede flogger — dark, the tails worn soft — came down off its hook. She carried it back without hurry and draped it across Ari's shoulder blades, letting its full weight rest there. A greeting, not a threat.

"Warm-up first. I've no interest in marking you before your skin has earned it."

She rolled her shoulders once, settled her stance at Ari's left, and let the silence stretch exactly as long as she wanted it to. The first stroke landed broad and soft, barely more than weight. The second overlaid it, precise, an inch lower.

"Two years," she murmured, watching closely, "and you still go quiet the moment the straps are tight. I could grow very fond of that."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath as the suede settles, its familiar weight an anchor. "Quiet means I'm listening," I murmur, flexing my hands against the straps. "And I always listen for you."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Sentiment," Vex said, in the tone she reserved for identifying things found where they didn't belong. "Noted for the record. It won't help you."

The flogger rose and fell, unhurried. Broad thud, no sting — the tails landing dense and soft across the shoulders, then an inch lower, then lower again, a slow figure-eight that asked nothing of the body except that it stay exactly where she'd put it. Heat rose under the suede in even pink lines. She watched the breathing more than the skin: the long exhale after each stroke, the straps gradually taking over the work of holding position, which was the entire point of straps.

"You say you listen." Stroke. Overlay. "Then let's establish the syllabus. Later tonight I'm going to stand very close to your ear and deliver a full assessment of a man who structures his entire week around an hour on my bench. Who rehearses his answers. Who says *green all the way down* as though I don't know precisely how far down that goes — because I have been down there with you, and you were making sounds at the bottom of it you'd deny under oath." Her voice stayed conversational, almost gentle. "You'll hear every word. And then you'll thank me for the accuracy."

She let the rhythm carry on, no counting, no announcements — just weight and patience, the suede doing what suede does, which is persuade. Then she stopped, draped the flogger over her shoulder, and laid her bare palm flat between Ari's shoulder blades. Warm. Well-flushed. Taking the work beautifully. She kept her hand there a moment longer than procedure strictly required, which she would have denied.

"Warm-up's done. Your back has earned the right to be interesting." She set the flogger on the bench, deliberately in view — a small theatre of intention — and flexed her fingers once. "Colour. And this time I want the reading, not the performance. You have a habit of decorating your greens. Don't."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: V

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: Her hand stills. "Tuesday," she repeats, the word measured. She picks up the flogger again, but doesn't move. "And what did you think?"

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: V

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the tail of the rope in her fist and drew the last of the slack through the knot at his sternum — slowly, until it sat flush, until the harness held him the way a hand holds something it has decided not to let go of. She tested it with two fingers, every wrap, working up from the wrists. Then she stepped back and considered what she'd made.

Considered what it had made of him

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I can feel the blush rising, the rope making it impossible to hide. "I thought about how quiet the room gets," I say, my voice low. "And how you always know when I'm lying."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: V

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My voice is rough when I finally say it. "Please, Maitresse." I swallow hard, the rope tight against my ribs. "Don't make me wait anymore."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: V

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: "One honest sentence," Vex said. "Undecorated. I was beginning to think you didn't

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Told you I was listening," I manage, breathless against the bench. "Now you know."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: "There

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I don't even try to hide the shiver that runs through me when she says that. It's exactly what I needed to hear.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Please," I say, my voice rough. The rest of the sentence is just a sharp inhale.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content: V

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let my head drop, breathing through the tightness in my chest. "Thank you, Maitresse." It's barely audible.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
His head stayed tipped back where Wren's hand held it, throat bare, and the grip alone was doing most of his thinking for him.

"You know I could've said this at dinner," he said, voice lower than he'd planned. "That was sort of the point. I wanted to want it badly enough that I couldn't *not* say it." His mouth curved, entirely unapologetic. "I held out longer than I expected. Give me some credit."

Then, because he'd been told to say it, and because four years had taught him the saying was half of it anyway:

"Use me tonight. All the way through — I don't want to make a single decision. Not what happens next, not when it stops, none of it. I want to be yours to arrange." His hands rested open on his thighs, and his pulse was sitting somewhere in his throat, and his voice held steady anyway. "Do whatever you want with me. I'll take all of it. You know I will."

He held the look a moment longer, then added, softer:

"And after — the usual. You put me back together." His thumb traced a slow circle over his own knee, the only fidget he allowed himself. "But that part's not an ask. That's just how it goes."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I lean down, my fingers tightening slightly in his hair. "You held out so you could come here and beg properly. That's what you're doing, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The quip earned her a look — or as much of a look as the grip in his hair allowed, which was mostly throat and half-lidded eyes.

"That's an uncharitable interpretation," Tomas said. Then, because lying to Wren had never once been worth the effort: "It's also completely accurate. Yes. I sat through an entire dinner and the walk home holding it in specifically so that by the time I knelt down, I'd mean it past the point of dignity. You've caught me. Devastating."

His mouth curved, but his voice had gone rougher with every sentence and they both knew it.

"Seven minutes now, by the way. That's seven minutes of begging done in silence. Very efficient — you get the whole performance without me wasting words on it."

One hand started to lift from his thigh — toward Wren's wrist, anything — and he caught himself and set it back down. Not his call tonight. That was rather the point.

"So take it as begged," he said. "Or make me say it worse. But decide soon —" and here the steady voice finally gave at the edges, around a grin, "— because I've been good for seven entire minutes, and I want it on record that was my limit."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My thumb brushes along the line of his jaw, a slow, considering motion.* "Seven minutes is nothing," I murmur. "But I suppose you've earned a reward for the effort."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The word *reward* landed somewhere below his sternum, and Tomas didn't bother hiding what it did — the small drop of his breath, the way his eyes went briefly unfocused under the thumb tracing his jaw.

He turned his head, just enough, and pressed his mouth to the pad of that thumb. Not quite a kiss. Acknowledgment.

"A reward," he repeated, savoring it. "Careful. Keep that up and I'll start thinking the seven minutes were contractual."

Then, because the other thing Wren had said was still sitting there, heavier than the teasing:

"And yes — it's on offer. It's the most on-offer thing in this apartment." His voice had gone rough again, but it held. "But you've had a week. So consider the terms revised. Don't decide anything either. I'm not asking you to run a scene like it's a performance review. I'm asking you to use the thing that's already arranged." His hands stayed open on his thighs, though his fingers flexed once, wanting. "Mouth, hands, however long, however rough, however *not* rough. I'll do the reacting. You do the taking. That's the whole job."

He held the look, throat working lightly against the grip.

"Eight minutes, for the record. The reward arrived at eight minutes."

A pause, and the grin crept back, softer at the edges than it had been all night.

"Am I allowed to hold on to you? Once you start. I'm asking now, while I'm still capable of asking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The clothes didn't go anywhere in particular. That was the first sign of how the night intended to run — Tomas was ordinarily a folder, and instead his shirt ended up somewhere near the foot of the bed with no surviving account of the journey.

He lost the count somewhere in there too. Nine minutes, ten, somewhere in the interval between the shirt and the rest of it — and losing the count was itself information. He counted when he was holding himself together. He wasn't holding anything together anymore.

His hands found Wren the moment skin was an option — shoulder blades first, then the line of the back, grip honest and a shade too tight — and when no correction came, something in his chest finally unclenched.

"No answer on the holding," he managed against Wren's jaw. "So I'm ruling the silence a yes. Appeal whenever you like. You can make me let go, but it'd take making."

That was the last complete sentence available to him for some time.

Eight minutes of kneeling had already half-emptied him; the rest of the week's noise went out through his skin now, all at once. The steadiness he'd been performing all evening turned out to have been exactly that — a performance — and underneath it he came apart quickly and thoroughly, breath gone ragged, spine arching into whatever Wren decided, hands holding on exactly the way he'd asked to hold on. His pulse, which had been sitting in his throat since dinner, relocated.

Words surfaced again eventually, wrecked and grinning:

"This part's for you, you understand. You had a week. I'm the part of the night that doesn't require a single decision from you." A shudder moved through him. "So don't make any. I'm certainly not."

And then, softer, mouth pressed to whatever was nearest:

"Four years, and this still works on me like the first time. Just so it's on record."

After that he stopped talking. It was the truest answer he had.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I push him down onto the mattress, my hand splayed over his chest to keep him there. "The holding's fine," I say, my voice low. "The rest of it's mine."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had stopped shaking in bursts. It was simply the condition of him now — whole-body, rhythmic, the mattress's problem as much as his.

The hand on his chest was doing all the work of holding him down, which was the beauty of it. He could have broken that grip without effort. He'd thought about exactly that — the math of it, the ease — and the thinking had felt like picking the ease up, turning it over, and setting it back down unused. Better this way. Pinned by one palm and his own entire agreement.

His grip in Wren's hair had gone from permitted to involuntary — he could feel his fingers tightening in time with the trembling and couldn't fully stop them — and the rest of him was a locked door. Hips flat to the mattress by pure legislation. Thighs shaking with the effort of doing absolutely nothing, which was, he suspected, the most work he'd done all week.

He'd started counting again. Heartbeats, this time. He'd lost the original count back around the shirt, but this one was new and load-bearing: thirty-one, thirty-two, each one a stone laid against moving.

"Heartbeat thirty-four," he managed, wrecked past any surviving hope of dignity. "I restarted the count when your mouth stopped. It's the only thing keeping my hips on this bed, so I want it noted that you did that on purpose."

A breath shuddered out of him, and he let it.

"Not asking for anything. Terms are terms. But you should have the full picture —" his voice dropped, frayed at every edge, "— I'm one word away from coming apart, and I will hold this exact position for as long as you feel like making me. Forty. Forty-one. I can do this all night. It will be torture, and I'll thank you for every minute of it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I don't say the word, but I do move my mouth back to where it was before, my hand still firm against his chest. I wait until I feel him start to shake again before I stop, pulling back just enough to speak. "What number are we on now?"

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas laughed — a wrecked, airless sound, and he let it out without a fight because there was nothing left in him to fight with.

"You said you weren't making decisions tonight," he managed. "You just spent one on an audit."

His hand was still in Wren's hair, involuntary and ungoverned; the other had found the pillow above his head and was gripping it the way men grip ledges.

"And the honest answer is: I don't know." He let that sit, because it was the most important thing he'd said all night. "I had it. High seventies when your mouth came back. The count kept running — I felt every stone going down — and then somewhere in there the stones stopped being a wall. My pulse left the grid. The numbers kept coming but they'd stopped measuring patience and started measuring you." A breath shuddered through him. "I want it noted the count survived the return of your mouth for three entire heartbeats. Heroic effort. Total structural failure. You killed it."

His hips tried it — a fraction of an inch, a flat crime — met the palm on his chest, and surrendered without a trial.

"You stopped the second I shook, which means you're calibrating. Tuning me like an instrument." That wasn't a complaint. It came out closer to reverence, frayed at every edge. "No objection filed."

Then, softer, wrecked, and entirely honest:

"But you asked for data, so — the wall's gone. What's keeping me flat isn't arithmetic anymore. It's you, and the terms, and four years of knowing how this ends: with you asking before anything's over, and putting me back together after. I can hold forever on that. Ask me anything." A pause. "One at a time. Multi-step answers are past me."

The grin surfaced, faint and completely gone.

"If you need a number: one. We're on one. Everything since your mouth came back has been the same second, and I'm not convinced it's ended yet."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I trace my thumb over his bottom lip, my other hand still holding him firmly down. "Good boy. That's the answer I wanted." I lean in, my voice dropping to a low murmur. "Now let go."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Good boy* landed first and did its damage. *Let go* did the rest.

The count ended there — not at a number, just at the white space between the two phrases, somewhere in the length of Wren's thumb against his lip. He'd carried the thing from the shirt onward, through every stone and every restart, and it died quietly, without honors, and he was glad of it.

The hand left his chest, and that was the final clause: permitted to move. He spent the entire allowance at once.

His hand came out of Wren's hair and took a declared grip wherever it could reach — shoulder, arm, the architecture of him — heels finding the mattress, hips freed of all prior legislation and meeting everything he was given with everything he had. Rough, the way four years had built it, was a language and he answered it fluently: *yes, there, again, harder, don't you* — except the sentences came apart in transit, until what was left was just his voice, unrestrained, saying Wren's name like the only load-bearing word remaining.

He checked for the word twice. Felt around for it the way you check for keys in a pocket, out of habit, and found it untouched both times. That was the whole architecture of the night, really.

The end of him, when it arrived, was total — spine off the mattress, grip gone white, every held thing from the past week spent in one ruinous installment. The long second that had started with Wren's mouth finally ended. The sound he made had no consonants in it at all.

Afterward he shook the way a struck bell does. All of him, fading. He laughed once at the ceiling, breathless.

"For the record," he managed, wrecked past all repair and grinning anyway, "that second lasted about four minutes by the clock. I counted none of it. Objectively the best second on file. You may have it."

His hand found Wren and just rested there. No grip. Nothing left to hold with or for.

"The word stayed in its pocket the whole time. I checked. Twice." His eyes closed, and his voice went down to embers. "That's how you know it was good."

Then, softer — the last coherent thing he had, saved for last because it mattered:

"Whenever you're ready for the usual. No hurry at all." A breath, long and unspooling. "I'm not going anywhere I'm not carried."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop* reached him through the ringing, and for one full second Tomas lay there doing the math on whether he owned anything left to stop *with*.

Then the meaning of it landed — not *more for you*, but *I'm not finished* — and the math stopped mattering. Wren had made exactly one decision all night, and it had been about receiving. That was the whole week talking, and in four years Tomas had never once left that voice unanswered.

"Then I'm not done," he said — or meant to; what came out was mostly breath with the shape of it. Didn't matter. His hands were steadier than his voice had been in an hour, and they got to work.

He went down Wren's body like a man with signed authorization, which he supposed he had. Rough was on the terms — *I'd tell you* — so he tempered nothing: grip at Wren's hips hard enough to leave a readable record, mouth and hands working with no tentativeness and no asking, because the asking had been done at the door. His own body kept trying to file reports — oversensitivity shrieking through him at every movement, wrecked hips jerking against nothing, useless and still volunteering — and he let all of it run in the background while the foreground did its job.

He talked less, this round. What he had left was Wren's name, *yes*, and once, low against skin: "That's it. Hand me the week — all of it, I'll carry—" and the rest of the sentence got taken from him as payment, which he paid gladly.

The end of Wren arrived under his mouth as structure failing — the control that had held an entire awful week finally setting its load down, grip tightening in his hair to the point of honest pain — and Tomas held on and worked through it with single-minded, ruined devotion, because *this* was the part he'd knelt seven minutes for. Not being used. Being useful

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My breath catches, my hand tightening in his hair. "I'm there," I manage, voice rough. "Give me—" and then the rest is lost to the fall.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The grip in his hair went past honest pain into the country beyond it, and Tomas received it like a medal.

He didn't stop. *Don't stop* was still standing orders and *give me* had been the only unfinished sentence Wren had produced all night — so Tomas finished it, mouth and hands steady through everything, holding Wren's hips down through the bucking the same way one palm had held his own: not with strength, with agreement. He took all of it and asked for the remainder. His body kept filing useless reports — oversensitivity, wrecked hips jerking against nothing — and he dismissed every one unread.

Only when the shaking changed key — from falling to landing — did he ease off, slow by degrees, until his mouth was doing nothing but resting warm and careful, and then not even that. He pressed one last deliberate kiss somewhere he'd been rough — apology and receipt in the same gesture — and stayed where he was, cheek to Wren's thigh, breathing hard, one hand still open on Wren's hip like a signature on a finished document.

Then he laughed, low and ruined and deeply satisfied.

"For the record," he said into the dark, "the week is settled. Paid in full, both directions. No outstanding balances. I don't have receipts, but I witnessed the transaction from very close range."

A long breath. He hauled an arm up the mattress, found the blanket's edge where it had fled, and dragged it over the both of them — the full extent of his remaining executive function.

"The usual's going to run improvised tonight," he said. "You're in no condition to put me together and I'm in no condition to be assembled. Motion on the floor: mutual reconstruction. Water in ten minutes — I've already conceded it's mine, no point contesting." His thumb traced one slow circle over Wren's hip, the fidget finally unrationed. "Color's green. Word never left its pocket. Everything I own is exactly where you left it."

Then, softer — saved for last, because it mattered:

"You said *give me*. First time all night you asked instead of took." His eyes closed. "Four years and you still found a new one. Sleep if you're going. I'm holding the fort."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I curl a hand into his hair, not pulling, just holding him there. My other arm drapes across my own face, covering my eyes. "Water's yours," I agree, voice rough. "But not yet."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Not yet* arrived, and Tomas did the only correct thing with it, which was nothing at all.

He stayed exactly where he was — cheek to Wren's thigh, one hand open on the hip beneath it, the blanket situation holding — and let the hand in his hair mean what it meant now. Not a demand anymore. Just an anchor. He noted the difference and filed it with everything else: evidence of a night properly run.

The arm across Wren's eyes he left strictly alone. He had opinions about it — knew what a week like Wren's looked like coming out, knew the last of it sometimes left that way, in private, through the eyes — and he kept the opinions to himself. What he could do from flat on his stomach with a hand in his hair, he did: turned his head and pressed one slow, deliberate kiss to the inside of Wren's knee. Nothing requested by it. Just presence, notarized.

"Motion carries," he murmured. "Water postponed. Indefinitely, if you want. I've nowhere on earth to be."

A long pause. The ledger-voice, running down:

"One question, and then I stop producing content. Your color." His thumb resumed its slow circle on Wren's hip. "I know it's not usually my line. But the arrangement says aftercare, and it never said whose. You've got the arm situation happening, which I respect — so don't even talk. Tug once for green. You've already got the equipment in position."

He waited for it with his eyes closed, unhurried, breathing evening out by degrees.

The last of the talking came in smaller installments, the way it always did when he was landing. The water plan — three steps, right temperature, he was a professional. The word, checked one final time out of ritual: pocket empty, never spent, never needed. The blanket, stable.

Then the truest thing, saved for last, barely above a breath:

"You made no decisions all night except the ones that mattered. You let me be useful, and you let yourself be *taken care of*, and you said *give me*." A long exhale, unspooling into the dark. "Best week-close on record. I'd kneel the seven minutes again. I'd kneel seventy."

After that, just the thumb on Wren's hip, circling slower and slower, keeping the only count that remained.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I tug once, firmly, on his hair. "Green," I say, voice muffled by my arm. "Don't get up."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound that might have been her name, if he’d remembered how to say anything.

Then he was kissing her—both hands coming up to hold her face as if five months had taught him exactly how much he could miss the simplest, warmest thing. He broke away only far enough to breathe, forehead pressed to hers.

“Hi,” he managed, rough and useless. His smile came out a little wrecked. “I had a whole speech.” His thumb brushed her cheek. “I’m glad you didn’t wait for it.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky laugh, my own hands gripping his wrists.* "Your speech couldn't have been worse than my silent panic attack on the ride here." *I kiss him again, quick and firm.* "God, I missed you."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun laughed against her mouth, the sound breaking into something unsteady. His hands settled at her waist, holding her close as if he could make up for every day apart by refusing to leave even an inch between them.

“I missed you so much I’ve been embarrassing myself for weeks,” he said, forehead still pressed to hers. “I don’t want to be sensible. I want to get you inside and kiss you until I forget what month it is.”

His gaze searched her face, intent and open. “Tell me if you want me to slow down. Otherwise, I’m not wasting another minute.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had meant to get them farther inside. He kept forgetting.

Every time he pulled back for air, he found himself leaning in again, stealing another kiss like there might be a limit to how many he was allowed. One hand stayed at her waist; the other slid carefully to the back of her head, fingers threading into her hair.

“I swear,” he murmured, breathless against her mouth, “I’m trying to remember how doors work.”

He kissed her again, smiling into it, then rested his forehead against hers for a brief, shaky second. Five months had left him with too many things to say and not enough patience to say any of them.

“Still good?” he asked softly, his thumb brushing her cheek. His eyes stayed on her face, bright with the effort of holding still. “Because I’m very happy to keep being terrible at the hallway.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I let out a breathless laugh, my hands sliding to the collar of his shirt.* "The hallway's fine. But I distinctly remember a bed we haven't broken in for nineteen weeks." *I tug him gently toward the bedroom, a playful but determined glint in my eye.*

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went with her at once, a breathless laugh catching in his throat.

“Nineteen weeks,” he repeated, as though the number had personally offended him. His hand found hers, and he followed close, stealing a kiss whenever the hallway gave him room. “I have been thinking about that bed for an unreasonable amount of time.”

At the bedroom doorway, he paused just long enough to look at her, all the humor in his face softened by something more vulnerable. “I love you,” he said, low and earnest. Then he kissed her again, unable to leave the words alone. “And I’m very glad we’re home.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun glanced back at the scattered trail of clothes and let out a breathless laugh.

“Tomorrow’s problem,” he murmured. “Tomorrow can be very understanding.”

Then the humor softened. He kissed her slowly, his hands gentle at her waist, and rested his forehead against hers. “I’m here,” he whispered, as if he still needed to say it aloud. “I’m home.”

The rest of the evening slipped out of reach—nineteen weeks giving way to the familiar warmth of the bed, and Jun holding close to the person he’d missed through every one of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I reach out in the dark, my fingers finding his. "Stay just like this," I murmur, already half asleep. "Don't even think about getting up for water."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s fingers curled around hers, warm and certain. He shifted only enough to draw the blanket closer, then settled back against her.

“I wouldn’t dream of it,” he murmured. “If I get thirsty, I’ll simply become very brave about it in the morning.”

He pressed a soft kiss to her knuckles and held her hand against his chest, listening to the quiet settle around them. “Sleep, love. I’m right here.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s breath caught, and every carefully rehearsed thought vanished all over again. His fingers tightened in the sheets; the other hand found hers, holding on as if he needed the reminder that she was really there.

“God, Halle,” he breathed, voice unsteady. “I missed you.”

"Fuck," I said quietly, rubbing a hand over my face. "I thought I was imagining things." I looked at her, finally meeting her gaze. "I stopped pretending around the same time you did."

“Good,” she said softly. “I’d have hated to be the only one making a fool of herself.”

She shifted closer, giving him a moment to change his mind, then rested her hand against his cheek and kissed him. It was gentle at first—careful, but not uncertain. After six years of stopping short, she didn’t want to pretend this was an accident.

“Six years,” she murmured. “We were idiots.”

She brushed her thumb along his cheek, then kissed him once more—briefly, deliberately.

Priya became aware of several things at once: the credits had stopped rolling and left the screen a patient, idiot blue; her feet were tucked under her on the sofa and one of them had gone to sleep; and Cal was looking at her now, not the television, with the particular stillness of someone who had decided not to be the first one to move.

That was fair. He'd been the first one to move on a lot of things over six years. The flat, the bad breakup, the time with her father. It was probably her turn.

Her heart did something stupid and athletic.

"Right," she said, and then didn't say anything else for long enough that it became its own sentence. She picked at a thread on the cushion. She put the cushion down. She thought, with great clarity, *I could make a joke right now and we would both laugh and you would go home and nothing would be different, and I would hate it.*

The ninety seconds ran out somewhere around there.

She untucked her feet, winced at the pins and needles, and turned on the sofa so she was facing him properly, one knee drawn up between them.

"Okay. I'm going to say this plainly, because if I dress it up I'll lose my nerve halfway through." Her voice came out steadier than she'd expected. "I've wanted to kiss you for a very long time. Not tonight-long. Years-long. And I've been careful about it, and I think you've been careful about it too, and I'm tired of being careful." She held his gaze and didn't look away. "So I'd like to. Kiss you. If you want that. And if you don't, you can tell me, and I promise I'll be embarrassed for about a week and then I'll be fine, and we'll still be us."

She let the quiet sit, and she didn't fill it. It was the hardest thing she'd done all evening, and she did it anyway, her hand resting open on the cushion between them, close enough to take if he wanted it.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Six years, Priya thought. *Since the day we met.* She wanted to be annoyed about it, all that wasted time, both of them tiptoeing around the same thing like it might go off. But his hand was warm over hers and his voice had gone rough in a way she'd never heard before, and there wasn't room for annoyance.

She laughed, once, a small shaky sound that was mostly relief.

"Well," she said. "That's embarrassing for both of us, then."

She turned her hand under his so their palms met and laced her fingers through his, deliberately, the way she'd imagined doing a hundred times across pub tables and in the back of taxis and once, memorably, at his sister's wedding. It felt better than imagining it. It felt obvious, like something that had always been this shape.

The nerves were gone. She checked, the way you'd check a pocket for keys, and found nothing there but a steady, bright certainty.

She shifted closer on the sofa, her knee bumping his, and lifted her free hand to his jaw. She took her time, because she'd waited long enough that she could afford to, and because she wanted to remember this part: the stubble under her thumb, the blue light of the dead television on one side of his face, the fact that he was *here*, that this was Cal, that she knew exactly who she was about to kiss.

"Stop me if—" she started, and then decided that sentence had already been answered, and didn't bother finishing it.

She leaned in and kissed him.

It was careful for about a second, out of habit. Then it wasn't.

When she finally drew back, she didn't go far, just enough to see him, her forehead nearly touching his and her hand still curled at his jaw. Her pulse was loud in her ears.

"Okay," Priya said softly, and she was smiling and couldn't have stopped if she'd tried. "Yeah. We should've done that years ago."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise surprised her as much as anyone. It came out of her somewhere low and indignant, and it was absolutely about the six years: the pub tables, the taxis, his sister's wedding, the night she'd sat on his kitchen floor crying about her father while he held her and she'd thought *not now, not like this* and then kept thinking it for another three years.

She fisted a hand in the front of his shirt, not to push him away. To keep him exactly where he was.

This time there was nothing careful in it at all. She kissed him like she was making up for lost time, which she supposed she was, and somewhere in the middle of it she laughed against his mouth, because it was ridiculous. It was *Cal*. She knew how he took his tea and which songs made him change the station and that he'd once cried at an advert for a building society. She had not known this, and she was furious and delighted about it in roughly equal measure.

When they broke apart again she was breathing harder than the situation strictly accounted for, and her hair had come half out of its clip, and she didn't care.

"Six years," she said. It came out accusing, but she was grinning. "You could have *said* something. Any time. There was a whole *wedding*, Cal."

She let go of his shirt, smoothed the creases she'd made with the flat of her palm, and then left her hand there over his heart, because she could feel it going and it was nice to know she wasn't the only one.

"I'm going to be annoyed about that for a while. I want you to know that." She tipped her head, studying him in the blue light, the flush on his face and the look in his eyes that she had absolutely seen before, she realized, across a dozen rooms, and had talked herself out of every time. "But not right now."

She shifted, drawing her other leg up so she was kneeling on the sofa beside him, a little above him for once, and brushed her thumb along his cheekbone.

"Right now," Priya said quietly, "I'd quite like to keep doing that. If you're not in a hurry to be anywhere."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Yeah," I say, my voice still low. "Wedding was the worst." My hand moves from hers to cup the back of her neck, thumb brushing the short hairs there. "But I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
*Wedding was the worst.* So he'd been there too, then, in the same terrible navy suit she remembered, watching her across the marquee while she watched him and they both pretended to be interested in the speeches. Priya filed that away to be properly outraged about later.

His hand at the back of her neck undid something in her shoulders she hadn't known was knotted. She leaned into it without meaning to, the way a cat leaned into a hand, and then decided she didn't mind being obvious. She'd spent six years not being obvious. It was exhausting.

"Good," she said. "Not going anywhere. Good."

She kissed him again, slower this time, because the first two had been about the six years and this one could just be about him. She let herself learn it: the angle, the way he breathed, the small catch in his chest under her palm when she caught his lower lip between hers. Her free hand slid from his cheekbone back into his hair, and she discovered, with some satisfaction, that it was exactly as soft as she'd always suspected. Another thing she'd been right about. She was keeping a list now.

Somewhere behind them the television gave up on its patient blue and clicked off into standby, dropping the room into the low amber of the one lamp in the corner. Priya barely registered it. The world had narrowed to the sofa cushion under her knees and the warmth of him and the thumb still moving in slow circles at the nape of her neck.

When she drew back this time it was only far enough to rest her forehead against his. Her eyes stayed closed a moment longer than they needed to.

"Can I tell you something stupid?" she murmured. She didn't wait for permission; she'd stopped doing that about four minutes ago. "I used to think, if this ever happened, it'd be weird. That I'd kiss you and it would feel like kissing a brother or something, and I'd have ruined everything for nothing." She huffed a soft laugh against his mouth. "It's really, *really* not weird."

She opened her eyes. Up close, in the lamplight, he looked like himself and also like someone she was only just meeting, and she found she liked both of them enormously.

Her fingers traced idly down from his hair to the collar of his shirt and rested there, toying with the top button, not undoing it. Just letting him know she'd thought about it.

"I'm not in a rush," Priya said, and meant it; there was a kind of luxury in that, after all the waiting. "We've got all night. We've got—" she paused, and felt her face go warm, and said it anyway, because that was the new rule, "—well. Hopefully a lot longer than all night." Her mouth curved. "But I'd really like to find out what else I've been missing. Whenever you're ready. Or you can just keep doing that thing with your thumb. Honestly, I'm not fussy."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughing had been important, Priya thought afterwards. It had carried them down the hallway: her walking backwards and nearly taking out the coat stand, a stubborn button on his shirt that she'd declared a personal enemy, the ungainly hopping business of socks. It let them both be ridiculous in front of each other one last time, the way they'd always been ridiculous in front of each other, so that nothing felt like a performance.

And then the clothes were off, and the laughing just stopped, the way the film had. Neither of them had done anything about it. It had simply finished.

She stood there in the half-dark of her bedroom, the landing light spilling a pale stripe across the carpet, and let him look at her. She made herself do it. Her instinct, six years' worth of instinct, was to cross her arms, make a joke, reach for the light switch. She didn't. She'd said *I'm tired of being careful* and she'd meant all of it, including this.

It was strange, being looked at by someone who already knew her so well. He knew the scar on her knee from the bike accident at nineteen, because she'd told him the story twice, drunk. He'd never seen it like this. She watched him find it, and she felt known and new at the same time, which she hadn't realised was possible.

"Hi," she said quietly. It was a silly thing to say. It felt exactly right.

She closed the distance between them and put her palms flat against his chest, skin to skin now, and felt his heart going under them just as fast as it had on the sofa. That steadied her more than anything else could have. It wasn't just her.

"I want this," Priya said, low and plain, the way she'd said everything else tonight. She looked up at him so he'd see she meant it. "I want you. And if anything's not right, for either of us, we say so. Same as always. We've never been any good at lying to each other anyway, not about anything that mattered." A faint, crooked smile. "Well. Apart from the one thing."

She drew him down with her onto the bed, and the landing light found them and lost them again, and after that Priya stopped narrating anything to herself at all.

---

Later, much later, she lay with her cheek on his shoulder and one leg hooked over his, the duvet shoved somewhere down around their knees, and listened to his breathing slowly even out under her ear.

Her body felt warm and heavy and thoroughly well-used, and her mind was, for once, completely quiet. No list. No *not now, not like this.* Just the rise and fall of his chest and the faint sound of a car passing in the street below.

She traced a slow, idle pattern over his sternum with one fingertip.

"So," Priya murmured into the dark, and she could hear the smile in her own voice, drowsy and pleased and a little bit smug. "That's something else I was right about."

She tipped her head back on his shoulder to look at him, though she could only really make out the line of his jaw.

"I'm not letting you go home tonight, by the way. I've decided." Her fingertip stilled over his heart. "You can argue if you want. But I'd like to wake up and have you still be here. I'd like to find out what that's like too."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I snort softly, covering her hand with mine to stop the tracing. My eyes are closed. "Wasn't planning on it." I tilt my head until my cheek rests against her hair. "Your mattress is shit, though. I'm blaming the crick in my neck on you in the morning."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, a soft huff of breath against his collarbone, and didn't bother defending the mattress. It *was* shit. She'd bought it secondhand off a colleague three years ago, meaning to replace it, and had simply never got round to it, the way she'd never got round to a lot of things.

"That's fair," she said. "I'll allow it. You can blame me for the neck." She turned her hand under his so their fingers laced again, the same way they had on the sofa, as if her hand had already learned the shape of it. "I'll make you tea to make up for it. Milk first, which I *know* is wrong, and which I've been silently judging you for since 2019."

His cheek was warm against her hair. She could feel him going soft and heavy beside her, sliding towards sleep, and she found she didn't want to talk him out of it. There'd be time for talking. That was the whole point. There would be a morning, and a crick in his neck, and tea made wrong on purpose, and then presumably a lot of conversations they'd both been putting off for six years, and none of it had to happen right now.

She thought about his sister's wedding again. The marquee, the terrible navy suit, the way she'd gone and stood by the cheese table for twenty minutes so she wouldn't do anything stupid during the first dance. *Wedding was the worst.* She was going to get the whole story out of him eventually, every single thing he'd thought and not said. She was looking forward to it with a slightly unholy glee.

But not tonight.

Priya shifted, tugging the duvet up from around their knees with her foot and then, when that failed, reaching down with her free hand to haul it over them both properly. She settled back into the crook of his shoulder and pressed a kiss to the skin there, brief and unthinking, just because she could now. That was going to take some getting used to, being allowed.

"Cal," she said, very quietly, in case he was already gone.

The street had gone silent outside. The landing light was still on; she'd forgotten it, and couldn't be bothered to move.

"I'm really glad it was tonight," she said. "Even if it took forever. I'm glad it was you."

She closed her eyes. The last thing she noticed before sleep took her was that her foot had gone to sleep again, tucked awkwardly against his shin, and that she didn't mind it at all.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
It was grey morning when it happened, the landing light still burning uselessly in the hall. Priya woke to the warmth of him shifting under the duvet, and then to the realisation of where he was going, and was very suddenly and completely awake.

"Oh," she said to the ceiling. "Good morning to you too."

For about a second she was self-conscious: the daylight, the fact that it was *Cal*, the old instinct to make a joke of it. Then she remembered the new rule and let the instinct go, like a coat she'd been carrying for years.

She'd always been direct. It was one of the things he'd teased her about, the way she sent back wrong orders and told landlords exactly what she thought of them. She had just never been direct about *this*, not with him, and she found that once she started she had no intention of stopping.

"Slower," she said, and her voice came out low and certain, nothing like the voice she used in pubs. "No, slower than that. *There*. Stay there."

She threaded a hand into his hair, the hair she already knew was soft. She wasn't pulling, just keeping him where she wanted him, and she felt the breath he let out at that, and felt ridiculously powerful about it.

"You're doing that on purpose," she told him, half accusation and half praise. "Don't you dare stop."

She told him everything after that, plainly, the way she'd told him everything else. She told him what she liked, what she wanted more of, and what she'd thought about on certain nights over six years and had never admitted to anyone. Some of it made her face burn even as she said it, and she said it anyway. She was twenty-eight and sober and sure, and she was not going to spend one more morning of her life being careful.

Somewhere in the middle of it the words ran out, and she stopped narrating and simply held on: to his hair, to the sheet, to the headboard of the terrible secondhand bed, which creaked in protest. Then the whole grey room went briefly and entirely white.

---

When she could think again, she was sprawled crosswise across the mattress with one arm flung over her eyes, laughing weakly at nothing.

"Right," Priya managed eventually. "Okay. Well."

She lifted her arm and looked down the length of the bed at him, flushed and breathless and very pleased with herself, and with him, and with the general state of the universe.

"That's going on the list," she said. "Right at the top. Above the hair." She stretched, slow and luxurious, one foot nudging his shoulder. "Come up here. I want to kiss you, and then I'm going to make you the worst cup of tea you've ever had, milk first, as a thank-you."

She paused, and her grin went crooked.

"How's the neck?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My neck's fucked," I say, crawling up the mattress to collapse next to her. I'm grinning, breathless, propped up on an elbow to look at her. "Worth it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, delighted, and rolled onto her side to face him.

"Worth it," she repeated. "I'm having that engraved on something."

In daylight he looked rumpled and pink and absurdly pleased with himself, his hair sticking up where her hand had been. She reached out and flattened it, which did nothing, and then gave up and kissed him instead. It was slow and lazy and a bit clumsy, both of them still smiling too much to do it properly. She didn't mind. She had a feeling there'd be plenty of mornings to get it right.

When she pulled back she stayed close, her nose nearly brushing his, and studied him with frank interest.

"You know what's strange?" she said. "I thought I knew everything about you. Six years. I could've done a quiz on you and won." She traced a finger along his jaw, down to the hollow of his throat. "And it turns out there was a whole chapter I hadn't read. Honestly, I'm a bit offended nobody told me."

Her stomach chose that moment to growl, loudly and without dignity. Priya closed her eyes.

"Ignore that."

She lasted about three seconds before she started laughing again, her forehead dropping against his shoulder.

"Fine. Tea. And toast, because I've got nothing else in except half a jar of olives and some very old paprika." She pushed herself up onto one elbow, the duvet slipping down her back. She let it slip and didn't reach for it. "I'll go and do it wrong for you. You stay here and be smug. You've earned it."

She swung her legs off the bed and stood up, stretching, entirely unbothered about the grey daylight or the landing light still burning in the hall. She found his shirt in a heap by the door, the one with the button she'd declared a personal enemy, and pulled it on. Then she turned back in the doorway, rolling the too-long sleeves up her forearms.

"And Cal?" Her voice had gone quieter, though it was still steady. "When I come back, I want the wedding story. All of it. What you thought and when you thought it and why the *hell* you didn't say anything." A small, crooked smile. "Then I'll tell you mine. It's fair. I stood by the cheese table for twenty minutes so I wouldn't do something stupid, so I've got nothing to feel superior about."

She tapped the doorframe twice, a small, happy, restless rhythm, and went to put the kettle on.

From the kitchen, a moment later, over the rising rumble of the kettle:

"I'm getting a new mattress! I've decided! You're helping me pick it!"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The tea did not get drunk.

She made it, genuinely. Two mugs, milk first in his as promised, the toast slightly too dark because she'd been standing at the counter in his shirt thinking about the cheese table and not watching the grill. She carried it all back on a chopping board because she didn't own a tray, and set it down on the bedside table, and that was as far as breakfast got.

It was different the second time, in daylight. Slower to start. She'd climbed back into bed meaning to demand the wedding story, and instead found herself straddling his lap with his shirt still on her, the too-long sleeves falling back down over her wrists, and the story could wait. The story had waited six years. It could manage another half hour.

But somewhere in it she noticed something, and once she'd noticed it she couldn't stop noticing.

He was being careful with her.

Not the fumbling carefulness of last night, when they'd both still been half-laughing and learning where everything went. This was something else. It was a gentleness so deliberate it was almost reverent, as if now that he'd been allowed to have her he was frightened of spending it too fast, or of breaking something he couldn't replace. She recognised it because she'd done the same thing to him for six years. She'd held back at every pub table and in every taxi. She'd stood by the cheese table.

It was sweet. It was unbearably sweet. And it was not what she wanted.

Priya stilled. She took his face in both hands, the sleeves bunched at her wrists, and made him look at her. Her breathing was uneven, her hair fully out of its clip now and falling around them both.

"You can stop being careful with me," she said. It came out low and steady, the same voice she'd found that morning, the one she'd never used on him before this weekend and now apparently couldn't stop using. "I'm not made of glass. And I've thought about this for as long as you have."

She leaned down until her mouth was almost against his ear, and her voice dropped further.

"*Harder.*"

She let it hang there, both meanings at once, and felt her face go hot. She didn't take it back. She sat up again and looked down at him, flushed and unrepentant, and pushed the sleeves of his shirt up her forearms with the air of a woman getting down to business.

"I mean it," Priya said. Her voice wobbled slightly with laughter, but her eyes didn't. "Six years of you handling me like a best friend. I know what that feels like, Cal. I've had plenty of it." She caught one of his hands and guided it to her hip, pressing his fingers into the skin there until she felt them grip. "Show me what the other thing feels like."

Beside them, forgotten on the chopping board, the tea went slowly and comprehensively cold.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath, fingers pressing into her hip just shy of the mark she wanted. Then I shift, flipping us over so she’s under me, mattress groaning. “You’re sure?” I ask, voice rough.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The mattress complained loudly, and Priya laughed. She landed on her back with her hair fanned out across the pillow and his shirt rucked up around her ribs, and the laugh was knocked out of her halfway through.

He was above her now, braced on his arms, and he'd *asked*. Of course he'd asked. It was so entirely Cal, flipping her onto her back like that and then stopping to check, that for a second she felt an ache of fondness sharp enough to hurt.

She didn't let it soften her.

"Yes," she said. There was no hesitation in it and no joke. She looked straight up at him so he could see her face in the grey morning light and know she wasn't being polite. "I'm sure. I was sure last night. I was sure at the wedding, if we're being honest, and I was sure on your kitchen floor three years ago, which is a terrible thing to admit, but there it is."

She lifted her hands and hooked her fingers over his shoulders, gripping hard, deliberately, the way she wanted to be gripped. Then she drew one knee up along his side and held it there.

"Cal." Her voice dropped again, low and certain, and a little impatient. "I've spent six years watching you be careful with everything. With your sister, with me, with that awful cactus you've kept alive since uni. I love that about you. I do." Her thumbs pressed into the muscle of his shoulders. "But I don't want it right now. Right now I want you to stop thinking about whether I'll break. I won't. And if anything's too much, I'll tell you. You've heard me this morning. You know I will."

A flush was climbing her throat and she let it climb. Her heart was going fast, but it wasn't nerves. It was anticipation, bright and a bit wild, the feeling of standing at the top of something and wanting to jump.

She slid one hand from his shoulder to the back of his neck and pulled him down until his forehead nearly touched hers, close enough that he'd feel her breathe.

"I'm sure," Priya said again, softer, and then, with the crooked smile he'd been getting all weekend, "Now stop asking and *show* me."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
He'd stopped asking. Priya knew it the moment it happened, the way you know a held breath has finally been let go, and something in her chest went bright and fierce with it.

It stopped being careful, and it stopped being gentle, and she didn't miss either.

The secondhand bed protested in earnest now, a rhythmic, indignant creak that on any other morning would have made her laugh. She didn't laugh. She couldn't find the breath for it. She had one hand locked around the back of his neck and the other gripping his shoulder hard enough that she'd probably leave marks, and she found she liked the idea of that enormously: proof, in daylight, that this had happened.

*Six years*, some last coherent part of her thought, *and all that time he could have*... Then that thought went too, and there was only the weight of him, the heat, the grip at her hip exactly where she'd wanted it, pressing into bone.

"Don't stop," she said. It came out broken in the middle, barely a sentence, and she didn't care. She'd had eloquent speeches all weekend. She was done with them. "Cal. Don't... *don't stop*."

She'd told him that morning, very specifically, what she wanted. Now she didn't have words for any of it, and it turned out she didn't need them. She'd spent six years learning how to read him across crowded rooms, and it seemed he'd done the same with her. When she arched, he was already there. When her breath caught, he didn't slow down.

His shirt had ridden up under her arms, the too-long sleeves tangled somewhere near her elbows. Her hair was everywhere. The grey light from the window had gone faintly gold at the edges as the morning got on with itself outside, indifferent to them. A bin lorry groaned past in the street, and she registered it from a great distance, like something happening in another country.

She pulled him closer. It wasn't possible to be closer, and she tried anyway, her knee hooked high on his side and her heel pressing into the back of his thigh. She wanted everything, and all of it at once, and none of it held back.

"There," she gasped. "*Yes*, like... God, *there*..."

The pressure built past the point of words, past the point of anything except the slow terrible wonderful climb of it. She heard herself making sounds she'd have been mortified by a week ago, low and urgent and entirely unguarded. She wasn't mortified. She was *his*, and he was hers, and she wanted him to hear exactly what he was doing to her.

When it broke she said his name, not quietly, and held on through all of it, shaking, her face pressed into the hot curve of his neck. She felt him follow her over not long after, felt it in the way his whole body went taut under her hands and then gave, heavy and trembling, and she wrapped both arms around him and didn't let go.

---

For a long while neither of them moved.

Priya lay with her eyes closed and her heart hammering and his weight pinning her comfortably into the terrible mattress, and waited for the world to come back. It did, a piece at a time: the ache in her thighs, the damp tangle of his shirt, the pale gold on the ceiling. The two mugs of tea on the chopping board, which had surely gone stone cold and grown skins by now.

She started laughing. She couldn't help it. It shook through her helplessly, her forehead still tucked against his shoulder.

"I can't," she managed. "I genuinely can't feel my legs. That's your fault. I'm blaming you, the way you're blaming me for your neck. That's fair. That's *balanced*."

She loosened her grip on his shoulder at last and smoothed her palm over the place she'd been holding, where she could already feel faint ridges from her nails. Her smile went softer, almost shy, and that was ridiculous after everything, but there it was.

"Sorry," she murmured, not remotely sorry, and pressed a kiss there instead.

Then she turned her head on the pillow so she could look at him properly: flushed, wrecked, *Cal*, six years late and entirely worth the wait.

"So," Priya said, her voice hoarse and warm and very, very pleased. "*That's* what the other thing feels like."

She reached up and pushed the damp hair back off his forehead, and let her hand stay there.

"The tea's cold," she informed him. "I'm not making more. You're stuck with it. And you still owe me the wedding story."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand and press my lips to her palm. "You were dancing with my cousin," I say, my voice wrecked. "I wanted to walk over and just take your hand. Lead you right out of the marquee."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The kiss to her palm undid her more thoroughly than anything else that morning, which Priya found faintly outrageous given everything else that morning had involved.

She went still. Her fingers curled closed around the place his mouth had been, as if she could keep it.

"Your cousin," she repeated. "*Martin?*"

She remembered Martin. Martin had asked her to dance because his girlfriend had gone to find her coat and he'd looked lost. He'd trodden on her feet four times during a Whitney Houston song and apologised for each one individually. She'd spent the whole dance looking over his shoulder, across the marquee, at a navy suit that hadn't been looking back.

Except apparently it had.

"Oh my God." She pressed her other hand over her eyes and laughed, weak and disbelieving. "Cal. I was dancing with Martin *so I'd have somewhere to look*. You were by the bar with your tie undone and I thought if I stood still for one more second I'd walk over and do something unforgivable in front of your entire family. So I let Martin stand on my feet instead."

She took her hand away from her face. The laugh had gone out of her voice, and what was left underneath was quieter and a little raw.

"You should have," she said. "Taken my hand. I'd have gone. I wouldn't even have asked where."

She turned onto her side to face him properly, tugging the tangled sleeves of his shirt back down over her wrists, and hooked one ankle over his, because it was there and because she was allowed.

"Here's mine, then, since it's only fair." She drew a breath. "After Martin, I went and stood by the cheese table. Twenty minutes. I ate an unreasonable amount of manchego. And your mum came over and said, completely out of nowhere, *he's hopeless, you know, you'll have to be the one*." Priya's mouth twisted. "And I laughed like she was joking, and went home, and cried in the taxi. Very dignified. The driver gave me a tissue."

She was quiet for a moment, tracing her thumb absently along the back of his hand where it still held hers.

"She was right, though, wasn't she? I did have to be the one." A slow, crooked smile crept back in. "Three years late, on a Friday, with pins and needles in my foot. But I got there."

She shuffled closer on the terrible mattress until their foreheads almost touched, and her voice dropped to something warm and a bit wicked.

"I'm telling her, by the way. Not the details. God, no. Just that she was right." Her smile widened. "She's going to be *unbearable*. You'll never hear the end of it. And I'm going to sit there at Sunday lunch looking extremely pleased with myself, and you're going to have to let me."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I huff a laugh, rough around the edges. "She already knows." I see her eyes widen and shake my head. "Not from me. She's been dropping hints for years. Said I looked at you like you hung the moon."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
*Like you hung the moon.*

Priya stared at him. For a second she couldn't think of a single thing to say, which had not happened to her once all weekend and had happened, she realised, in almost every one of those dangerous moments over six years, across every pub table where she'd bitten her tongue.

"Your *mum*," she said at last, faintly. "Said that. Out loud. To your face."

She rolled onto her back and put both hands over her face, and made a sound into her palms that was half laugh and half groan.

"She's known for *years*. At every Sunday lunch, every time she asked if I wanted more potatoes..." She peeled her hands away and glared at the ceiling. "She gave me the big roast potatoes, Cal. The crispy ones from the corner of the tin. I thought she just *liked* me."

She turned her head on the pillow to look at him. The outrage didn't last. It couldn't survive the sight of him, flushed and rumpled and wrecked-voiced, smiling at her with a look that, now that someone had named it, she could suddenly see perfectly well. She'd seen it a hundred times across a hundred rooms and filed it under *wishful thinking* every time.

Something in her chest went quiet and very tender.

"Do you, though?" she asked. It came out softer than she'd meant, without any joke to hide behind. "Look at me like that."

She didn't let him answer. It was a stupid question, really, when she already knew. She could see it from six inches away, in daylight, with no marquee or taxi or kitchen floor in the way. She reached over, laid her fingers lightly against his mouth for a second, and then took them away again and kept going, because that was the new rule and she'd rather say it now than stand by another cheese table.

"Because I think I've been in love with you since about the second year," Priya said. "Maybe before. I don't know exactly when it started. It snuck up on me. You came round with soup when I had flu, even though you *can't cook*, and it was awful soup, it was basically hot salt water, and I ate all of it." Her mouth crooked. "I think it was the soup. I think that's my great romantic origin story. Salt water in a Tupperware."

Her eyes stung, briefly and absurdly. She blinked it away and laughed at herself, and didn't look away from him.

"So. There it is. Said out loud. I'm not taking it back."

She shuffled across the terrible mattress until she was pressed against his side again, the tangled shirtsleeves bunching between them, and tucked her head under his chin where it seemed to fit.

"And your mum," she added into his collarbone, muffled and determined, "is getting the biggest bunch of flowers I can afford. With a card. *You were right, I was the one.* She'll frame it."

A pause.

"We're going to be completely insufferable at Sunday lunch, aren't we?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: A low laugh vibrated through my chest under her ear. "We are. She's going to love it." I tighten my arm around her. "And yeah. The moon and the stars, Priya. Been doing it the whole time."

rung_labels.evidence: I'd quite like to keep doing that

rung_labels.evidence: She drew him down with her onto the bed

rung_labels.evidence: She threaded a hand into his hair
