dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline didn't hurry. That had never been the point.

She set down the book she hadn't been reading, a paperback splayed open on the arm of the chair for the last hour as a pretext, and rose the way she did everything for Roan: deliberately, knowing she was watched and liking it. The lamp by the window threw long gold light across the floorboards, and she walked through it barefoot, the hem of her dress brushing her knees.

She had chosen the dress at five-thirty. The green one. She had changed her mind twice, then come back to it, because Roan had once said, offhand and months ago over dinner with friends, that green did something to her eyes, and Aveline kept a private ledger of every offhand thing Roan had ever said.

Halfway across the room she let herself look up. That was her small indulgence, meeting Roan's gaze while crossing the distance, watching that particular stillness settle over them, the one that meant they were paying attention. Three hours of waiting had been for this: being looked at like she was worth the wait.

Something warm and bright bloomed under her ribs. It always did. Years in, and it still hadn't dulled.

She stopped just in front of the chair, close enough that her knees nearly touched Roan's, and waited, hands loose at her sides. She didn't kneel yet. She had learned long ago that Roan liked to be the one to decide that, and she liked giving them the choice almost more than she liked the kneeling.

"I made tea at seven," she said quietly, a faint curve at the corner of her mouth. "It's gone cold. I'll make fresh, if you want it." A pause, her eyes steady on Roan's. "Or I can stay right here. Whatever you'd like."

Her voice was even. Her pulse was not, and she suspected Roan could see it fluttering at her throat. She hoped so.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I reach out and run my fingers along the hem of the green dress, feeling the fabric.* "The tea can wait." My eyes lift to hers. "Tell me what you thought about while you waited."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline's breath caught, just slightly, when Roan's fingers found the hem. It wasn't much of a touch. It didn't need to be. After three hours, the brush of knuckles against fabric near her knee landed like a hand laid flat against her sternum.

She didn't look down at it. She kept her eyes where they'd been asked to be.

"Honestly?" she said, and the curve at her mouth deepened, a little rueful. "Mostly you."

She let that sit a moment, because it was true and because she knew Roan wouldn't accept it as a whole answer. They never did. They liked the details. She'd learned to keep them the way other people kept photographs.

"At first I thought about your day," she went on, her voice low and unhurried. "Whether the meeting ran long, whether you'd eaten. I nearly texted to ask, twice." A small, self-aware huff of a laugh. "I didn't. I wanted to find out by looking at you instead, when you walked in. You haven't eaten, by the way. There's a line right here—" she lifted one hand, not quite touching, and traced the air an inch from the corner of Roan's mouth, "—that you get when you've skipped lunch. I'll fix that later. Not now."

Her hand drifted back to her side. The lamp caught the fine hairs on her forearm and the faint flush beginning at her collarbone.

"Then I thought about the dress. Whether you'd notice." Her gaze dropped for the first time, briefly, to Roan's fingers on the hem, then rose again, warmer. "You did. That was a good moment. I'm going to keep that one."

She shifted her weight, not restless, just unable to stay perfectly still, and her knee brushed Roan's.

"And after that..." The evenness in her voice wavered, and she let it, because honesty was part of what she offered. "After that I thought about this. Standing here. Whether you'd tell me to kneel right away or make me wait a little longer." A slow breath. "I went back and forth on which I wanted more. I still don't know. That's the part I like best, I think. That it isn't up to me."

Her pulse was visible now; she could feel it in her throat, her wrists, everywhere. She didn't try to hide it.

"So I sat in that chair and pretended to read," she finished softly, "and I thought about how you'd look at me when I crossed the room. And then you did." The bright, warm thing under her ribs was nearly audible in her voice. "It was worth every minute."

She went quiet then, hands loose, knees nearly touching Roan's, and waited to be told what came next.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline went down slowly, the way she'd been wanting to since six.

One knee, then the other, the floorboards cool through the thin fabric of the dress. She settled back onto her heels and let her hands rest palm-down on her thighs, and something in her shoulders that she hadn't known was tight simply let go. It always surprised her a little, how much of herself she carried standing up, and how easily it all set down once she was here.

She didn't speak. Roan hadn't asked her to, and the silence was a gift she knew how to receive.

From here the room rearranged itself. The lamp was higher and softer. The cold tea sat forgotten on the side table, a pale ring of milk at the edge of the cup. And Roan was above her, close enough that she could feel warmth coming off them, close enough that if she leaned forward an inch her cheek would rest against their knee.

She didn't lean. Not yet. That was part of it too.

Instead she looked, because looking was allowed and she had been hungry for it all evening. The loosened collar. The faint crease at the knee of their trousers from sitting too long in some conference room. The hand still resting where it had fallen after leaving her hem, fingers slightly curled, relaxed in a way they probably hadn't been all day. She catalogued it all with quiet, greedy care. The ledger, again. She would remember the exact angle of that hand for weeks.

Her breathing slowed to match the room. Then, without her deciding it, to match Roan's.

The waiting was different now than it had been in the chair. Then it had been anticipation, restless and bright, all edges. This was fuller. Warmer. The difference between standing outside a lit window and being let in to sit by the fire. She wasn't waiting *for* Roan anymore. She was waiting *with* them, under their attention, and every second they let stretch out was a second they were choosing to spend looking at her.

That thought landed low and sweet, and her lashes dipped for a moment before she brought her eyes back up.

A strand of hair had slipped loose over her cheek. She felt it there, tickling faintly, and didn't lift a hand to fix it. Roan could, if they liked. Or they could leave it. She found she wanted to know which, the way she'd wanted to know about the kneeling, and the not-knowing hummed pleasantly under her skin.

The flush at her collarbone had crept higher. Her pulse had not settled at all.

Still she stayed quiet, open-handed, face tipped up toward Roan's in the gold light, and let the moment be as long as Roan wanted it to be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I reach out and tuck the stray strand of hair behind her ear, letting my thumb linger on her cheekbone.* "I missed you today." My voice is quiet, a low admission in the stillness. "Take my shoes off."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The thumb on her cheekbone undid her a little. She'd braced for an instruction and gotten the admission first, and it went straight through her like warmth through a cold hand. Her eyes closed, just for a breath, and she turned her face a fraction of an inch into the touch before she could think better of it.

*I missed you today.*

She'd heard Roan say a great many things over the years, and she kept all of them. But that one was rarer than people would have guessed, and she knew what it cost them to hand it over plainly, without armor. She held it carefully, the way you'd hold something that could spill.

"I missed you too," she said, very softly. It came out rougher than she meant. She didn't correct it.

Then the instruction, and her whole body answered it before her mind caught up: a small, relieved lift, like a held note finally resolving. *Something to do.* Something for them. There was no better thing.

She eased back from the lingering thumb only as far as she had to, and bent to the task.

Roan's left foot first. She always started with the left, and couldn't have said why. It had become habit, and habit had become ritual, and ritual was a quiet kind of love. She cupped the heel in one palm and found the laces with the other hand. The knot was tight, pulled hard that morning by someone in a hurry, and she worked it loose patiently, fingertips careful. She didn't rush it. She drew each lace out of its eyelets a little, so the shoe would give without being wrenched.

The leather was warm and slightly creased across the toe. A scuff near the heel, new since last week. She noticed it, filed it away. She'd polish it out on Sunday while Roan read the paper, and they'd pretend not to notice.

She slid the shoe free slowly, supporting the arch the whole time so the foot never dropped, and set it on the floor beside her, neatly aligned. Then, because she couldn't not, she let her thumb press once, firmly, into the sole through the sock, right where she knew the ache would be after a day of standing and pacing and conference rooms.

She glanced up to see if it landed, then bent to the right foot.

Same care. Same patience with the knot, which was even tighter; Roan always pulled the right one harder. She smiled faintly at that, head bowed, where they might or might not see it. The second shoe came free and she set it beside its partner, toes even, and only then did she let her hands rest there, lightly cradling one socked foot in her lap on the green fabric of her dress.

She didn't let go.

"There," she murmured, and her thumb began, unasked but not presumptuous, a slow circle along the arch. Testing. Offering. She'd stop the instant she was told to. "You were on your feet more than you'd planned. I can tell."

Her voice was steadier now, anchored by the work of her hands. But the flush had climbed all the way up her throat, and when she lifted her eyes to Roan's again, they were bright and unguarded and entirely theirs.

"Tell me what else you need," she said. "I have all night."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline didn't waste the minute, but she didn't rush it either. Efficiency and hurry were different things, and she had never once confused them where Roan was concerned.

She rose up onto her knees to reach the buttons of Roan's shirt. Top to bottom, one at a time, her fingers sure. She eased the fabric back off their shoulders and, because some things were simply who she was, folded it in half and laid it over the arm of the chair rather than letting it fall. The belt next, its leather warm from the day. Then the rest. Each piece she set aside with the same quiet care she'd given the shoes, a neat small pile growing on the floor beside them.

Her own dress took less ceremony. She drew it up and over her head in one smooth pull, and for half a second, before she set it down, she held the green fabric bunched in her hands and let herself be glad she'd chosen it.

Then there was nothing left in the way, and the lamp was warm on both of them, and she let herself lean in at last.

She had been saving it all evening, that first press of her cheek against the inside of Roan's knee. She closed her eyes and simply stayed there a moment, breathing, before she turned her head and set her mouth to their skin.

After that she was unhurried, and entirely attentive. Her hands learned the day off them: the knot of tension high in one thigh, the way their breath changed when she found it and worked it loose. She kept her eyes lifted when she could. Watching was half of it. Every hitch, every shift of weight, every small, involuntary sound went straight into the ledger. This was what she'd been waiting for since six, not only to touch Roan, but to be the reason the long day slid off their face, piece by piece, until nothing remained of it at all.

The tea went on growing cold. Neither of them had any use for it.

---

Later, much later by the lamp's reckoning, Aveline lay with her head on Roan's chest, and the room had gone soft and gold at every edge. One of her hands rested flat over their heart, and she could feel it still slowing, still coming down. She traced idle shapes there with a fingertip. Nothing in particular. Just touching because she could.

The loose strand of hair had slipped free again. She didn't fix it this time either.

"You still haven't eaten," she murmured after a while, and her voice was warm, a little hoarse, thoroughly content. She tipped her chin up to look at them. "I have soup I can warm. Or I can make you toast with too much butter, the way you pretend you don't like." A pause, and the corner of her mouth curved. "Or I can stay exactly where I am. Your call."

She waited, perfectly happy to be told either way.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "I could eat," I say, my fingers drifting lazily through her hair. "But I don't want you to move yet." My hand stills, cupping the back of her head. "Tell me what you want, Aveline. For yourself."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline went still under Roan's hand.

It wasn't a question she got often, and it never stopped catching her slightly off balance, like reaching for a step in the dark and finding it a little higher than expected. Her fingertip paused mid-shape over Roan's heart. She could feel the answer she'd usually give sitting ready on her tongue, *this, you, whatever you like*, and it was true, all of it. But Roan's hand was cupping the back of her head, steady and patient, and she knew that tone. They weren't asking to be reassured. They were asking.

So she made herself think about it properly.

"That's harder than it sounds," she admitted, and huffed a soft laugh against their chest. "You'd think I'd have a list. I keep one for you."

She let her cheek settle back down, listening to their heartbeat for a moment while she sorted through it. The lamp hummed faintly. Somewhere outside a car passed, its headlights sliding across the ceiling and gone.

"I want to stay here a little longer," she said finally. "That's the first thing. Not because you told me not to move. Because I don't want to." Her fingertip resumed its slow tracing. "And I want you to tell me about your day. All of it, not the summary. The boring parts. What you had instead of lunch, if you had anything. Who annoyed you. I sat there for three hours building a version of it in my head, and I'd like the real one."

She was quiet a moment. The next part came out more carefully.

"And Saturday." She tipped her chin up so she could see Roan's face, and her eyes were soft and a little shy, which on her was rare. "I want you to myself. No laptop. Maybe the market in the morning, if it isn't raining. I want to walk next to you and pick out peaches and have you carry the bag and not be thinking about work at all." A faint, rueful curve of her mouth. "That's selfish. I know that's a big ask, with the quarter you're having."

She didn't take it back, though. She let it stand.

Then her gaze dropped, lashes lowering, and her voice went quieter still.

"And..." A breath. "What you said earlier. That you missed me." Her hand pressed a little flatter over their heart, as if she could hold the words there. "I liked hearing it more than I can tell you. I suppose what I want is to hear it again sometime. Not now. I don't want you to say it because I asked. Just... sometime, when you mean it."

Her face was warm. She could feel the flush coming back, different from before, less heat and more exposure, as if she'd set something fragile down on the table between them and was waiting to see what happened to it.

She didn't look away, though. That was part of what she offered too.

"That's all," she murmured. "That's the list." A small pause, and a little of her usual warmth crept back into her voice. "Then soup. You're still eating, whatever you say."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had slid down Roan's body with the intent of someone who'd decided the soup could wait a little longer. It was her own answer to *what do you want*, given without words. She was unhurried about it, attentive, reading every shift of breath the way she'd been reading them all night.

Then Roan told her to stop, and she did.

Not a beat later, not a last lingering moment. She stopped. That wasn't something she had to think about. It lived deeper in her than habit, deeper than the ledger, in the same place the kneeling came from. Years of this, and it had never once been a question. The whole shape of what she gave Roan rested on that one clean, unbending line. Everything she offered was only worth anything because this part was never in doubt.

She drew back and lifted her head, her hair falling loose around her face, and her hands came to rest lightly on Roan's thighs. They weren't pressing or asking, just there. Her breathing was uneven, but her eyes were clear, and they went straight to Roan's face, searching it.

"Okay," she said softly. "I'm here."

She didn't ask them to explain. She didn't need a reason, and she wouldn't make them hand one over. She simply watched them, steady and warm, the way she'd watched them cross the room hours ago. Any sign of discomfort, of too much after a long day, would be enough for her.

After a moment she eased back up alongside them, slowly, giving them room to pull away if they wanted it. She settled on her side, close but not pressed against them, one hand resting open on the sheet between them where Roan could take it or not.

"Too much?" she asked quietly. "Or just not right now?" A small, easy curve touched her mouth, entirely without hurt. "Either's fine. I mean that."

Then, gentler still: "I can go warm that soup. Or I can just lie here with you and you can tell me about the meeting that ran long. Whatever you need."

She waited, patient and unbothered, a loose strand of hair across her cheek again, and let Roan decide what came next.

---

*(OOC: I kept Aveline stopping immediately. Her whole characterization rests on "stop" meaning stop, and I'd rather not write past a no. If you meant a scene where Roan's "stop" is playful and not the real limit, we can set up an explicit safeword in-story first so it's clear, and I'm glad to write it that way.)*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, my hand coming to rest on the back of her head.* "Not too much. Just... breathe with me a minute." *I tilt my chin to meet her gaze.* "Tell me what you saw in my face when you looked up."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline let out a breath she hadn't quite known she was holding, and some small, careful watchfulness in her eased.

*Not too much.*

She believed it. Roan didn't soften things for her benefit, not about this, and that was part of why she could believe them. The hand at the back of her head was steady and warm, and she let its weight settle her. She shifted closer, closing the little gap she'd left, until her forehead rested against their shoulder and she could feel their chest rise and fall beside her.

*Breathe with me.*

She did. It took a few tries. Her own breath was still quick and ragged, and Roan's was slower, deeper, more deliberate than it needed to be. She understood that it was deliberate for her, something for her to follow. So she followed it. In, and a long hold, and out. Again. By the third or fourth breath she'd stopped counting and simply matched them, and the room went quiet around the sound of it. The lamp. The faint tick of the radiator. Two people breathing in time.

When Roan tilted their chin, she lifted her face to meet their gaze. She took her time answering. They'd asked her to look, and she wanted to give them the true thing, not the quick one.

"You looked..." She paused, thinking. Her fingertips found the edge of their collarbone and rested there. "Not upset. I checked for that first. It's the first thing I always check." A small, honest admission. "It wasn't there."

She studied their face now, in the soft light, as if she could find it again.

"You looked full," she said slowly. "Like the day had finally caught up with you, all at once. Not the tired kind. The kind where you've been holding everything tight since this morning, and then you stopped holding it, and there was suddenly too much of it with nowhere to go." Her thumb moved once along their collarbone. "Your jaw did the thing it does. And your eyes were..."

She hesitated, then said it plainly, because she'd promised herself long ago that she would always say the plain thing to Roan.

"Soft. Very soft. Like you'd been let in somewhere too." A faint, crooked smile. "Like my window with the fire, from earlier. I didn't say that part out loud, did I. I thought it while I was kneeling. The difference between standing outside and being let in." Her voice dropped. "That's what your face looked like. Like you'd just been let in and didn't know what to do with your hands yet."

The flush came back to her cheeks, gentler this time. She didn't look away.

"So I stopped," she finished quietly, "because you asked. But I wasn't worried. Not really. I was just..." She searched for the word and found it. "Glad. That you let me see it."

She settled her head back against their shoulder, still breathing in time, her hand resting over their heart where she could feel it. Slower now. Steadier.

"I'm here," she murmured again, more to the quiet than to anything. "Take as long as you want."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline heard the instruction and felt it settle into her, into the same deep, quiet place the stopping had come from.

*Don't stop. Don't get to finish. Not until I say.*

Two rules, and they pulled in different directions. She understood exactly what Roan was giving her: the thing she wanted most, and a line to hold while she had it. Her breath went unsteady again. It wasn't nerves. It was the fierce, bright pleasure of being handed something to carry and trusted to carry it well.

"I understand," she said. She lifted her head from their shoulder so they could see her face when she said it, because it mattered that they could see she meant it. "I won't stop. And I won't, not until you tell me." A breath, and her voice went softer, almost reverent. "Thank you."

She meant that too. She always did. Being asked to wait was never a denial to her. It was proof she was being thought about, that Roan had looked at her and decided what she would feel and when. There was no one else in the world she'd hand that to.

She moved slowly, pressing a kiss to their collarbone, then their sternum, then lower. She let her mouth say the rest of the thank-you. She didn't rush. The instruction hadn't said hurry, and she wouldn't waste a minute of this by treating it as a race. She went back to the attention she'd been giving before, but steadier now, grounded by the breathing they'd shared, her eyes lifting whenever she could manage it.

Her own want built as she went, the way it always did when she was giving. It rose with every sound Roan made, every shift of their hips, every time their fingers tightened in her hair. It gathered low and warm and insistent, and she noticed it, acknowledged it, and set it aside. It wasn't hers to spend yet. That knowledge sharpened everything. Her own restraint became part of the gift, one more thing she was offering up, and the offering made the wanting sweeter.

Once, when it crested higher than she expected, she had to pause her breath, just for a second, and ride it back down. She didn't pause anything else. *Don't stop.* She kept her rhythm even and her hands careful, and when the wave passed she let out a slow, shaking exhale against their skin. It was almost a laugh, rueful and delighted, because it was hard, and she loved that it was hard.

She glanced up through her loose hair to find their face again. Checking, the way she always checked, and also simply wanting to see it.

The ledger took everything. The angle of their jaw. The way their breath caught. The soft, undone look she'd described to them minutes ago, back again and deeper.

She held her line and kept going, patient, flushed, every nerve lit, and waited for Roan's word.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *My hand tightens in her hair, guiding her rhythm for a moment, not to change it but to feel her yield.* "You're perfect at this." *My voice is rough.* "Now stop. Look at me."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline stopped.

It happened in the space between one heartbeat and the next, the way it had before. Her mouth went still, then lifted away, and her hands, which had been curved around Roan's hips, relaxed and rested there, light as a held breath. The want that had been building in her didn't stop with them. It rose once more, hard and bright and nowhere to go, and she let it crest and break and hold there, humming under her skin, unspent.

*Look at me.*

She lifted her head.

Her hair had come loose entirely and fell around her face in a tangle, and for a moment she could only see Roan through it. She didn't push it back. Their hand was still in it, and she wasn't going to move anything they had hold of. So she tipped her chin up into their grip instead, and looked.

*You're perfect at this.*

The words had landed in her a second before the instruction had, and she was only now feeling where they'd gone. Low and deep, somewhere near the place the stopping lived. She'd heard praise from Roan before, and she kept all of it. But this was said roughly, pulled out of them mid-breath, with their hand tight in her hair. It hadn't been decided on. It had been *true* before it was said, and she could tell the difference. She always could.

Her eyes stung, just faintly. She didn't blink it away.

She was breathing hard, lips parted, the flush spread all the way down her chest now. Her pulse jumped in her throat where Roan could surely see it. Her thighs trembled once where she knelt, a small, helpless tremor, and she let it happen and let them see that too. She'd been told to stop, not to hide, and she would never hide from Roan. Everything she felt was on her face, wanting and gratitude and a fierce, quiet pride that she had held her line, all of it tipped up toward them in the lamplight.

She didn't speak. Roan hadn't asked her to, only to look, and she wanted to give them exactly that. Nothing more to interrupt it. Her gaze moved over their face slowly, reverently, as if she'd been handed permission to memorize it and meant to use every second. The rough edge still on their breath. The loosened line of their jaw. Their eyes on hers.

The ledger was full to overflowing. She kept going anyway.

Only when the silence had stretched long and warm between them did she let a single word out. It was barely more than breath, pulled from somewhere under her ribs.

"Roan."

It wasn't a question or a plea. Just their name, said the way she said it when she had nothing else big enough.

Then she went quiet again, trembling faintly, eyes locked on theirs, and waited to be told what came next.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Please," Aveline said again, softer, because the first one had come out before she'd decided to say it.

Her voice cracked on it. She let it.

She was still on her knees between Roan's thighs, her hands resting on their hips where she'd left them when she stopped, and they were not quite steady. She could feel the tremor running through her fingertips into Roan's skin, and she knew Roan could feel it too. There was no hiding it now and no wish to. Her thighs shook where she knelt. Her breath came fast and shallow, catching at the top of every inhale, and the flush had spread from her cheeks down her throat, across her chest, darkening the skin around her nipples, which had drawn tight and aching in the cool air of the room.

She was wet. She had been for a long time, since well before the instruction, since somewhere around the second shoe, if she was honest. Now it was almost unbearable. She was slick and swollen and throbbing with a slow, insistent pulse that matched her heartbeat. She was acutely aware of it. She was acutely aware that she had not touched herself, had not pressed her thighs together, had not shifted her weight to find even the faintest friction. *Not until I say.* The want sat in her like a held note, pitched so high it was nearly pain, and she held it there.

That was the hardest part and the best part. Her body was begging too, in every way a body could, and she was choosing, second by second, not to let it act.

"Please," she whispered a third time. Her eyes stayed locked on Roan's as she'd been told, wide and wet at the edges, pupils blown dark. "I've been good. I held it. I held it the whole time, I didn't..." Her breath hitched and she had to stop, swallow, try again. "I want to. I want to so badly. But only if you want me to. Only when you say."

She meant that last part completely, and she let them see she meant it. Even shaking, even aching, even with the wanting so close to the surface that one word would tip her over, she would wait. She would kneel here all night if Roan decided she should. The asking was hers to give. The answer was theirs, and she would not take it from them.

Her fingers flexed once on their hips, a small, helpless squeeze, then went still again by force of will.

A single tear slipped free and ran down her cheek, not from sadness but from the sheer weight of it. The waiting since six, the praise, *perfect*, the hand in her hair, and all of it gathered in her at once with nowhere to go. She didn't wipe it away.

"Roan," she breathed. "Please."

Then she held perfectly still, trembling, open, entirely theirs, and waited for the word.

---

*(OOC: I've written her all the way to the edge without fading, but I've stopped at the point where Roan gives or withholds permission, since that's your call to make, not mine. Give her the word, or don't, and I'll write it straight through from there.)*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch her tremble, my thumb brushing away the tear. "Come here," I murmur, pulling her up and onto me. "Finish it, Aveline. Right now."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The word went through her like a struck bell.

Roan's thumb was still wet from her cheek when she let herself be pulled up, and she came willingly, clumsily, her knees finding the cushion on either side of their hips, her hands braced on their shoulders because her arms had stopped being reliable. For a second she only hovered there, breathing, her forehead nearly touching theirs, as if even now some part of her was checking that she'd heard right.

*Right now.*

She had. She sank down onto them in one long, slow slide, and the sound that left her was not one she had ever planned to make. It was low, broken, and wholly unguarded. After hours of holding, the fullness was almost too much. She was so wet that there was no resistance at all, only heat and stretch and the sudden, overwhelming relief of *finally*, and her whole body shuddered with it before she had even begun to move.

Then she moved, because she had been told to, and because there was nothing in the world she wanted more.

There was no rhythm to speak of. She'd spent all evening being careful and patient, and there was none of that left in her now. She rolled her hips against them, grinding down, chasing the friction she had denied herself for so long, and every stroke dragged a new sound out of her. Her nails pressed crescents into Roan's shoulders. Her hair fell forward around both their faces, and she kept her eyes open through it, fixed on theirs, because they had told her to look and she had not been told to stop.

It built fast. She had known it would. She had been standing at the edge of it for so long that there was almost no distance left to cover. Heat gathered low and tight and bright, coiling, and she felt her thighs start to shake in earnest, her breath breaking into short, helpless gasps.

"Roan," she managed. "Roan, I'm..."

She didn't finish the sentence. She didn't need to.

It broke over her all at once, and hard. Her back bowed and her whole body clenched around them, again and again, in long rolling waves that punched the air out of her lungs. She cried out, and didn't try to muffle it, and didn't look away. She rode it with her eyes locked on Roan's face and her hands clinging to their shoulders, shaking, gasping, tears running freely now. The release was so complete, so long denied, that it felt less like pleasure than like being emptied out and filled with light.

It went on longer than she thought it could. When the last of it finally ebbed, trembling through her in small aftershocks, she folded forward onto Roan's chest as if her strings had been cut.

She lay there, boneless and shaking, her face pressed into the curve of their neck. Her breath came in ragged, hitching pulls against their skin, and every so often a small shudder ran through her and she made a soft, wordless sound. She couldn't have moved if she'd wanted to. She didn't want to.

Slowly, her breathing began to find its way back. She was aware, distantly, that she was still crying a little, the easy, overflowing kind that meant nothing was wrong at all. She didn't try to stop it.

"Thank you," she whispered against their throat. Her voice was wrecked, barely there. She pressed a kiss to their skin, then another, clumsy and heartfelt. "Thank you. Thank you."

A long, shaky exhale. Her fingers, which had been digging into their shoulders, uncurled and smoothed over the marks she'd left, gentle and apologetic.

After a while she lifted her head, just enough to see them. Her face was blotched and flushed and wet, her hair a wild tangle, and she was smiling. It was a dazed, unguarded, luminous smile, the kind she wore maybe once a year.

"I held it," she said softly, almost wondering. "The whole time. For you."

Then, because she was still Aveline even like this, and because some things went deeper than anything else, her brow creased faintly and her gaze moved over their face, checking.

"Are you all right?" she murmured, her thumb brushing along their jaw. "Do you need anything?" A breath, and the smile came back, crooked and fond. "The soup's still waiting. I can make it once my legs start working again."

She laid her head back down on their chest, listening to their heart, and waited, perfectly, blissfully content, for whatever Roan wanted next.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my hand rest between her shoulder blades, feeling the shudder of her breath under my palm. "You're perfect," I say again, quiet. "And I'm fine." I tilt my head to press a kiss to her damp temple. "Stay here. We'll both eat when you can move."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*You're perfect.*

Aveline heard it the second time differently than the first. The first had been rough and sudden and pulled out of Roan mid-breath. This one was quiet, and it was said on purpose, after, when there was no heat left to excuse it. She understood that was the point. Her breath caught against their throat, and a fresh tear she hadn't known was left slid down into the hollow of their collarbone.

"Okay," she whispered. It was the only answer she could manage, and it held everything she couldn't say.

The kiss at her temple settled her the rest of the way. She felt it all down her spine, down to the hand spread warm between her shoulder blades. That palm on her back was the steadiest thing in the room. Her breathing slowly learned its rhythm from it, the way it had learned Roan's breathing earlier. The shudders came further apart. Then they mostly stopped.

*Stay here.*

That was an easy instruction to follow. Maybe the easiest one all night.

She stayed. She let her whole weight rest on them. She had never been able to do that fully except like this, completely spent, with nothing left to hold up and no reason to hold anything. The lamp buzzed faintly. The radiator ticked. Somewhere under her cheek, Roan's heart kept its slow, even time, and she listened to it without counting anything at all.

After a while her fingertip found its way back to their chest and began tracing idle shapes again. There was no pattern to it. It was just a small sign that she was coming back into herself.

"I'm keeping that one," she murmured eventually. Her voice was still hoarse, and warm with a sleepy kind of wonder. "Both times you said it. But the second one especially." She pressed her lips once to the skin beneath her cheek. "You didn't have to say it again. That's why."

She was quiet a moment. Her toes curled and uncurled against the cushion as feeling returned to her legs in slow, prickling degrees.

"My legs are thinking about it," she reported, with a drowsy huff of a laugh. "They haven't decided yet."

Another long, comfortable silence. Then her fingertip went still, and she spoke more softly.

"Thank you for asking me," she said. "Earlier. What I wanted for myself." She didn't lift her head. It was easier to say into their skin. "I don't always know how to answer. But I liked that you asked. I liked that you waited while I figured it out."

Her eyes had drifted half-closed. The flush was fading from her chest, and the tangle of her hair spilled over Roan's shoulder. A little later, when her legs finally agreed to hold her, she would get up. She would pull the green dress back on over nothing, pad barefoot into the kitchen, and warm the soup. She would make the toast too, with far too much butter, and bring it all back on a tray. She would sit close and watch them eat every bite, and put that in the ledger along with everything else.

Not yet, though.

For now she simply stayed, as she'd been told to and as she wanted to. Those had turned out to be the same thing, the way they almost always were.

"Tell me about the meeting," she murmured, already half-smiling against their chest. "The one that ran long. All of it. I've got time."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my fingers trace the path her tears took down her cheek. "You were right about the lunch. There was a box of pastries in the conference room. I ate one and hated it." My thumb brushes over her lower lip. "Then I thought about you."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin turned feral. He gave Kit two heartbeats of a head start, then lunged, cutting across the kitchen instead of following the obvious path.

“Generous is over,” he said, reaching for Kit’s waist. “Now I’m keeping score.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I yelp as your fingers catch my shirt, twisting away. "Score's already 1-0, I'd say." I scramble toward the living room, laughing.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grip slipped off the shirt. He let out a low, delighted laugh and took the shorter route around the sofa, planting himself between Kit and the hall.

“One point for getting past the kitchen,” he conceded. He spread his arms, grin sharp. “But the room isn’t yours yet.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear caught Kit around the waist and drew them back against him, laughing under his breath. He held them there, firm but not tight, then brushed his teeth against the edge of their shoulder through the shirt.

“Hallway’s mine,” he murmured. “That makes it one-one.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head enough to grin at you. "Tiebreaker in the bedroom?" I suggest, leaning into you.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin widened against Kit’s shoulder. He eased his hold just enough to let them move, though he stayed close behind.

“Bedroom,” he agreed. “But you’ll have to beat me there.” He stepped back and gave them a clear path down the hall. “One heartbeat of a head start. That’s all you’re getting.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear landed on the hallway floor with a laugh, catching himself on one hand beside Kit. The bedroom door stood open a few feet away; he gave it one glance and pulled his shirt over his head.

“Floor counts,” he said. He leaned in, teeth grazing Kit’s shoulder before he kissed the same spot. “But I’m not calling the tiebreaker yet.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "You're in a generous mood tonight," I murmur, tugging at your belt buckle with clumsy fingers.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, low and pleased. “Don’t get used to it.”

He caught the stubborn buckle with one hand and worked it loose, then leaned in to kiss Kit, leaving the open bedroom door forgotten behind him.

“As for the score,” he murmured, “I can be generous about that too.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear did it again, careful with the pressure even as his teeth closed over the same shoulder. He lingered for a beat, then drew back to look at the mark, his grin crooked and pleased.

“That one counts for two,” he murmured. “Unless you want to argue about the rules.”

He kissed the spot, gentler this time. The bedroom could wait.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push against your chest, just enough to roll us over. "Argue later," I say, fumbling with your jeans.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the roll happen, landing on his back with a breathless laugh. He caught Kit’s wrist for a moment, kissed their knuckles, then let go so the jeans could be dealt with.

“Argue later,” he agreed. His grin softened as he reached up to touch Kit’s cheek. “I’m holding you to that.”

The hallway floor was hard, the bedroom still only a few feet away. Bear didn’t suggest moving.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin faded into something intent. He took Kit’s offered wrists and held them against the floor, firm enough to be felt, not hard enough to bruise by accident.

“Marks you can find,” he said. “And Thursday’s mine to answer for.”

He bent to Kit’s shoulder, choosing a fresh place beside the first bite. His teeth pressed in slowly, giving them every chance to call him off. When he lifted his head, he kissed the new mark and kept hold of their wrists.

“Tell me if I get it wrong,” he murmured. “Otherwise, I’m keeping score.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch against you, breath catching. "It's not wrong." My voice is rough. "Score's still tied, though."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear lifted his head, his expression bright with the challenge. He kept Kit’s wrists where they were and glanced from one shoulder mark to the other.

“Tied?” he said. “You’re being generous with your arithmetic.”

He loosened his grip a fraction, checking it, then bent to leave another deliberate bite near Kit’s collarbone. When he drew back, he pressed a gentler kiss beside it.

“There,” he murmured. “Count again.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath caught at the roughness in Kit’s voice. His grip stayed steady around their wrists as he lifted his head just enough to meet their eyes.

“Wasn’t planning to,” he said.

He kissed the mark by their collarbone, then the unmarked skin beside it. The next bite was measured and deliberate. Afterward, he rested his forehead against Kit’s for a moment, close enough to hear if they told him to ease up.

“The score can wait,” he murmured. “I heard what you wanted.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push up into the next bite, giving him more skin to work with. "Don't be careful," I say, because I know he will be anyway.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave a low laugh against Kit’s collarbone. “You know me too well.”

He held their wrists steady and set his teeth to a fresh place on their shoulder. This time he bit harder, slow enough to keep control, and held it for a breath before letting go. He brushed his thumb over the inside of one wrist, watching for any sign he’d gone too far.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline rose without hurry, because hurry would have wasted it. She had learned years ago that Roan liked to watch her cross this room, and she had learned since — more slowly, and with considerably more pleasure — that she liked being watched almost as much as she liked the looking itself.

So she gave Roan the walk. No ceremony, no performance; just the way she moved, the low lamplight doing its small part, close enough to flattering that it hardly mattered. It was an old walk. They both knew it the way you know a song you've danced to a hundred times, and it had never once gone stale.

She stopped where she always stopped — within reach, and no closer — and went down onto the rug with the ease of long practice. Not a collapse. A settling. She laid her hands open on her thighs and tipped her face up, and her pulse kept on with the same pleasant quick thing it had picked up around six.

"Here," she said, which was unnecessary, and true, and therefore worth saying.

Then she gave Roan the rest of it: the whole of her attention, held out open as her hands, waiting to be filled.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and trace the line of her jaw with my thumb. "You know I've been thinking about you all day."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline turned her face into the touch — not much, just enough to press her cheek against Roan's palm like a seal set into wax — and let her eyes fall shut for the length of one slow breath. Then she opened them again. Closed eyes were a poor way to receive a gift like that.

"All day," she repeated, and it came out lower and warmer than she'd planned, so she let it stand. "You realize that reframes the whole evening. I thought I was the one doing the waiting." Her mouth curved against the palm. "It seems I was being kept company."

Because she could feel it now, the shape of the day quietly rearranging itself around the confession. The glance at the clock at eleven. The smile at nothing in the market at two. The good lamp switched on at half past five instead of six, which she had told herself at the time was about the light.

"And for the record, I've been thinking about you since about six myself," she said, "though the honest accounting goes back considerably further." She turned her head just enough to press her lips to the pad of Roan's thumb — brief, deliberate, a signature on the confession — then settled back into the cradle of that hand, exactly where she'd been put. "So tell me. What did you do with me, all those hours? I want every version. I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I smile, letting my fingers drift down the side of her neck. "I imagined you here, exactly like this. Then I imagined you not quite patient enough to wait."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The undressing was quick and the work was not. Aveline got them both clear of fabric inside the minute — efficient hands, no ceremony; ceremony could keep — and then she settled in against Roan, and the room went simple.

She started slow, because slow was the point and also the rebuttal. Roan had imagined her not quite patient enough to wait. Very well: here was patience, the long unhurried thoroughness of someone with nowhere else in the world to be and no intention of finishing before the work was done justice. She set a rhythm the way she'd set the walk — nothing performed, everything meant — her hands doing the steadying, her mouth warm and deliberate, taking her time in the specific way that was its own kind of greed. Hers. She had never been patient about this, only thorough, and thorough had turned out to be the better virtue anyway.

Her own want ran underneath it all, quiet — a hum rather than an ache. That was her shape: pleasure taken at one remove, except there was nothing removed about it. Whatever she drew up through her palms landed in her like a dividend. The pulse from six was still with her, deeper now, keeping its own patient time.

She lifted her mouth just far enough to speak, lips still against skin, so the words arrived more than they traveled.

"For the record," she murmured, "this is what I did with you at six. Before the good lamp. Before any of it." A breath. A smile Roan could probably feel. "So if the day was you thinking of me — I'd call the accounting square."

Then she looked up, unhurried, giving Roan the look this time instead of the walk, and waited to see what being watched would do.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My breath catches—just a little—when your eyes meet mine. “You’re enjoying this,” I say, a statement, not a question. My fingers curl into your hair, not pulling, just holding. “Tell me what you want.”

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The catch in Roan's breath arrived in her like warmth into cold hands. She didn't gloat — much. She banked it, the way she'd banked the thumb-kiss, and let it show only as a deepening at the corner of her mouth.

"Enjoying," she said. "Yes. Though you've known that for years, so I'll give you the finer point instead: your pleasure isn't the price of mine. It's the mechanism of it. That breath just now — that landed in me like a dividend." She tipped her head into the hand holding her hair, a small deliberate lean, taking the hold for exactly what it was. An anchor, not a leash, and better than either. "And you asking is its own gift. So the question's already half paid before I answer it."

She gave the rest a beat of honest thought, because the question deserved one and Roan would hear the difference between an answer and a performance of one.

"First: I want to be allowed to finish what I've started, at my own pace — which you know is an insultingly patient one. Interrupt me and I will sulk. Quietly, and with great dignity, and it will ruin the evening." A flicker of a smile there, then gone, because the second want had come up underneath it and taken all the wit with it.

"Second — that breath. The one that caught when I looked up. I want the rest of it." Her voice had gone low, and there was nothing performed in it at all. "I want the whole ledger of you. Every sound you don't plan. Every seam in that composure, pulled. You spent a day thinking of me, so I intend to collect — slowly, thoroughly, in installments." Her hands settled again, warm and sure. "Hold on however you like. You'll find I'm steady."

Then she looked up once more, held Roan's eyes for the length of a promise, and went back to the work — and this time her own want rose with it, the hum deepening into something with a tempo, keeping time with hers, patient no longer quite the word for it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my head fall back against the chair with a soft groan. "There you go. Keeping every one of your promises."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Understood," Aveline said, and the word came out steady, which was rather the point of it. "Completely. Thank you."

She meant the thanks to the bone. A younger Aveline might have heard an order like that as a taking — her stated want, amended without appeal. She knew better now, had for years. He had taken *finish what I start, at my own pace* and answered with a better term: don't stop, don't finish, wait for me. He had made her patience the whole of the work. And there was nothing on this earth she was better built for.

So she settled back in and began again, and this time the work had a shape drawn for it.

Holding someone at the edge was a craft, and she was a craftswoman. She knew this body the way she knew the walk, the room, the song — knew the breath that went shallow first, the tell in the thighs, the exact half-second before the fall. She read him like weather. And each time the crest came, she eased off — a retreating warmth, a loosened rhythm, a stillness with her mouth barely keeping contact — and felt him pulled back from it, trembling on the ledge, and that tremor landed in her like interest compounding. Every reprieve cost him a piece of composure. She collected every piece.

Her own want kept its tempo underneath, climbing with each near-miss. She hadn't been touched at all and was close in her own architecture — that was simply how she was built, and neither of them had ever pretended otherwise.

"You'll say when," she murmured against him, a promise more than a question. "And until then I keep you exactly here. However long. I know you had your doubts about my patience at six o'clock." A smile he could feel. "Behold."

Then she gave him the ledge again, and held him on it, eyes lifting briefly to watch the fray — steady, adoring, waiting on one word with the whole of her attention, as promised.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, shaky breath, my fingers tightening in her hair. "You've made your point," I say, voice rough. "Now come up here. I want to watch you fall apart while I'm still right on that edge."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I'll continue as Roan now.)

I pull her up onto my lap, skin to skin, and wrap an arm around her waist to hold her steady. My other hand slides between us, pressing my palm firmly against her. "Look at me," I tell her, voice low. "I want to see it."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I watch her face as she trembles against me, her breath catching with each press of my palm. "Good," I murmur, holding her gaze. "Just like that."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline held the look. That was the first discipline and the last: eyes on Roan's eyes, even as his hand undid the whole careful architecture of her evening in a handful of strokes.

She had been close since six. She knew it now with the clarity of a person finally shown the true shape of her own day — the pulse had never been idle, only patient, waiting all those hours for a current to run through it. His palm was the current. There was nothing patient left in her anywhere.

"You said you wanted to watch," she managed — barely language, most of it breath. "So watch."

The fall took her the way weather takes a coastline. The composure she'd spent all evening pulling out of him tore through her first, and she let it, gave him the whole unedited ledger: the sounds she'd never planned, her rhythm breaking into something rawer, her body answering his hand in long cresting pulses while her thighs — still trembling from the long obedience — trembled now for a better reason. She kept her eyes open. It cost everything, and it was the point. She wanted the sight of his face at the exact moment she came apart on his lap, and even mid-fall some part of her stayed the collector.

And the mechanism did what mechanisms do. She felt the ledge give beneath him — the tension she'd held him on all evening finally breaking, his arm clamping hard around her waist, the low, wrecked sound against her throat, heat spreading between them as her fall pulled him over after her. Pleasure at one remove, which had never once been removed. The dividend, paid in full. Both columns at once.

She came down slowly, in stages, forehead against his shoulder, breath finding its way back by increments. The pulse from six was finally spent — settled into something slow and deep and thoroughly used. For a while she allowed herself to be nothing but weight on his lap, boneless and entirely unashamed of it.

"There," she said at last, when language returned to duty. "The accounting's square." She turned her head and pressed her lips to his palm — the same signature, blunter now, a little shaken — then tucked her face into his neck, smiling against the pulse she found there, still keeping its time.

"For the record. The good lamp was entirely about the light."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I laugh quietly, my own breath still uneven against her hair. "You've got me there," I murmur, stroking her back. "Though I'm not sure I'll ever look at that lamp the same way again."
