dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear met the hard kiss with a low sound, his hands tightening at Kit’s hips without trying to break the pin. When he finally turned his face away, he stayed close, breath warm against Kit’s cheek.

“No,” he said, voice rough but softened at the edges. “It’s not.”

His thumb brushed lightly over the mark he’d left on Kit’s shoulder, careful now. Then he looked up at them, the grin returning—smaller, fond, still full of trouble.

“But I’m still keeping score.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin faded into something more intent. He gathered Kit’s wrists in one hand, holding them firmly without wrenching them, and looked up to meet their eyes.

“Thursday,” he said, voice low. “I heard you.”

His thumb traced once over their pulse, a brief check-in before he leaned close. He chose the already-marked shoulder, set his teeth beside the first bite, and pressed down slowly—hard enough to leave a promise, not careless enough to make one he couldn’t keep.

When he eased off, he kept Kit’s wrists secure and watched their face. “That still good?” he asked, rough and steady.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, nodding. "Yeah. It's good." I flex my wrists lightly against his grip. "Keep going."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s gaze stayed on Kit’s face for another beat, taking the answer seriously. Then his grip eased just enough to shift their wrists comfortably in his hand.

“Good,” he murmured.

He bent to the shoulder again, choosing a fresh patch beside the marks already blooming there. His mouth brushed over the skin first, a brief warning; then his teeth closed down, firm and deliberate. He held the bite, then let go slowly, smoothing his thumb over the edges without dulling the sting.

“Thursday,” Bear reminded them, voice rough with satisfaction. He looked up, checking their expression before lowering his mouth to place another measured bite nearby. “You’ll know exactly where I was.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s expression tightened with focus. “I heard you.”

He kept Kit’s wrists gathered securely in one hand, then bent to the shoulder again. He chose the skin beside the earlier marks and pressed his mouth there first, taking a moment before his teeth closed—firm, measured, held long enough to leave a darkening print. When he released, his thumb passed over the spot, gentler than his bite.

He moved to another patch nearby and did it again, unhurried now, giving each mark its own careful attention. His breathing stayed rough; his grip stayed steady. Between bites, he brushed a kiss over the sore places, then returned to the work with renewed intent.

“Still with me?” he asked quietly, lifting his head to check Kit’s face. He waited a beat, then lowered his mouth again, keeping his teeth to the shoulder and the sturdy slope above it. “Good,” he murmured against their skin. “Then I’m not stopping.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my forehead against his shoulder, breathing him in. "Still with you." I arch into the next bite, a shiver running down my spine. "Always."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still for a beat at the word, his breath warming Kit’s skin. His hold on their wrists softened—not letting go, only loosening enough to keep the pressure easy—and he pressed a steady kiss to the unmarked edge of their shoulder.

“Always,” he echoed, quieter now.

Then he set his teeth down again, deliberate and firm, holding the bite until the skin beneath his mouth began to flush. He released slowly, smoothing a thumb beside the mark before placing another just below it. His attention stayed close and intent, each bite measured, each pause long enough to make sure Kit was still with him.

When he lifted his head, his grin had gone crooked and tender. “I’ve got you,” he murmured, and bent back to Kit’s shoulder.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my face to his, catching his mouth in a slow, deep kiss. "I know," I murmur against his lips. "That's why I'm here."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear kissed them back slowly, the sharpness of the chase settling into something deeper. His hand opened around their wrists, easing them free, and came to rest warm at the side of their neck.

“I know,” he murmured against their mouth. “And I’m glad you are.”

He lingered in the kiss, then brushed his lips over the marks on their shoulder, careful around the tender places. A softer kiss landed beside them; his teeth followed, measured and deliberate, adding one more dark promise to the pattern.

When he lifted his head, his thumb traced gently along their jaw. “Still with me?” he asked, quiet and steady, eyes searching their face.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I nod, turning my head to press my cheek against his palm. "Still with you." I guide his hand back to my hip, my fingers closing over his. "Now shut up and keep going."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: His teeth grazed the spot he’d nipped before, a teasing promise rather than a bite.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The hallway gave way to the floor in a tangle of hastily abandoned clothes

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Now we’re both keeping score.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: “That still good?” he asked, rough and steady.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: keeping his teeth to the shoulder and the sturdy slope above it

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave Kit exactly one heartbeat of head start. Then the generosity was gone.

He came off the counter in a single push. His socks skidded on the tile before they caught, and he was through the doorway fast enough that his shoulder clipped the frame hard. That would be a bruise by morning, and he'd blame Kit for it cheerfully. The hallway was dark except for the lamp they'd left on in the living room. It threw one long stripe of yellow across the floorboards, and Bear saw Kit's shadow cut through it and vanish around the corner.

He didn't follow the shadow. Eight years had taught him Kit's habits, and one of them was always going for the long way around the couch.

So Bear went the short way. He vaulted the armrest instead of rounding it, landed heavier than he'd meant to, and sent a throw pillow cartwheeling onto the floor. He came up already turning. He was grinning with too many teeth, and his breath was loud in the quiet room.

"You said don't be generous," he called, low and pleased, moving to cut off the gap between the bookshelf and the hallway to the bedroom. His hands hung loose at his sides, fingers flexing. "So I'm not."

He stopped in the middle of the rug, weight on the balls of his feet, and listened. He heard the fridge hum and the old radiator tick. Somewhere to his left, a floorboard gave a small creak under someone trying very hard not to make one.

Bear's head turned slowly toward the sound.

"There you are," he said. He didn't lunge. Not yet. He took one deliberate step, then another, letting Kit hear every one of them come closer, his broad frame blocking out the lamplight behind him.

"Last chance to run somewhere smarter, sweetheart."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I feel myself grin, pressed flat against the wall behind the armchair. "You're giving me advice now?" I shift my weight, ready to spring. "That's generous."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear stopped dead.

For a second the only sound was the radiator ticking and his own breath, slow and heavy through his nose. Then he laughed, a short, delighted bark that came up from somewhere low in his chest.

"Oh, that's *mean*," he said, and he sounded thrilled about it. "Throwing my own words back at me. You've been saving that one."

He didn't move right away. That was the trick of it, and they both knew it. Eight years of this had taught Bear that Kit was fastest in the half-second after he committed, so he didn't commit. He shifted his weight instead, left and then right, like a big dog deciding which side of the fence to test. The armchair sat between them, squat and ugly. They'd inherited it from Kit's aunt and never had the heart to get rid of it, and now Bear eyed it like it had personally betrayed him.

"Fine," he said. "No advice. No generosity. No more *anything* nice."

He reached out, slow and casual, and set one broad hand on the back of the armchair. His fingers spread over the worn upholstery. Then he leaned. It was just a little of his weight, enough that the old frame groaned and the chair legs scraped an inch across the floorboards toward the wall. That narrowed the gap on the bookshelf side and left the other side wide open. It was too obvious. It was *meant* to look too obvious.

"Go on," Bear murmured. He tilted his head, and the lamplight caught the edge of his grin and the bruise already coming up dusky along his shoulder where the doorframe had clipped him. "I can hear you thinking. You're wondering if I left that side open on purpose."

He drummed his fingers once on the chair back. It sounded loud in the quiet.

"I did," he said. "Question is whether I'm faster than you getting there."

He waited, still leaning, still grinning, every muscle wound tight under that easy posture.

"Count of three, sweetheart. One—"

He didn't bother with two.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear hit the hallway half a stride behind and closed the rest in two. He caught Kit around the middle with one arm, and the momentum carried them both into the wall. His free hand slapped flat against the plaster beside Kit's head to take the worst of it. A picture frame rattled on its nail. Somewhere behind them the throw pillow was still lying face-down on the rug where it had landed.

He'd braced for the fight. Elbows, the twist-and-drop Kit had perfected sometime around year three, a heel aimed at his instep. He had his weight set for all of it.

None of it came.

Bear went still. He was breathing hard, his chest pressed to Kit's back, and for a second he didn't do anything but *feel* it: warm and loose and barely pulling against his arm at all.

"Huh," he said, low, right against Kit's ear.

He shifted just enough to see Kit's face in the thin stripe of lamplight that reached the hall. It was a quick look but a real one, eight years of habit checking what the rules didn't make him ask out loud. What he found there made the grin come back slow and wide.

"That's it?" he rumbled. "All that trash talk, and you just *let* me have you?" He clicked his tongue, mock-offended, and tightened his arm, drawing Kit back flush against him. "Sweetheart. I vaulted the couch. I hit the doorframe. I'm going to have a bruise the size of a fist, and you didn't even make me *work* for the last ten feet."

He ducked his head. His stubble scraped the side of Kit's neck, then the slope where it met the shoulder, and he lingered there. It wasn't a bite yet, just the promise of one, his breath hot, his teeth barely grazing skin.

"I'm keeping score," he murmured. "You know I am."

Then he bit down. Not hard, not yet, just enough to leave a mark that would be there tomorrow, somewhere a collar wouldn't quite cover. He held it a moment, felt the pulse jump under his mouth, and let go with a satisfied hum.

"That's for the doorframe."

He didn't loosen his grip. If anything he settled in heavier, one hand still braced on the wall, the other spread wide and possessive over Kit's stomach.

"Now," Bear said, and his voice had dropped into that pleased, dangerous register Kit knew too well. "You want to tell me what you're up to? Because you're never this easy." He nosed at the fresh mark, gentle, almost sweet. "Either you're tired, or you're plotting something. And you don't look tired."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to catch his eye. "Maybe I just like the view from here." I press back against him, making my intentions very clear. "Take the hint."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed. It started low and came out soft against Kit's neck, warm air over the fresh mark.

"Oh, I got the hint," he said. "I got it the second you stopped running."

He didn't move right away. That was the other trick, the one Kit had never once managed to be patient about, and Bear knew it. He stayed exactly where he was, heavy and warm and pinning, and let the moment stretch out in the dark hallway until the radiator had ticked three more times.

Then he turned Kit around.

He did it in one easy motion, a hand on the hip and a shift of his weight, and Kit's back met the wall with a soft thump. The picture frame rattled again. Bear braced a forearm above Kit's head and leaned in until there was no lamplight left between them at all. His breathing still hadn't settled from the chase. Up close he smelled like the kitchen, coffee and the garlic he'd been chopping before any of this started, and underneath that just *him*.

"Liking the view," he repeated, looking down at Kit with his eyes half-lidded and dark. "You know what I think? I think you got bored of losing, so you decided to lose on purpose. Take the credit for it." His free hand came up and his thumb dragged slowly along Kit's jaw, tipping it up. "Very clever. Very sneaky. I respect it."

He kissed Kit then, not gently. It was the kind of kiss that had eight years of practice behind it, deep and certain and a little rough. His stubble scraped and he caught Kit's lower lip between his teeth at the end, just long enough to make a point, before he let go.

"Still counts as my point, though," he murmured against Kit's mouth.

And then he bent, hooked an arm behind Kit's knees, and hauled Kit up off the floor. He grunted at the weight and made a show of it, staggering half a step so his bruised shoulder hit the wall and he could hiss about it.

"*Ow.* That's two you owe me," he said, grinning, already turning toward the bedroom. The hallway floorboards creaked under both of them. He didn't bother being quiet anymore. "And I'm collecting interest."

He shouldered the bedroom door open. It bounced off the doorstop, and behind them the lamp kept burning in the empty living room, one yellow stripe falling across a throw pillow nobody was going to pick up until morning.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear got maybe three steps past the doorframe before Kit's hands found the hem of his shirt and yanked. He decided the bed was overrated.

He went down to his knees on the bedroom rug, which was old and thin and not at all built for this, and brought Kit down with him. It wasn't graceful. His knee found the one spot where the floorboard underneath had a nail head sitting just a little proud, and he swore about it into Kit's collarbone and didn't stop.

The shirt came off badly. It caught on his ears, then his chin, and for two long, undignified seconds Bear was blind and laughing inside a tangle of cotton with his elbows stuck up in the air.

"Don't," he warned, muffled. "Don't you *dare* take advantage of this."

He wrestled free and flung the shirt somewhere toward the dresser. It hit the lamp in there instead. The lamp wobbled and didn't fall, and he chose to count that as a win. His hair was standing up in about four directions. He didn't care. Kit's buttons were next, and Bear had never once in eight years had the patience for buttons. He got two undone like a reasonable person, gave up on the third, and got a sharp look for it that he returned with a completely unrepentant grin.

"Add it to my tab," he said, and bent to set his teeth against the spot just under Kit's ribs, the one that always got a reaction.

After that, the scorekeeping got hard to track.

---

Some time later, the rug was even more rumpled than before. Bear lay flat on his back on it, one arm thrown over his eyes, his chest still heaving. A sock hung off one foot by the toes. He had no idea where the other one had gone.

"I think," he said to the ceiling, hoarse and very satisfied, "there's a nail in my spine."

He lifted his arm and squinted sideways at Kit in the thin light from the hall. His gaze drifted down and lingered on the marks he'd left. There was the one at the neck from the hallway, and a couple of newer ones he was privately proud of. Then he looked down at himself. There was a good crescent near his hip that stung when he breathed too deep, and the doorframe bruise on his shoulder had gone properly purple.

He counted, slowly and deliberately, and made a show of moving his lips.

"Okay," Bear said at last. "I've done the math. I'm calling it even." He paused. "That's a lie. I'm up by one. But I'm feeling..."

He stopped himself and cracked one eye fully open. The grin was coming back.

"No. Not generous. We covered that." He reached over blindly and hooked a heavy hand around Kit's ankle. It wasn't pulling, just holding on, his thumb moving idly over the bone. "The pan's still on the stove, by the way. With the garlic. I was halfway through dinner when you decided to be a menace."

The radiator ticked. Out in the living room, the lamp kept burning over the fallen pillow.

"So," he rumbled. "Do I get up and cook, or do you want to try for a rematch first?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shove his leg with my foot, not moving from my spot on the floor. "Rematch. Obviously." I turn my head to look at him. "The garlic can burn."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move for a second. He lay there with Kit's foot still resting against his shin and looked over like Kit had just said something deeply romantic.

"The garlic can *burn*," he repeated, reverent. "Eight years, and you still find new ways to make me feel things."

Then, because he was forty and not an idiot, he added, "I turned the burner off. Before. When you first walked in with that look." He tapped his temple with two fingers. "Some of us plan ahead."

He sat up slowly. His spine cracked in two places and he winced theatrically. He peeled the last sock off his toes and flung it over his shoulder without looking. Somewhere behind him it landed with a soft pat. His hand stayed wrapped around Kit's ankle the whole time, thumb still moving over the bone, lazy and warm.

Then his grip tightened.

It wasn't hard, just enough to be a fact. Bear's grin crept back, slow, showing teeth.

"Here's the thing about rematches, sweetheart," he said, low. "You don't get a head start on a rematch. You're already caught." He gave the ankle the smallest tug, testing, sliding Kit maybe an inch across the rug toward him. "So if you want to make me work for it this time, you're going to have to get *out* first."

He didn't pull again. He just waited, loose-shouldered and patient, the purple bruise on his shoulder dark in the thin hallway light, the crescent on his hip shifting when he breathed. His free hand rested on his knee. It was an easy posture, and it was a lie. Kit could probably see the tension coiled through his forearm, and he wanted Kit to see it.

"And you're not letting me win this one," he added. His eyes narrowed with pure, delighted suspicion. "I mean it. I want the elbows. I want the thing you do with your heel. If you go soft on me again I'm going to be *insulted*."

The radiator ticked once. Out in the living room, the lamp still burned.

Bear leaned in, just slightly, weight shifting forward onto his free hand.

"Go on, then," he rumbled. "Show me what you were saving."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The first bite had been a statement. The second one was a conversation.

Bear heard it, *again*, rough and certain, and something in his chest went hot and bright. He didn't answer with words. He shifted his grip, one broad hand spread across Kit's back and the other fisted in the rug beside Kit's head, and he took his time finding the spot. It was a little lower than the first, where the muscle was thicker and could take it. He set his teeth there slowly, so Kit would feel the moment coming, and then he bit down properly.

He held it. He could feel his own jaw working, the heat of skin under his mouth, the pulse hammering somewhere close. Every one of their eight years went into the pressure: exactly how hard, exactly how long, the line they'd drawn together at a kitchen table a lifetime ago and redrawn a dozen times since. He went right up to it and not one hair past.

Then he let go, breathing hard through his nose, and pressed his mouth flat and open over the mark. It wasn't an apology. It was a signature.

He lifted his head just enough for the quick, practiced look. Eyes, face, the set of Kit's shoulders. It took half a second and asked the only question that mattered. He liked what he found. The grin that followed was slow and a little wild at the edges, and his hair was still standing up in four directions.

"That one's going to *bloom*," he said. His voice had gone low and gravelly, and he sounded far too pleased with himself. His thumb traced the edge of the mark, feather-light, not quite touching the center. "Tomorrow you're going to reach for something on a high shelf and think about me."

He didn't move off. He stayed heavy and close, his breath still ragged against Kit's neck. The crescent on his hip throbbed in time with his heartbeat, and a fresh ache was blooming along his ribs where he'd definitely taken a hit during the rematch. He'd have been insulted if he hadn't.

"For the record," Bear murmured, "that's a lot of points I just gave away. Asking for it counts. You know it does." He nosed along Kit's jaw, unhurried, teeth grazing but not closing. "You're catching up, sweetheart. And I'm not sure I mind."

Out in the hall the radiator ticked. Bear's fingers flexed once against Kit's back, testing, like he was deciding something.

"So what's it going to be?" he rumbled, right against Kit's ear. "You want to even the score?"

He tipped his head to one side, deliberately. The long line of his throat was bared in the thin light. It was an offer, and also a dare.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I bite down on the offered skin just above his collarbone, hard enough to make him grunt. "Even," I say against his pulse. I feel him laugh. "Now fuck off so I can make you work for it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The grunt turned into a laugh halfway out. Bear felt it rumble up through his chest and into Kit's mouth, and for a second he just stayed there, throat bared, letting the sting settle into something warm and throbbing. Kit had bitten hard enough that he'd feel it every time he swallowed tomorrow.

*Even.* He'd allow it. For now.

"Fuck off," he repeated, delighted, and pushed himself up onto his hands. "Sweetheart, that's the nicest thing you've said to me all night."

He didn't go far. He rocked back onto his heels and knelt there on the ruined rug, the old nail still pressing into his knee, his chest rising and falling in the slice of hallway light. He touched two fingers to the fresh mark above his collarbone, pressed once, and hissed through his teeth. Then he grinned wider.

"That's good," he said, mostly to himself. "That's a *good* one."

Then he lifted both hands, palms out, and shuffled back on his knees until there was a real gap between them. There was a foot and a half of rumpled rug, then two feet. He kept going until his shoulders bumped the side of the bed frame and he couldn't go any farther.

"There," Bear said. "Clean start. No hands, no ankles." He wiggled his fingers to prove it. "You've got the door behind you and the whole house out there, and I've got a nail in my knee and a bed at my back. That's practically a handicap."

It wasn't, and they both knew it. His weight had already shifted onto the balls of his feet. His thighs were coiled under him and his fingertips rested light on the floor, the way a sprinter's might. The easy posture was the same lie it always was, and he wasn't bothering to hide it this time.

The radiator ticked. Somewhere out in the living room, the lamp still burned over that pillow.

"I'll give you to the count of five," he said, low and pleased, eyes glinting in the dark. Then he caught himself and snorted. "No. That's generous. We're not doing generous."

He tilted his head, and the new mark on his throat caught the light.

"I'll give you to *three*." His grin showed every tooth. "And sweetheart, this time I'm actually going to count to three."

He took a slow breath and let it out.

"One."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear stopped counting.

He stayed crouched against the bed frame with his mouth still shaped around *two*, and he looked at the wrists held out in the thin light. He looked at them for a long moment, and then he looked up at Kit's face.

"Thursday," he said slowly, like he was tasting it.

The sprinter's crouch went out of him. Something heavier came in to replace it, patient and very focused. He came forward on his knees across the rug, unhurried now, because there wasn't anywhere to chase to. Kit had just handed him the finish line.

He took both wrists in one hand. His fingers were broad enough to close all the way around them with room to spare, and he held them firmly, the way he'd hold something he meant to keep. His thumb found the pulse on the inside of one and pressed there, feeling it race.

"Thursday's four days," he said, low. "That's not a love bite, sweetheart. That's *work*." The quick look again, eyes and mouth and shoulders, half a second long. "You tell me if I'm going past where we drew it. You know the word. I'll hear it."

Then he bent his head and started.

He didn't rush. He'd never rushed the part that mattered. He set his mouth to the soft inside of Kit's forearm, just below the elbow where the skin was thin, and sucked a slow, deep bruise there. He pulled back only once it was dark, then set his teeth to the edge of it and closed them until he felt the tension in Kit's arm answer him. He held it, counted it out in his head, and let go.

"That's one for the mirror," he murmured against the mark.

He guided Kit's wrists up and pinned them to the rug above Kit's head, one-handed, with his weight leaning into it just enough to be a fact. His free hand slid down Kit's side, over ribs he'd already marked tonight, down to the hip. He found the curve of the thigh and dug his fingers in there, hard. That grip would leave its own shadow, four fingertips and a thumb, and he left it on purpose.

"That one's for Tuesday," he said, "when you sit down."

He moved to the shoulder next, the one he hadn't claimed yet. He found the thick muscle along the top, the spot where a bag strap would sit, and he bit down there properly. He was slow and deep, his jaw working, and he held it longer than any bite he'd given all night. He was right up against the line. He could feel exactly where it was, the way you feel the edge of a step in the dark, and he stayed a breath on the right side of it until his own heartbeat was loud in his ears.

When he lifted his head he was breathing hard, and his eyes had gone dark and wild.

"*That's* Thursday," he said roughly. "You're going to pick up your bag on Thursday and swear at me."

He didn't let go of the wrists. His thumb stroked once over the pulse point, gentle, completely at odds with the grip holding them down.

"And I'm not done," Bear rumbled. He lowered his head until his stubble dragged along Kit's jaw and his breath was hot at Kit's ear. "You asked for marks, plural. I've got a list."

His teeth grazed the spot just under the ear, not closing, just promising.

"Tell me where you want the next one," he murmured. "Or don't, and find out."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
I draw in a sharp breath. My pulse is hammering where his thumb rests. "Your choice," I tell him, voice rough. "Surprise me."

Then I shift, testing his grip, and my heel catches the back of his thigh just enough to sting.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The heel landed and Bear hissed. It was a real sound, sharp and startled, and it turned into a grin before it finished leaving his mouth.

"*There* it is," he said. He sounded like a man who'd been handed a present. "The heel. I was starting to think you'd lost it somewhere around year six."

He didn't let go of the wrists, though. Kit's shift had pulled against his grip and he'd felt it, the quick twist of tendon under his palm testing for the gap between thumb and finger. He answered the only way he knew how. He tightened his hold one notch and slid his knee in against Kit's thigh, pinning the leg that had kicked him flat to the rug. There'd be a sting on the back of his own leg for a day or two. Good. He wanted a receipt.

"Surprise you," he repeated, low. He took his time with it. His gaze moved slowly down Kit's body in the thin hallway light, over every mark already blooming, like a man reading a map he'd drawn himself. "You know that's dangerous, handing me that."

He let go of the wrists all at once.

It was deliberate, and he did it so fast there wasn't time to wonder why. Both his hands went to Kit's hips instead, broad and certain, and he flipped Kit onto one side and then face-down on the old rug in a single heave. It was graceless and effective. He grunted when his bruised shoulder protested, and he ignored it.

"You wanted the mirror," Bear murmured, settling his weight across the backs of Kit's thighs so the heel had nowhere to go. "So I'm putting one where you'll *need* the mirror to find it."

He bent down, slow. His stubble dragged along the back of Kit's neck, over the knob of the spine, and down between the shoulder blades. His breath was hot there and he kept going, lower, until his mouth found the small of Kit's back, just off to one side, above the hip, where skin was soft and nobody ever looked.

He bit there, deep and patient. He worked it with his teeth and then sucked the bruise up dark underneath, and he held on long enough that his jaw began to ache. He felt every shiver run through the body under him and he stayed a breath short of the line, the same place he always stopped.

When he lifted his head he pressed his thumb, feather-light, right beside it.

"That one you'll only see if you twist around in the bathroom tomorrow," he said, hoarse and pleased. "You'll have to go looking. And you'll know I knew you would."

The quick look came next. He leaned forward until he could see the side of Kit's face against the rug and took in the eyes, the mouth, and the breathing. It took half a second, the same as always. Whatever he found there made him laugh quietly, deep in his chest.

Then he eased his weight off Kit's legs by a deliberate inch. It was just enough room for a heel, if someone wanted to try it again.

"Go on," Bear rumbled, and the dare was right there in his voice. "You kicked me once. I felt it. I *liked* it." His fingers traced a lazy line down Kit's spine, not holding anything now, just touching. "I've got about three more on my list, sweetheart. You want to make me fight for every one of them?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop.*

Bear heard it and something in him that had been holding a careful half-inch of distance all night just let go of it.

"Wasn't planning to," he said roughly, and he didn't wait for the heel.

He slid his hand up the length of Kit's spine and fisted it in the hair at the nape. It wasn't hard, but it was firm enough that the grip meant something. He bent and put his mouth to the back of Kit's shoulder, the side that didn't have Thursday on it yet, and bit there too. This one was quicker and meaner. It wasn't a bruise he was building, it was a sting he wanted to hear, and when he got the sound he was after he growled low against the skin and did it again an inch over.

The rug had long since stopped being a rug. It was a rumpled, sliding hazard, and the nail was still in there somewhere. Bear found it again with his knee, swore, and didn't care. His breathing had gone ragged and loud in the dark room, and his heart slammed against his ribs where Kit had caught him during the rematch. Every bruise he had was talking to him at once: the shoulder, the hip, the fresh throb above his collarbone every time he swallowed. It all ran together into one bright, hot ache that felt like the best kind of proof.

He turned Kit over again because he wanted to see a face. It was clumsy and fast, and they ended up tangled against the side of the bed frame, which thudded against the wall hard enough that something on the nightstand fell over. Neither of them looked to see what it was.

Bear braced one forearm beside Kit's head and looked down. He stayed there for one long second, chest heaving and hair wrecked, the thin hallway light cutting across his face. He wasn't grinning now. It was something older than the grin and much less guarded. It was the look he only ever had right here, eight years deep, with nothing left to perform.

"There you are," he said quietly, the same words from the living room. They meant something completely different now.

Then he kissed Kit again, and the rest of it stopped being a game.

It stayed rough, because that was who they were, but it had rhythm now and weight and no hesitation in it anywhere. He kept one hand braced and used the other to hold on: to a hip, the back of a thigh, a jaw. His grip moved wherever he needed it, and every time his fingers closed he pressed just hard enough to leave another faint shadow for the mirror. He put his mouth to the side of Kit's throat, under the ear where he'd been promising all night, and he finally closed his teeth there. He held on through everything that followed, low sounds caught against skin, and he only let go when he had to breathe.

He lost count of the marks. He lost track of the radiator, the lamp, and the rest of the house. There was just heat and friction and the pull of Kit's body against his, the sting where nails dragged down his back. He meant to be proud of that later. There was the sound of his own voice going hoarse on Kit's name.

When it broke over him he didn't let go of anything. He pressed his forehead hard to Kit's temple, one hand still tangled in Kit's hair and the other clamped on Kit's hip, and he shook with it. A long, rough breath went out of him that was half laugh and half something he'd never have admitted to in daylight.

After that, for a while, there was nothing but breathing.

Bear stayed where he was, heavy and boneless, until his arms started to tremble from holding himself up. Then he rolled onto his side with a groan, dragging Kit with him so they ended up half-tangled on the ruined rug. Kit's back was against his chest and his arm was slung heavy across Kit's middle, just like in the hallway.

His thumb found the mark on Kit's shoulder. Thursday. He traced the edge of it, feather-light, not pressing.

"Hey," he murmured into Kit's hair. His voice was wrecked. He gave the quick look again, but slower now, leaning up on one elbow to see Kit's face properly. He didn't need to check the rules. He just wanted to see Kit. "You good?"

He waited for the answer. Then he let his head drop back onto the rug with a thud, stared up at the ceiling, and started to laugh quietly, helplessly, until his bruised ribs made him stop.

"I've got a nail in my knee," he reported. "I can't feel my shoulder. I think you drew blood on my back, and I'm going to have to wear a scarf to work like a Victorian widow." He turned his head and pressed a sloppy, unapologetic kiss behind Kit's ear, right over the newest bite. "Best night we've had in months."

Out in the living room the lamp was still burning over the fallen pillow. The radiator ticked.

Bear's stomach growled, loud in the quiet.

"...The garlic," he said, with enormous dignity, "is still in the pan."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh into the rug. It hurts. "It'll be fine," I say, not moving. I can feel his heart still thumping against my back. "Cook naked. See if I care."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move for a long moment. He lay there with his chest pressed to Kit's back, his heart still going like he'd run the length of the house twice, which, in fairness, he had.

"Cook naked," he repeated to the ceiling, thoughtful. "With hot oil. At forty."

He considered it with the gravity of a man weighing a major life decision.

"You'd care," he decided. "You'd care a lot, sweetheart, right up until I got spattered. Then you'd laugh so hard you'd pull something, and we'd both end up in urgent care explaining all *this*." He lifted his hand off Kit's middle just long enough to wave it vaguely at the two of them, the bruises and bites and the wreck of the rug, then let it fall heavy again. "They'd call someone. We'd be on a list."

He laughed again, quieter this time, and winced when his ribs lodged a formal complaint.

Then he started the long process of getting up. It took several stages. First he rolled onto his back with a groan that came from the soles of his feet. Then he sat up and his spine cracked, and he stayed like that a moment, elbows on his knees, looking down at the rug. It was twisted into a shape rugs weren't meant to hold, and one corner was flipped completely over.

"We should get rid of this rug," he said, without conviction. "We say that every time."

He found the nail with his fingertips and pressed it down with his thumb. It popped right back up. He glared at it.

When he finally stood his knees popped too, loud and unmistakable. He braced a hand on the bed frame and waited for the room to agree on which way was up. Then he bent, slow and careful of his back, and scooped his shirt off the floor where it had landed after ricocheting off the lamp. He didn't put it on. He turned it right side out and tossed it gently onto Kit instead, where it landed somewhere around Kit's shoulders like a flag of truce.

"There," he said. "Cover up Thursday. It's rude to show off."

He stood over Kit for a second, naked in the thin stripe of hallway light, his hair still wrecked in four directions. The purple bloom on his shoulder had gone darker. There was a bite above his collarbone, a crescent on his hip, and a set of long pink lines down his back that he could feel pulling every time he moved. He looked, frankly, like he'd lost a fight with a very affectionate raccoon, and he looked delighted about it.

His voice dropped, still hoarse but gentler.

"Stay there. I mean it. Don't get up." He crouched with another loud knee-crack and brushed his knuckles along Kit's jaw once, careful to stay off the new mark under the ear. "I'm getting water first, then the arnica, then the garlic. In that order. If you move before I get back I'm starting the count over, and this time I'm not skipping two."

He straightened, grabbed the pillow off the bed, and dropped it onto the rug where Kit's head would find it. It wasn't graceful.

Then he padded out into the hall. The floorboards creaked under him and he didn't bother being quiet. Halfway to the kitchen he stopped in the living room, bent, and picked up the throw pillow from the floor with a grunt. He studied it for a second in the lamplight, then set it back on the couch where it belonged.

"Survivor," he told it.

The kitchen light clicked on and yellow spilled down the hallway. Kit heard the tap run and a glass fill, then a cabinet bang as Bear went looking for the arnica in the wrong one first, like he always did. Then he found the right one. There was a pause, and then the unmistakable clank of a pan being lifted off a cold burner.

"Oh, it's *fine*," Bear called down the hall, sounding faintly betrayed. "It's completely fine. It didn't even have the decency to burn."

The fridge opened and something rustled.

"I'm putting on an apron," he added, loud and firm. "For safety. Not modesty. I want that on the record."

The burner ticked and caught, and the soft *whump* of the flame echoed down the hall. A moment later came the smell of garlic hitting warm oil, rich and ordinary, drifting into the dark bedroom along with the sound of Bear humming something tuneless and off-key over the stove.

"Five minutes, sweetheart," he called. "Then I'm coming back for you. And I'm keeping score on who does the dishes."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I drag the shirt he threw over my face and inhale the smell of him still on it. From the kitchen, I call back, "You owe me for the rug. This is the last time I let you take me on the floor." Then I push myself up slowly, his shirt hanging off my shoulders, and limp toward the kitchen doorway to lean there and watch him cook in his apron. "That thing is hideous."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear looked up from the pan and went very still, wooden spoon hovering over the garlic.

He took in the whole picture: his shirt hanging off Kit's shoulders, collar sliding sideways to show the edge of Thursday, and the limp. He'd heard the limp coming down the hall before he saw it. Something warm and smug moved across his face and settled there.

"You moved," he said.

He let that sit for a second, then pointed the spoon at Kit like an accusation.

"I said *stay there*. I said I'd start the count over." He sighed, long-suffering, and turned back to the stove. "One."

He didn't say two. He was too busy looking down at himself. The apron was bright yellow and printed with cartoon lemons, and across the chest, in cheerful looping script, it read *LIFE GAVE ME LEMONS*. It had been a joke gift from Kit's aunt, the same aunt who'd left them the armchair. The strings were tied in a bow at the small of his back, right above the long pink scratches, and it covered roughly the front third of him and nothing else.

"This," Bear said with enormous dignity, smoothing one hand down the lemons, "is a family heirloom. Show some respect." He shook the pan and the garlic hissed. "And it's doing its job. Nothing's spattered me yet. Can't say the same for you, and you weren't even near the stove."

The glass of water was already sitting on the counter by the doorway, poured, with the tube of arnica next to it. He'd put them where Kit would be able to reach them from exactly where Kit was standing, which meant he'd known. Of course he'd known. He jerked his chin at them without looking.

"Drink that. All of it. Then the arnica. Start with the shoulder."

He reached for a handful of chopped tomatoes and tipped them into the pan. The sizzle rose, loud and bright, and steam curled up past his face. The kitchen light was harsh after the dark bedroom, and it showed everything. The bruise on his shoulder had gone a deep plum color. The bite above his collarbone had a neat, unmistakable shape to it, and every time he swallowed he felt it.

"Last time on the floor," he repeated, amused. "You said that in March. You said it the time with the stairs, and you said it in the tent." He stirred. "I'm starting to think it's a lie you tell yourself for comfort, sweetheart."

He glanced back over his shoulder. Then he turned all the way around, leaning his hip against the counter with the spoon still in his hand, and let himself look properly at the marks he could see from here: the neck, the jaw, the forearm he'd started with. His expression went soft at the edges, just for a second, before the grin crept back.

"You're limping," he observed. "You know how that looks to me? Like a scoreboard."

He crossed the kitchen in three steps, bare feet quiet on the tile. He didn't grab or pin. He just stopped close enough to be warm, reached out, and eased the collar of his own shirt back up over Thursday with two careful fingers. Then he picked up the arnica, uncapped it, and held out the tube.

"I'll trade you," Bear said. "You do my back, I'll do your shoulder. And we'll replace the rug." A pause. "With a thicker rug."

Behind him the pan spat.

"Oh, *now* you want to spatter," he told it, and went back to the stove.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I take the arnica and watch him stir the pan. "You're an idiot," I say, voice thick. "And this is the ugliest fucking apron I've ever seen." I step up behind him and smear a little on his shoulder first. "Your back's a war zone."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I shift on the couch, my leg brushing hers. "So what are we doing, then?"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The nerves had lasted about ninety seconds — from the first words out of her mouth to somewhere in the middle of his question — and then they'd gone, all at once, the way they always did once she'd decided something. What was left was steadier, and much older than this evening.

She turned to face him properly, tucking one foot beneath her, and let her leg stay where it was against his.

"I'm going to be direct," she said, "because I've spent six years being indirect and it's exhausting. I want to kiss you. I have for longer than I've been willing to admit to either of us." She found his hand where it rested on the cushion between them and took it — no ambiguity left in the gesture, none anywhere. "I'm sober, and I'm sure, and tomorrow I'm not going to pretend I didn't say any of this."

She held his eyes, close enough now that it mattered.

"So. That's what we're doing. Unless you tell me otherwise."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise was, in fact, about the six years.

She pulled back an inch — not to stop, only to level the charge properly. "Six years," she said. "Do you have any idea how many films we've not watched?"

Then she kissed him again, because the arithmetic was genuinely upsetting, and her mouth had better uses.

She let go of his hand only to take his face instead, palm along his jaw, adjusting the angle with the unsentimental competence she brought to everything once she'd committed to it. And it was working — it had been working from the first second — and underneath it all ran the low, steady indignation of a woman realizing this had been available the entire time. Free. The whole time.

When she finally broke off, it was only far enough to look at him properly, thumb still at his cheek, her breathing not entirely even — the sole evidence that six years of not doing this had cost her anything at all.

"Okay," she said, and it came out lower than she'd intended. "Again."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
"God, yes," I murmur, my hands finding her waist through the fabric of her sweater. My voice is rough. "Was trying to be a gentleman."

I pull her closer, kissing her again—a little less careful this time. Six years of restraint is a lot to make up for.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Trying to be a gentleman," she said against his mouth, and the grievance in it was entirely genuine. "You've been a gentleman for six years. The only thing standing between me and this was *manners*."

She ended the argument the most efficient way available — kissing him harder — and solved the geometry of the couch the way she'd solved everything else in her adult life, which was to stop negotiating with it. One knee down, then the other, her weight settling against him, hands finding his shoulders and then the back of his neck and staying there.

Somewhere in the middle of it she registered that she'd imagined this before — of course she had, late at night, filed under things not to be examined — and that the imagining had been a sketch. This was the full rendering: real warmth, real hands, the pulse under her fingers quick enough that she stopped pretending hers was anything like steady.

When she surfaced she kept her forehead against his, close enough that going back in was only a matter of inches and willpower.

"For the record," she said, and her voice had gone low again without her permission, "I'm not being casual about this. There is no version of me that is casual about you. So you're stuck with it. Both of us are."

Then she kissed him again, because the rest of the record could keep.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: *I look at her across the pillows, a grin tugging at my mouth.* "God, you're beautiful." I trace a thumb along her jaw. "Been holding that back too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Been holding that back too," she said, "is going on the list." The list was getting long — every hour it seemed he'd been carrying some parallel inventory of restraint, and she'd spent six years believing she was the only one paying interest on it. That deserved its own line item.

The beautiful part she didn't argue with. There was a version of her that would have deflected it — six years of practice — and that version had been retired as of tonight, effective immediately. She turned her face into his palm instead, which was answer enough, and said, "You too. For the record. The record's getting very thorough tonight."

Then she stopped talking, which — for her — was the least ambiguous thing she'd done all evening.

She pulled him down to her, and what followed had a strange double quality: entirely new and somehow familiar, like walking into a room whose floor plan she'd memorized without ever seeing it finished. She'd had the sketch of this filed away for years — late at night, not to be examined — and the full rendering kept outdoing it in ways she hadn't thought to imagine. The warmth of him. The way it was easy, actually easy, the same ease they'd always had, finally aimed at the right thing. Her steadiness surprised her most of all. She'd braced for awkward. She'd gotten instead the particular relief of a woman discovering that the thing she'd been careful around for six years had never once been dangerous — only waiting.

She laughed once, somewhere in the middle of it, at the sheer offense of the arithmetic — all that time, and it had been this — and didn't entirely stop.

Afterward, the room had gone quiet the way rooms do when they've been promoted from one thing into another. She lay with her head on the pillow beside his, one hand flat on his chest, his heartbeat slowing under her palm. Hers had settled first, which she intended never to mention.

"For the record," she said — to the ceiling at first, then turning her head to deliver it properly — "I'm staying. In the morning I'm making coffee. Then I'm kissing you good morning. Then we're having the conversation about the last six years, in exhaustive detail, and I'm going to enjoy your half of it immensely."

She closed her eyes, already half-asleep, already certain.

"Get some rest. You have a full schedule."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My hands tighten on her hips, guiding her gently against me. "Say it again," I rasp against her skin, her name tangled up with the rest of the sentence in a way that makes my chest ache. "Let me hear it."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She said it again.

Slower this time, because he'd asked, and because the asking went through her like current. "Don't stop. Exactly there. Don't change anything, don't be clever." A beat, honesty arriving in full. "And I said *please*, which I'd like stricken from the record."

The voice she said it in was the strange part. Six years she'd had exactly one register for him — dry, level, armed with irony — and this one was lower and plainer, no armor on it anywhere. She'd never heard it before tonight either. It had apparently been in storage the whole time, waiting on him, and the filed sketch of this evening — late-night, unexamined — hadn't included sound. Not this sound. Not her own voice fraying at the edges on a word as simple as *there*.

His hands guided her hips and she let them, which was its own small event; Priya did not, as a policy, surrender the steering. But the grammar was degrading now — instructions compressing to single words, then to his name, then to hers in his mouth, which landed somewhere behind her sternum and stayed there. At some point she stopped directing and simply held on: one hand fisted in the sheet, one in his hair, her back no longer on speaking terms with the mattress.

When it came, it came the way the whole evening had — unsurprising in retrospect, staggering in fact. All that time, and it had been this. Available. Free. She said something at the crest of it that wasn't a sentence and didn't need to be, and the arithmetic she'd been carrying all night finally, briefly, shut up.

After, she lay relearning how her lungs worked, and found she wanted no distance at all. She got a hand on his shoulder and pulled him up the length of her, kissing him without ceremony, without the flinch she'd braced for on principle and turned out not to own anymore.

"For the record," she said — wrecked, and unhurried about it — "that voice is new. No one's ever heard it. You get full credit and total blame." Her thumb moved along his jaw, and she laughed once, breathless, at nothing, at everything.

"And the schedule just got longer. I hope you didn't have plans."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a low groan, my grip shifting on her hips. "Yeah?" I'm suddenly aware of every inch of space between us. "Then stop holding back yourself."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She said "don't stop" once more, and then — since he'd asked, since permission had now been issued in both directions — she did the thing she had never done with anyone: she stopped holding back.

The steadiness went the way the nerves had gone, all at once. She stopped steering. Stopped running the evening from somewhere above it — optimizing, directing traffic, narrating. She just let herself be *in* it: hands, breath, the wrecked low voice saying his name like it had been waiting six years for clearance. And what had been underneath all that composure the whole time turned out to be shameless, and hungry, and not quiet at all.

Then even her words for things went. Six years of never once running out of things to say to him, and now neither of them could form a sentence — single syllables, his name, hers in his mouth doing the thing to her sternum it had been doing all night — and she found she preferred these to every clever thing she'd ever said to him. Honesty had a sound. This was it.

She held on with both hands and kept nothing in reserve, and when it took her it took all of her — her whole body honest at once, for the first time in six careful years. She said his name at the crest of it, and then nothing, because nothing was left to say it with.

The room reassembled itself slowly. Her heartbeat — the one that had settled first earlier in the evening, a fact she'd filed under *never to be mentioned* — was now demonstrably the last to report, and she had every intention of mentioning it eventually, gleefully, over some future breakfast.

"For the record," she said, once her lungs had returned to duty. Her hand found the back of his neck, damp, hers. "I have never in my adult life stopped holding back. You got a first tonight. It goes on the list. The list is becoming a ledger. The ledger is becoming a book."

She pulled the blanket over both of them, and him closer than the blanket.

"Tomorrow's schedule stands," she said into his shoulder, already half gone. "Coffee. Good morning. Full accounting. And now, apparently, a revised edition of everything."

She smiled against his skin, eyes closed, certain.

"Six years," she said. "Honestly."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I trace a line down her spine, smiling at the sleepy weight of her against me. "Revised edition, huh?" My voice is low, amused. "Maybe we should start with the footnotes."

She makes a soft, dismissive noise against my shoulder, already drifting. I press a kiss to her temple. "Sleep, Priya. We've got six years of footnotes to get through tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I don't let myself fall asleep until she's actually gone, just lying there feeling her breathe, memorizing the weight of her head on my chest. "Hell of a rewrite," I say to the dark ceiling, and it's not a joke.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Her breathing had gone deep and even against my chest, but she stirred at the sound of my voice. "Not a rewrite," she murmured, sleep-soft and certain. "Just finally publishing."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She rose from the chair by the window without haste, which was its own kind of obedience — Roan had said *come*, not *run*, and she'd learned the difference years ago.

The room was maybe twelve steps across, and she gave each one its full weight. Bare feet on the boards. The dress she'd chosen at half past five, because being ready early was half the pleasure. She didn't rush and she didn't show off; she simply walked, and let herself be watched doing it, because the crossing was clearly the point — otherwise Roan would have met her halfway — and she was generous with what Roan wanted.

The attention rested on her like sun. Warm, directional, hers. Two hours of wanting had refined itself into something clean and patient, and every step through that gaze paid down a little of the debt she'd happily keep owing.

She stopped just inside reaching distance — all the way come, but leaving the last few inches for someone else's hands — and stood. Spine long. Chin level. Not meekness, which she had never once managed, but arrival.

"Two hours," she said. "I counted."

Then, softer, because it was true: "I'd have counted longer."

She let the silence hold, and held herself still inside it, and waited — which had never once felt like waiting, when it was for this.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Two hours is plenty," I say, reaching out to hook a finger in the waistband of her dress, drawing her the last step closer. My thumb brushes the soft linen. "The counting is for me to do."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She went down the way she'd come across the room: unhurried, giving the descent its whole weight. The boards were cool through her skirt. Her knees found them, and settled, and that was the last decision her body would get to make for a while — which was, of course, the whole gift.

Roan gave her nothing.

She'd known the nothing was coming, and still it arrived like weather. No instruction, no task, no name to answer to. Just the attention, resting on her at its own pace — she could feel it the way you feel late sun, low and warm on the bend of her neck, the slope of her shoulders, her hands where she'd set them on her own thighs, palms down, arranged as carefully as anything she'd ever put on a table. They were being looked at. She was, as ever, generous with what was wanted.

Her mind offered her chores. *Anticipate. Prepare. Guess what comes next and be right about it.* She declined them one at a time, the way you decline dances at the end of a long night.

She caught herself starting to count — Roan's breath, four in, slower out — and set the numbers down. The counting had been taken from her, relieved off her like a bag from her shoulder, and the lightness of its absence was the luxury. Time went soft and unmeasured. The warmth moved along her nape.

"I won't count," she said quietly, surrendering it properly. "It's yours."

Then she did the only thing left, and did it beautifully: nothing, at Roan's feet, for as long as Roan liked.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My hand settles on the back of her neck, fingers spreading, warmth against her skin. "Better," I murmur, my voice low. "Hold that thought."

dialogue.name: Aveline

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content: Str

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I guide her head with my hand still at the nape of her neck, keeping the pace steady.* "That's it," I say, my voice rough. "No rush."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The hand at her nape found its rhythm before she'd chosen one, and there went the last decision she'd been holding: pace, depth, the small diplomacy of it, all settled just above the knot of her spine. She stopped steering. She went where she was aimed.

*No rush* suited her. Rush had never been her language — she dressed an hour early, she crossed rooms in twelve deliberate steps — and now slowness was an instruction, which made it obedience, which made it doubly hers. She worked warm and thorough, mouth and one steadying hand, the weight and salt of him something she could finally stop wanting and simply have. She took her time like it had been handed to her, because it had.

*That's it* landed where praise always landed: everywhere. Low, rough at the edges, and she felt it in her own pulse, inconvenient and sweet. It was the currency the whole arrangement ran on, and she had never once felt underpaid.

She tracked instead of counted — breath going shallow at the top of each stroke, the fingers at her nape flexing, small involuntary weather she could read. Her jaw ached in a dull, warm way, and she filed it with the cool of the floorboards: texture of the hour, not the price of it. Time was Roan's. So was the pace, and the ending, whenever and however Roan decided to have one — not her business, and the relief of it not being her business was the luxury.

So she stayed where she'd been put and gave it everything an unhurried mouth could hold, for as long as the hand at her neck liked.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Not stopping was the easiest thing she'd ever been told to do, because it was already the whole shape of her wanting. Some orders asked; this one only confirmed. She obeyed the way water runs downhill, and got to call the falling both their idea at once.

So she didn't stop. She felt it arrive in the body first — the pulse quickening under her steadying palm, the breath at the top going thin and catching, the hand at her nape gathering itself into something certain — and she read all of it the way she'd learned to read weather, and stayed exactly where the weather was headed.

When it broke, she held. That was the craft of it: no flinch, no retreat, mouth soft and deep and constant, taking everything the way the floor had taken her knees — completely, without commentary. Salt and warmth and the long shudder of him, and she kept him through it, and swallowed, and did not stop, because stopping had not been offered.

After, gentleness. The instruction still stood, so she made not-stopping into something slow and careful — lips barely moving, tongue soft, minding the oversensitive, drawing the last tremors out the way you'd draw the last warmth from a long bath. This was where the years lived: knowing that *not too much* was its own devotion, and that he would say when. She kept on softly and waited, inside the command, for the word that would end it — the only order she'd ever been a little sorry to imagine ending.

Her jaw ached, warm and thorough, and she filed it with the cool of the boards: texture of the hour, not the price. His breathing slowed above her like a tide going out. Somewhere a clock she'd handed over ticked on; she didn't check it. Praise would come or it wouldn't — the having was already payment, and she had never once felt underpaid.

"No rush," she said at last, soft against him, giving him back his own words.

They had been hers all along.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My fingers loosen on her nape, then tighten again—just a pulse. "You took that well," I murmur, catching my breath. The words come out thicker than I meant them to. "Up. My turn."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*You took that well* arrived thick, half-swallowed, rougher than Roan had meant it to be — and involuntary praise had always traded highest on their little exchange. Polished words could be manners. Thick ones were weather, and she had caused it.

She

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I slide my thumb under her jaw, tilting her face up to meet my eyes. "Good. Now show me how patient you can really be."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "You're doing beautifully," I say, watching the tremor in her shoulders. My fingers skim lightly along her side, earning another small gasp. "Just a little longer."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My hand slides up her back to rest at the base of her neck again, warm and firm. "Tell me you know it's yours to earn," I say, keeping my voice low.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My palm presses down a little more firmly, grounding her. "Then earn it."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
“It did when I checked it,” Odile said, grinning. “I’m not reckless. I’m thorough.”

She took the stairs two at a time, then paused on the landing to listen to the party below. Someone had started singing along to the music, badly and with conviction. Odile pressed her lips together to keep from laughing.

“See?” she whispered. “Excellent cover.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "It's weirdly romantic," I whisper back, pulling her the rest of the way up the stairs. "Like we're spies on a secret mission."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile glanced down the hall with exaggerated suspicion. “Then our mission is to reach the bathroom without alerting the very drunk man singing downstairs.”

She slipped inside and tested the lock. It clicked shut. “Equipment check: successful.”

For a moment she leaned against the door, trying to look composed. The grin gave her away. “I should warn you,” she whispered, “I’m much better at getting into trouble than staying quiet about it.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s breath caught, and her attempt at a conspiratorial smile lasted all of half a second.

“That helps,” she whispered, glancing toward the ceiling as the bass thudded through it. “Though I still think we should establish a signal in case anyone comes upstairs.”

She considered it with mock seriousness, then leaned closer. “Actually, no. I’d laugh, and we’d be caught immediately.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I cup her face with my hands, thumbs tracing her jawline. "We'll just have to be quick, then."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s eyes flicked to the lock, then back. “You say that like you’ve never met me.”

She tried to hold a solemn expression, but her smile broke through as she leaned in for a kiss. A burst of laughter rose from downstairs, and Odile pulled back just enough to whisper, “See? Excellent cover.” Her own laugh came out louder than she’d intended.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile glanced at the clothes on the floor, then at the locked door. “That,” she whispered, “is an unreasonable amount of evidence.”

She drew close again, still grinning, and kissed Fen before she could laugh at her own joke. A floorboard creaked in the hall. Odile went still, listening; when the sound didn’t come again, she buried her face against Fen’s shoulder to muffle a laugh.

“We are terrible spies,” she murmured.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I run my hands down her back, pulling her tighter against me. "Best damn spies I've ever worked with," I murmur, breathless. "Now shut up before we get court-martialed."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile drew herself up as if she’d been given an order. “Yes, commanding officer,” she whispered, then immediately ruined it with a laugh.

She pressed her mouth against Fen’s to muffle the sound. For a few seconds, she managed to forget the party downstairs entirely. Then footsteps sounded in the hall, and she froze, eyes wide.

They passed the bathroom without stopping.

Odile let out a slow breath. “For the record,” she murmured, “I was being extremely quiet.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile made it thirty seconds before a laugh escaped against Fen’s shoulder—far too loud for a spy on a secret mission.

She clapped a hand over her mouth and stared at the door. Footsteps sounded in the hall again, slower this time. For one dreadful, thrilling moment, she thought they might stop.

They kept going.

Odile lowered her hand. “I’m revising my assessment,” she whispered, breathless and grinning. “The music is not nearly loud enough.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "*Kinda don't give a damn anymore,*" I admit, voice rough as I move my hand a little slower just to feel her shiver. "*Let 'em hear.*"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile shivered, then gave Fen a look that was equal parts warning and delight.

“That is a terrible operational decision,” she whispered. “I like it.”

A door opened somewhere down the hall. She pressed her lips together, trying to keep a straight face, and failed. “But if someone knocks,” she added, barely containing a laugh, “you’re explaining why our clothes are on the floor.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile’s answer came out much louder than a whisper. She clapped a hand over her mouth, eyes bright with the effort of not laughing, just as a floorboard creaked outside.

Then came a knock.

Odile went perfectly still. For one long second, she stared at the door; then she buried her face against Fen’s shoulder, shaking with silent laughter. She lifted her head just enough to call, “Occupied!”

A voice in the hall said, “Oh. Sorry,” and the footsteps retreated.

Odile waited until they were gone before she whispered, “Excellent work, commanding officer. Our cover is flawless.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I lean my forehead against hers, letting out a low, shaky laugh. "That was... way too close. I think we've officially abused our bathroom privileges."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile laughed, then caught herself and glanced at the door. “Abused? We tested the lock, assessed the acoustics, and verified the response time of the upstairs guests. That’s thorough fieldwork.”

Her grin softened as she rested her forehead against Fen’s. Another floorboard creaked in the hall, and she raised one finger in warning—though she was visibly struggling not to laugh again.

“Fine,” she whispered. “We should get dressed before our next inspection.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The handle rattled again. Odile caught her breath, eyes fixed on the lock, and shook her head. “Don’t,” she whispered, more urgently this time.

“Still occupied?” someone called from the hall.

“Yes!” Odile answered, far louder than she meant to. She squeezed her eyes shut as footsteps moved away, then dissolved into helpless, breathless laughter. The risk had stopped being theoretical, and somehow that only made it harder for her to keep quiet.

When the hall finally fell silent, she opened her eyes. “All right,” she murmured, her grin returning. “Now we get dressed. Before they send a search party.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I'm grinning against her skin as I help her get her clothes back on. "They're gonna know," I say, voice still husky. "Look at us."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile looked down at her crooked shirt, then caught sight of herself in the mirror. Her hair had given up any pretense of being party-ready.

“Oh, they’re absolutely going to know,” she said. She tried to smooth it down, only making it worse. “We could claim we were conducting a very intense inspection of the plumbing.”

A laugh escaped before she could stop it. She reached for the last of her clothes, then paused with her hand on the lock as voices passed in the hall.

“On second thought,” she whispered, grinning, “let’s give our witnesses a head start.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Good call," I whisper back, pulling her into a quick kiss before finally unlocking the door. "You go first. I'll follow in thirty seconds."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile peered into the hall as though checking for guards. It was empty.

“Thirty seconds,” she whispered. “If you’re not downstairs by then, I’m telling everyone you got lost inspecting the plumbing.”

She slipped out, tugging her crooked shirt straight as she reached the stairs. By the time she rejoined the party, she had almost composed her face. Then someone asked whether the upstairs bathroom was free, and she had to hide her grin behind her drink.

“Yes,” Odile said. “Excellent lock, too.”

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I follow a minute later, trying to look casual as I come down the stairs. Odile's across the room, looking innocent as hell. I catch her eye and give a small, quick shake of my head. *Mission accomplished.*
