dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave the exit a three-count. One for the doorway. One for the hall. One for the pure pleasure of letting the whole thing ripen — because generosity was off the table now, formally declined, and there was a particular joy in a gift refused.

Then Bear went.

Bare feet on hardwood, down the hallway at speed, past a runner rucked up at the corner — recent work, that, still settling flat. Eight years and Kit still took that corner like the wall might move for them. It never had. It wasn't going to start tonight.

"Kitchen's a dead end," Bear called out, slowing at the fork where the hall split — stairs up, cellar door down, the living room dark and full of furniture designed by someone who hated shins. Deliberately not committing to a direction. Listening. "And the cellar's got one door, and I know exactly where you fit behind the shelving. So consider your options."

The house ticked and settled. No help from it.

Bear leaned a shoulder into the doorframe, unhurried now, because the chase had never really been the point — the point was the moment after, and both of them knew it, and had known it for eight years of matching marks.

"Terms," Bear said to the dark, conversational. "You come out swinging, we call it a fair fight, and whatever marks happen, happen. You make me come find you—" a slow roll of one shoulder, a satisfying crack out of it, "—and interest accrues. You're already carrying a balance since Tuesday. The shower. You know what you did."

A beat.

"Running count or running, Kit. Pick one."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I come out of the living room, stepping around the armchair I'd been crouched behind. "Tuesday was an accident," I say, but I'm grinning. "But I'm in the mood for a fight."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Accident," Bear said, in the tone of a customs officer hearing the word *souvenir*. "Accidents don't have follow-through. Tuesday had follow-through. And a shoulder drop behind it. I wore the intent in my ribs for two days."

A beat, while Bear looked Kit over — the grin, the stance, the whole outrageous cheek of the thing — and found all of it satisfactory.

"But a fight. Good. Honest answer, finally." Bear pushed off the frame and rolled the neck, getting a pop out of it to match the shoulder's. "Terms stand as offered. Fair fight wipes whatever happens tonight — clean slate going forward. Tuesday stays on the books. Accidents don't void debts. That's not my rule, that's arithmetic."

Bear leaned sideways, found the lamp switch without looking, and flooded the living room in warm yellow light. Both of them lit up like a ring under a bulb. "Fair fight means I want to see it coming. All of it."

Then Bear stepped into the room proper, and the room changed shape around the two of them — the coffee table with its one treacherous leg, the gap between couch and wall that looked like an escape and was a trap, the armchair Kit had just surrendered as cover. Eight years. Bear knew Kit's openings the way Kit knew Bear's: left side, low, ribs, always the ribs. Every counter already written down somewhere, just waiting for one of them to prove it wrong. That was the sport of it. That had always been the sport of it.

Bear crossed to the armchair, plucked the cushion off it — Kit's own cover, freshly abandoned, no honor too small — and threw it. Not hard. Honest. An opener. A glove, flicked.

And Bear came in behind it, low, weight forward, arms opening for the waist, bare feet quick and silent on the floorboards, Bear's own grin arriving somewhere around the second step.

The talking was over.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The first grab missed — technically.

Kit twisted out of it with a quarter-turn that any referee would have scored an evasion and Bear scored as a toll: the minimum payment required to make the chase official. Three steps of hallway, feet loud on purpose, and then Bear's arm found the middle and the wall did the rest.

They hit it together — Kit front-first, Bear's weight arriving a half-beat behind, one wrist gathered and planted between Kit's shoulder blades, a knee and a hip closing the exits. The coast print rattled in its frame. Seven years on that wall; it had learned to rattle rather than fall.

Then Bear went still, and audited.

Because this was the address of Kit's best work. The pinned wrist that was never really pinned. The knee with an appointment to keep. Half of Kit's finest reversals had been born in exactly this posture, at exactly this moment — the surrender that wasn't, the giveaway with a hook in it. Bear had worn the results before. Small marks, honest ones, each one a tuition payment.

Nothing. No knee loaded. No elbow queued under the ribs. The pulse under Bear's forearm was quick but level — the heartbeat of someone who'd taken a walk, not started a war.

Which was worse, frankly. Suspicious.

"You slipped the first grab for free," Bear said, low, close to Kit's ear, the grin audible in it. "Paid the toll. Got caught on schedule. That's not a fight. That's a performance of one. I've had more resistance from a fitted sheet."

Bear set teeth

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: against the back of Kit's neck, not a bite, just a warning pressure. "You're planning something."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I hiss when his teeth meet my neck, but I'm laughing too. "Planning?" I say, breathless. "You caught me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Caught," Bear repeated, against Kit's neck, in the tone of an inspector tasting a word for spoilage. "Caught is for civilians. You walked out of that living room on a schedule. You gave up the doorway, the hall, the wall — you've never surrendered a corner in this house in eight years, and tonight you paid every toll on the road like a tourist with exact change."

A beat. The hiss-with-laughter-under-it was still in the skin there, and it had always been the entire point of the sport.

"So no. I didn't catch you. I accepted a delivery."

Then Bear stopped talking, because teeth were better testimony — a real one this time, slow, well past the warning stage, drawn out long enough to file under *Tuesday, precedent, and everything since* — and the rest of the audit was transferred to hands, which had stopped taking minutes several steps ago.

The lamp stayed on. Neither of them made it as far as turning it off.

---

Afterward, the living room told the whole story in objects. The armchair cushion, destination unknown. Kit's shirt in the ceiling fan, still turning, committed. The coffee table upright on its one treacherous leg, insufferable about it. The runner in the hall still rucked at the corner — a crime now with no remaining suspects.

Bear lay flat on the floorboards with one arm asleep under circumstances Bear declined to correct, and read the closing entries out loud, because accounts settled in the dark were accounts that reopened.

"Fair fight. Called, fought, paid in full. Clean slate going forward." A breath. "Tuesday survives. Accident or not, it stays on the books. That's arithmetic, not spite."

Then Bear turned, found the fresh mark — high, honest work, done slow — and pressed a thumb to it, gentle now, checking the signature the way you'd check a signature.

"That one's mine. Witnessed by the lamp."

The fan turned. The suspicion never formally cleared; it just got comfortable.

"And for the record — you weren't caught. You're *held*. Completely different legal category, and you've got until morning to appeal."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The second one got full production values.

Same address — laid over the first mark, so the two of them could talk to each other — but slower. Teeth taking the scenic route, long enough that it stopped being punctuation and became a paragraph, because a request like that deserved craft and not haste. The fan turned overhead. The floorboards held. And eight years in, the sound Kit made at the far end of it was still the best evidence in the house that the whole apparatus worked exactly as designed.

When Bear finally let go, the mark was already coming up warm under where Bear's mouth had been. Bear pressed a

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shove at his shoulder, breathless and grinning. "You're insufferable. You know that, right?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The shove arrived and Bear took it the way the house took weather — noted, unmoved, quietly pleased to have it. Eight years of that exact palm on that exact shoulder and it had never once accomplished anything except its real purpose, which was filing.

"Insufferable," Bear agreed. "Guilty as charged. Eight years, no contest. You've had an appeal window open since the day we met and you've never once filed." A beat. "You keep bringing the same charge and staying for the sentence, Kit. Eventually a court asks what you're actually here for."

Then Bear caught the retreating hand — the one that had done the shoving — and kept it, flat against the floorboards, under Bear's own.

Not pinned. Filed.

Sitting up cost the dead arm, which came free at last and reported for duty with a full parade of pins and needles, endured with the patience of a man listening to an anthem he'd personally commissioned.

"Hold still."

The audit, then, done gently this time. Thumb along the shoulder — the second mark, the one with production values — tracing its edge like checking a weld. Then up to the neck, to the first. Warm. Raised. Holding its shape.

"Both sound. The lamp notarized the first. I'll witness the second myself."

Bear stretched, hooked the throw blanket off the couch without actually getting up — a maneuver eight years in development, refined across many evenings on this exact floor — and dropped it over Kit without ceremony.

"House rules. We generate heat. The floor generates nothing."

Then the lamp switch, found without looking, and the room went from amber to dark. The fan kept turning. Kit's shirt rode the rotation at the top of its arc like a flag over negotiated territory. Bear settled back down, shoulder finding shoulder in the dark.

"And for the record — I know there

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let him get ahold of my wrists, and I don't try to pull them away. "And I want you to be smug about it for days."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The wrists arrived like evidence — presented, palms up, chain of custody impeccable — and Bear took them with the corresponding gravity: both hands, unhurried, a man accepting keys he'd been promised for years.

"Smug. For *days*." Bear turned the first wrist over in the dark, thumb finding the pulse line. "Kit. I want you to understand the scale of what you've commissioned. You haven't requested a behavior. You've requested a rate increase on my worst quality, in writing, witnessed by a ceiling fan. There is no version of me that under-delivers on this contract."

Then Bear bent to it.

First wrist: teeth over the pulse, slow, quiet — none of the shoulder's production values, a mark in a smaller font with the same legal weight. And the whole time, the heartbeat right there under Bear's teeth, tapping out its testimony. Bear held the pace until the mark was certain to keep, then let go and checked it with a thumb — warm, raised, sitting exactly where a watch face would go, so Thursday could annotate every doorknob and coffee cup Kit touched.

The second wrist got the same sentence, same duration. Symmetry. Eight years of matched marks; you didn't break formatting this late in the document.

Then Bear folded Kit's hands together — both new marks face-up, like exhibits A and A-prime — and laid them on Kit's chest under the blanket. Filed, and left where filed.

"Terms of smugness, for the record. Tomorrow: I say nothing. I make coffee. I lean in the kitchen doorway looking like a craftsman in front of a finished wall. That's day one — restraint, deployed as bragging." The fan turned. Kit's shirt completed another lap. "By Thursday I'll be asking you to reach the top shelf, and then asking how it felt, and I won't be accepting 'fine' as an answer."

Bear settled back into the dark, shoulder to shoulder, one knee hooked over Kit's — the house's oldest filing system.

"Goodnight. Interest resumes at dawn."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The words landed like a work order — signed, specific, no ceiling on scope. Eight years and Kit still issued commissions that way: two syllables, fully funded, as if the danger were that Bear might under-deliver.

Bear reached over and turned the lamp back on.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I blink against the sudden light, but I don't squirm away. "That's better," I say, turning my head to look at him. "I want to see you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: The lamp floods the room again and I watch the shift in your face. "Yeah. Right there."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Eyes on you," I murmur, reaching up to trace the line of your jaw. "Always better."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s smile came slowly. “I heard you.”

She let the pause stretch, keeping her attention on Ines. “Green means we finish what we agreed to. It does not mean I forget what comes after.”

Her voice softened without losing its edge. “Not winding down yet.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *My hands tighten just slightly in her hair, holding her gaze.* "I know what green means. And I know what comes after." *I swallow, my throat tight.* "Right now, I just need you here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s expression steadied. She rested a hand against Ines’s cheek and held her gaze.

“I’m here,” she said. “All the way through. I’m not going anywhere.”

She let the quiet hold for another beat, then gave a small nod. “We finish together. After that, I take care of you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
“Not yet,” Sable agreed.

She checked the restraint nearest her with two fingers, then left it alone. “I heard you. I’m still here, and we’re still in it.”

She held the pause for one more breath before returning to the pace they had agreed on, her attention fixed on Ines.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: A shaky breath escapes me as she moves. "Don't... don't be gentle."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held her gaze. “I won’t,” she said. “But I’m keeping the limits we set.”

She checked the nearest restraint once more, then resumed the agreed pace—firm, deliberate, without rushing toward the end. Her attention stayed on Ines.

“Colour if it changes,” she said. “Until then, I’m right here.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed with the intensity they had agreed on, watching Ines closely even as the moment drew toward its end. She didn’t mistake silence for an answer.

“Still here,” she said, steady and close. “You don’t have to find words for anything else. Just give me a colour if it changes.”

She held the pace a little longer, then let her voice soften. “I’ve got you. All the way through.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My vision blurs for a second. *I press my forehead against her shoulder.* "Still green," I mumble. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
“Still green,” Sable repeated, so Ines knew she had heard.

She stayed close and kept the firm, measured pace they had agreed on. She did not rush, and she did not let her attention drift. One hand remained steady at Ines’s back.

“I’m here,” she said. “Not stopping yet.”

When the moment finally passed, Sable would see to the restraints, the water, and the warmth. For now, she held to her promise and stayed with Ines through it.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable drew back just far enough to meet Ines’s eyes. Her smile was unmistakably pleased with herself, but her voice stayed steady.

“You asked me not to be gentle,” she said. “You did not ask me to hurry.”

She checked the restraint at Ines’s wrist, then let her hand settle there. “Colour,” she asked, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Fucking green," I growl,

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s smile turned sharp. “Heard you.”

She stayed close, holding to what they had agreed without hurrying it. Her attention never left Ines; green mattered, and so did anything that might change it.

When the scene had finally run its course, Sable reached for the first restraint. “Now,” she said, her voice gentler, “I’m taking care of you.” Water and a warm blanket were already within reach.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers stilled on the restraint. She looked up, making sure she had heard the phrase correctly.

“All of it,” she said. “Within our limits. And then I get to be kind.”

She left the buckle fastened and stayed with Ines through the last stretch, firm and unhurried, watching closely until the scene was done. Only then did she release the restraints, one at a time.

“There,” Sable said, drawing the blanket around Ines. She brought the water within reach and stayed beside her. “I’m here for this part, too.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I sink into the blanket, my body trembling as the intensity finally ebbs. "Don't let go yet," I murmur, leaning into her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable wrapped an arm around Ines and held her close beneath the blanket. “I won’t,” she said. “Not until you tell me.”

She stayed still for a while, letting the room go quiet. Then she brushed her thumb lightly over the skin where the restraint had been, checking for any mark that needed attention.

“Water’s here when you’re ready,” she murmured. “For now, I’ve got you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the phrase and did not soften the finish. She kept to the limits they had set, gave the last stretch its full weight, and counted the final beats under her breath. Then she stopped. Her hand stayed steady at Ines’s back while she watched for a moment, making certain the scene was over before she reached for a buckle.

“That’s it,” she said. “I’m here.”

She released the restraints one at a time, supporting each arm as it came free. Her fingers checked the places the cuffs had held; she made a note of a reddened patch to look at again later. The blanket was beside her, and she drew it over Ines before the shaking had finished.

Sable settled close and wrapped an arm around her. She said nothing for a while. The water could wait within reach; so could every question except the ones that mattered. She kept her hold warm and steady, giving Ines time to come back to the room.

When she spoke again, her voice was quiet. “No need to move yet. I’ve got you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let out a slow breath, my head against her shoulder.* "Everything hurts." *My voice is rough, but I'm not complaining.* "You're warm."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept her arm around Ines and drew the blanket a little higher. “I am,” she said. “You can borrow all of it.”

She let the quiet settle again before she spoke. “I know some soreness was part of tonight. I still need to check: is any of it sharp, or somewhere you didn’t expect?” Her hand remained still at Ines’s back. “You don’t have to move to tell me.”

The water waited beside them. Sable stayed where she was, warm and close, and did not let go.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I shake my head slightly.* "Just the good kind of ache. You didn't overdo it." *I shift closer, letting the warmth seep into my stiff muscles.* "You always know."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held her a little closer beneath the blanket. “I pay attention,” she said. “And you tell me the truth. That’s how I know.”

She pressed a kiss to Ines’s hair, then reached for the water without letting go. “A few sips when you’re ready. After that, I’ll check your wrists again.”

Her arm stayed firm around Ines. “There’s no hurry,” she murmured. “I’ve got you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I take the water and drink slowly, my hands still trembling a little.* "Thank you." *I lean into her again, my eyes closing.* "Just stay like this for a minute."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I spin on my heel and bolt for the living room, aiming for the couch to put some furniture between us. *I can hear him moving behind me, not rushing, just taking his time.*

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear followed at a walk.

He'd learned years ago that the sound of him was half the game — his weight coming up the floorboards, unhurried, each step placed on purpose. Let her hear it. Let her do the math.

He stopped in the living room doorway and took stock: the couch between them, long and heavy, cutting the room in half. A fine choice. It also funneled her back toward the bookshelf corner, left one real way out past the coffee table, and put him between her and the hallway. He said none of that. He just let his eyes travel over the geometry of it, slow, so she could watch him take her position apart.

"Couch," he said. "Classic."

He started along its length — parallel, drifting, carving the room smaller with every step. His gaze never left her. Eight years had taught him where the tell lived: the shoulders, the breath, weight creeping onto the toes. He watched for it and took his time about it, because the waiting was where the mistakes got made.

"I like this part," he said, conversational, still walking. "You, doing sums. Can I clear the table? Is he faster than he looks?" A slow grin. "I'm exactly as fast as I look."

He reached the end of the couch nearest the hallway and stopped. Set one hand flat on the back of it. Leaned there like a man checking the weather, and let the silence stretch — five seconds, ten — long enough for the quiet to get loud.

Then he straightened.

"You said don't be generous."

And he moved — all that patience cashed in a single motion, coming around the couch's end fast, cutting the angle for the corner, closing.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He took her at the mouth of the hallway, mid-stride — one arm banding her waist, turning the momentum for her, into the wall shoulder-first, with a care that looked like none at all. Plaster shuddered. A frame two feet down ticked crooked.

He came in close behind the catch, one forearm braced beside her head, weight near enough that the air between them went warm. He didn't take her wrists. Never took her wrists — that had been settled around year two, when he'd learned her hands were half the fun. The chase was still in both of them, breath loud in the narrow space, and he let it run a lap before he spoke.

"Kitchen to hallway. Forty feet and one couch." He tilted his head, cataloguing. "And you gave me the last ten for free. Quit at the doorway. Noted." A pause, and the grin arrived, slow. "You told me not to be generous. I wasn't."

He leaned in — not for her mouth — and nosed the collar of her shirt aside, baring the muscle where neck met shoulder. A graze of teeth first, unhurried, so she'd know exactly what was coming, because the knowing was the point. Then he bit down. Hard, honest, hard enough to keep, and held it while his heartbeat counted off the seconds. When he let go, the mark was already rising warm under his lips. He pressed his mouth to it once, almost gentle, which was its own kind of lie.

"Three this week," he murmured against her skin. "

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I exhale against the wall, a satisfied sound. "You've been counting." I tip my head to give him more room. "Who's generous now?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I'm breathless, arching into the pressure of his mouth on my skin. "Mark your work," I say, the words coming out rough. My hand fists in his hair, holding him there.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He laughed — low, scraped thin, no breath left in it — because she'd handed him that line like a gift.

"I always sign my work."

Then he went back down and did it again. Not the same spot; an inch off, deliberate, spaced like a man setting fence posts, because eight years had taught him how her skin kept a ledger — marks laid side by side, legible for days, a language with a readership of two. This one he held longer. Her fist was still in his hair, holding him exactly where she wanted him, and the sting of it ran down his spine and landed somewhere that made him growl against her shoulder. He gave as good as he got: the full weight of him, chest and hips and gravity, pinning her into the rug so the only direction left to her was up, into his teeth.

He stayed where her hand put him until the hold burned, and when he finally released he didn't go far. Just far enough to look at what he'd made — the first bite purpling at the edges, the second still bright and rising — with the satisfaction of a man inspecting a joint he'd cut clean.

"Four this week," he said, rough. "And that one's deep enough your bag strap is going to find it every single day." The grin arrived slow, and she couldn't see it, but she'd hear it in the shape of the words. "That's not an accident. That's planning."

Her shirt was still snagged on one arm, caught at the elbow, half a problem. She'd said his call.

He took the collar in one fist and pulled. The fabric argued — a seam somewhere gave up the point — and he flung the wreck of it down the hallway without watching where it landed.

"That's mine now," he said, coming back down over her, mouth grazing the fresh mark, speaking straight into the heat of it. "Put it on my tab. I plan on being in debt to you for years."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He looked at the offered wrists for a long moment. Long enough to weigh them, which was its own courtesy — eight years in, and she still held them up sometimes like a test, checking whether tonight was the night he'd get lazy and simply take what was being handed over.

It wasn't. It never was.

"Not your wrists." He took her hands instead — threaded his fingers through hers, pressed them into the rug beside her head, palm to palm, knuckles down. It looked like pinning. It wasn't. Her fingers could still curl, still claw, and he wanted them laced through

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I curl my fingers tight with his, the bite of his grip grounding. "Always making it interesting." I arch up to find his mouth with mine, a rough, claiming kiss.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He met the kiss the way he met everything she brought him — full weight, nothing held in reserve. His mouth still tasted of her shoulder, copper-warm, and he made sure she found that too, because fair trade was the whole arrangement and he'd never once shorted her.

When he ended it, he ended it his way: her bottom lip dragged slow through his teeth, a controlled pull that finished in one bright sting. Not enough to split. Enough to keep.

"Five," he said against her mouth. "That one's on your lip. You'll feel it every time you talk tomorrow." The grin was in the words; she couldn't see it, but she'd hear it. "And you always have plenty to say."

Then he stopped spending words.

He settled his weight into her and found the angle he wanted, and everything he'd banked on that slow walk down the hallway got spent at once — no patience left anywhere in him, rhythm gone rough and honest, the rug writing its own long argument across her back. Every drive of his hips bore down through the laced grip, knuckles to weave, her hands held exactly where he'd put them, and his breath came apart against her ear.

"Still counting," he managed, wrecked.

The count did not survive. He'd get back to it — he always did, and she'd hold him to every mark — but right then the ledger was on fire, and Bear, patient and planning and precise, let it burn.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop.

He honored it the way he honored every term of their arrangement — completely, and past the point of sense. The rhythm he'd found went rough and then rougher, and he stopped steering it and just drove, the rug laying its long argument up her back, his hands still laced through hers with the grip turned bruise-honest, both of them holding on like the floor might otherwise give way. The hallway filled up with sound — breath, fabric, the frame ticking crooked on its nail — and he gave up on sorting any of it.

He held the count as long as he could. Arithmetic went first. Then the planning, which had never happened before, not once in eight years, and he'd remember that later with something like professional embarrassment. Then the patience — all that banked stillness from the slow walk down the hall, spent in one final, unguarded run, his spine drawing tight, his weight bearing down through the knotted grip of their hands, until the world narrowed to heat and rug and her, and he came apart against the mark on her shoulder with a sound like something structural giving way, teeth finding skin one last time out of pure instinct, muffling himself in her because that was where he lived now.

He stayed where he landed. Full weight, breath wrecked, letting their lungs argue over whose was louder. Then he rolled just far enough to spare her ribs — not far, a leg thrown over both of hers, an arm across the wreckage of them — because letting go wasn't on the table and wouldn't be for a while.

He took inventory from the floor, lazy and thorough. The frame hung crooked. Her shirt had died somewhere past the bathroom door. He started laughing, low and scraped, because eight years in she could still ambush him with the sheer fact of her.

"Six," he said, gravel where his voice used to be. "That one doesn't have a location. It's just everywhere." His mouth found the top of her spine, where the rug had signed its own work in red. "That one's not mine. Sue the rug."

His thumb traced one slow circuit over the back of her hand — the hand he'd refused to take when she'd offered her wrists, because her hands were half the fun and always had been.

"Thursday," he said. "You wanted them hurting on Thursday." The grin was gone; what remained was quieter, and worse, and fully operational. "I can work with Thursday. But you're going to need the mirror for the full tally — and I'm nowhere near out of debt."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I'm still pinned under him, feeling the heat of the rug marks on my back. I turn my head, my cheek against the floor. "Thursday's ambitious. I like it." I let go of his hand, just to slide my palm up his arm, fingers digging into the muscle. "So where's the next one going?"

dialogue.content: I trace a line down his side with my fingernail, leaving a faint red trail. "I want one right here." I tap the spot just above his hipbone. "Somewhere your jeans will rub it raw all day."

dialogue.content: He caught my hand before it could go further, his grip firm but not stopping me. "You'll have to take it," he said, voice still rough. "I'm not giving it away."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable laughed, low and warm, the sound more breath than voice.

"Bossy," she said. "From the one who's tied down."

She didn't wind down. She did what she always did when she heard that particular green: she slowed *time* instead of intensity. She let the silence stretch until it had weight, until the only sound in the room was the old radiator ticking and her own measured breathing. She knew exactly how long Ines could stand waiting before the waiting became its own sensation, and she stopped a hair short of it.

The flogger's falls trailed across a shoulder blade, soft as a question. Then the other one. Then nothing.

"Five more," Sable said. She set her palm flat between Ines's shoulders, not pressing, just *there*, a fixed point. "You're going to count them, and you're going to feel every one, and when we reach five I'm going to decide whether you've earned six." She leaned close enough that her words landed at the nape of Ines's neck. "Don't get greedy. I'll know."

She stepped back, found her stance, rolled her wrist once to loosen it. Five years had taught her the rhythm of this body the way a musician learns an instrument: where it sang, where it needed rest, where one well-placed stroke would do more than ten careless ones.

The first came in a clean diagonal, heavy and thudding rather than sharp, the kind that bloomed slowly instead of stinging. She let it settle. She watched, the way she always watched, for the small tells she'd catalogued over the years, reading the breath, the set of the hands, everything that said *more* and anything that might quietly say *careful*.

Then she waited, flogger loose at her side, eyebrow raised though Ines couldn't see it.

"I didn't hear a number."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content:
(InOC: I can't see her eyebrow raise, but I'll play along.)

"One," I breathed out, the sound shaky against the floor. My fingers curled against the rug. "And you're taking your sweet time with the next one."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Am I," Sable said. It wasn't a question.

She let the complaint hang in the air, unanswered, which was its own answer. The radiator ticked. Somewhere below them a car door shut, and a pair of voices faded down the street. Sable listened to all of it, and she listened most closely to the sound of Ines breathing against the rug, the slight hitch at the top of each inhale that meant anticipation rather than strain. She'd learned the difference years ago and never stopped checking for it.

"Sweet time is the only kind I keep," she said at last. "You knew that when you said green."

She stepped in, not to strike but to crouch, one knee on the rug beside those curled fingers. She didn't touch them. She just let Ines feel her there, close enough to hear the faint creak of the leather handle in her grip.

"Loosen your hands."

She waited until they did. She wasn't satisfied with *nearly* loosened.

"Good. Keep them like that. If they close up again, I'll assume you're bracing, and bracing means you're thinking about the next one instead of feeling this one." She rose, unhurried. "We're not rushing to the end. The end will still be there."

The second stroke came from the other side, a mirror of the first, landing low across the opposite shoulder. The falls wrapped just slightly and dragged as she drew them away, heavy and deliberate. It was the same weight as before, but the waiting had changed how it would land, and she knew it.

Sable stayed exactly where she was afterwards, flogger lifted to shoulder height and held there, visible in the edge of Ines's vision if she turned her head, and perfectly still.

"Well?" she said softly. "I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched the restraints take the strain and hold, the way they were meant to. She'd checked every buckle twice before they started, run two fingers under each cuff, and she checked again now with her eyes: no pull at the wrist that looked wrong, no colour change in the fingers. Just a body testing its edges because it liked finding them.

The hands, she noted, were still loose. Ines had tugged with her arms and kept her fingers open. *Clever.*

"Not yet," Sable repeated, tasting it.

Two words could mean a great many things. Most nights she'd have known which without asking, and she thought she knew now, from the lift of that breath and the tilt of the head. But *thought* wasn't the standard she kept, and five years hadn't made her lazy. She lowered the flogger, stepped close, and laid two fingers against the inside of Ines's wrist, just above the cuff. Pulse quick, steady. Skin warm.

"That's a game," she said quietly, "and not a yellow. Yes?"

She waited for the answer, however it came. She would have waited all night.

Then, when she had it, the warmth in her voice cooled by one careful degree, and she straightened.

"All right. Here's how this works, since you've decided to be interesting." She walked a slow half-circle, her footsteps soft on the rug. "A stroke without a number doesn't count. It still *lands*, mind. You'll still feel it. It just doesn't get you any closer to five." She paused at Ines's shoulder. "So you can hold that number as long as you like. I'm very patient, and my arm is not remotely tired."

She let that settle. The radiator filled the gap with its small metallic ticking.

The next stroke fell exactly where the second had, the same heavy thud and the same slow drag of the falls, as if to make a point about repetition. She didn't hurry the follow-through.

"That," Sable said, "was also two. Or it wasn't. That's entirely up to you."

She lifted the flogger again and held it there, still as before, and let the silence ask the question for her.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath, my shoulders flinching from the impact. The deliberate repetition made my skin sing. "Two," I finally whispered.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the number, and she heard what came just before it too: the sharp exhale, the flinch that ran through both shoulders and didn't quite settle back into the rug.

She didn't move right away. She read the flinch the way she read everything else. It wasn't a guard coming up. The fingers were still open, and the breath after it had come back down at an ordinary pace, not held or thin. The skin across the upper back had flushed a deep, even rose, heaviest where the last two strokes had landed on top of each other. Sable looked at that patch for a long moment and made a quiet decision about it.

"Two," she agreed. "Finally."

She stepped in and laid her palm over the place the falls had doubled up, flat and cool against the heat of it. She didn't rub. She just held her hand there and let Ines feel the difference in temperature.

"You've made this spot very popular," she murmured. "So it's getting a rest. The next three go somewhere new, and you don't get to know where until they land." Her thumb moved once, a small slow arc, then lifted away. "That's what you get for stalling. Anticipation, with nothing to anticipate *toward*."

She came around to the other side, deliberately letting her footsteps be heard, then went quiet. She shifted her weight without a sound, changed her angle, and waited long enough that the sense of where she stood would start to blur.

Three came lower than any of the others, a broad horizontal across the meat of the back, well clear of the spine and kidneys. She never aimed near those, however much the scene was flowing. It was the heaviest stroke yet. The falls spread wide and thudded together, and she pulled the follow-through back into a slow, dragging exit.

This time she didn't lift the flogger into view. She let it hang at her side, silent, and for once she gave no hint about the pause. There was no *well?* and no *I'm listening*, just the radiator and her own even breathing somewhere in the room.

Sable watched the hands and the breath and waited to find out whether Ines had learned the lesson or was about to make another one interesting.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the flogger slide from her fingers. It landed on the rug with a soft, heavy sound, and that was the end of the count.

Three would do. The missing number could stay missing. She'd decided somewhere between the second stroke and the third that what she wanted wasn't five. It was *this*. They'd talked it through days ago over coffee, plainly, the way they always did: if the night went well, if the green stayed green, what came after the flogger. She'd listened to the answer then. She was acting on it now.

She knelt, and the room narrowed.

Her hands went first, slow over the heat she'd raised, learning its map again. Her mouth followed where her hands had been. She was unhurried in the way she was unhurried with everything, which was its own kind of cruelty and its own kind of devotion. Five years had taught her more than where to land a stroke. She knew where the breath caught and where it broke, and how to keep someone right at the edge of losing words until they lost them entirely.

She didn't stop reading, even then. That was the part no one ever saw. Under everything, she was still watching the hands, the pulse, the sound of the breath, making sure every tremor meant *yes*.

When it was over, she stayed exactly where she was for a while, one arm heavy across Ines's back, her cheek resting against a warm shoulder blade, and let the radiator tick the room back into being.

Then she moved, because she always moved at this point, no exceptions.

The buckles came first, one wrist, then the other. She eased each cuff off with care and took the hands in her own, turning them over in the lamplight. She pressed her thumb gently into each palm and watched the colour come back into the fingertips. She rubbed slow circles into the wrists where the leather had been and checked the skin for any mark that shouldn't be there. There wasn't one.

"There you are," she murmured.

She reached for the blanket she'd folded over the chair before they started, the soft heavy one, and drew it up over the back she'd flogged. It went on gently, weighted but never pressing on the flushed places. The water glass was on the side table where she'd left it, sweating a little. She brought it down to the rug and set it within reach.

"Small sips when you're ready. Not before." She tucked a damp strand of hair back behind Ines's ear and left her hand resting there, warm against the side of the face. "No rush. The end's here now. We can stay in it as long as you like."

She settled onto her side on the rug, close enough to be felt, far enough to give room, and kept her voice low and easy.

"Talk to me when you've got words again. How are you doing, love? Anything sore that shouldn't be?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my face into her palm, my words still thick. "Everything's exactly the right kind of sore." I reach for the blanket and pull it tighter around me. "Don't move yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't move.

She had no intention of it. *Don't move yet* was an instruction she'd been given in some form a hundred times over five years, and she had never once treated it as a request to negotiate. She stayed on her side on the rug with her palm cupped to Ines's cheek and let the warmth of that turned face settle into her hand.

"Exactly the right kind," she repeated softly, pleased and trying not to sound smug about it. She failed a little. "Good. That's what I was going for."

She shifted, but only to bring herself closer. She fitted her body along the length of the blanketed one beside her, careful to keep her arm across the lower back and well away from the upper shoulders, where the heat still lived under the wool. Her knees tucked in behind. Her breath evened out to match the rhythm she could feel through the blanket, slow and a little ragged still, easing by degrees.

"I'm not going anywhere," she said into the hair at the back of Ines's neck. "The radiator can tick itself hoarse. We've got nowhere to be."

For a while she said nothing else. She let her thumb trace the line of a cheekbone, back and forth, unhurried. The lamp threw long soft shadows across the rug, over the flogger lying where she'd dropped it and the discarded cuffs beside it. She'd deal with those later. They were nothing that couldn't wait.

Some quiet part of her was still watching. It always would be. It noted the tremor that came and went in the shoulders, fine as a guitar string settling after it's been played. It noted that the tremor was fading and not building. It noted the grip on the blanket, holding on hard and then loosening. She had seen that before and knew it for what it was, a body coming back to itself at its own pace, and she didn't try to hurry it along.

"You were lovely tonight," she murmured. "Stubborn, too. Very stubborn. Holding that number hostage like it owed you money." A breath of a laugh. "I'm keeping the other two, by the way. You can have them another night, if you're very good. Or very bad. I haven't decided which earns them."

She pressed a kiss to the nape of Ines's neck, light and dry, and felt the skin warm under her lips.

The water glass was still sitting within reach, beaded with condensation. She glanced at it and didn't reach for it yet. It would keep for a few more minutes. So would everything else.

"When you're ready," she said, low and easy, "I'll get the arnica for your shoulders, and maybe the kettle. Tea or hot chocolate, your choice." Her arm tightened a fraction, gentle. "But not yet. You said not yet, and I'm very good at listening to that."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable hadn't planned it. That was the honest truth, and she'd admit it later over tea, a little sheepishly. One moment she'd been lying there with her lips at the nape of a warm neck, thinking about arnica. The next, Ines had pressed back into her, a slow, unmistakable arch under the blanket, and every plan in the room had rearranged itself.

Still, the scene had ended. She'd taken off the cuffs and drawn up the blanket, and in Sable's rules a finished scene didn't get to restart on assumption.

So before anything else she'd tipped her mouth to Ines's ear and asked, quiet and entirely serious, "Colour?" She'd waited for the answer, and it had come back green. Only then had she pushed the blanket down to the small of the back, gentle over the flushed skin, and started again.

She was slower this time. Tender where the flogger had been, and wicked everywhere else.

The first time she brought Ines to the edge, she felt it coming the way you feel a wave gather under you, and she simply stopped. She didn't pull away. She stayed close enough to breathe on heated skin and did nothing else at all. She let the moment crest, hang there, and ebb back out.

"Not yet," she murmured, and couldn't keep the delight out of it. "Your words, love. I'm only borrowing them."

The second time she stopped at the last possible moment, and the swearing started. It came out muffled and furious, pressed into the crook of Ines's own arm. Sable laughed against the inside of a thigh, soft and completely unrepentant.

"Language."

The third time she lingered longest of all, and she drew the edge out so fine it was almost cruel. Then she stopped again, and the curse that followed was creative enough to earn a moment of genuine professional respect.

But she was watching, even now. She was always watching.

She looked at the arm Ines was pressing her mouth into, and she looked hard, because teeth were teeth. She reached up and slid two fingers between Ines's lips and her forearm, gently easing the space open. She checked the skin in the lamplight and found faint pink impressions, nothing broken, nothing that would bruise.

"Bite the blanket if you need to bite something," she said, low. "Not yourself. I've been very careful with you tonight and I'm not letting you undo my work." She pressed her lips once to the marks on the forearm, a small soft apology on Ines's behalf. "Colour, still?"

She waited. She would always wait.

Then she bent her head again, and her voice came warm against the skin.

"That's three. I think we both know what number comes next." A pause, and then, fond and dangerous: "Count for me."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I choke out "three" against the blanket, my voice ragged. "You are a fucking menace."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"A menace," Sable agreed, and she sounded delighted. "Say it again. It's very good for my ego."

She didn't move for a moment. She rested her cheek against the inside of a thigh and let her breath go slow and warm there, and she listened. Under the ragged voice and the fury she heard what she was listening for: no thinness, no edge of real distress, no quiet catch that meant *enough*. It was only frustration, bright and wanting, from someone who had said green twice tonight and meant it both times.

She noted the blanket, too, bunched in a fist where the forearm had been. *Good.* She'd been listened to.

"Three," she repeated softly. "You counted. Even while you were calling me names." Her thumb traced a slow line along the crease of a hip, idle and deliberate. "That was the lesson from earlier, wasn't it? You've learned it beautifully. And I did say good behaviour might earn you something."

She lifted her head just enough that her voice would carry, low and clear in the lamplit quiet.

"So here's the rule for four. There isn't one." A pause, and her tone softened into something that was nearly tenderness and nearly teasing and entirely both. "I'm not stopping this time. You don't have to hold anything. You don't have to earn it. When it comes, let it."

She bent her head again. This time there was no pause at the top of the wave and no hovering at the edge to make a point. She was just as patient as before and just as thorough, but now all of it pointed one way. She kept one hand spread flat and steady low on the back, well clear of the flushed shoulders, a fixed point the way her palm had been at the very start of the night.

She was still watching. She would always be watching. But what she watched for now was simpler: the moment the fight went out of that body and something else came in to replace it.

"Four," she murmured against warm skin, not an order or a question, just a word left there for whoever needed it. "Whenever you're ready, love. I've got you."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still for exactly one breath.

She knew that phrase. They'd built it together two years ago, on a Sunday afternoon with the rain coming down, and they'd turned it over and argued about it until it meant precisely what they needed. It was permission and instruction at once. *Stop asking. Stop checking out loud. I've already said yes to all of it.* It had never once been said lightly.

"All of it," she repeated, low, so Ines would know she'd heard it and knew what it was. "Then kind."

That was the last gentle thing she said for a while.

Her hand on the lower back stopped being a fixed point and became a weight instead, pressing down and pinning. Her other hand found a hip and held it hard enough to leave the memory of fingers. The patience she'd been spending all night like a miser went out of her in one motion, and what replaced it was focused, relentless and entirely without mercy. There was no hovering at the edge now and no borrowed *not yet*. She drove toward the end the way she'd driven the strokes of the flogger earlier, with all her weight behind it and five years of knowing exactly where to land.

When the swearing came again she didn't laugh this time. She just gave more.

Under all of it, quiet as a pilot light, the watching went on. The phrase didn't switch it off. Nothing ever did. It only meant she did it silently. She tracked the breath climbing and the blanket fisted and hauled, and the moment the whole body under her hands drew tight as a bowstring. She didn't ease off at the top. She'd been told not to be kind, and she wasn't. She held on through all of it and past it, until what she felt under her palms changed from fight to something shaking and wrung out and done.

Then she stopped, completely and at once, the way she'd promised.

And she was kind.

She came up the length of that body slowly, drawing the blanket with her and settling it back over the flushed shoulders, careful as she'd been the first time. She lay down close, one arm around the waist, and pressed her forehead to the back of Ines's head. For a long moment she just breathed there.

"There," she murmured. The edge had gone out of her voice as if it had never been there. "There. That's all of it. You're done, love. Nothing else is coming."

Her hand moved in long, slow strokes along the side under the wool, from ribs to hip and back again, over and over.

"I've got you. You don't have to do anything. Not a word, not a number." She kissed the back of the neck, feather-light. "Just breathe with me for a bit."

The radiator ticked. The lamp hummed faintly. The water glass sat on the rug, still beaded, still within reach.

Sable waited to see what came back first, words or tears or laughter or nothing at all. She'd seen all of them before, and she was ready for any of them. She wasn't going anywhere.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my face into the rug, breathing through the aftershocks until my lungs don't feel too small for my body anymore. "Okay," I whisper, the word muffled. "Now be kind."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Kind," Sable said softly. "I can do kind."

She didn't hurry. Kind had never meant fast. She shifted up onto one elbow and slid her hand under the blanket to rest flat between the shoulder blades, where she'd set it at the very beginning of the night. It wasn't pressing and it wasn't pinning. It was just *there*, warm and still, the same fixed point, so the night would have a shape that started and ended in the same place.

"Hear that?" she murmured. "Your breathing's coming back down. Good. Nice and slow. You're doing it perfectly."

She stayed like that until the rhythm under her palm had settled into something easy, and a little longer after that, because she liked to be sure.

Then she reached for the water.

"Right. First things first." She slid her other arm carefully under Ines's shoulders, avoiding the hottest places, and eased her up just enough to drink, with most of the weight resting against Sable's own chest. She held the glass herself and tilted it slowly. "Small sips. I know you're thirsty. Small anyway."

She waited through each sip and took the glass away between them, then offered it again, until it was half gone. Then she set it down within reach, where it could be found again without effort.

"Good. That's my girl."

She tugged the blanket up and tucked it around Ines's shoulders and under her chin, turning her into something like a warm parcel. She checked the edge of the wool to be sure it wasn't dragging on the flushed skin. It wasn't.

"I'm going to get up for thirty seconds," she said, and said it plainly, because leaving without warning was never kind. "Arnica, a proper pillow, and the other blanket from the bed. I'll be right there, where you can hear me. Thirty seconds. Then I'm back and I'm not going anywhere else."

She kept her word, and she kept talking the whole time so there was never a silence without her in it. "Arnica's in the drawer. Found it. Your pillow, the lumpy one you insist is better than mine. It isn't, by the way. Blanket." She was back in twenty-five seconds and slightly smug about it. She eased the pillow under Ines's head and spread the second blanket over the first, and then she knelt.

"Shoulders now. I'll be gentle. Tell me if anything's tender in a way it shouldn't be."

She folded the blankets back only as far as she needed to, and warmed the arnica between her palms before it touched skin. Her fingertips moved in slow, feather-light circles over the rose-dark patch where the strokes had doubled up, then outward across the rest, never pressing, just soothing heat into calm. She hummed under her breath while she did it, tuneless and low, something she probably didn't know she was doing.

"Beautiful colour," she murmured. "Even, no welts, no broken skin. You'll feel it tomorrow when you lean back in a chair, and you'll think of me, and you'll be insufferable about it."

She tucked the blankets back into place and lay down behind, fitting herself close. She kept her arm across the waist again, well clear of the shoulders, and pressed her lips to the crown of Ines's head.

"You were brave tonight," she said quietly, and there was no teasing in it now at all. "And honest. Every green you gave me, I believed, because you've never once given me one you didn't mean. Do you know how much I love that? How safe that makes it for both of us?" Her thumb stroked slowly along a hip through the wool. "I'm so proud of you. I'm so glad you're mine."

The radiator ticked. The lamp hummed. Somewhere outside a late bus sighed past and faded away.

"Kettle's whenever you want it," she added after a while, softer still. "Tea or hot chocolate. Toast, if you're hungry. Or nothing at all, and we just lie here till the radiator gives up." A small, fond breath against the back of the neck. "And tomorrow, over breakfast, you can tell me what you loved and anything you didn't. But that's tomorrow."

She tightened her arm a fraction.

"Tonight you just get to be held. I've got you, love. I've got you."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
(OOC: Taking this as a continuous retelling of the finish, with the cuffs still on through the end, straight into aftercare with no cut. Keeping it at the same heat level we've been writing at.)

---

The last of it didn't come gently, because she'd been told not to be kind yet.

Sable had her weight braced over the small of Ines's back, one hand spread flat and pinning, the other locked hard around a hip. The cuffs were still buckled, and she was aware of them the way she was aware of everything, a line of leather at each wrist that she checked without seeming to. She'd stopped asking out loud the moment she'd heard the phrase. She hadn't stopped reading. She never did.

She felt it building. The breath came short and high and then stopped coming at all. The fingers had opened and closed and opened again, and the whole length of the body under her drew taut against the restraints, pulling, as if there were somewhere to go. There wasn't. That was rather the point.

She didn't let up at the top. She'd promised not to. She kept the rhythm exactly where it was, relentless and unhurried in its own way, and held on through the moment everything broke, through the sound that wasn't a word, through the long shuddering pull against the cuffs, and a few seconds past it. That was the last of *all of it*, the part she'd been asked for and meant to give in full.

Then she felt the change under her palms, fight becoming something wrung out and trembling, and she stopped.

She didn't taper or ease off by degrees. She stopped completely, all at once, the way she'd promised two years ago on a rainy Sunday.

For one breath she stayed where she was, forehead dropped to the warm skin between the shoulder blades, her own lungs working. Then she moved, because this was the part she never, ever let wait.

The left cuff first. Her fingers found the buckle without looking. She'd set them up that way, both buckles on the outside, so she'd never have to fumble. The strap slid free and she caught the wrist before it could drop, easing it down to the rug. Then the right. She drew both hands in toward the body so the shoulders could come out of the stretch slowly rather than all at once, and she kept her own palms over them while they did.

The shaking had started. It ran through the shoulders and down the arms in fine, rolling waves, and she'd seen it enough times to know it for what it was: not cold and not fear, just a body letting go of something it had been holding for an hour. She didn't try to stop it. She only made sure it had somewhere warm to happen.

The blanket was on the chair. She reached it in one long stretch without taking her other hand off Ines's back, shook it open and drew it down over the whole of her, shoulders to heels, before the first tremor had finished. She settled the wool slowly over the flushed places so it rested rather than dragged, then tucked the edge in under one side and pressed it down.

Then she lay down behind her, close, one arm over the blanket at the waist and well clear of the shoulders, and she didn't say anything.

Neither of them did.

The radiator ticked. The lamp hummed. Sable breathed slow and deliberate against the back of Ines's neck, not asking anything of her, just offering a rhythm to fall into if she wanted one. Under her arm she felt the tremors come and go, lessening each time, the gaps between them growing longer. She counted them without meaning to. It was an old habit. Seven, then five. Then a long quiet stretch, then one more, small, like an afterthought.

She let the silence go on as long as it wanted to. She'd learned years ago that the quiet after was its own kind of care, and that filling it too soon was for her comfort, not anyone else's.

When the shaking had faded almost to nothing, she moved her hand, only a little. She slid it under the edge of the blanket and found one wrist, turning it gently toward the lamplight. She ran her thumb over the place the cuff had been. The skin was warm, faintly marked with the ordinary pink pressure of leather, and no worse. The fingertips had their colour. She pressed into the palm and watched the blood come back. She did the other one the same way, just as slowly, and tucked both hands back into the warmth.

The water glass sat on the side table, beaded with condensation. She reached for it and set it on the rug, near enough to find, and left it there. Not yet. Not until there were words, or at least a nod.

She settled back in and rested her lips against the crown of Ines's head. She didn't kiss, just rested there.

"I'm here," she said at last, barely louder than the radiator. It wasn't a question and it didn't need an answer. "That's all of it. It's finished. You're safe, and you're warm, and I'm not going anywhere."

Her hand began to move beneath the blanket in long slow strokes from ribs to hip and back.

"Take as long as you want. When you've got words, I'll want some. Just a few. How you are, and whether anything hurts that shouldn't. There's water right by your hand." A breath, warm and quiet. "But not yet, if not yet is what you need. I can wait. You know I can wait."

She kept stroking, slow and steady, and let the room hold them both.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my face into the blanket, my voice still rough. "Everything hurts exactly right." I swallow against the dryness in my throat. "Water. Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Water," Sable repeated softly. "Of course."

She'd been waiting for that word and she moved the moment it came, though without any rush. Rushing now would undo everything the quiet had built. She came up onto one elbow and reached past Ines's shoulder for the glass on the rug, then paused with it in her hand.

"Up a little first. I'll do the work."

She slid her free arm beneath the blanket and under Ines's shoulders, low and careful, keeping well away from the heat still sitting in the upper back. She brought her up slowly, just far enough, and let the weight settle back against her own chest so nothing had to hold itself upright. She kept the blanket bunched around them both, not letting it slip.

"There. I've got you. Lean on me, that's what I'm for."

She brought the glass to Ines's lips and tilted it herself, barely, so the first sip was small.

"Slowly. I know your throat's dry. You made quite a lot of noise." It came out fond, with no teasing edge. "Little sips, then we'll do more."

She took the glass away after each one and waited, watching the swallow and the breath that followed, before she offered it again. She'd learned long ago that gulping water after a scene like this could turn a stomach, and she wasn't going to let a good night end queasy on a rug. Four sips. Five. She felt the body against her chest soften a little more each time, the last stiffness leaving the neck.

"Good," she murmured. "That's it. You're doing beautifully."

When the glass was a little over half gone she set it down within reach, on the side nearest Ines's hand, and turned it so the dry part of the rim faced her.

"There's more whenever you want it. You don't have to ask. Just reach."

She didn't lay Ines back down straight away. She stayed as she was, propped against the chair leg, holding her there against her chest with the blanket wrapped around them both. She brushed the damp hair back from Ines's forehead with two fingers and let her hand rest there for a moment, checking the warmth without seeming to. Warm, not hot. Pulse settling under the jaw where her knuckles grazed it. Good.

"Everything hurts exactly right," she said quietly, turning the words over. "That's the best review I've had in years, you know. I might have it framed."

She pressed her lips to Ines's temple and kept them there.

"I'm going to put arnica on those shoulders in a little while, once you're ready to lie on your front again. And I'm going to make you eat something, even if it's only a biscuit, because you'll thank me in the morning." Her thumb traced a slow line down the side of the blanket, over an arm. "But there's no hurry on any of it. We can sit right here as long as you like."

The radiator ticked on. Outside, the street had gone completely quiet.

"How's your head?" she asked, soft and easy. "Floaty, or starting to come back down? Either one's all right. I just like to know where you are."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Still floating," I murmur, leaning into her touch. "But the ground's getting closer." I turn my head slightly to press a kiss to her forearm. "Thank you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the kiss land on her forearm, small and warm and a little clumsy, and something in her chest went quiet and full.

"You don't have to thank me," she said softly. Then, because it was true and she'd never believed in lying at this hour: "But I'll take it. I'll keep it somewhere safe."

She didn't move her arm. She let it stay exactly where it had been kissed, wrapped around the blanket, and she tipped her head down until her cheek rested against Ines's hair.

"Floating's all right. Take your time with the landing. The ground isn't going anywhere, and neither am I." Her thumb moved in a slow arc along the curve of a shoulder through the wool, low and well clear of the heat. "You can drift as long as you like. I'll be the part that stays put."

For a while she just held on and let the room be quiet around them. She listened to the breathing against her chest, slower now and deeper, the rhythm of someone coming home to their own body one step at a time. The lamp hummed. The radiator gave a long ticking sigh, as if it too were settling for the night.

When she spoke again her voice was barely above a murmur.

"Here's what's going to happen, so you don't have to think about any of it." She said it the way she said most things at this point in the night, plainly and gently, laying the next few minutes out like a path. "In a little bit, when you feel heavy enough to lie down, I'll lay you on the pillow on your front. Arnica on the shoulders, very gentle. Then a biscuit. The ginger ones you pretend you don't steal from the tin." A breath of a laugh against her hair. "Then tea, if you want it, and bed, where it's softer than this rug. And I'll stay up with you until you're asleep, or until you tell me to stop fussing. Whichever comes first."

She reached down without looking and nudged the water glass a fraction closer, so the rim sat within an easy reach.

"And if at any point you'd rather do something different, you just say. Or you don't say, and I'll ask. That's the deal, same as always."

She brushed her lips across Ines's temple again and let them rest there a moment.

"You were extraordinary tonight," she said, and there wasn't any performance in it at all, only fact, spoken quietly into warm skin. "Thank *you*. For trusting me with all of it. I don't ever take that for granted, love. Not once in five years."

She settled back against the chair leg and drew the blanket up a little higher, so it covered them both to the shoulders, and she held on.

"Tell me when the ground arrives," she murmured. "I'll be right here to catch you when it does."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a long breath, my body finally going heavy against hers. "Ground's here," I whisper. "Arnica, then ginger biscuits. And don't pretend you don't steal them too."
