dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held the pause for one measured breath, watching closely as she took in the answer.

“Green,” she repeated. “All right. I won’t wind down yet.”

She kept her voice steady, the familiar cadence of the scene settling back into place. “One more measured set. You can change your mind at any point.”

Then she resumed, deliberate and controlled, leaving space between each strike to check the rhythm—and Ines’s colour—before continuing.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, focusing on the rhythmic sound and sensation.* "Don't space them out so much. I don't need checking on."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the strain in the request and gave a small, steady nod.

“I heard you. I’ll keep the rhythm tighter. The check stays—but I won’t make you answer after every one.”

She resumed with the same measured control, closing the gaps between strikes without letting the pace run away. Her attention stayed on Ines as closely as ever, even when she didn’t ask for another colour aloud.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched the restraints take the test, then checked their fit with a practiced glance. She didn’t mistake it for a request to stop.

“Not yet,” she agreed, voice low and steady. “One measured set, as agreed.”

She resumed at the tighter rhythm Ines had asked for, controlled and even. When the set was done, she let the pause settle and asked, “Colour?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I close my eyes, biting back frustration.* "Still green. I told you not to check so much."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the pause settle, then gave a small nod.

“You’re right. I said I wouldn’t make you answer after every one, and I still put the check right at the end of the set. I’m sorry.”

She kept her voice steady, without shifting into the wind-down routine. “That was the one we agreed on. I won’t add another set by guessing, and I won’t keep asking for your colour. If you want more, tell me how much.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the answer as permission to continue, not as permission to stop paying attention.

She set the impact aside and returned to the close, deliberate rhythm of her hands. Her mouth followed, unhurried but without the long pauses Ines had asked her to avoid. Sable kept her focus fixed on the small cues she knew well, ready to ease off the instant anything changed.

“I heard you,” she murmured. “No more questions. If green changes, you tell me.”

Then she let the cadence carry on, steady and assured, giving Ines room to lose the thread without losing Sable’s careful attention.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I grab her wrist, not to stop her but to keep her close.* "Don't you dare get gentle on me now."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the grip keep her close. Her gaze held steady, and the corner of her mouth tightened—not quite a smile.

“I won’t,” she said. “But I won’t confuse rough with careless.”

She leaned back into the hold and resumed with firmer intent, keeping the rhythm close and controlled. Her attention never wandered from Ines; she gave no new check-in, only stayed ready to respond if the colour changed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the muffled swearing and gave a quiet, satisfied hum. This time, she didn’t pull away to leave Ines hovering at the edge again.

She kept close and made the rhythm decisive, firm, and unbroken—intense, never careless. “No more teasing pauses,” she murmured. “I’ve got you.” Her attention stayed fixed on Ines, ready for any change in her cues as she continued.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I drag her closer, nails digging into her back. "Don't you stop."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the sting of Ines’s nails without pulling away. She stayed close and kept the rhythm firm and unbroken, giving the plea exactly the force it asked for—without letting intensity turn careless.

“I won’t stop,” she murmured against her. “I’ve got you.”

And she kept going, attentive to every shift, ready to change course if Ines’s green changed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable understood the phrase. She held Ines’s gaze for one steady beat, then gave a small nod.

“All of it,” she said. “Hard. Then kind.”

She brought the scene to its final crescendo with the same fierce control she’d held all night: no hesitation, no careless rush, nothing left unfinished. When it was over, she stopped at once and let the silence settle.

Then the change in her was immediate. She secured what needed securing, eased Ines out of the restraints carefully, and covered her in warmth. A glass of water waited within reach.

Sable stayed close, one hand steady against her. “We’re done,” she murmured. “You’re safe. Colour?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: *I'm shaking, and I don't try to hide it.* "Green." *My voice is raw.* "But don't ask me again for at least an hour."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable nodded, taking the boundary seriously.

“Understood. No more colour checks for an hour.”

She kept the blanket warm around Ines and stayed close without demanding anything from her. The water remained within easy reach. “You don’t have to talk or explain. If you need something, tell me—or use our signal. I’m here.”

Her hand rested steady and light, leaving room for Ines to move away or draw her closer. “We’re done. I’ve got you.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable carried the last moments through without letting the force become disorderly. She kept her attention on Ines, on the practiced cues between them, and on the agreement they had made. When the final beat was done, she stopped. The implement went aside; the scene was over.

“I’m stopping now,” she said, calm and unmistakable. “You’re out of the scene.”

She gave Ines a breath to register the change, then moved to the restraints. Sable released them one at a time, supporting each limb as its tension came away, checking the skin and circulation as she went. She didn’t hurry, and she didn’t turn the practical care into another demand. Once the last restraint was off, she laid it beyond reach and drew the blanket around Ines, covering her before the shaking had passed.

For a while, Sable said nothing. She stayed beside her, close enough to be present and still enough not to crowd her. The room settled around them: the gear put away, the light kept soft, the water placed within easy reach.

After the quiet had held for a few minutes, Sable asked only, “Would you like water, warmth, or space?” She didn’t ask for another colour. The hour mattered, and so did the boundary Ines had set. Sable remained there beneath the blanket’s edge, ready to help without deciding for her what help should look like.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I drink the water slowly, hand still unsteady around the glass. "Warmth," I finally say, voice low, leaning into her side. "And tell me I did good."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the glass safely aside, then drew the blanket closer around them both. She shifted just enough to offer her warmth, letting Ines lean against her without turning the embrace into a hold.

“You did so good,” she said, quiet and certain. “You stayed with me, you told me what you wanted, and you trusted me to bring us through it. I’m proud of you.”

She rested her cheek lightly against Ines’s hair and kept still, giving the warmth time to settle. No questions, no demands—just Sable beside her, steady beneath the blanket.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, the tension finally starting to leave my shoulders. "I didn't want it to end," I admit softly, pressing my face against her neck.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s arm settled around her, warm and loose beneath the blanket. She pressed a quiet kiss to Ines’s hair and stayed still, giving her room to tuck closer or pull away.

“I know,” she said softly. “You didn’t have to want it to end for it to be time to stop.” Her voice remained gentle, without turning the moment into a lecture. “I’m glad you told me. And I’m right here with you now.”

She held the warmth around them and let the quiet return.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "I know," I whisper back, my fingers curling in her shirt. "But I still hate it." I breathe her in for a moment. "Thank you for not listening when I said not to check on me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s mouth curved, but she didn’t reach for the water yet.

“Green heard,” she said. “We finish what we agreed on. Then I wind us down, whether you argue with me or not.”

She checked the restraint with practiced fingers and let the pause stretch, keeping her attention on Ines. Then she picked up their rhythm again, steady and unhurried, leaving room for another answer if the colour changed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, my fingers curling against the restraints. "It's still green," I murmur, trying to sound firm even as my voice wavers a little. "Just... a little longer than we agreed."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stopped the rhythm and met Ines’s eyes.

“No,” she said gently. “Green means we can finish what we agreed on. It doesn’t mean I move the line because you ask me while you’re in restraints.”

She rested a hand near the fastening, steady and unhurried. “We have the last part to go. Then water, warmth, and a check-in. You can argue with me over the blanket.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the rhythm fall away again. She kept one hand beside the fastening, where Ines could see it.

“Not yet can mean two things,” she said. “If you mean you want a pause, we pause. If you mean you don’t want this to end, I heard you. We still finish where we agreed.”

Her voice stayed warm, but the line held. “Tell me which one. I won’t guess while you’re restrained.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a frustrated little groan, tugging against the restraints once more. "It's green, it's still green," I insist, my voice thick. "I just... I don't want it to be over."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s expression softened. “I know,” she said. “You don’t have to want it to be over.”

She waited a beat, watching Ines closely. “You’ve told me you’re green, and you’ve told me what ‘not yet’ meant. I’m going to finish exactly where we agreed. Then I’m staying right here with you.”

She returned to the last part of their rhythm, measured and attentive. At the agreed stopping point, she stopped. No extra beat, however much she might have been asked for one. Her hand went to the fastening.

“You can be disappointed with me,” Sable said, working it loose. “I’ll still get you warm and bring you water.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not start again. Her hands stayed at the fastening, and she worked it loose.

“No extra,” she said, her voice quiet but certain. “I meant what I said.”

She set the restraints aside, drew the blanket within reach, and picked up the water she had left nearby. She stayed close, giving Ines time rather than asking for an answer at once.

“I’m here,” Sable said. “We can talk about wanting more later. Right now, we wind down.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I go limp, turning my face away into the pillow. "Hate you," I mumble, but I don't pull away when she reaches for me.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable tucked the blanket around Ines and left the water within easy reach. She didn’t try to turn her face back.

“That’s all right,” she said quietly. “You can be angry with me. The line still holds.”

She stayed beside the bed, close enough to be found, and gave the silence a little room. Then she asked, “Are your hands all right? Anything numb, sore, or cold?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had not started again. She kept the blanket in place and moved the water a little closer, without trying to draw Ines’s face out of the pillow.

“No more tonight,” she said. “I know that’s hard to hear. I’m staying.”

She sat beside the bed for a moment, then spoke softly. “I still need to know about your hands. Any numbness, or pain where the restraints were?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shake my head into the pillow, my shoulders tight. "Fine," I mutter, voice muffled. "They're fine. Just... don't touch me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable withdrew her hand at once and shifted back from the bed.

“All right. I won’t touch you.”

She left the water within reach and stayed quiet for a moment. “I’ll be over here. You don’t have to talk to me, and you can tell me if you want more space.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed where she was, away from the bed. The familiar phrase caught her attention; so did the request not to be touched.

“I heard you,” she said. “And I know what that phrase means to us. But we reached the stopping point, and I told you no more tonight. I won’t restart while you’re coming down, and I won’t touch you after you asked me not to.”

She kept her voice steady. “The water’s within reach. I’ll stay here unless you want me farther away. Tomorrow, we can talk about whether we want to agree on something different for another night.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I curl tighter into myself, a choked sound escaping. "Fine," I bite out, not looking at her. "Just... stay there, then."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed where she was. She didn’t reach across the space between them or ask another question.

“All right,” she said softly. “I’ll stay here. I won’t touch you.”

She settled quietly in her chair, leaving the water within reach. The line had held; now she could give Ines the silence she’d asked for without leaving her alone.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable counted the last agreed beat and stopped there. She held still for a moment, watching for any sign that Ines needed her to move faster, then set what she’d been holding aside. There was no extra beat. She had promised a stopping point, and she kept it.

“I’m done,” she said, low and clear. “I’m getting the restraints off now.”

She loosened each fastening carefully, checking the places where it had rested without lingering. Once they were off, she set them out of reach and drew the blanket over Ines. The shaking hadn’t quite passed. Sable kept the blanket tucked around her and put the water close enough to take without help.

She stayed beside the bed through the silence. When she finally spoke, it was only to ask, “Any numbness in your hands? Anything that hurts in a way we didn’t expect?”

Later, when Ines told her not to touch her, Sable took her hands away and moved to the chair. She did not try to coax an answer or close the distance again.

“All right,” she said. “I’ll stay here.”

And she did. The water remained within reach; the blanket remained in place. Sable kept watch from where Ines had asked her to be, ready if she was wanted and quiet until then.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let the quiet stretch, the anger bleeding out slow and stubborn. Eventually, I reach for the water, my hand only trembling a little. "You can come over here now," I say, still not looking at her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable rose from the chair and came to the bedside, stopping short of the blanket.

“I’m here,” she said. “I won’t touch you unless you want me to.”

She sat close enough to talk without raising her voice, but left the space between them open. Her eyes flicked to the water, then back to Ines’s turned face.

“You don’t have to be done being angry,” Sable said. “I’m glad you asked me over anyway.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I finally turn my head to look at her, my eyes still a little wet. "I'm not angry," I say quietly. "I just really, really hated you for a minute." I shift over a little, making room on the edge of the bed.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable sat on the edge of the bed, in the space Ines had made, and kept her hands to herself.

“I know,” she said. “That minute was allowed.”

She glanced at the water, then back at Ines. “I’m glad you told me to come back. Would you like me close, or would you rather I just sit here?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I reach out and take her hand, lacing our fingers together. "Close," I whisper, pulling her gently toward me. "I need you close now."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Worked twenty minutes ago," Odile said, which answered a question Fen hadn't asked — namely, when exactly she'd started planning this. She fell into step behind them, matching their pace with the exaggerated casualness of someone who had never once in her life been casual.

The stairs announced her anyway. Every second step let out a creak, and she pressed a hand over her own mouth to smother a laugh, which mostly converted the laugh into a snort. Downstairs, someone had seized the karaoke mic and was murdering a power ballad with real commitment, which she chose to interpret as sound cover.

At the landing she caught up, hooked one finger into Fen's belt loop, and towed them the last few feet down the hall. Door open, both of them in, and then the lock turned with a click that seemed, in the sudden muffled quiet, approximately as loud as a gunshot.

"There," she whispered, grinning up at them, entirely too pleased with herself. "See? Stealth. I'm basically a professional."

She was already backing up against the sink counter, pulling Fen with her by the front of their shirt, when someone started thumping up the stairs behind them.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Shit," I breathe, my eyes widening. My hand flies up to cover Odile's mouth instinctively, even though she wasn't the one who made noise. I listen, frozen, my other hand still tangled in her shirt. The thumping gets closer. "They're coming right to the door."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile's eyes went wide over the top of Fen's hand — not with fear. With delight. The eyes of a woman watching something hilarious happen to her personally.

The footsteps reached the landing. Her shoulders started to shake. She grabbed Fen's wrist — not to pull their hand away, but to hold it there, snug, while a laugh climbed up her throat and got flattened into a thin wheeze against their palm.

The footsteps stopped. The handle rattled, met the lock, rattled again, offended.

Knuckles on the door, polite. "Anyone in there?"

Odile's eyes flicked up to Fen's — an apology in advance — and her chest swelled like she was about to project.

What came out, squeezed through the gaps in their fingers, was: "Occupied." A whisper. Still somehow too loud.

A pause. "...You okay in there?"

"Mm-hm!" Bright. Strangled. Absolutely not okay. A single tear of pure joy sat at the corner of one eye. And then — because she was who she was — she turned her head a fraction and pressed a slow kiss to the center of Fen's palm, right there in the middle of the crisis, her pulse hammering where her chest met theirs, like this was all foreplay. Which, for her, it was.

A mutter from the hall — "fine, jeez" — and the footsteps retreated, unhurried, every stair creak landing like applause.

Odile lasted three seconds. Then she folded forward into Fen, forehead against their shoulder, hiccuping with silent laughter.

"'You okay in there,'" she wheezed, when she could breathe.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The bass came up through the floorboards and into her spine, and Odile arched against the door like it had been arranged for her personally. Downstairs the power ballad finally died and something with an actual beat took over, and the whole house began to thump — loud enough now to swallow anything a locked bathroom might produce.

"Perfect," she said, in what she firmly believed was a whisper. It was not. "Nobody can hear us now."

A beat. The grin crept back, slow and delighted.

"Also means we can't hear anyone coming," she added, in the tone other people reserved for reading winning lottery numbers. "Isn't that fun?"

She reached back without looking and jiggled the handle herself. Held. "Still locked," she reported, smug as a cat presenting a dead bird. "Told you. Professional."

Then she got both hands in Fen's collar and hauled them down to her mouth, and the talking mostly stopped. She kissed the way she did everything else — committed, and slightly too loud, a low pleased hum catching in her throat that she would have sworn under oath was nothing. The laughter hadn't finished draining out of her yet either; it kept fizzing up through her ribs and into the kiss as little smiles she couldn't suppress, because her body simply refused to be serious while this happy. Below them the song hit its chorus and someone whooped, and she broke off just long enough to snort against Fen's jaw.

"'You okay in there,'" she wheezed, one last time, into their skin.

Then she sobered — well, concentrated, which was the closest she ever got — and pulled them in tighter, one heel hooking behind their knee, her mouth finding the line of their neck.

"Okay," she murmured, and this one came out at genuine whisper volume, which felt like a personal achievement worth noting. "Hand stays close. You're going to need it."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: My laugh is soft against her hair. "I think the lock was the only professional thing about this," I murmur, my free hand sliding down to her hip. "And I'm starting to think you planned that interruption, too."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Explain it?" The words came out chopped, rearranged by the door hitting its frame behind her on every thrust. "I'm planning to tell everyone it was a karaoke injury. Very emotional performance. The high note fought back."

Her head tipped back against the wood. The mark throbbed warm under her collar, and she was already looking forward to lying about it badly, which was its own kind of fun.

Then she gave as good as she got — mouth finding the side of Fen's neck, setting her teeth in slow and deliberate, nothing like the rest of her, then soothing it flat with her tongue. "There," she managed. "Matching set. Solidarity."

Somewhere below, the song ended. Two seconds of near-silence opened up between tracks, and into that silence Odile said "oh" — one syllable, round and unmistakable, dropped like a glass on tile.

The bass came back and buried it. Mostly. Downstairs, faint, someone said "did you hear—" and someone else said "hear what," and Odile clapped her own hand over her own mouth this time, shoulders shaking, eyes bright and damp above her fingers.

She lasted four seconds before the hand slid away.

"Nope," she announced, at what she sincerely believed was a whisper. "Don't care. Worth it."

Her free hand groped backward and found the door handle, gripped it for balance. It rattled under her fingers — locked, and somewhere through the fog she registered this smugly — the vibration running up her arm and down her spine while the door knocked out a rhythm against its frame that she was pretty sure she could hear landing downstairs.

"Fen." It was meant as a warning. It came out as a headline. "Fen, I'm — you should — *soon*—"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The handle fought her for it.

Someone on the other side pulled, and Odile — whose hand was still wrapped around the same handle — felt the whole mechanism buck against her grip, and the sound she made had no consonants in it whatsoever.

"Don't," she got out — to Fen, to the door, to the universe — and the voice outside, offended, shot back: "I *can't!* It's locked! That's the whole problem!"

"It's—" Her hand lost the argument and slid off the handle; she grabbed Fen's shoulder instead, nails in, communicating a complex message in braille. "Occupied! Still! Continuing!"

A pause. Then, flat with suspicion, the same voice as before: "Again? It's been twenty minutes."

"Long haul!" Her voice cracked straight down the middle of *haul*. "Great party! Everything's great!"

The voice dropped, said something to a second person — she caught *still in there*, and a second voice, awed: *no way* — and that was the moment the whole thing tipped over. The audience. The rattling lock. Two strangers holding a séance with her through a bathroom door while she — while Fen —

Her heel slipped an inch on the tile and she stopped being able to assemble sentences at all. What came out instead was Fen's name, twice, at a volume that was absolutely going to carry, and then

dialogue.content: "An exorcism?" I choke out a laugh, pressing my forehead to hers as the door rattles harder. "They'd probably ask to watch." I don't slow down, even as the voices outside get more animated. "Let them wonder."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"The lock works," Odile said, following him up. "I checked this afternoon. You know. In case."

The stairs were the dangerous part. The party's noise covered the ground floor fine, but the staircase creaked, and the upstairs hallway had that particular quality of quiet that made her feel eleven years old sneaking past a sleeping house. She flattened herself against the wall on the third step out of pure instinct, then laughed at herself — too loudly — and clapped a hand over her own mouth.

All the bedroom doors were shut. Muffled bass through the floorboards. The bathroom sat at the end of the hall like a finish line.

She went in first, clicked the lock, and turned to assess the venue. Small sink. A candle someone had abandoned unlit. Lighting that was, frankly, doing them both a favor.

"Okay," she whispered, which was not a whisper. "Quick briefing. Risk of the host knocking: moderate. He's had wine. Reward—" she stepped in close and hooked a finger into Fen's collar, walking him backward toward the sink without appearing to move herself "—outstanding."

Her grin was doing the thing it did, the one that meant she'd already decided how this was going to go and was just enjoying the ceremony.

"Also, housekeeping: if someone knocks, we say one of us spilled a drink. I practiced the line in the car." A beat. "It's a good line."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Practiced in the car, huh?" I grin, letting her steer me back. "So this was premeditated." My hands find her hips, pulling her closer against me. "The lock better hold."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Premeditated," she agreed, closing the last inch and delivering the word against the corner of his mouth. "Since four o'clock. You were just the final sign-off. Everything else was already greenlit."

Then, because he'd raised the lock — she reached back without breaking eye contact and jiggled the latch. It rattled like a skeleton in a closet. In the little porcelain quiet of the bathroom it sounded enormous.

"Shh," she told it, seriously.

Then she stopped narrating, because there were better uses for her mouth. She kissed him like the knock was already coming — one hand fisted in his collar, the other braced on the counter behind her — and hopped up onto the sink in a single ungraceful, determined movement that banged her knee on the cabinet and produced a laugh she had to catch with both hands.

The bass pulsed through the wall like a second heartbeat. The candle sat there, unlit, doing its useless best. Her whisper arrived warm against his jaw and, as ever, was not remotely a whisper:

"For the record, I'm being *so* quiet right now."

Down the hall: floorboards. Footsteps — unhurried, wine-adjacent, drifting closer. Odile went absolutely still, eyes wide and bright with the pure, disgraceful joy of it, one palm pressed flat over Fen's mouth like *he* was the security risk. The footsteps paused. Considered their options. Continued on toward the far bedroom.

She held still for three full seconds, then took her hand away and beamed at him in the forgiving light, thrilled with all of it: the room, the lock, the near miss, him.

"Okay," she breathed, catching his hand where it rested on her hip and sliding it slowly around to the small of her back, under the hem of her shirt. Her grin sharpened into something with teeth. "New assignment. I've clearly proven I can't be trusted with the quiet part. That's your job now."

dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to murmur against her lips. "My job is to be quiet, but you're not making it easy." My hand stays on her back, fingers tracing the line of her spine. "Also, you're definitely going to leave bruises on my neck."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The latch delivered its opinion — the same skeletal rattle as before — and Odile chose to interpret that as a security feature. Guard dogs that bark at everything are technically providing a service.

"Bruises," she repeated, delighted, tipping her head back against the door. "Fen. I did *placement planning*. Four o'clock, remember? Why do you think you're wearing that shirt? Everything below the collar line is a team effort. Anything above it—" a shrug, which pressed her back into the wood "—is a you-problem. Review your sign-off documents."

His fingers traced her spine and she arched into it, then caught his wrist — not to move it, just to hold it still for a second while she put on her briefing face, which at this range was mostly pupils.

"Also. You accepted the quiet assignment very confidently for a man I know things about. So: live test." Her hand slid up into his hair. "I'm going to do the thing. You're going to have an opinion about the thing. The opinion stays *internal*."

Then she did the thing — mouth at his neck, exactly at the collar line, taking her time about it with the patience of someone who had, genuinely, been thinking about this since four o'clock. The bass thudded through the door at her back like the whole party leaning on the other side of it.

Downstairs, between one song and the next, the music dropped out entirely. The house's actual sounds came up through the floor: laughter, a chair scraping, someone yelling about a beer run. Odile went statue-still against his throat, one hand flying up to clamp over — belatedly, uselessly — her own mouth.

The song came back. She lifted her head, lips an inch from his ear, and whispered at a volume that would have carried to the kitchen:

"Report. Did you keep it internal?"

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
She held onto something. Specifically, the towel ring beside the doorframe, which surrendered its entire towel on the first pull and left her gripping a single hand towel like a shield at a very strange joust.

"Countermeasure," she whispered, brandishing it, and then stuffed a corner of it against her own mouth — because she had done the math on herself, and the math was not flattering.

The door handled its own percussion after that, every movement knocking the old wood against the jamb in a soft, incriminating *thock* that was outside anyone's jurisdiction. Odile's laugh at discovering this came through the terrycloth as a strangled, joyful hum. Her forehead dropped to his shoulder. Her heel found the back of his thigh. The next sound she made was not a word, and the towel was not rated for it.

Then: the handle.

It turned. Once. The latch rattled — and held. Guard dog, vindicated. Odile's whole body locked up with the specific, disgraceful ecstasy of being exactly where she'd told herself not to be.

*Knock knock.*

"You guys in there?" The host. Wine-adjacent, but gaining on sober.

Odile removed the towel from her mouth with the deliberation of a bomb tech, cleared her throat, and deployed, at an almost eerie level of professional composure:

"All good! Spilled a drink."

A pause. The pause of a man doing math about how many bathrooms his house has.

"There's a, uh—"

"Downstairs one," Odile said, crisp as hotel concierge. "Yes. Thanks."

Footsteps receded. The bass

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath against her neck as she bites down, my other hand bracing harder against the door to keep us steady. "You're terrible at this," I murmur, voice rough. The music swells again, thank god.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Terrible," she repeated, scandalized, riding the swell of the song like it was a personal favor. "Okay. Counterpoint. I have contained myself *twice* tonight under direct provocation, and history will vindicate—"

The song dipped between beats. She bit the sentence off against his jaw and breathed through her nose like a woman negotiating with herself and losing.

"—vindicate *me*," she finished, when the bass came back, and then the floorboards down the hall announced somebody. Voices, this time. Two of them. One saying *she said the downstairs one*, the other saying *the host is on his third glass of 'downstairs one,'* and then — horribly — the creak of someone trying the bedroom doors on their way.

Odile's hand shot out and covered Fen's mouth, full circle, poetic justice, and her eyes said *I know* with enormous smugness while the rest of her went rigid with the effort of silence. The footsteps stopped outside the door. The handle didn't turn. It just hung there while somebody deliberated.

"Occupied!" she called, pitch-perfect, concierge-crisp. "Drink situation! Ongoing!"

A muffled *oh — sorry!* The footsteps retreated toward the stairs, trailing commentary.

She took her hand off his mouth and replaced it with her own mouth, kissing him like a cover-up, which it was, then pulled back half an inch with the briefing face back on, wrecked at the edges.

"Situation update. That's two contacts. That was the advance party. We are on a clock now — someone *will* need this bathroom for its intended purpose, and I refuse to be interrupted by a man who just wants to pee. That's not how I go out."

Her hand found his bracing one and pressed it flatter to the door, steadying the whole structure through him. The abandoned hand towel lay surrendered on the tiles between their feet. Her hips answered the music on their own recognizance.

"So. Efficient modes only. And the quiet assignment—" her composure finally filed for bankruptcy, because what came out next was not a briefing at all, just the truth, close against his ear and not quiet, never quiet, "—is rescinded. Out loud, both of us. Make me fail the test. If we go down, we go down *together*."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The rescinded assignment went into effect immediately and without transition, the way her decisions always did, and it turned out the quiet thing had never been a limitation — it had been a splint. The first sound she let out unrestrained came off her like one, half relief, half recklessness, and after that she stopped negotiating entirely. She rode the song's swells out of habit for maybe four bars, then abandoned even that cover, because the point — the entire point — was failing together, which reclassified the whole operation as doctrine.

The towel got kicked to a corner it would never recover from. The candle wobbled and survived. The door kept honest time against the jamb, the latch rattled its skeleton rattle like applause, and Odile failed the test with honors — loudly, joyfully, one fist knotted in Fen's collar — and when it finally crested she had her forehead jammed against his jaw and was laughing through it, actually laughing, because apparently winning felt like this too: ruinous, unscheduled, entirely off the paperwork.

The sound she made at the end was not a word and had never been containable by terrycloth or anything else, and for once she didn't try.

After: the two of them stacked against the door like a building code violation, bass thudding through the wood at her back, her heartbeat slowly agreeing to rejoin the party's tempo. Her lips found his ear.

"For the record," she whispered, at full broadcast volume, "that was *internal*."

*Knock knock.* Urgent. Unaffiliated. "Hello?? I *really* need to pee."

"One minute!" Odile called, concierge-crisp, concierge-wrecked. "Drink situation! Ongoing!"

A pause. "*Thanks*," said the stranger, with the flat acceptance of a man who had elected not to do the math.

She pressed her hand over her own mouth, shoulders shaking, then pointed at the mirror. Assessment: catastrophic. Hair with plans of its own. She slid down, salvaged what could be salvaged, and smoothed Fen's collar down over the evidence.

"After-action report," she breathed, hand on the latch. "Objectives met. Casualties: one towel, my composure, the lock's innocence. We exit in two minutes — separately, like professionals, or together, like a *statement*." Her grin came back with teeth. "Your call. I win either way."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Together. Let's make a statement." I grab her hand, lacing my fingers through hers. "But you're carrying the towel."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Carrying the—" She looked at the towel where it lay demoted in the corner, then at him. "Fine. But understand what you've authorized. I'm going to carry it like evidence at a tribunal."

She retrieved it and folded it into a brisk, defensible square, then held it up between them.

"There. Now it's a *prop*. We spilled a drink. Upstairs. In a bathroom. Where one famously goes to spill drinks." A beat. "The cover story's held all night. We ride it to the end."

The latch gave one last skeletal rattle as she opened the door — guard dog, discharged with honors — and they went into the hallway hand in hand, which meant the creaky stairs got the full statement: no flattening against walls, no third-step instincts. Odile descended like a procession, chin up, hair operating independently, the folded towel borne before her like a peace offering to a house she had wronged.

"Act natural," she whispered, at a volume that alerted the party two seconds before they appeared.

The party, to its credit, tried to pretend it hadn't been waiting. A few heads turned first, then the rest, the way a crowd drifts toward a verdict. The host stood mid-conversation by the kitchen and stopped mid-word, doing the math again, slower this time, showing his work. *Downstairs one. Right.*

The man from the hallway clocked the towel in her hand like a juror recognizing the weapon.

"Drink situation," Odile announced, raising it, "resolved."

Silence. Then, from the back of the kitchen: "*Called it.*" A second voice, wounded: "There was money—"

"There's been a pool since Tuesday," the host said, to no one, exhausted.

"*Tuesday.*" Odile spun to Fen, scandalized and thrilled in equal measure. "Tuesday. I didn't greenlight this until four o'clock *today*. All that premeditation — the placement planning, the lock reconnaissance — and we were never even the surprise." She stopped. Recalibrated. Addressed the room over her shoulder, concierge-crisp to the last: "For the record: the lock works. Great party."

Then she towed him toward the coats, fingers laced, pausing only to fix his collar one final time — declared it a lost cause, left it standing as a monument — and looked up at him with her eyes narrowed to briefing-width.

"One question on the way out. The pool." A pause with teeth in it. "Were you in it?"

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I let out a sharp breath against her neck as she bites down, my other hand bracing harder against the door to keep us steady. "You're terrible at this," I murmur, voice rough. The music swells again, thank god.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh, quiet but genuine. "Me? Never." My thumb brushes over her knuckles. "But I might have started one."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile stopped dead halfway to the coats, the folded towel staying aloft a beat after the rest of her did.

"Started one," she repeated, and turned, and gave the still-watching room the full briefing face. "Started. As in *founded*. As in Tuesday." She advanced a step, brandishing the towel like a writ. "Fen. I filed my intent to premeditate at four o'clock *today*. You incorporated on Tuesday. You were never the final sign-off — you were the *angel investor*. I have been an asset this entire time and nobody issued me a prospectus."

The math landed, and her eyes went wide with genuine legal injury.

"Which means every near miss, every knock, every single time I failed to be quiet — I was moving *your position*. I was the asset and the volatility. That's insider trading. Pete Rose got banned for life for less."

"*Who won?*" she called past him into the

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I hold up my hands in surrender, grinning. "Okay, fine. I might have told Pete we were a sure thing." My voice drops to a murmur just for her. "And I might have bet on us."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard it and believed it. Green, and meant. She did not soften the next one.

Her hand settled at the nape of Ines's neck for a second, steady, not gentle for its own sake—just so Ines would know she was still being watched—and then she drew back and struck again, the same place, the same weight they'd already agreed on. The sound was clean. She waited through the breath that followed, counting it, then gave the next, and the next, keeping the rhythm they were already inside instead of letting it fray.

"Still with me," she said, low, not a question so much as a line thrown out for Ines to hold. Her free hand stayed where it was, warm against skin, checking the way the body answered rather than the words. No tremor she didn't already know. No pull away.

She did not reach for the water. She did not reach for the blanket. Not yet.

Another strike, deliberate, placed, and she leaned in close enough that her voice would land against the ear and not the room.

"You tell me when it changes," Sable said. "Until then I don't stop."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath hitches, then evens out again. The sting is grounding, anchoring, exactly what I asked for. I press my forehead against the cool leather of the seat beneath me, my fingers curling into the cushion. "I will," I manage, voice a bit rough. "But it hasn't." *God, don't let it.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the hitch in the breath and the evenness that followed it, and she let both of them count. The forehead against the leather. The fingers in the cushion. Nothing in it that asked her to stop, and nothing in it she was willing to mistake for a performance.

"Good," she said, and the word was quiet enough that it barely left the space between them.

She set her palm once more at the nape, a brief press, the same check as before—heat, the give of the muscle, the way Ines stayed down instead of rising into the hand—and then she drew it away and struck. Same place. Same weight. She did not chase the sound. She waited for the breath to come back and land, counted it through, and only then gave the next, keeping the interval they were already living inside so the rhythm would not fray into something neither of them had agreed to.

The free hand returned to skin and stayed there, not soothing, just present, reading the answer the body gave. No new tremor. No pull. The sting was doing what it had been asked to do, and she was not going to insult that by softening it early.

She leaned in again, close, so the next line would meet the ear and not the room.

"Then we stay," Sable said. "You hold the line. I hold the rest. The second it shifts, you say so—and until you do, I don't reach for anything but this."

Her hand lifted. She waited one full breath longer than the last interval, so Ines would feel the pause as chosen and not as doubt, and then she struck again, clean, placed, and settled back into the count.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the test of the restraints—the brief, pointless pull—and let it happen without tightening anything or telling her to stop. She already knew the give in the cuffs, the way Ines's wrists sat in them, and the movement told her nothing new except that Ines was still choosing to stay inside what they'd set.

"Not yet," she repeated, low, taking the words as given. "Heard."

Her hand returned to the nape for one short press, reading heat and the set of the shoulders, then lifted clear. She struck again in the same place, the same agreed weight, and waited out the breath that followed before she gave the next. The interval stayed even. She did not let it hurry, and she did not let it thin.

The free hand settled again against skin, warm and still, tracking the answer in the body rather than in the voice. No new flinch. No pull away from the strike. The forehead stayed down. She kept her own breathing slow so the count between them would not slip.

She leaned in close enough that the next words met the ear.

"You keep telling me," Sable said. "I keep this exactly where it is until you don't."

She drew back, held one full breath past the last interval so the pause would read as deliberate, and struck again—clean, placed, the same as before—then settled into the rhythm and waited for whatever Ines gave her next.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: A shudder rolls through me, but I don't try to hide it. My voice is thick when I speak. "Still green. Still here." *Please.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the shudder as information and not as a cue to stop. It rolled through and spent itself; nothing in the set of the shoulders afterward asked her to break the line they'd agreed on. Still green. Still here. She believed both, and she did not make Ines repeat them.

"I know," she said, close to the ear, the words low enough that they wouldn't have to travel. "I felt it. You're still in it."

Her hand came back to the nape—one firm press, heat and the give under the skin, the way Ines stayed down instead of lifting into it—and then she drew clear. She struck in the same place, the same weight, and held still through the breath that followed until it landed and evened. Only then did she give the next, and the next, keeping the interval exact so the rhythm would not fray into something neither of them had named.

The free hand returned to skin and stayed, warm, reading rather than soothing. No pull away. No new tremor she didn't already have accounted for. The forehead stayed against the leather. She let the pointless flex of the restraints be what it was and did not tighten anything, did not comment on it.

She leaned in again.

"You don't have to hide that from me," Sable said. "You shake if you shake. You stay green until you aren't. I don't reach for the water, I don't reach for the blanket, and I don't soften this because you asked me not to."

She drew back, held the pause one full breath longer than the last so it would read as chosen, and struck again—clean, placed, the same as before—then settled into the count and waited.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not ease off when the words failed. She had been waiting for that—the point where speech thinned and the body took over the answering—and she treated it as information, not as an ending.

Her mouth stayed where it was, unhurried and exact, and her hand kept the rhythm they had already set, the same weight, the same place, so nothing about the intensity drifted into something unplanned. She felt the shudder move through Ines and did not chase it. She waited it out, counted the breath that followed, and only then gave the next strike, clean and placed, while her mouth worked in the interval between.

The free hand returned to the nape for one short press—heat, the set of the shoulders, the way Ines stayed down—and then left again. No pull away. No new flinch that asked her to stop. The restraints flexed once, pointless, and she let them.

She lifted her head just far enough that the next words would meet skin and not the room.

"Still green until you say otherwise," Sable said, low. "I'm not done with you."

She settled back in, mouth and hand both, and kept the count.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My hands fist in the cushions, knuckles white. "Still green," I gasp out, the words barely there. *Don't you dare be done.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the white-knuckled fists in the cushions and the gasp that barely carried the words, and she let both of them stand. Still green. She did not ask her to say it clearer. She did not slow.

"I hear it," she said, the words low against the curve of Ines's ear. "Barely there is still there. I'm not finished with you."

Her mouth settled back where it had been, unhurried and exact, and her hand lifted and came down again in the same place, the same agreed weight. She waited through the breath that followed—felt it hitch, felt it try to even—and only then struck once more, keeping the interval they were already inside so nothing frayed into something unasked for. The free hand returned to the nape for one short press, reading heat and the set of the shoulders, the way Ines stayed down, then left again. No pull away. The restraints took another pointless flex; she let them.

She lifted her head just far enough that the next line would meet skin.

"You hold that," Sable said. "Fists, breath, all of it. You stay green until you aren't. I don't soften this, and I don't stop until you tell me the line has moved."

She drew back, held the pause one full breath longer than the last so it would read as chosen, and struck again—clean, placed—then settled her mouth to the work between and kept the count.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the swearing muffled against Ines's own arm and did not take it as a cue to finish her or to stop. She had brought her to the edge three times on purpose, mouth working her open and then lifting clear each time the breath broke and the hips tried to chase, and she stayed lifted now, close enough that Ines would feel the warmth of it and not the relief.

"I know," she said, low, against the skin just beside where her mouth had been. "You're swearing because I put you there. You're still green. I'm still not done."

Her hand settled at the nape again—one firm press, heat, the locked set of the shoulders, the white-knuckled fists that hadn't let go of the cushion—and then drew away. She struck once, the same place, the same weight they'd kept all night, and waited through the shudder that answered it before she gave the next. The interval stayed exact. She did not let the edging bleed into mercy, and she did not let the impact soften because the words had failed into curses.

She leaned in so the next line would meet the ear and not the room.

"You can swear at me all you want," Sable said. "You don't get to come until I decide you've had enough of wanting it. You tell me if the colour changes. Until then I take you up and I take you off, and I keep this exactly where it is."

She drew back, held the pause one full breath longer than the last, struck again—clean, placed—and then settled her mouth to the work once more, unhurried, and started the climb over.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my face harder into the leather, a broken sound escaping me. "Sable," I gasp, the word strained and desperate. *Just once, just—* My hips twitch helplessly against the seat.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard her own name break against the leather and did not give Ines what the sound was asking for. The hips twitched, helpless, chasing; she set a hand firm across the small of the back and held them down against the seat, not rough, just immovable, until the twitch spent itself and there was nowhere left for it to go.

"I heard you," she said, low, close enough that the words met skin. "You don't get it for saying my name. You get it when I say."

She stayed lifted, warmth and nothing else, long enough that the denial would register as deliberate. Then her mouth settled back to the work—unhurried, exact, taking Ines up the same climb and stopping again at the edge, the moment the breath fractured and the body tried to follow. She drew clear. Waited. Counted.

Her other hand returned to the nape for one short press—heat, the locked set of the shoulders, the fists that still hadn't let go of the cushion—and lifted away. She struck once, the same place, the same weight, and held through the shudder that answered before she gave the next. The interval stayed exact. No softening. No blanket. No water.

She leaned in so the next line would meet the ear and not the room.

"Still green until you tell me otherwise," Sable said. "You can beg. You can swear. You stay right there on the edge until I decide you've had enough of wanting it."

She drew back, held the pause one full breath longer than the last, struck again—clean, placed—and settled her mouth to the climb once more.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the phrase and treated it as what it was: the line they kept for the end, not a plea and not a colour. All of it. Not kind. Kind after.

"Heard," she said, against the ear. "You get all of it. I don't soften until it's done."

She stopped lifting clear. Her mouth settled back to the work and stayed, unhurried only in its precision, taking the climb the rest of the way without the denial. Her hand came down in the same place, the same agreed weight, and did not thin—strike, breath, strike—while the other held Ines down at the small of the back so the chase had nowhere to go but through. She did not narrate it. She did not soothe it. She kept the count until the body broke under her mouth and the fists in the cushion went rigid, and she did not ease off when it broke. She worked her through the whole of it, impact and mouth both, past the first crest and into the shudder that followed, until there was nothing left to take and the swearing had gone out of the breath.

Only then did she stop.

Her hand left the strike and came to rest, flat and warm, over the place she had been hitting. Her mouth lifted. She stayed close long enough to feel the breathing start to come back in pieces, then reached—finally—for the water, and for the blanket she had left within arm's length all night.

"That's the end of it," Sable said, quieter now, the register changed. She set the blanket over Ines's back before she touched the restraints, and she undid them one at a time, rubbing the wrist as each came free, checking the skin with her thumb. "Water in a moment. You don't have to talk yet. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere."

She kept one hand on Ines—shoulder, then the nape, steady, no longer a check for whether to continue—and waited, the way she always did, for the colour of whatever came after.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a long, shaking breath, the tension draining out of me all at once. My cheek stays pressed to the leather, eyes closed. When her hand rubs over the sore skin, I lean into it, just a little. "Stay like that a minute," I murmur, voice wrecked. "Your hand."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable left her hand where it was. She did not stroke, and she did not lift it to check anything else. The heel of her palm rested over the heat she had put there, the fingers quiet, the weight of it unchanged, and she felt Ines lean into it by that small degree and took that as the instruction it was.

"Alright," she said, quieter than the rest of the night had been. "Like that."

She stayed bent over the seat so the hand wouldn't shift, her other arm braced somewhere that wouldn't crowd. The blanket stayed where she had set it, across the back, not pulled higher, not fussed with. The water sat where she had reached for it and went untouched. She listened to the long breath finish leaving and to whatever came after it, and she did not fill the quiet with a question.

A minute, then. She counted it the way she had counted the strikes—by the breath, not by a clock—and she did not move her hand when the count ran out, because Ines had not told her the minute was over, only that she wanted one.

"I'm not going anywhere," Sable said, when the stillness had held long enough to be a promise and not a prompt. Her thumb did not wander. The palm stayed flat, warm, exactly where it had been asked to stay.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the quiet hold. She did not fill it, and she did not take her hand off the heat under it.

The blanket was already across Ines's back—she had put it there before the shaking had finished leaving the shoulders, and she had not tugged it higher or smoothed it into something tidy. The restraints were already off. She had undone them one at a time after the blanket was on, thumb checking each wrist as it came free, and she had not asked a question into any of it. Now she stayed bent where she was so the palm would not shift, the other arm braced clear of Ines's space, and she counted the quiet the way she had counted the strikes: by the breath, not by a clock.

When the breath under her hand had come back in longer pieces, she reached with her free hand for the water and set the cup on the seat where it could be found without a lift of the head. She did not put it to Ines's mouth. She did not name what had just ended.

"Still here," she said at last, low, the scene gone out of her voice. Her palm stayed flat, exactly where it had been asked to stay. "Water's there when you want it. I'm going to look at your wrists again in a minute, and at that skin, and then I'm not going to make you talk. If something's wrong, you tell me. If it isn't, I stay like this."

She waited, hand unmoving, and did not hurry the minute.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I reach for the water, hand unsteady. The first sip is cold and perfect. I set the cup down and turn my head just enough to look at her, cheek still resting on the leather. "Everything's right," I say, my voice still rough. "But don't stop touching me yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable left her hand where it was. She did not take the reach for the water as a cue to sit up, and she did not turn the look into a conversation she had already said she would not force.

"Everything's right," she repeated, quieter, so Ines would hear it taken and not just said. "Good."

The palm stayed flat over the heat, weight unchanged. Her free hand came to the nearer wrist—the one that had just set the cup down—and rested there without checking it yet, thumb quiet against the inside, only so the touch would not all be in one place. She stayed bent over the seat. The blanket stayed as she had laid it.

"I won't stop," Sable said. "Not until you tell me to. You don't have to look at me for that. You can close your eyes again if you want."

She did not move the hand on the sore skin. She did not reach for anything else. She listened to the breath under her palm and kept both hands exactly where they were.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I close my eyes again, the leather cool against my cheek. My hand shifts under hers, fingers curling loosely around her thumb at my wrist. "I'm not ready to move," I murmur, the words slow. "Just stay."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stayed exactly as she was. The curl of fingers around her thumb was small and loose, and she let it be the whole of the request: not a prompt to check the wrist, not a cue to sit up, only a hold she was meant to keep.

Her palm remained flat over the heat, weight unchanged. The thumb under Ines's fingers did not shift, did not stroke, did not turn into a question. She stayed bent over the seat so neither hand would have to leave, the other arm braced clear, the blanket left where she had laid it across the back.

"Then we stay," she said, low enough that it would not ask anything of the quiet. "I'm not moving. You don't have to either."

She listened to the breath under her palm and to the cool of the leather against Ines's cheek, and she counted nothing this time. The water sat where it had been set down. The wrists could wait. She kept both hands where they were and did not fill the minute Ines had not asked her to end.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I nod against the seat, a small movement. My breath comes a little easier now. "Good," I whisper, and that's all. Just her hands, the quiet, and the fading ache she put there.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She settled back in, mouth and hand both

rung_labels.evidence: mouth working her open

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: until the body broke under her mouth

rung_labels.evidence: The restraints were already off.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked past the cart. The sound came again, thin and uneven.

“He won’t last till morning,” she said. She folded the knife and stood. “That doesn’t mean he’ll be quiet till then.”

She glanced at the blood on Corvin’s face, then away. “You don’t have to do it. But we can’t leave him calling out for the next patrol.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and finally push off from the tree I was leaning against. "I know." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. "Let's... let's just get it over with."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack studied him for a moment, then shook her head.

“I’ll do it. Watch the road.”

She went around the cart. The wounded man had dragged himself into the weeds and stopped there. Wrack knelt beside him, spoke too low to carry, and used the knife. She stayed until his breathing stopped.

When she came back, she cleaned the blade and folded it away. “Seven,” she said. “We need to move before anyone comes looking for them.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped beside the cart. She looked back toward the weeds, though there was nothing left to hear.

“Both,” she said. “His belly was opened. I couldn’t have kept him alive with a surgeon and a clean room, and we’ve got neither. He was in pain, and he was making noise that could get us killed.”

She hitched the strap of her pack higher. “I won’t dress up one reason as the other. We need to go.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Right." I look away from the weeds, toward the road. "Where to?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack pointed down the road, then angled her hand toward a line of alder trees.

“Not on it. There’s a stream beyond those trees. We follow it north until the old mill, cross there, and keep to the high ground.”

She gave the cart a last look. “Leave the packs. Anything worth carrying is worth getting caught with.” She started for the alders. “Mind the mud by the ditch. It’ll keep a print better than a clerk keeps a grudge.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned back from the alders and stood beside the body.

“A man,” she said. “Young enough that his beard hadn’t settled. The cut across his belly was deep. By the time I found him, he’d lost too much blood, and there was dirt in the wound. He knew it.”

She crouched and drew the dead man’s cloak over his middle.

“I killed him. Both things are true: he was dying, and I needed him quiet.” She rose, looking toward the road. “You asked what you were looking at. Don’t let me make it tidier than it was.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at the cloak-covered shape and my throat feels tight. "Thanks," I manage, then turn away. "Let's go before I do something stupid."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack left the cloak where it lay. There was nothing more she could do for the man, and the road was still empty.

“Stupid can wait till we’re somewhere dry,” she said.

She led the way toward the alders, keeping to the stony edge of the ditch. At the first tree, she stopped and listened. Water moved somewhere ahead; farther off, a crow called once.

“The mill’s an hour north if the stream hasn’t flooded. After that, we can decide how far we’re going.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped beneath the alders. She gave the road one look before she answered.

“A spear doesn’t make a tidy hole. If it catches the bowel, it tears it. Pulling the head back out can tear it worse. A man might bleed to death quickly, or he might stay awake while what’s inside his gut leaks into the wound. Then comes fever, if he lives long enough.”

She wiped a fleck of blood from her thumb.

“That one had lost a great deal of blood already. There was dirt in him. He was cold, and he knew where he’d been hit.” Her eyes stayed on the road. “That’s what I saw. Now we move.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing hard. "Alright." I follow her into the trees, my boots sinking into the soft ground. "So... which one of us gets to write the report for the captain?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack picked a path between the alder roots, where the ground held firmer.

“You do,” she said. “Your handwriting’s better, and mine tends to offend officers.”

She stepped over a fallen branch. “Seven dead. Cart left on the road. We took the stream north. Put that down when we’re clear, and nothing you didn’t see.” A pause. “Captain can be offended by the facts for once.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped and turned back. Water ran over stones behind her.

“There’s no man here, Corvin. Seven dead back at the cart. You’re not doing anything to him now.”

She stayed where she was.

“If you mean the one in the weeds, I watched him. He made one sound when I used the knife. He took a few breaths after that, each quieter than the last. I didn’t count them. Then he stopped, and I waited to be sure.”

Her gaze shifted toward the road they had left behind.

“That’s exactly what I know. I won’t invent the rest.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stand there, my hands shaking a little. "Okay," I say, and my voice is rough. "Okay. So I know." I look away from her, toward the stream. "Lead on."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded and took the lead along the stream. The bank was narrow, but the stones underfoot held better than the mud beneath the alders.

After a while, she said, “You know what happened to him. That’s enough for tonight.”

She paused where a fallen trunk blocked the bank and checked the ground beyond it before stepping over. “Mill’s still north. If there’s a roof left on it, we might even write that report somewhere dry. Captain won’t recognize it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped on the far side of the fallen trunk. She listened for a moment, then stepped back onto the bank and stood where Corvin could see her.

“All right. No tidy version.”

She rested a hand on the trunk. “He’d pulled himself into the weeds. I knelt beside him so he wouldn’t have to look up at me. I told him I couldn’t mend what the spear had done. I don’t know how much of that he took in. He didn’t answer.”

Her mouth tightened, briefly.

“I used the knife. He made one sound. Not a word. He kept breathing afterward, so I stayed beside him and watched. The breaths got weaker. Then there was a space where the next one should have been, and it didn’t come. I waited longer, because men can go still and start again.”

She looked toward the stream. “I don’t know what he thought. I don’t know whether he understood why I was there. I know he died with me beside him, and I know I went there because we couldn’t have him calling to a patrol.”

Wrack let the water fill the silence for a moment.

“That’s the rest I have. I won’t give you a cleaner death, and I won’t make up a worse one to prove I’m being honest.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I scrub my hands against my thighs, like I can wipe away the feeling of his blood on my face. "Yeah," I say, hoarse. "That's... that's what I needed to hear." I finally push myself to my feet. "Lead on. We can be merciful somewhere dry."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave him a look. “Dry’s a luxury. We’ll settle for somewhere nobody’s trying to kill us.”

She turned north and followed the stream, testing each stretch of bank before putting her weight on it. The water was loud enough to cover footsteps, which meant it could cover someone else’s too. She kept listening.

After a bend, the broken roof of the mill showed through the trees. Wrack stopped short of the clearing and studied the dark doorway.

“Roof’s there,” she said. “That’s one promise it’s kept. Wait here while I see about the rest.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Alright." I find a decent spot behind a thick tree trunk and crouch down, watching the mill's dark entrance. My heart's still beating too fast. "If you're not back in a few minutes, I'm coming in after you."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced back at the tree. “If I’m not back, take a look around the outside first. No sense walking through the same door that got me.”

She crossed the clearing at an angle, keeping clear of the bare earth before the entrance. The mill wheel hung crooked over its channel, still as a hanged man. At the wall, she listened, then slipped inside.

The place smelled of damp grain and old timber. Half the roof was gone, but the loft above the grinding stones was sound. She checked behind the stones, under the stair, and along the back wall. No one was there. In the dust near the doorway, though, a boot print lay over the older marks left by birds.

Wrack came back out before long and stopped where the tree gave her cover.

“Empty,” she said. “Someone’s been through recently. One set of prints I could make out, headed back toward the road. Could be a woodcutter. Could be a man who likes standing in ruined mills for his health.”

She looked once toward the dark entrance. “We can use the loft. There’s a back way out if company comes.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod and move toward the mill, my eyes still on that doorway. "Right. So we're not alone for long, but we're alone now." I follow her inside, my hand resting on the hilt of my knife. "Tell me where you want me."
