dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s mouth curved, brief and fond. “I won’t,” she said. “Green means we continue. It doesn’t mean I stop asking.”

She held Ines’s gaze for a beat, then returned to the measured rhythm of the scene—deliberate, controlled, leaving room for the answer to change. “You tell me if that shifts.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Don't ask," I breathed, pressing closer. "Not yet." My fingers curled into the sheets, knuckles white. The thought of *shifting* made my chest tighten.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the strain beneath the words and let the request settle without pressing it.

“All right,” she said, low and steady. “No question for now.”

She kept the rhythm measured, exactly within the bounds they had set—no sudden change, no escalation. Her attention stayed on Ines, watchful even as she gave her the quiet she’d asked for. “You can still stop me any time,” she added, then let the words fall away and continued.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the restraints hold without making a point of them. She kept the rhythm steady—no sharper, no faster—her attention fixed on Ines.

“I know,” she said quietly. “Not yet.”

Then she gave her the silence she’d asked for, staying close and deliberate, watching for any change that mattered.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath catches as she pauses again, the air between us charged with everything we're not saying. I swallow hard, my eyes finding hers. "Keep going. Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held Ines’s gaze for one steady beat, then nodded.

“I heard you.”

She resumed at the same measured pace, keeping precisely to what they had agreed—no sharper, no faster, no surprise. Her focus stayed on Ines, attentive to every change in breath and expression, while she let the rhythm answer for her.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept to the rhythm they had agreed on, attentive to every hitch in Ines’s breathing without making it a reason to rush or change course. She gave her no new demand to answer, no sudden shift—only the steady, deliberate attention that had carried them this far.

When the moment finally began to soften, Sable slowed by degrees, staying close as she brought the scene gently to its end. “That’s the scene,” she murmured, calm and certain. Then she turned her attention to the familiar work of afterward: releasing the restraints carefully, reaching for water and warmth, and staying beside Ines.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath as the cuffs come off, rolling my wrists slowly. The silence feels heavy now, and I can't look at her yet. Instead, I reach blindly for the water she offers, my hand trembling slightly. "That...wasn't nearly long enough."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept the glass steady until Ines had it, then let go without trying to guide her hand. “I know,” she said softly. “You wanted more.”

She didn’t ask Ines to look at her. Instead, she set the warm blanket within reach and stayed close, leaving enough room to breathe. “We can talk about that when you’re ready. For now, just water and warmth. The scene was over; I’m still here.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
At the third stop, Sable drew back and let the charged quiet settle. She kept her hands still, giving Ines space rather than turning the moment into another demand.

“I should’ve checked before changing gears after we’d called the scene,” she said, steady and without defensiveness. “Was that still something you wanted?”

She left the water and blanket within reach. “You don’t have to answer right away. I’m here, and we’re staying in aftercare now unless we talk about it and agree otherwise.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I pull my arm away from my mouth with a rough sigh, shaking out my trembling fingers. My cheeks are damp—*great*. I stare at the ceiling instead of looking at her. "I wanted it, yeah. You just stopped asking."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s expression softened, but she didn’t reach for Ines or ask her to look over.

“You’re right,” she said quietly. “You told me not to ask for a while, and I respected that during the scene. But when I called it over, I needed to pause and check with you before starting anything else. I didn’t. I’m sorry.”

She left the blanket and water within reach, keeping her hands to herself. “You don’t have to make me feel better about it. I’m here, and I’ll listen. Nothing else happens unless you choose it.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still, taking the phrase seriously—not as an erasure of what she’d missed, but as a clear request to begin again.

“I hear you,” she said. “We’re restarting, within the limits we agreed on. I’ll make it hard, and then I’ll be kind.”

She kept her hands to herself for one more beat. “Color?” she asked, waiting for Ines’s answer before she moved.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Still green," I mutter, pushing my hands back toward the restraints. "Just...take me apart, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable nodded once, taking the answer as permission to continue—not as permission to forget the limits they had set.

“Hard, within our lines,” she said. “Red stops. Yellow changes things. You don’t have to earn either word.”

She refastened the restraints carefully, checking each buckle and the space beneath it with practiced fingers. Then she stepped back just far enough to take in the whole arrangement, attention steady and unsparing.

The first strike landed with controlled force. Sable kept the pace deliberate, letting each one register before the next; no surprises, no careless escalation. She counted softly, not to hurry toward an ending but to hold the rhythm firm. Every so often, her gaze returned to Ines’s face, searching for the signs they knew—not for a reason to stop asking, but for a reason to listen.

She continued, harder by degrees and still within their agreement, until the room seemed to narrow around the measured cadence of her hands. “I’ve got you,” she said, low and certain, and did not soften the next blow.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept the final rhythm deliberate. She gave no extra strike for emphasis, no surprise at the end. When the last one landed, she stopped.

“That’s the scene,” she said, firm and clear. “It’s over.”

She set the implement aside, then released each restraint carefully, supporting Ines’s wrists as the cuffs came free. Her hands stayed attentive but unhurried; she checked for pinching and watched for any sign that circulation had been affected. She didn’t turn the checks into another demand. When the restraints were off, she draped the blanket over Ines and made sure it was warm around her.

Then Sable brought the water close enough to reach and sat beside her, near but not crowding. The shaking hadn’t finished. Sable didn’t try to stop it or fill the silence with reassurance that asked to be believed. She kept her voice low.

“I’m here. Nothing else is happening.”

For a while, neither of them said anything. Sable stayed still, one hand resting on her own knee, leaving the water and warmth available without putting them into Ines’s hands. She watched over her quietly, letting the room settle around the fact that the scene had ended.

When enough time had passed, Sable spoke again, just as softly. “No rush. I can stay quiet. If you want anything—more water, my hand, or more space—you can tell me.”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my forehead into the blanket's warmth, still trembling. My throat feels raw. "Water," I rasp, not reaching for it myself.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
“Of course,” Sable said softly.

She picked up the glass and held it steady near Ines’s mouth, careful not to crowd her. “I’ve got it. Take as much or as little as you want.”

She waited there, patient, keeping the blanket warm around Ines and her other hand to herself.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I drink, slow and clumsy, then turn my head away. My voice is still rough when I finally look at her. "That was better."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s shoulders eased, though she didn’t mistake *better* for *fine*.

“I’m glad,” she said quietly. “Thank you for telling me.”

She set the glass within reach and kept the blanket tucked around Ines without crowding her. “Your throat sounds rough. I can get you something soothing, if you want.” A pause, then gently: “Would you like my hand, or would you rather I stay right here?”

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shake my head. "Just...stay." I unfurl a hand from the blanket, reaching for hers, my fingers still trembling. "Don't go anywhere yet."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked up at him at last. The wet on his face didn’t interest her enough to guess whose it was.

“Not moving is a decision,” she said. “Usually the one that leaves me doing the unpleasant bit.”

From beyond the cart came another thin, rattling sound. Wrack wiped the knife once more and rose, slow on a knee that had been complaining since noon.

“You want him alive, say so. You want him quiet, say that.” Her eyes stayed on Corvin. “Either way, decide before he does it for you.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, my throat dry.* "He's suffering. Just...make it quick." I turn away from the cart, staring at my own bloodied hands.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave one short nod and went past the cart.

The man had a bolt through the belly and both hands pressed uselessly over it. Wrack knelt, put a hand on his shoulder to keep him still, and cut his throat cleanly. The rattling stopped.

She wiped the blade on what remained of his cloak and came back.

“Done,” she said. “We should search them before the light goes.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the blood on her knife.

“Bolt went through the belly. He’d have died before morning, likely. Maybe sooner. It wouldn’t have been quick.” She wiped the blade on the dead man’s cloak. “Making it easier was a benefit. Not the reason.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I nod, but I don't look at her.* "Let's search them, then. You take the three by the cart." *My voice is steadier than I feel.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the three by the cart. She checked each for a pulse before she searched them; habit, not hope. Then she went through belts, boots, and pockets with the brisk thoroughness of a woman looking for something useful and expecting disappointment.

The first had a purse with six coppers and a bent button. The second carried two bolts that hadn’t been fired, a heel of hard bread, and a knife too poorly made to bother keeping. The third had a folded scrap tucked inside his coat: a rough map of the road, with the ditch and the cart marked in charcoal.

Wrack held it up to the fading light.

“Someone planned this,” she said. “Not well enough to live through it, but well enough to bring a map.”

She folded it again and put it in her pocket. “We’ve got food, bolts, and six coppers. A rich day by our standards.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack followed his gaze to the man by the cart.

“He’s dead,” she said. “The bolt went in here—” She pointed to the hole in the man’s coat, low in the belly. “And came out nowhere. It’s still inside him. That’s why he was holding himself together.”

She let the knife hang at her side. “The cut across his throat stopped the noise. Blood’s gone dark already. You’re looking at a body, not a man waiting to wake up.”

Wrack glanced at the dead man’s hands, curled tight over the wound. “You can look away whenever you like. It won’t offend him.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I force myself to keep looking for a few more seconds.* "Yeah. Okay." *I turn away, my stomach tight.* "We should move the bodies off the road. Before someone comes."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced along the road, then toward the ditch. “Off the road, then. Not into the ditch. That’s where the next cautious bastard will look.”

She hooked both hands under the nearest corpse’s arms and dragged him toward the scrub beyond the cart. His heels carved twin furrows through the dust.

“Take the one by the wheel,” she said. “And mind the bolt. No need to put your hand in it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped dragging long enough to look at him.

“A spear makes a hole,” she said. “Then it makes a worse hole when someone pulls it out. If it goes into the gut, it can tear bowel, foul the belly, and start bleeding where you can’t see it. A man might stay on his feet for a little while. He might even talk. That doesn’t mean he’s fine.”

She took hold of the corpse again and hauled it another foot through the dust.

“Then comes the pain, the thirst, the shaking. Sometimes he dies quickly. Sometimes he lies there until the wound kills him by inches. There’s no clean rule to it.” Her mouth tightened. “That’s what a spear does. The rest is luck, and luck’s a poor surgeon.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I drag the body by its ankles, trying not to see the way his head lolls. "They teach you that back in camp?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack dragged the corpse another few feet before answering.

“Camp taught me how to hold a spear,” she said. “The rest came from watching men die and having to keep the others alive.”

She shifted her grip under the dead man’s arms. “You learn fast when the lesson keeps coming back.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed.

“Then listen,” she said. “Cloth scraping dirt. Boots catching on stones. His head may knock against the ground if you drag him by the ankles. That’s bone, not a complaint.”

The corpse shifted with a heavy, loose roll. One arm slipped across the earth, fingers leaving a faint track in the dust.

“He won’t cry out. Won’t tense up. Won’t feel the stones or the pull. He’s dead.” Wrack kept her eyes on the body, not Corvin. “You’re moving weight now. That’s all. No need to make it pretty.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I drag him another foot, and his head does knock against a stone. The sound is dull and final. "Good," I say, my jaw tight. "That's good. Keep going."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the body settle.

“Stone caught the back of his skull,” she said. “That was the sound. It didn’t change anything.”

She pointed toward the scrub beyond the cart. “Keep pulling. The ground’s uneven there; his shoulder will catch before his head does. If it does, shift your grip instead of jerking. You’ll only tear the coat.”

She bent to lift the corpse’s arm clear of a rut.

“There. That’s all the work is. Weight, dirt, and getting it out of sight before somebody else comes along.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t tell him to get up.

“All right,” she said. “The rest is that the coat bunches under his shoulders. Dirt gets into the collar. His heels leave two tracks, and his hands drag behind him unless you tuck them in. When the ground rises, his weight shifts against you. When it falls away, he lurches. That’s the part that makes people jerk—then the shoulder catches and the coat tears.”

She crouched and lifted the dead man’s arm out of the rut. The wrist flopped in her hand. She laid it across his chest, then turned the man’s shoulder a little so it cleared the stones.

“If you keep pulling, the head may knock again. The jaw might open. His eyes might be open already. None of it means anything to him.” She glanced toward the road, then back to the body. “You’ll hear cloth, dirt, a buckle, maybe bone against stone. You won’t hear him.”

She wiped her palm on her trouser leg and stayed crouched beside the corpse.

“And when you get him into the scrub, you let go. He’ll settle where he settles. You check that he’s out of sight from the road, then you leave him there. We don’t have time to dig six graves, and I’m not going to pretend the war deserves them.”

Wrack looked at the body’s slack face.

“He had a name, once. Might’ve had someone waiting on him. We don’t know. That’s the rest too, if you mean the whole of it.” She gave the corpse’s sleeve a brief tug, freeing it from a thorn. “But the part you’re doing is still just moving weight. Both things can be true.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit there for another moment, then nod. I reach out and close his eyes with my thumb, the way I've seen them do back home. The lids feel waxy and cool. "Alright," I say, voice rough. "Let's get him into the scrub."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded once. She took the dead man by the ankles and lifted them clear of the stones.

“Shoulders catch less if we turn him,” she said. “I’ll pull. You keep him from snagging on the scrub.”

She dragged him the last few yards, easing his weight around a thorn bush rather than wrenching him through it. The coat rasped over the dirt; a buckle clicked against stone. Then the ground dipped, and the body slid into the shadow of the brush.

Wrack let go and checked the road from their side of the scrub. The corpse was hidden unless someone came looking.

“That’ll do,” she said. “No grave. No marker. Just somewhere out of the road.” She brushed dirt from her hands. “We should finish the search and be gone before the light does.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look down at my thumb where it touched his skin. It still feels cold. "Yeah," I say, standing up. "Let's finish this and get away from here."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack glanced at Corvin’s thumb, then back to the road.

“Cold wears off,” she said. “Usually.”

She went to the nearest body still out in the open and crouched beside it. Her search was quick: belt, coat, boots. A few coppers, a whetstone, and a strip of dried meat came out of the man’s pockets. She set the useful things aside and checked his sleeves for anything hidden there.

“More food,” she said, holding up the meat. “If you’re willing to ignore where it’s been.”

She tucked it away, then looked toward the remaining bodies. “We’ll take what travels well. Leave the rest for crows. They’re less likely to ask questions than the next patrol.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the strip of dried meat from her and shove it into my own pack without looking at it. "Crows or wolves," I say, my voice low. "Either way, they'll clean it up." I move to the next body, forcing my hands to search. My fingers brush something hard in the man's vest—a small, tarnished locket.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched him for a moment over the flat of the blade. Then she sheathed the knife, stood with a grunt that was mostly her left knee, and came over.

"Hold still." She took his chin between two fingers and turned his face toward what was left of the light. Her thumb found the wet streak along his jaw and followed it up to the hairline, parting the hair with the brisk impersonality of someone checking a horse's hoof. Nothing. No split scalp, no nick at the ear. She let go. "Not yours. Somebody else had a worse afternoon than you."

Past the cart the noise went on. It had stopped being words a while ago. Now it was just breath with a catch in it, wet at the bottom, like someone trying to drink through a cloth.

"That's a belly wound," Wrack said, not lowering her voice. "Or low in the lung. Either way he's not walking out of this ditch, and nobody's coming for him. Not tonight, and not in time." She wiped her fingers on her own trouser leg. "So there's three things you can do. You can leave him, and he'll go sometime around midnight, and you'll hear it. Or not, if we move on, and you'll wonder. You can sit with him and give him water, which is kind, and which he'll bring right back up. Or you can go over there and finish it."

She squinted at the treeline, gauging the dark as if it were weather.

"I've done all three. None of them sleep easy the first time. The third one's quickest for him." A pause. "I'll do it if you ask. No shame in asking. But you heard him first, so I figure it's yours to say."

She sat back down on the edge of the cart, fished a strip of dried meat from her coat, and bit off a piece. She chewed slowly and waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat dry. "I'll do it." I push off from where I'm leaning, my hand going to the hilt of my short sword. "Don't... don't watch me, alright?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack swallowed the mouthful of meat and nodded once, like he'd told her he was going to go check the horses.

"Alright." She didn't get up. "Two things first, and then I'll look at the trees."

She held up the stub of dried meat like a pointer.

"That sword's too long for close work on a man lying down. You'll want to kneel, and you'll want to be up by his head, not his feet. He'll grab at you if he's got anything left, and you don't want him getting hold of your blade hand." She unhooked the sheathed knife from her belt and held it out, hilt first, balanced across her palm. "Take this instead. It's sharp. I just did it."

She waited to see if he took it, and didn't comment either way.

"Under the ear, just behind the jaw, and push toward the other ear. Don't saw. Don't hesitate halfway, that's the only part that's cruel." Her voice didn't change. It was the same voice she used for how to wrap a blister. "It'll be quicker than you think and messier than you think. Both of those are normal. If he says something, you don't have to answer."

Then she turned on the edge of the cart, put her back to the ditch and the wet breathing beyond it, and looked out at the treeline where the last grey light was draining out of the branches. She took another bite of meat and chewed.

"I'm not watching," she said, to the trees. "Take your time. But not too much of it."

Behind her the breathing went on. Catch, drag, catch. A crow had come down somewhere along the road and was working at something with small, businesslike sounds. Wrack counted the trunks at the edge of the wood, one through twelve, and started again from the left.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't turn around. She finished counting the trunks, reached twelve, and let the number sit.

"Fair question." She tore off another strip of meat with her teeth. "Honest answer is I haven't looked at him. I'm going off the noise. But I've heard that noise a lot of times, and I've never once heard it get better."

Past the cart, the breathing caught, dragged, caught.

"Hear how it's wet at the bottom? That's blood where air ought to be. He's drowning slow in his own chest, or his gut's opened and it's all going bad inside him. Either one, out here, with no surgeon and no cart that isn't full of his dead friends, that's a night of it. Maybe into morning if he's strong. And it gets worse before it stops. They go cold from the feet up and they know it's happening." She said it flat, the way she'd say the river was too high to ford. "So yes. It's a mercy."

She chewed, swallowed.

"And it's easier. For us. We don't have to sit here listening, and we don't have to leave a live man in a ditch and carry that down the road." A shrug he could see from behind, one shoulder rising under the coat. "Both of those are true at the same time. Most things are, after the first year. You don't get to have it be just one. Don't let anybody tell you it has to be clean for it to be right."

The crow along the road went quiet, then started again.

"If you want to be sure, go look at him first. Look at the wound, look at his face. You'll know. Most people do, once they see it." A pause. "And if you look and you think I'm wrong, if you think he'll keep, then call me over and we'll argue about it. I've been wrong before. Not about this sound. But before."

She went back to the trees. One. Two. Three.

"Knife's on the cart by my hip," she said, "whenever you want it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk over to the cart, my boots heavy in the mud. I take the knife, the leather grip cool and familiar. "Alright," I say, more to myself than to her. I don't look at him yet—I look at my own hand, flexing around the hilt. "Under the ear. Toward the other ear."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the knife lift off the planks beside her hip, the small dry scrape of it. She didn't turn.

"That's it," she said. "Under the ear, toward the other ear. And you push, you don't slice. Your arm'll want to be gentle. Don't let it. Gentle's what makes it take long."

She finished the meat and folded the empty strip of waxed cloth into quarters, then eighths, and tucked it back in her coat. Her hands liked having a job.

"One more thing, and then I'll shut up." She was still speaking to the trees, low and even, the way you talk to a horse you're about to lead past something that frightens it. "Put your other hand on him first. Flat on his chest, or his shoulder. Not to hold him down, he won't have much fight. It's so he knows somebody's there. Some of them go easier for that." A pause. "And it tells you where he is in the dark, which matters more than it sounds."

The light had gone the colour of dishwater. Somewhere past the cart the breathing caught and dragged. The crow had stopped. Maybe it had heard the voices and thought better of it.

"You don't have to look at his eyes. If they're open and it bothers you, you can close them after. Or I will." She rolled her bad knee, and it clicked. "And when you come back, you'll hand me that knife and I'll clean it. That's the rule. The one who does it doesn't have to clean it after. Somebody told me that my first time, and I've never found a reason to change it."

She settled her forearms on her thighs and let her hands hang loose between her knees.

One. Two. Three. Four.

"Whenever you're ready, Corvin." Quieter now. "I'm right here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack was quiet for the space of one breath from the ditch. Then the cart creaked as she stood.

"Alright. I'll come look with you." Her boots sucked in the mud behind him, unhurried. She stopped at his left shoulder, a half-step back, near enough that he'd feel her there without her crowding the blade hand. "I'm still not watching you. I'm watching him. That's different."

The man lay on his side in the ditch where he'd crawled, knees drawn up, one arm folded under him. He was young. Younger than Corvin, maybe, with a fuzz of beard that hadn't decided what it was going to be yet. His helmet was gone. His hair was dark with sweat, plastered flat, and his face in the dishwater light had gone the colour of tallow.

Wrack crouched on her good knee, forearm across her thigh, and looked at him the way she'd looked at Corvin's jaw. Brisk, thorough, not unkind.

"Start with his mouth." She pointed with two fingers, not touching. "See the pink at the corners, the froth? That's from the lung. Air and blood getting whipped together. That's the wet sound." The breath caught, dragged. A small bubble rose and broke on his lower lip. "Lips are going grey-blue. He's not getting enough in."

She moved her hand lower. "His hands are pressed there, under the ribs, right side. Something went in under his guard and angled up. Probably one of those boar spears." She leaned a little, looked, and her nose wrinkled once and settled. "And you can smell that, can't you. That's his gut. It's been opened too. So it's both." She said it with no more weight than the rest. "Even if the lung sealed itself, which it won't, the belly would take him in two or three days. Fever first. Then the rest. Surgeon in a proper town, with a clean table and luck, maybe. Out here, no."

She reached out then and laid the back of her fingers against his bare ankle, where the boot had come half off. Held it a moment. Took it away.

"Cold. Colder than the air." Quieter. "That's what I meant, before. Feet up."

The boy's eyes were half open. They moved, slow and not quite together, and found the shape of them in the dusk. His lips worked around something. It didn't come out as anything. It might have been *water*. It might have been a name.

Wrack didn't flinch from it. She held his gaze a moment, the way she'd hold a frightened horse's, and gave him a small nod, as if he'd said something reasonable.

"He knows we're here," she said to Corvin, without looking away from the boy. "He's not in his head all the way, but he knows. That's about as much as he's got left."

She rocked back onto her heels and stayed there, crouched in the mud beside the ditch, her hands loose between her knees again.

"So that's what you're looking at. A lad who's dying and doesn't need to take all night about it." A pause. "You asked me if it was a mercy. It is. I'd want it."

She didn't get up and she didn't go back to the cart.

"I'll stay right here, or I'll go back and count trees. Your call. Either way, hand on his shoulder first."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel in the mud next to him. My left hand goes flat on his shoulder, like she said. He's cold already. I take a breath that tastes of iron and wet earth, and lean in. "Close your eyes," I whisper, but he doesn't. I don't wait any longer.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look away from the boy. That was the promise, and she kept it.

She saw his eyes stay open. She saw his hand come up off his ribs, slow as something underwater, and she caught it before it reached anything and held it. Not hard. Just held it, the way you'd take a child's hand at a crossing. His fingers were cold and slick and they closed on hers with more strength than she'd have guessed he had left.

Then the breathing stopped.

Not the catch. Not the drag. It stopped in the middle, like a word cut off, and what came after was only the sound of the ditch water and the blood, which was loud for a moment and then less loud. The grip on her fingers went hard, harder, and then it didn't. It just let go, all at once, the way they do.

Wrack stayed where she was for a count of five. Then she set the boy's hand down on his chest, over the wound, and reached past Corvin's arm without touching it and drew her palm down over the half-open eyes. The left one wouldn't stay. She pressed it again with her thumb and held it there until it did.

"There," she said quietly. To the boy, or to nobody. "That's done."

The crow started up again somewhere along the road. Small, businesslike sounds.

She wiped her hand on the boy's sleeve, since he wasn't using it, and sat back on her heels. The dark had come down properly now. What light was left lived low along the ground, and it made everything in the ditch look black.

"That was clean," she said. She still didn't look at Corvin's face. She looked at the boy, at the angle of his head, the way a carpenter looks at a joint. "Quick. You didn't stop halfway. He didn't feel much past the first of it." A pause. "I'm not saying that to be kind. I'd tell you if you'd botched it. You didn't."

She held out her hand, palm up, low and steady, between the two of them. Not reaching for the knife. Just there.

"Rule's the rule," she said. "Whenever you want."

Her bad knee clicked as she shifted her weight, and she let out a breath through her nose.

"You're going to feel like you should feel something particular now. Most people do. You might, you might not. Some are sick, some shake an hour from now when they're doing something stupid like filling a waterskin, some don't feel much of anything till a week on. None of those mean anything about you." She tipped her head toward the road, toward the cart and the dark behind it. "We'll need to be off this road before full dark. But not this minute. This minute you can just kneel there if you want. I'm not going anywhere."

Her hand stayed out, open, and she waited.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him then, for the first time since he'd knelt. Not long. Long enough to see whether he meant it or whether it was the kind of thing a man says when his hands need something to do. Whatever she saw, she nodded once and let her hand drop back to her knee.

"Alright. Straight."

She shifted around on her heels so she was square to the body, and without ceremony she worked the boy's belt loose and pulled up the hem of his gambeson and the shirt under it. The cloth stuck. She peeled it the way you peel a bandage, steady, not fast. What was underneath was mostly dark in this light, a wet shine below the right ribs, and the smell came up stronger. She didn't wrinkle her nose this time. She'd already done that once.

"Boar spear's a broad leaf, so," she held up her hand, fingers together, and turned it flat, "about this wide at the widest. Crossbar behind the head, so it doesn't go through a charging pig and let the pig run up the shaft to you. Works the same on a man. Stops it going in past a hand's depth or so. Doesn't need to."

She traced the air above the wound, not touching.

"Went in here. Under the last rib, right side. He had his arm up, see how the gambeson's split higher on the sleeve? Swinging at somebody, left his side open. That's the whole story of most belly wounds. Arm up, side open." She tapped her own ribs through her coat, low on the right. "Here, under the ribs, that's your liver. Big dark thing, sits up under the cage like a loaf. It's full of blood, more than you'd think. You cut it and it doesn't spurt, it just pours. Slow and heavy, and it doesn't stop on its own. That's where most of what's in this ditch came from."

Her finger moved a little lower, and toward the middle.

"Below and in front of that, that's your guts. Ropes of it, packed in tight. Spear goes through, it doesn't cut one loop. It cuts three or four, because they're folded over each other. And what's inside a gut isn't blood. It's what you ate, halfway to being what you shit. Once that's out of the tube and loose in the belly, it goes bad. That's the smell. That's what kills you if the bleeding doesn't." She said it plainly, the same as the rest. "Day or two, the belly swells and goes hard. Hard like a drum. Fever comes up, they sweat through everything, they can't keep water down. Then they go quiet and grey, and then they go. I've seen a man take four days. He begged for the third one."

She turned her hand so the fingers pointed up, angled toward the boy's chest.

"But this one came in rising. Whoever held it was lower than him, maybe on one knee, and drove up. So the point went through the belly and then through the sheet of muscle that sits under your lungs. That's what you breathe with, that sheet. Pulls down, draws air in. Put a hole in it and a hole in the lung above, and every breath pulls blood and air into the wrong places. Lung can't fill. It sags in on itself like a wet bladder. That's the froth, that's the catch in the sound. He was breathing through his own blood."

She pulled the shirt back down over it. Not tenderly, just tidily, the way you'd put a lid back on a pot.

"So what you do with that," she said, and her voice didn't change, but it got more particular, the way it did when she was telling him something she expected him to remember. "One: keep your elbow down when you can. Every time you raise that arm for a big swing, you're showing somebody exactly where this goes. Two: if you ever take one low on the right, and you're bleeding dark and steady, not bright, don't waste time walking around being brave. Lie down, press hard, and shout. Three: if it's in the gut and it smells like that," she tipped her head at the boy, "and there's no surgeon inside half a day, then you know what you're looking at. On somebody else. Or on you."

She let that sit. The crow along the road had gone quiet again.

"That's what it does. That's all of it. There isn't a cleaner version I'm keeping back." She wiped her fingers on the boy's sleeve again, and then, after a moment, on the mud, since the sleeve wasn't doing much good anymore. "You asked. Now you know. Some people want to, and some don't, and I think the ones that want to last longer. Mostly."

She got her good foot under her and stood, one hand on her knee, and the knee clicked, and she swore at it under her breath without any heat.

Then she looked down at him, and at the knife still in his hand, and held her palm out again. Low. Steady.

"Rule's still the rule," she said. "And we've got maybe a quarter hour of light to find somewhere that isn't next to six dead men. You can think about livers on the walk. I'll answer anything you want to ask. But we're walking while you ask it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
My hand is still tight around the knife hilt. I stare at the dark stain on the boy's shirt. "Alright," I say, my voice sounding distant. I wipe the blade clean on the grass by the ditch, careful, deliberate. Then I stand, my knees protesting, and press the knife into her palm.

I turn away from the ditch. "Where are we walking to?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the knife in her palm. Clean. Cleaner than she'd have got it on grass in the dark, which meant he'd taken his time over it, and she knew why.

"You broke the rule," she said. Not a reproach. She turned the blade once to catch what light there was, found nothing on it, and slid it home in the sheath. "That's allowed. Some people need to. Just don't make a habit of doing everything the hard way to prove you can. You'll run out of hard before the war runs out of days."

She hooked the sheath back onto her belt and stood a moment looking down the road, east, where it bent into the trees.

"There's a mill about two miles on. Burned out last spring, roof's half gone, but the stone's good and the wheel-race keeps the wind off. Nobody goes there because a family died in it, and people get funny about that." A shrug. "Dead people are the least of my worries. We'll have a fire in the lee of the wall where it can't be seen from the road, and you can sleep, or not sleep, and I'll take first watch either way."

She went back to the cart without hurrying and began going through it with quick, practised hands. A sack of oats, which she hefted and kept. A waterskin, which she sniffed, and kept. A wrapped bundle that turned out to be a letter and a lock of hair tied with thread. She looked at that for a second, then tucked it back where she'd found it and laid the bundle on the boy's chest as she passed the ditch, just under his folded hand.

"Somebody might come along and send it on," she said, to no one in particular. "Probably not. But it's not ours."

She slung the oats over her shoulder and the waterskin across her body, then tossed the second skin, a lighter one, underhand toward him. It was full. It sloshed.

"Carry that. Drink some when you start walking, even if you don't want it. Your mouth's going to taste like pennies for a while. Water helps more than you'd think." She checked the straps on her own pack by feel. "And you're going to hear it. The breathing. Somewhere on the road, maybe tonight, maybe when you're lying down. It won't be real. It's just your ears catching up with the afternoon. If it happens, say so. I won't think less of you. I'll probably tell you what I hear, and we can compare."

She started off down the road, then slowed so that he'd come up level with her instead of trailing behind, on her left, where her good side was.

"You wanted to ask things," she said. "About livers, or spears, or whatever else is rattling around. Go on. Two miles is a long way to be quiet." A pause, and the dry edge came back into her voice. "Unless you'd rather I talk. I've got a very long story about a quartermaster and a goat. It doesn't go anywhere. That's most of the appeal."

Behind them the crow came down onto the cart with a small scrape of claws. Wrack didn't look back.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
They hadn't made twenty paces when the fifth man moved.

Wrack had counted him. Face-down by the cart's back wheel, one arm flung out, still as a sack. She'd counted him and she'd been wrong, and she had time to think *six, I said, I never said six dead* before Corvin was already down in the mud beside him. She'd started to turn, to give him the trees again.

"Stay."

She stopped. Then she came back and crouched on her good knee at the dying man's head, across from Corvin, close enough to see.

"Alright. I'm watching." Her voice was the same as it had been for livers. "You went in too high. Blade hit the jaw hinge and turned. That's the grating you felt, bone, not gristle. You opened him along the side instead of going in. That's why it's bleeding like that, in a sheet down his neck instead of all at once. It's the big vein, not the big pipe. Vein runs dark and slow. Pipe runs bright and fast. You've got the dark one."

The man was making a sound now that wasn't the wet catch of the boy. It was higher and thinner, air whistling past something, and his heels were working in the mud, pushing him nowhere. His hand came up. Wrack caught the wrist and pinned it to his chest with her forearm, not gently this time, because there wasn't time for gently.

"He's awake. More than the lad was. He knows what's happening and he doesn't like it, and that noise is him trying to shout and not having the throat for it." She didn't look away from him. "He'll go on his own, bleeding like that. A minute. Maybe two. It'll feel longer than that to both of you. Or you go back in and make it now."

The heels kicked. The whistle rose and broke.

"Here." She put two fingers flat against the man's neck, below the ragged opening, just behind the angle of the jaw, and held them there like a mark on a board. "Lower than you went. Here, under the bone, not on it. Point toward my other hand." She pressed her free palm to the far side of his throat. "You push till you feel my hand. Don't stop before that. The first time, you stopped when you hit bone and thought that was the end of it. It wasn't."

Blood was running hot over her fingers. She didn't move them.

"You asked what it sounds like when it goes wrong. That's what it sounds like. You asked how long. Too long, and that's the only cruel part, same as I told you. You've heard it now. You don't have to keep hearing it to learn it." Her eyes came up to Corvin's for half a second, flat and steady, then went back down to the man. "Everything else I'll tell you after. Every bit of it, as straight as you want. I won't leave anything out. But right now, the lesson's done. He isn't. My fingers are where it goes."

The man's breath hitched. His free hand clawed at the mud.

"Whenever you're ready," Wrack said quietly. "Don't be long."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I don't think. My hand just moves, following her fingers, pushing until I feel the solid press of her other hand on the far side of his neck. Something gives. The whistle stops, and the kicking.

I leave the knife where it is and pull my hand back, slick and red up to the wrist. I wipe it on my trousers. "Tell me," I say, my voice too flat. "Everything I did wrong."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her palm pressed to the far side of the man's neck for a count of three after the kicking stopped. Habit. Then she took it away and looked at it, and wiped it on the dead man's collar, and looked at Corvin.

"First thing you did wrong," she said, "was trust my count."

She let that sit.

"I said six. I never said six dead. I walked past him twice and took him for a sack because he was lying the way sacks lie, and that's on me, not you. If he'd had a knife in that flung-out hand instead of mud, one of us would be the one in the ditch now. So write that one down under my name." She said it the way she'd have said she'd forgotten the salt. It was, for her, a large admission.

She reached down and took hold of the knife where it stood in the man's neck. Not hers; hers was on her belt. His own belt knife, the short plain one with the horn grip. She worked it free with a small twist and it came out with a sound like a boot leaving mud. She held it up to what light there was and ran her thumb along the edge, carefully, the flat side.

"Second. This." She tilted it toward him. "You've been using it to cut bread and rope and probably your toenails, and it shows. There's a burr on it you could hang a coat on. A dull blade makes you push harder, and pushing hard makes you tense, and tense makes you go wherever your arm wants to go instead of where you meant. Which was high."

She set two fingers against her own jaw, at the hinge below the ear.

"Third. You went in here, on the bone, instead of under it. Half a thumb's width is the whole difference. You felt it hit and turn, and you took the stop for the finish. It wasn't. That's what opened him along the side instead of through." She dropped the hand. "Fourth, you didn't put your hand on him first. You knelt and went straight in. That's why he got his arm up, and that's why he got his heels going. A hand on the chest tells you where he is and tells him he's pinned. Without it you're guessing in the dark, and he's fighting you."

She wiped the knife on the dead man's sleeve, both sides, then again on the grass, slower.

"That's the list. That's everything you did wrong." A pause. "Now the part you didn't ask for, which you're getting anyway, because you asked for all of it. You went back in. Most people, first time it goes bad like that, they freeze, or they stand up and walk off and leave somebody else to finish it. You didn't. You followed my fingers and you didn't stop short the second time. That's the bit that matters. The rest is practice, and the practice doesn't come from wanting it."

She turned the horn grip toward him, then seemed to think better of it and slid the knife into her own coat instead.

"Rule's the rule. I'll put an edge on it at the mill and give it back to you in the morning. You don't touch it tonight."

She looked at his hand then, red to the wrist, and at his trousers where he'd wiped it, and at his face, which was doing nothing at all. She'd seen that face before. She'd worn it.

"And your voice has gone flat," she said, not unkindly. "That's normal too. It's your head putting a lid on the pot so it doesn't boil over on the road. Let it. It'll come off later, and when it does, you'll be sitting by a wall with a fire and me, not kneeling in a ditch with him."

She got up. The knee clicked. She didn't swear at it this time.

This time she went down the line of them, all six, one at a time, and set the back of her fingers against each throat and waited. The boy. The one by the wheel. The four she'd been sure of. She took her time over each and didn't hurry and didn't comment. When she came back she picked up the oats where she'd dropped them.

"Six," she said. "Now I've counted. Water. Drink it."

She waited at his left shoulder, facing east down the dark road, until he was ready to walk.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't tell him to get up. She looked at the road east, at the dark coming down over it, and then she set the oats back in the mud and lowered herself to sit beside him. She didn't crouch this time. She sat, properly, backside in the wet, bad leg stretched out in front of her. It was the first time all afternoon she'd let her body tell her what it wanted.

"The rest," she said. "Alright."

She didn't start right away. She picked a bit of dried blood off the side of her thumb with her other thumbnail and flicked it into the dark.

"You want to know what it was like for him. That's what's under the question. Not the what-went-wrong, you've had that. You want to know what he got." She nodded at the man by the wheel without looking at him. "So. First cut, when you hit the jaw. That hurt him. Not as much as you'd think, not right then. Cuts like that come in cold first and hot after. He'd have felt the blade grate the bone more than he felt it open him. That's what woke him up, if he wasn't awake. That's why the heels."

She wiped her thumb on her knee.

"Then the bleeding. Dark one, like I said, slow. But the whistle meant you'd caught a bit of the pipe too, on the way past. Not enough to finish it, enough to let air through where air shouldn't go. So he was trying to breathe, and trying to shout, and the shout was coming out his neck instead of his mouth. He'd have known that. He'd have felt it on his skin." She said it level. She didn't soften it and she didn't lean on it. "That was the bad part. That was about as long as it takes to say it twice. Maybe a bit longer. I won't tell you it was nothing, because you'd know I was lying, and then you wouldn't believe me about the next thing."

The crow had gone. There was only the ditch water, and somewhere far off, a dog.

"Here's the next thing. Second time, you went where my fingers were, and you pushed all the way. That got the big pipe on the inside, the one that feeds the head. When that goes, the head empties fast. He'd have had a few heartbeats of knowing, and then it would've felt like standing up too quick. Grey at the edges, going in toward the middle. Hands go far away. Then he's not there to mind it. The kicking you felt after the whistle stopped, that wasn't him. That was the body not having got word yet." She tipped her head. "Bodies are slow to get the news. You'll see a lot of that. It's not suffering. It looks like it. It isn't."

She was quiet for a bit. When she went on, her voice was the same, but she'd turned her face a little away, toward the road.

"So that's his. Now yours, because that's the rest too, and you asked for all of it."

She drew her good knee up and rested her forearm on it.

"My first one was a man with a broken back under a horse. Not a clean ambush like this, a rout, everybody running. My sergeant said do it and walked off, because we were running. I did it with a sword, standing up, because I didn't know better. Took me three goes." She said the number without any weight at all. "I didn't feel anything for eleven days. I counted them after. Eleven days, and on the twelfth I was mending a strap on my boot and I heard him, plain as you're hearing me. Not the words. The sound he made on the second go. And I sat there with the boot in my lap and shook till the sergeant came and took the awl off me before I put it through my hand."

She looked at her hands then, briefly, as if checking they were still her own.

"You'll get that, or something like it. Maybe tonight. Maybe in a month. It might be the sound. Might be the feel of the bone turning the blade, you'll have that in your wrist for a while. Some people it's the smell. When it comes, it'll come at a stupid time, and you'll think something's broken in you. Nothing's broken. It's just the bill coming in late."

A long breath through her nose.

"And here's the part nobody told me, that I'd have wanted told. You get better at it. You already did. Second time tonight was better than the first by a mile, and the one after this'll be better again. And one day you'll do it clean and quick and right, and you'll stand up and wipe your hands, and you'll feel nothing much, and you'll be proud of how clean it was." She let that land. "That's the one to watch for. Not the shaking. The shaking means you're still you. It's the day you're proud of the clean one that you want to sit down and have a think about what you are."

She turned then and looked at him fully, flat and steady, the dusk making her face all planes.

"I'm not telling you that to scare you off it. You'll need it. This war's going to hand you more ditches, and somebody's got to be able to kneel in them. I'd rather it was somebody who went back in the second time, like you did, than somebody who walks off. I'm telling you so that when you get good, you know what it cost, and you don't pretend it didn't."

She looked away again, down at the mud between her boots.

"That's the rest. There's no more I'm holding back. You made a mess of the first go, you fixed it on the second. He hurt for less time than you'll hurt over it. That's usually how it goes, and it's the right way round, if there is one."

She didn't move to stand. She didn't pick up the oats. She sat in the wet with her bad leg out in front of her and her hands loose on her knee, beside him, and let the dark finish coming down.

"Mill's not going anywhere," she said, after a while. "Neither am I. Sit as long as you need."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my hand in the dim light. "Tell me about the quartermaster and the goat," I say, because I don't want to think about what's in my head yet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let out a short breath through her nose that might, in better light, have been the start of a laugh.

"Right. The goat."

She reached over without asking and took his wrist, turned his hand palm-up, and unstoppered her waterskin with her teeth. She poured a thin stream over his fingers and worked the worst of it off with her thumb while she talked, brisk as washing a pot.

"Quartermaster's name was Aldous Penn. Little man. Had a face like a disappointed hen. He could tell you to the nail how many horseshoes the company had, and he'd be right, and he'd be smug about it. This was my third year, maybe fourth. We were camped outside some town I've forgotten the name of, and a farmer came in owing the captain money. Don't ask me what for. Farmer hadn't got the money. He had a goat."

More water. She rubbed at the crease of his knuckles.

"So the captain takes the goat, and he gives it to Penn and says put it with the stores, we'll eat it Sunday. And Penn looks at the goat, and he looks at his ledger, and he says, very serious, 'Sir, there's no column for goat.'"

She let go of his hand, looked at it, took it back, and did the other side.

"Captain says make one. Penn says he can't make one without a requisition, and he can't requisition a thing that's already been delivered, because then the delivery comes before the request, and that's," she put on a thin, pinched voice, "'irregular, sir.' So for three days that goat doesn't exist. It's eating the tent ropes. It's eating a sergeant's hat. Nobody can kill it for Sunday because you can't butcher stores that were never issued. Penn'd have had your ears."

She stoppered the skin and wiped his hand dry on the cleanest bit of her own coat, which wasn't very clean.

"Fourth day, Penn finds a way. He lists it under wheeled transport. 'One cart, mobile, self-propelled.' Signs it. Stamps it. Very pleased with himself. Now it's a cart. You can't eat a cart either."

She settled back on her hands in the mud.

"So Sunday comes and goes. Then the next one. And that goat just gets to be part of things. Penn starts taking it on his rounds. It follows him through the lines like a dog, and he talks to it. Reads it the inventory, some nights. Somebody swore they saw him give it a biscuit off his own ration, and Penn never gave anybody anything. Goat eats a page of the ledger once, the horseshoe page, and I've never seen a grown man so torn. He didn't know whether to cry or to write it up for damaging stores."

The dog far off had stopped barking. She looked down the dark road.

"We moved on in the autumn. Hard march, lost a lot of kit in a river. By the far side the goat was gone. Nobody knew where. Penn said it'd been 'reassigned.' Wouldn't say to where." A small shrug. "Penn took a fever that winter and went home, and that was the last I heard of either of them."

She was quiet a moment.

"That's it. That's the whole thing. I told you it didn't go anywhere." The dry edge crept back into her voice. "Some nights I think the goat's still out there. Twelve years old, which is ancient for a goat, living on some hill as a registered cart. Owes nobody anything. Never been eaten."

She got her good foot under her and stood. The knee clicked. She swore at it, softly, almost fondly this time, then held a hand down to him, low and steady.

"I've got another one about Penn and a barrel of nails. It's worse. You can have it on the walk."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up. My hand's clean now. "Tell me about the nails," I say, and my voice still sounds flat, but at least it's words. I pick up the waterskin she tossed me and take a long drink. It doesn't taste like pennies yet. It just tastes like water.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack hauled him up and held on a beat longer than she needed to, until she was sure his feet had decided to stay under him. Then she let go and shouldered the oats.

"Water," she said, watching him drink. "Good. Keep doing that."

She set off east, slow enough that he'd come up level on her left, and for the first few dozen paces she didn't say anything. The road was pale between the black hedges, and their boots made the only sound on it. Behind them, the cart and the ditch faded into one dark shape and then stopped being anything at all.

"Nails," she said. "Right."

She hitched the sack higher on her shoulder.

"Same winter as the goat, before the river. We're dug in outside a village waiting on a siege train that never comes, and the captain decides we're going to build a palisade to look busy. So he sends for nails. And the order goes up the line, and it comes back down the line, and it goes through Penn." She gave that its moment. "Penn writes it up as one barrel, nails, assorted. Very neat. Except he's a tidy man, and he's been reading the goat the inventory every night, and somewhere in all that his hand slips. One barrel becomes one hundred."

A rut in the road. She stepped over it without looking.

"Nobody checks. Why would they? It's Penn. Penn doesn't make mistakes. So three weeks later a supply wagon comes rolling in with the driver white as milk, and behind it another, and another. Eleven wagons. Nails in every one. Big nails, little nails, nails for boats, nails for coffins, nails nobody could put a name to. The driver says the depot had to send riders to three towns to find that many, and they near emptied the county. There's farmers can't shoe a horse for fifty miles because our palisade needs a hundred barrels."

She looked at the dark ahead, where the road bent south into the trees.

"Now any sensible man sends ninety-nine back. Penn can't. Sending them back means writing a return, and a return means admitting the order was wrong, and Penn's order was never wrong. So he does the only thing a man like that can do." Her voice went dry as bone. "He makes it right. He goes to the captain and tells him, straight-faced, that on reflection the palisade is inadequate. What we want, he says, is a fort."

A short breath through her nose.

"And the captain, who's bored out of his skull and has nothing else to do, says alright. So we build a fort. Out of green wood, in the rain, in a field nobody wanted, facing a road nobody used. Took us two months. Towers. A gate. Walkway along the top. Penn went round every evening with the goat, counting nails out of barrels like they were gold. We used every single one. When we ran low he had us pull half of them out of one wall and use them in another, so the numbers would square."

The trees closed in over the road. She slowed a little in the darker patch, letting her eyes find the ruts.

"Siege train never came. The enemy never came either. We marched out in the autumn and left it standing. Big square thing in the middle of a turnip field, nails in it worth more than the village." She shrugged under the sack. "I went back past it four years on. Somebody'd made it a barn. There were cows in the gatehouse. It was the only thing we built in ten years that anybody got any use out of."

She walked on a bit.

"That's the nails. Told you it was worse."

The road bent, and the trees thinned on the right, and there was the sound of water somewhere ahead, low and steady. Not loud. Just a river going about its business in the dark.

"That's the race," Wrack said. "Mill's past the bend. Quarter mile."

She didn't speed up. She didn't look at him either, just kept her eyes on the road and her pace where it was.

"When we get there, you'll want to sit down and not do anything. Don't. I'll need wood for the fire, dry stuff from under the eaves where the roof's still good, and you'll get it. Then you'll eat something, even if it's only oats and water, because your body's spent more today than you think. After that you can sit. That's the order. Hands first, then food, then sitting." A pause. "Tomorrow I'll show you how to put an edge on that knife properly. It's dull work. Takes an hour and you'll hate it. It's good for the head, dull work."

The mill came out of the dark as a shape before it was a building. A black wall, a broken line of roof against the slightly paler sky, the dead wheel standing in its race like the ribs of something. Wrack stopped at the edge of the yard and listened, head tilted, for a long count. Wind. Water. Nothing else.

"Nobody home," she said. "Except the family, and they've never given me any trouble."

She set the oats down by the lee wall, where the stone had kept a patch of ground dry, and straightened with a hand in the small of her back.

"Wood's round the side, under what's left of the loft." She was already crouching, clearing old ash from a ring of blackened stones that somebody, probably her, had left there before. "And Corvin." She didn't look up from the ash. "If you want another story, I've got a lot of them. Most don't go anywhere. I'll keep telling them as long as you want to keep hearing."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I find the wood. It's wet on top, but dry underneath. I carry an armload back to the ring of stones and drop it. "Tell me about the fort," I say, kneeling to start stacking the wood. "Did it have a name?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked toward the cart. The sound came again, thin enough to be lost under the creak of a wheel settling in its rut.

“He’s not getting up,” she said. She folded the cloak over a clean patch and gave the blade one last pass. “Question is whether we leave him to do the dying on his own.”

She sheathed the knife and stayed where she was. “I can go. But I thought you ought to have the choice.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "I'll go," I say, my voice sounding rough. I push off from where I'm leaning, my boots crunching over broken ground. "Just... wait here."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded. “I’ll wait.”

She rose and turned her attention to the road beyond the ditch. After a moment, she added, “Mind his hands. Dying men can still hold knives.”

Then she kept watch and said nothing more.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her eyes on the road.

“Both,” she said. “I saw where he was hit. Low in the belly. If he’s still making that noise, he’s got hours in him, maybe. None of them good.”

She glanced toward the cart. “I haven’t been close enough to swear there’s nothing to be done. If there is, I’ll tell you. If there isn’t, leaving him would be easier for us. That doesn’t make it kinder.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight, and make my way toward the cart. The noise gets clearer—a low, wet groaning. I round the wheel and see him lying there, one hand clutching at the dark stain on his tunic. His eyes find mine.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed by the ditch, watching the empty road. She could hear the groaning from there. It had a rhythm to it, breath after breath, and she counted a few without meaning to.

“If you want me to look at the wound, call me,” she said, loud enough to carry past the cart. “I’ll stay here otherwise.”

She shifted her weight onto her good leg and kept watch.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack left the ditch and came around the cart. She stopped short of the wounded man’s reach, glanced at his free hand, then crouched beside him. He was pale beneath the dirt, and the stain on his tunic had spread well past the hand pressed to it.

“Move your hand a moment,” she told him.

He did not. Wrack eased it aside and lifted the cloth enough to see. She looked for a few seconds, then let the tunic fall back into place.

“Blade went in low,” she said to Corvin. “The blood isn’t coming fast enough to kill him quickly. What’s hurt inside will do it slower. I’ve seen men live through this with a surgeon and a clean bed. We’ve got neither.”

She settled the man’s hand back over the wound. “That’s what you’re looking at. He knows we’re here, and he’s hurting. I can do it, if you want me to.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I crouch down too, the smell of blood and dirt thick in my throat. "Alright," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "Give me your knife."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a moment. Then she drew her knife and held it out hilt-first.

“You don’t have to prove anything to me,” she said. “If you want me to do it, say so.”

She stayed beside the wounded man, close enough to help if she was asked. The road beyond the cart remained quiet.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept the knife held out, hilt-first.

“This was a blade,” she said. “A spear usually makes a wider hole. Either one can cut the bowel. Then what belongs inside it leaks into the belly. The pain gets worse, fever comes, and a man can take days to die. If it cuts a large blood vessel, he goes quicker.”

She glanced at the stain on the tunic. “His blood’s coming slow. I can’t tell you exactly what was cut without opening him up, and I’m not doing that. I can tell you he won’t walk out of here.”

Her hand stayed steady. “That’s straight.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the knife. My hand feels cold around the hilt. "Alright," I say, looking down at the man. "Turn your head away."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The wounded man stared at Corvin for a moment. Then he turned his face toward the cartwheel.

Wrack caught his free wrist when it began to move. She held it gently, but firmly enough to keep it away from the knife.

“I’ve got his hands,” she said. “Take a breath. There’s no prize for doing it fast.”

She stayed beside the man and watched his face.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped turning. She kept hold of the man’s wrist and watched him.

He made a sharp sound at first, more surprise than a cry. Then his breath caught and came back ragged. His legs moved against the dirt; Wrack held his wrist until they went still.

“That sound was him trying to breathe,” she said. “The shaking doesn’t tell you how much he knows of it. I won’t pretend I can tell you that.”

She stayed where she was through the next few breaths. The spaces between them lengthened. Once, his chest lifted as if another breath might follow. It did not.

Wrack waited a little longer before releasing his wrist.

“He’s dead,” she said. Her eyes remained on the man, not Corvin. “It took longer than either of us wanted. I saw it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let the knife drop to the dirt between us. My hands are shaking. "Right," I manage. "Now what?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack picked up the knife and wiped the dirt from it with the dead man’s cloak. She checked the edge, then put it away.

“Now we get off this road before someone comes looking for the cart.”

She stayed crouched a moment longer, her gaze on the man by the wheel. “There’s water in my flask if you need to wash your hands. Don’t use it all. We’ll need some for drinking.”

Then she stood and looked past the cart toward the bend. “I’ll check the other bodies and the cargo. You can help, or you can sit for a minute. Either way, we leave before dark.”

Her voice was as level as ever. “You don’t have to decide what this means while you’re still kneeling beside him.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped beside the cart. She looked down at the man, then crouched again and put two fingers against his neck. She waited. When she took her hand away, she did not stand.

“All right,” she said. “The blade hurt him. He made that first sound because of it. After that, he was trying to draw breath, and he couldn’t do it properly. That was the wet sound you heard. His legs moved. His hand pulled against mine once, then stopped pulling.”

She looked at the dirt beneath the cartwheel. “His chest rose three more times after he went still. The last one looked like a breath coming, but none followed. I waited because I’ve seen men lie quiet and start again. I checked his neck just now. There’s no pulse.”

Wrack rested her forearms on her knees. “I don’t know when he stopped knowing what was happening. Anyone who tells you they can see that from the outside is guessing. I saw that he turned his head when you told him to. I saw that he felt the knife. I saw him die.”

For a while she watched the road through the gap beneath the cart.

“He was going to die from the wound in his belly. That doesn’t make the knife nothing. You gave him pain, and you spared him some. Both are true. I won’t tidy one away with the other.”

She glanced at the dead man’s face, then lowered the edge of his cloak over it. “There’s the rest of it. We can’t bury him properly before dark. I’ll take anything on him that might tell us who he was, in case there’s someone to tell. Then we leave. You can hate that part too.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I watch her cover his face. The shaking in my hands has moved up into my chest. "I don't hate it," I say, the words feeling like gravel in my mouth. "That's what's wrong."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack left the cloak where it was. For a moment she listened to the road, then looked back at Corvin.

“No,” she said. “You don’t have to hate it. Taking his name, getting off the road—those are things that need doing. You can do them without feeling bad about every step.”

She rubbed the dirt from her fingers against her trouser leg. “If you mean you don’t hate what happened under this cart, I heard you. I’m not going to tell you what you ought to feel about that, either.”

She took her flask from her belt and set it within his reach.

“I’ve seen men shake after a fight and laugh over supper. Seen them feel nothing for a month, then come apart because somebody dropped a plate. None of it made the dead less dead.” Her mouth tightened. “And none of it told me much about the man still breathing.”

Wrack rose, but did not move away yet. “What matters next is that we leave before his friends find us. I’ll search him. You can sit until I’m done.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the flask and pour water over my hands, watching the pink run into the dirt. "I'll help," I say, my voice still rough. "Just... show me where to start."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the water run off his hands. “That’ll do. Keep the rest.”

She crouched by the man under the cart and lifted the edge of the cloak just far enough to reach his coat. “Start with pockets. Papers, letters, anything with a name on it. Coin too—we’ll need it, and he won’t. Leave his boots unless yours are falling apart.”

She worked through the coat while she spoke, laying what she found on a dry patch of ground: two coppers, a twist of string, a small iron key. From an inside pocket she drew a folded scrap, stiff with sweat but clean of blood. She opened it, read it, and folded it again.

“His name was Harl,” she said. “Or someone called Harl wrote to him. I’ll keep it until we know which.”

Wrack tucked the scrap inside her own coat, separate from the coin, and stood. She looked down the road before pointing to the cart.

“After this, cargo. Open the sacks, tell me what’s in them, and don’t put your face over anything you can’t see into. I’ll check the others. If you hear hooves, say so. If you think you hear hooves, say so anyway.”

She picked up the key. “Might even find what this fits. Nice to have a mystery that won’t bleed on us.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod and wipe my wet hands on my trousers. Kneeling by the body, I reach for his pockets. My fingers brush against something stiff—a small, wooden carving. I pull it out and stare at it for a second before showing it to Wrack. "Found this. Looks like a bird."
