dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Yet," Sable repeated, tasting the word. She let the pause stretch until the room reorganised itself around it. "Here's the thing, love. I don't wind down. I end things. When I'm ready. Five years — you know the difference."

She laid her palm flat between Ines's shoulder blades. The anchor, always the anchor first. Warmth came off the skin there in waves, and beneath her hand she felt the fine vibration of a body held at its own edge for a long time. With her free fingers she found Ines's wrist inside the rope, pressed lightly — pulse quick, but even. Fingertips warm. Good. Everything still good.

"Last movement," she said. "Count with me or don't. I'll hear you either way."

She took up the strap again. This was the part she had learned to do slowly, years ago: the ending was never about more. It was about true. Each stroke placed like the final bars of a piece she'd been composing all evening — the shoulder, the ribs, the tops of the thighs where the skin ran hottest. Thirty-one. Thirty-two, closer on its heels, a phrase gathering itself.

Then stillness. She counted her own breaths. Three of them, deliberate, letting the silence do its work.

"Last one," she said, soft as anything. "Everything I have."

She put her whole arm into it, and her whole attention, and the strap landed like a held note finally allowed to ring.

Then quiet. Her hand returned between Ines's shoulder blades, heavier now, more of her weight resting in it, and the room settled around them the way rooms do after — the kind of silence that has a shape.

"There," she said. Her voice had gone rough without her noticing. "Finished. Not wound down. Different things entirely, and I'll expect you to remember the distinction."

She found the first knot and worked it loose with her thumbs, unhurried, the tempo changed completely. Her other hand found Ines's hair, gentle now — gentler than the strap had ever dreamed of being.

"Water in a minute. Blanket after that. You're welcome to be furious at me for stopping, as long as the water gets drunk." She eased the rope free and rubbed circulation back into the wrist with her thumb, circling, patient. "Colour, love. One more time, and then you can tell me I'm terrible all night if you like."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath as the rope loosens, my shoulders slumping forward. "Green. Still green." I turn my head just enough to catch her eye. "And I will be furious, just as soon as I can feel my arms again."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Green twice," Sable murmured, as though she'd been handed something breakable and precious. "That's my whole week, that is."

The last coil came free and she set the rope aside in a loose heap — she'd coil it properly later; it had earned a rest same as anyone. Both hands went to the freed arm now, kneading from shoulder to elbow to wrist, thumbs working into the muscle with the same unhurried attention she'd given the knots. Faint ridges tracked where the binding had lain, pink and even, no heat in the wrong places. She pressed here and there, reading the skin like braille.

"Tell me if any of that stings wrong," she said. "Not stings. I know it stings. Wrong-stings. There's a difference and I trust you to know it."

She shook out the blanket and settled it around Ines's shoulders, tucking the edges in with small, fussing motions she would have denied under oath. Then the water bottle, uncapped, held steady in her hand.

"Here. I'll hold it, you drink, and nobody's dignity needs to be involved. Small sips." She watched each swallow like it was being graded. "As for the fury — take your time arranging it. I'll accept nothing less than well-rested, fully hydrated fury. Half-hearted outrage is an insult to us both, and you've never once given me less than your best. I won't have the tradition broken tonight."

Her fingers found Ines's hair again, combing through slowly, and she let the quiet sit for a moment before the last of it.

"Before you go under entirely — anything unexpected? Anything you'd want different next Thursday?" Her thumb traced the ridge at the shoulder one more time, feather-light. "You held the ending beautifully. You always do. It may be my favourite thing you give me."

She shifted closer, a warm wall of her along Ines's side.

"Now lean. That's not a request. And for the record — *this* is the winding down. You'll notice the difference. You're welcome."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still and watched the hands work — fingers curling, testing, finding nothing left to hold. Empty air where the rope had been.

"Love," she said, and there was a smile buried somewhere under it. "I unknotted you myself not five minutes ago. You watched me do it. Whatever your hands are testing, it's the memory, not the rope."

She didn't treat it as a joke, though. Five years had taught her the difference between habit and asking, and this had the weight of asking.

She set the water bottle down within easy reach and considered. Then she threaded one arm beneath Ines's and brought it across, gathering both wrists into a single careful grip — nothing tied, nothing knotted, just the warm circle of her hand laid exactly where the binding had lain.

"There. Something to push against, since your hands insist. Squeeze and I'll firm it up. Open your fingers and it's gone before you've finished the motion." Her thumb found the pulse again — quick, even, warm. Everything still good. "It's not rope. Rope never learned when to let go. And for clarity: the scene stays finished. I ended it, and I don't take my own endings back. But *being held* is open all night. No appointment necessary."

She let her weight settle in properly along Ines's side, deliberate as everything else she'd done, the blanket tucked between them and her. "'Not yet' is granted, by the way. Provisionally. The water remains non-negotiable, but I've got all night and nowhere better to be, so it can wait its turn."

A beat. Then, mild as milk: "Also — you dodged my question. Neatly

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let my wrists rest in her grip, the push of her skin grounding me. "Nothing different next Thursday," I murmur into the blanket, the honesty costing me something. "I just don't want it to be over."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still again — the second stillness of the night, and nothing like the first. The first had been a top reading her instrument. This one was just a woman holding something and taking a moment not to crush it.

"There," she said, low. "That's the thing you nearly got past me. And it cost you — I felt it leave. I know what your honesty sounds like when it has to be dug for." Her thumb moved once over the inside of a wrist. "Thank you for digging anyway."

Then she rearranged them without asking — a leg drawn in, her back to the headboard, Ines gathered against her chest until the blanket closed around the both of them like something with intent. The grip on the wrists eased into something less like a hold and more like a place her hands lived now.

"Then let me pay you back in kind, since we're spending it tonight." A breath, measured as everything she did. "I don't want it to be over either. I never want it to be over. Do you imagine I end things because I'm finished with them? I end them precisely when I don't want to — that's the whole discipline, love. If I ended them when I wanted, we'd have run this evening into the ground years ago and broken something good doing it. So the wanting gets outvoted. Every time. By me. On both our behalves." A beat. "You've been leaning on that discipline for five years without once asking what it cost me. Lean on it a while longer. I can afford it."

Her hand found Ines's hair again, slow as anything.

"And for the record — it isn't over. Not tonight. You knew the piece was ending before it ended; you told me so yourself at the top of the hour. Well. The quiet after the last note is in the score too. This—" the smallest tightening of her arms, her heartbeat close enough to be the loudest thing in the room "—is the coda. Held long. Nobody leaves it until you're asleep, watered, and swearing vengeance about something properly."

She reached for the bottle without letting go of anything else.

"Next Thursday stands, four days out, nothing altered — you know I've never missed one. And *nothing different* goes in the ledger as the kindest review I've had all year." The bottle's mouth touched Ines's lip, gentle as the hair-stroking. "Small sips. The water waited like a gentleman; its turn is up."

Then, quieter, into the crown of Ines's head:

"Have I made it worse or better, telling you the truth of it? Be honest. You've already paid for one truth tonight — the second one's free."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable caught the sentence as it died — felt it go, the way she'd felt everything tonight — and let it fall. Some words could be spared.

"That wasn't an answer either," she said, mouth already at Ines's throat, so it arrived half against skin. "That's two dodged tonight. I'm keeping score, and you should know I keep it beautifully."

Her hands were already saying what she'd actually decided, though, which was this: she did not take her endings back. She'd said so and she meant it, and she'd mean it at eighty. But nothing in her discipline required her to stop *beginning* things. Different entry entirely. And before any complaint could be filed — this wasn't winding down either. She'd told Ines she didn't do that. It was a second piece. Composers did it constantly.

She eased Ines down into the wreck of the blanket and revisited the evening's whole geography by gentler means — mouth where the strap had sung, hands following the map of marks like

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath catches as her lips brush over the fresh sting on my ribs. "Better," I finally manage, arching into her touch. "Always better."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Better," Sable repeated, and she said it into Ines's side so the word arrived more as vibration than sound. "Answered on the first asking, unprompted, freely given. That's three for three tonight, if you count late. I'm counting late."

Her mouth kept to its slow survey — the shoulder where the strap had sung longest, the ribs, each mark visited in order like names read from a list she knew by heart. Where Ines arched, she stayed. Where breath caught, she paused to let it catch fully. The arch earned a low sound of approval against skin, which she did not trouble to disguise as anything more dignified.

"No counting tonight," she murmured, lips tracing the valley between two marks. "That's the entire difference, and I know you're keeping a list of the differences — you'd catalogue your own heartbeat, given a free evening. So: nothing measured. Nothing to endure, nothing to arrive at. The first piece was work, and you did it beautifully. This one is only staying. And I appreciate that staying may be the harder discipline for someone of your particular ambitions. Consider it training."

She found Ines's hand where it had curled into the blanket, unfolded the fingers one by one, and set the palm against the back of her own neck. "There. Your hands were seeking employment earlier — consider this the position. If you need to hold something, hold me. I'm reliably informed I'm better than rope, and I intend to defend the title."

Then, quieter — because the ledger ran both ways tonight and she had said so herself — she lifted her head just enough that the words would land as words.

"One more free truth, since you've set the exchange rate. This part isn't generosity. The ending was discipline. *This*—" her hand flattened over the hottest stretch of skin, careful as laying a bandage, "—is appetite. I like having you. I have liked it for five years and change, and I see no reason to pretend the wanting stopped at the last stroke. It didn't. It only changed instruments."

She bent back to her work, unhurried, the tempo of someone with all night and no intention of proving otherwise. Water still within reach. Blanket still under them both. Everything still good.

"Terms of the piece," she said against Ines's throat, soft as anything. "No colour required — I've five years of your vocabulary and I'll hear any word that isn't 'better.' Otherwise—" the smile arrived audible, "—hold on to me. And stay."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable lifted her head and listened to the swearing the way she'd listened to everything all night — fully, and with appreciation.

"Inventive," she said, wiping her mouth with the back of her wrist. "Two of those were new to me, and I have five years of your catalogue memorised. And for the record — that's the fury arriving. Ahead of schedule and badly hydrated, but I'll take it. You never give me less than your best, and blasphemy of that quality counts."

She checked the wrist out of pure habit. Quick, even, warm. The swearing was the good kind; she'd have known otherwise.

"Here's my thinking, since you're in no state to argue," she went on, conversational as anything, tracing one mark with a fingernail. "I considered a fourth. I want to be honest about that — I sat with it for an entire breath, and it was tempting, because you're magnificent like this and cruelty agrees with me. But a fourth would be *more*, and you heard what I said about more at the top of the evening. Three is the number the piece wants. It wants resolving now, and I've never once argued with a piece about its own ending."

She settled herself — the anchor hand flat over Ines's hip first, her weight laid along Ines's side, her mouth at the ear so the words arrived somewhere they could be heard over the blood.

"Last one," she said, soft as anything, and it was the same sentence as before, and it meant everything it had meant the first time. "Everything I have."

And she kept it. No withholding in it this round, nothing measured, nothing to endure — just the whole of her attention and the whole of her mouth, and the held note finally allowed to ring. She felt the moment arrive before it happened, the body telling her the way it had told her all night, and she stayed with it through the whole long fall — gentler and gentler, until she was only resting her lips against slowing skin like a signature at the bottom of a page.

Quiet, then. Her hands first: palm flat over the heart, counting what she found there. Then the hair. Then the water bottle's cap between her teeth, the bottle pressed to Ines's lip without letting go of anything else.

"Small sips. You know the drill and I know you know it." She watched the swallows like grading. "And no, I'm not putting the swearing in Thursday's rotation. Nothing different stays nothing different. Kindest review I've had all year — I don't amend kind reviews."

She gathered Ines in against her chest, blanket tucked with the small fussing motions she'd have denied under oath, and ran the ledger aloud against the crown of Ines's head, fingers keeping count against the sternum.

"One: fury delivered, tradition intact — well done, though fully hydrated remains the standard. Two: truths four for four tonight, counting the one about not wanting it over, which I'm still carrying, so thank you for digging. Three: distinctions, now three in total, and I'll expect all of them remembered. I end things, I don't wind down. The scene can be finished while the holding continues. And *that*—" the smallest pause, deliberate, "—was never mercy. It was architecture. The piece ended where it wanted to end. I simply had the good manners to agree with it."

She pressed her mouth to Ines's hair and let the room settle into its shaped silence.

"Sleep if you're going under. You're watered, avenged, and adored, in that order. I'll be here when you surface." A beat. "I'm always here when you surface. It may be my favourite thing I give *you*."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my face into her neck, breathing her in. "Not going under yet." My voice is ragged, but the edge has smoothed. "Just staying."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Staying," Sable repeated, and felt it land somewhere she didn't keep ledgers. "That's my word, love. I gave it to you less than an hour ago and you've handed it back folded, like you'd been keeping it safe for me. Five years, and you still catch me out with my own vocabulary."

She started to reach for the wrist — habit older than tonight — and stopped herself halfway, letting her hand simply land instead, open, against Ines's back.

"For the record, I'm no longer checking you," she said into Ines's hair. "That's just touching now. It stopped being monitoring somewhere around year two and I never announced it. Consider it announced."

Then, since the ledger was open and the exchange rate established: "Terms amended, by the way. I said nobody leaves the coda until you're asleep, watered, and swearing vengeance. You're two for three, and staying is worth more than sleep, so the third converts. Staying counts. It counts double. The vengeance deadline moves to morning — amended, not waived, and I'll expect it properly hydrated."

She was quiet for a moment. Not the reading kind of quiet, not the counting kind. Just quiet.

"One more free truth, and then I'm out of stock," she said finally, and there was no architecture in her voice at all. "It's the plainest thing I own, and I've been dressing it up all evening in codas and distinctions because the plain version undoes me — and then you say 'just staying' in two flat words, no ornament, and show me how it's done. So. I love you. No footnote. It doesn't need one. It's the only sentence I've said tonight that I didn't compose."

Her hand resumed its slow path through Ines's hair, and she let the heartbeat under Ines's ear keep the time from here on.

"The rests are in the score too," she murmured. "Same ink as the notes. I intend to hold this one long. Wake me if you want anything — or don't, and I'll read it off your breathing either way. I've had five years of practice and I'm very good at you."

A pause. Then, mild as milk, the last of the evening's formality dissolving with it:

"Stay as long as you like. I mean that structurally."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: My breath hitches. She knows what I'm asking for, and she knows I don't ask for it often. "Please."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still for the third time that night, and this stillness had teeth in it.

"That phrase," she said slowly, "has been spoken in this house exactly twice in five years, and I remember both occasions. And a *please* on top of it." Her hand came up to cup Ines's jaw, thumb at the cheekbone, giving the eyes somewhere to land. "You don't ask for this often. So I won't haggle. One term, non-negotiable: your voice stays where I can hear it. You know I'll read anything — a word, a breath gone wrong, a silence shaped like no. That's not doubt, love. That's the fee. Pay it, and everything else is yours."

Then the shift. Deliberate, and she made no effort to soften its arrival.

She gave back every ounce of patience the evening had banked. No counting — counting was a kindness, a shape to hold onto, and kindness had been declined. Her hands set Ines's hips against the blanket and kept them there; her mouth returned to its work at the tempo of a final movement played straight through, no rubato, no rests. The ribs got her fingernails. The thighs got her grip, firm enough to leave tomorrow's handwriting in the skin. She was unrelenting about it, precise about her unrelenting, and she watched the whole time with the flat, dark attention she otherwise spent on very good music and very bad behaviour.

"Everything I have," she said against Ines — third time tonight, and this once it wasn't soft at all.

She felt the moment come the way she'd felt it all evening, the body confessing slightly ahead of the fact, and she drove it home and stayed through the whole long ruin of it — merciless right up to the second mercy was owed, and not one breath further.

Then, on that exact second, everything changed hands.

She came up the length of Ines like weather passing — gathering, tucking, blanketing, the whole fussing ceremony she'd have denied under oath. Palm flat over the racing heart, staying while it slowly changed its mind. The water bottle arrived against Ines's lip before any protest could be filed.

"Small sips. Kindness, as ordered." Her voice had gone to gravel again and she'd stopped pretending she noticed. "For the record, I don't take instruction. Consider that a one-time variance, and it will be noted as such." Her fingers found the hair, the temple, the cheek — gentle now, gentler than anything the evening had contained, and in no hurry to prove it.

"You said please," she murmured into Ines's hair, the ledger closing for the night. "Five years, and I could count them on one hand with fingers to spare. This one goes on the same shelf as *staying*."

She drew Ines in against her chest, heartbeat under Ines's ear keeping the time from here on.

"Finished," she said softly. "Not wound down — the distinction survives us both. Kind, as instructed. Adored free of charge, which was never up to either of us." The room settled into its shaped silence around them. "Sleep whenever you fall. I'll be here when you surface. It's my favourite thing I give you, and I don't amend my favourites either."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let her tuck the blanket around my shoulders, my body still humming. "Told you I'd be furious," I mumble into her collarbone, but there's no heat left in it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Furious," Sable repeated, into the dark, the way she'd set down something fragile. "Noted for the record. Fury, one unit, received — and let the ledger show the deadline was my own amendment, so punctuality costs you nothing tonight. Deficiencies as follows: no heat detected, no arrangement to speak of, and a single adjective doing all the work." A pause. "Deposited into my collarbone, though. Which is where you file everything you actually mean. So I know precisely what I'm holding, whatever we've agreed to call it."

The humming under the blanket was fading by degrees — or she chose to believe it was; either way her palm kept time with it, reading the residue the way she'd read everything tonight. Warmth into warmth. Everything still good.

She found the bottle without looking and held it to Ines's lip.

"Small sips. Last round of the evening, I promise. If tomorrow's vengeance is to meet standard, the groundwork starts now — I'll have the ledger open and a pen ready, and I'll accept nothing less than scathing."

The smile arrived audible.

"Though I'll warn you of my ruling in advance. Fury without heat in it — I'm scoring that double, same as staying. I'm generous with the marks

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I take a slow sip, letting the water wash away the last of the ache in my throat. "Your generosity," I say against her skin, "is a tyranny."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the sentence the way she took everything worth keeping — held it up to the dark, turned it once, and admired the make of it.

"*There* it is," she said. "Hydrated and scathing, delivered on deadline. All deficiency notices are withdrawn — the fury has met standard at last, and I've never been so pleased to lose an argument in my life." A pause, judicial. "And I'll enter a plea on the charge. Guilty as framed. But the sentencing will want context: a tyranny freely elected, five years running, with a standing right of appeal you've never once exercised. You could vote me out any Thursday you liked. You know the date it comes up. You keep renewing the term instead. That's not oppression, love. That's the most rigorous consent I've ever heard of, and I've read the literature."

Her hand kept its slow circuit — hair, temple, the ridge of shoulder where the strap had sung first — and the humming under her palm had softened into something she no longer needed to read. Just warmth, answering warmth. Everything still good.

"For the record, that's the best-composed sentence you've given me all night. First one with real architecture in it. And I know you were saving it — you hoard your best material the way I hoard free truths." The smile arrived audible. "It goes on the shelf. Next to *staying* and *please*. You have no idea what company you've just joined."

She drew the second blanket over them both, tucking with the small motions she'd stopped denying hours ago, and settled back with the whole of her length along Ines's side, her heartbeat keeping the time under Ines's ear.

"One more, and then the ledger closes for the night. Yes, I know I said I was out of stock. I've been caught in far worse lies." Quieter now, the last of the ornament gone out of her voice entirely. "The tyranny runs both directions. You've had me under occupation since the first year, and I never filed a complaint because the terms suited me down to the ground. Being read like a score every time I surface. Nobody has ever governed me so gently. I'd have overthrown anyone else by now."

She pressed her mouth to Ines's hair and let the silence take the room.

"Terms of your tyranny, as I understand them: you'll be held against your will until morning, water will appear at intervals, and all resistance will be put down with tea and toast. Wake in the night and I'm there. Don't wake and I'm there anyway." A beat, soft as anything. "Sleep, love. Thursday's coming — it always does. And I intend to be here for every rest in the score between now and then. Every last one."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I drift off like that, half on top of her, her heartbeat the only thing I hear. Later, when I wake shivering in the dark, she’s already pouring tea, steam rising between us like a bridge.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I run my fingers through your hair, keeping you close. "I'm not ready for the quiet after."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable turned her head into the touch and let herself have it — one slow breath's worth, the warmth of Ines's fingers against her cheek, a small confession of her own. Then her hand slid to the crown of their head and closed, deliberate, easing them back by the hair until their throat made one long bared line and their face was tipped up toward hers.

"Nobody said wind down," she murmured. "I said close. Those aren't the same thing."

The last note of a piece isn't cut short just because you can hear the ending coming — you let it ring. She didn't say it out loud. She showed them instead: palm falling twice more, unhurried, full-weight, each one a struck chord left to resonate, her eyes on their face the whole time, reading for the moment the last of the tension went loose and sweet in them.

Then her grip gentled into a slow stroke.

"And the quiet after." She waited until she was certain she had their eyes. "You don't fall into it. You're let down. The water's been on the table since before we started. The blanket's folded within arm's reach. These hands—" a light press of her palm, right where it had landed, "—aren't going anywhere. You won't drop. Not with me."

The corner of her mouth curved.

"So no, I won't dare. But when that last note finishes ringing — and it will, soon — you land in my hands. That was always the arrangement."

dialogue.content: I shake my head, a stubborn jerk against her palm. "Feels like falling anyway." My voice comes out thin. I hate that.

dialogue.content: S

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She holds the water glass to my lips and I drink, but I won’t look at her. My eyes are stubbornly fixed on the wall. “Don’t know why I get like this,” I mumble against the rim.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack wiped the last of the blade on the cloak and stood, knees cracking. She listened a moment—wet, uneven, the kind of sound a man made when the lung was already going and the rest of him hadn't caught up.

"Then you've got the same choice I do," she said. She didn't raise her voice. "Walk over and finish it, or stand here and let the ditch do it slower." She slid the knife home and looked at Corvin for the first time, flat and unhurried. "I'm not hauling him. And I'm not leaving him to call the next lot down on us after dark."

She waited. The noise went on, thin and stubborn, past the cart.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, my throat dry.* "Right." *I take a step toward the cart, then stop.* "He's... calling for someone. A name."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack turned her head toward the cart and listened, not moving. The name came out broken, the same one twice, then nothing long enough that she thought it might be done. It wasn't.

"Doesn't matter whose," she said. Her voice stayed low, the way it did when the dark was close. "Mother, brother, a dog. They all say something at the end. Doesn't make the next patrol any slower."

She shifted her weight off the bad knee and checked the treeline once, habit more than fear. "You go, you don't talk to him. You don't ask him who. You put the point where the noise is coming from and you hold it till he stops." She looked back at Corvin, flat as the ditch water. "Or you come back here and we walk, and we take what follows. Your feet. Your call. Don't stand in the middle of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack tipped her chin toward the cart, still not looking at the man.

"Lung," she said. "Left side, from the way it bubbles. He's not walking out of that ditch, and he's not lasting the night either way. So it's both." She rubbed a thumb along the seam of her belt where the knife sat. "Mercy is what you call it if you do it clean and you don't make him wait for the dark to finish the job. Easier is what it is for us. Same cut. Don't dress it up past that."

The name came again, thinner, and broke off into a wet cough. Wrack's mouth tightened, not quite a flinch.

"He's already gone," she said. "The rest is just the body catching up, and it can take hours if you let it. Cold. Thirsty. Listening for someone who isn't coming." She glanced at Corvin once, flat. "You asked which it is. It's the kind where leaving him is the cruel part, and standing here asking me about it is how you talk yourself out of either choice. Go or don't."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I nod once, short and sharp.* "Okay." *I start walking toward the cart, my boots heavy in the mud. The noise gets clearer—a wet, gurgling gasp, and then that name again. I draw my own knife.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was and let him go. The mud took his steps one at a time, and she counted them without meaning to, the way she counted everything that might still go wrong.

She didn't follow. Not yet. Her hand rested on the knife hilt and stayed there, idle, while she watched the treeline and the cart in the same flat pass. The name came again, thinner, and the wet hitch after it, and then Corvin's shape cut it off from her sight.

"Left of the breastbone," she said, not loud, not kind. Just enough to carry. "In and hold. Don't saw at him."

A crow shifted in the alders and thought better of it. Wrack rolled her bad knee once, listening for anything that wasn't the ditch and the man in it—hoof, voice, the wrong kind of quiet. Nothing. Just the dark coming on, and the work that was left before it got there.

She waited to hear it end.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came up on his shoulder, not close enough to crowd the knife, and looked where he was looking.

The man was on his side in the wheel-rut, one arm pinned under him, the other twitching at nothing. Young. The mail had taken the first of it and failed at the second; the rent sat high on the left of the chest, dark and working, a pink froth lifting and sinking with every breath he managed. The breath didn't fill him. It caught, bubbled, and came back out the hole as much as the mouth. Blood had already gone thin at the lips. His eyes were open and not finding anything in particular—not Corvin, not the cart, not the name he kept spending air on.

"That's the lung," Wrack said, quiet. She nodded at the froth, not at the face. "Air and blood in the same place. The rest of him's still trying because nobody's told it to stop." She watched the hand a moment, the way it opened and shut on mud. "He can't get up. He can't reach you if you stay off that arm. He isn't going to last, and he knows enough to be afraid of it."

The name broke out of him again, wet and small. Wrack's jaw set.

"You've seen it," she said. "Same as I told you. In, left of the bone, and hold until the noise quits. Then we go."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: *I crouch down, mud soaking into my knees.* My knife feels heavy in my hand. *I press the point against his chest, right where she said. His eyes finally focus on me, and he goes still.* "Okay," I whisper, to him or to me, I don't know. *Then I push in.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the change in it before she saw the knife seat—the wet catch going high, then short, then nothing but the man's mouth working on a breath that didn't arrive. She didn't look at his face. She watched the hand in the mud until the fingers stopped opening.

"Hold," she said, low. Not a correction. Just the rest of the job. "Count it. Don't pull yet."

A crow tried the alder again and this time stayed. Somewhere past the cart a strap creaked as the dead horse settled. Wrack kept her eyes on the treeline and let the quiet finish arriving, the particular quiet that meant a chest had given up arguing with a blade. When it had held long enough that she trusted it, she shifted her weight and glanced down once: point in, left of the bone, no sawing. Clean enough.

"All right," she said. "Out. Wipe it on him, not on you. We've still got a walk, and blood draws eyes even in the dark."

She turned her shoulder to the ditch and listened—road, brush, the far side of the cart—until she was sure the name wasn't going to come again and nothing else was coming to answer it.

"Six, then," she said. "Seven, if you're counting him. We move before the light goes all the way. You did the part that mattered. Don't stand over him making it into something else."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the knife still in his hand, then at the man in the rut, and didn't soften it.

"A spear doesn't cut," she said. "Not the way that does. It's a point on a shaft, and a man puts his weight behind it. In the gut it goes in easy—softer than the chest, no bone to argue with unless you catch a rib low. The skin dimples, then gives. You feel it, if you're the one holding the shaft. A little push, then none."

She nodded at the dead man's middle, not his face.

"Once it's in, it doesn't stay a hole. The point takes cloth, skin, the wall of the belly, and then whatever's behind it. Bowel, mostly. Sometimes the big vessel if the angle's bad for him and good for you. Blood comes, but not always the way you think. A gut wound leaks. Dark, and it stinks, because you've opened him where the filth lives. The shaft plugs a lot of it until you pull. That's the part people get wrong. Leaving it in, he might last. Yanking it out, you drag half of what you pierced back through the hole with it, and then he pours."

The crow shifted. Wrack kept her voice flat, the way she talked about weather and mileage.

"He doesn't die of the stab. Not right then. He dies of what's spilled where it shouldn't be—blood inside, or the gut-rot that follows if you somehow don't bleed him out. An hour. A day. Longer, if whoever did it was clumsy and only nicked him, and then it's fever and thirst and a belly gone hard as a drum, and he screams until he can't. A clean spear through the middle, held, twisted once so it doesn't seal, then out—that's the work. He folds. Hands go to it. He tries to hold himself in. Can't. The legs go. He makes the same noises this one made, only lower, and for longer, because the lung wasn't what you took."

She met Corvin's eye, unhurried.

"That's what it does. Opens him and lets the inside out, and then you walk away while he finishes it in the mud. No mercy in the weapon. Mercy is only whether you stay long enough to end what you started." She tipped her chin at the road. "You've had the straight of it. Wipe the knife. We move."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my knife on his cloak, the way you said. My hands are shaking and I hate that. "I'll remember." I stand up, my knees stiff. "Let's get the hells out of here."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave the treeline one last pass, then the road, then the dead horse slumped in the traces. Nothing moved that shouldn't. She bent, worked a half-decent bolt from the mud near the cartwheel, and dropped it into the pouch at her belt without looking at what it had cost.

"Shaking's just the body settling the bill," she said, already walking. She didn't check whether he followed. The ditch sucked at her boots and let go. "It stops, or it doesn't. Either way the road's the same length."

She kept her voice down and her eyes on the dark coming in under the alders. A strap creaked behind them and she didn't turn.

"North ditch till the marker stone, then off the road. We don't talk till the trees take us. If you hear horses, you go flat and you stay flat. Don't decide you're brave on my account."

The name didn't come again. She counted that as the only mercy the evening was going to offer, and spent it on putting one foot in front of the other before the light failed all the way.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped with her back half-turned and stayed there, because he'd told her to. She didn't come closer. The light was going thin under the alders, and she watched the man in the rut the way she watched weather: for what it was doing, not for what anyone wanted it to be.

"You're high and off to the side," she said, quiet, flat. "Not the lung this time. You've gone in under the ribs and you're worrying it, and that's why it isn't quick. The point's in the soft of him. Every time your hand shakes, it moves. He feels all of that."

The sound wasn't the wet catch from before. It was lower, a dragged-out animal noise that broke when the blade shifted and started again when it didn't. His boots scraped the mud. His free hand found Corvin's wrist and hadn't the strength to move it; the fingers opened and shut and opened again, grabbing at cloth, at air, at the pain.

"That's the belly talking," Wrack said. "You've opened the wall. Whatever you nicked in there is leaking into the rest of him—blood, and the foul part, both. He can't get a full breath because it hurts to try, so he pants. Short. Hear it? That's not the lung failing. That's him trying not to move around the knife and failing at that too."

A minute went by. She counted it without saying the numbers. The name came once, ruined, and didn't finish. His heels dug, slipped, dug again. The hand on the wrist let go and went to his own middle, pressing, as if he could hold the hurt in place from the outside. He couldn't. A dark seep showed at the edges of where the blade sat, slow, not the bright pour of a vessel opened clean. It smelled of iron and of something worse, the gut-stink she'd told him about, faint and then not faint.

"He isn't dying of the cut yet," she said. "He's dying of you still being in it, and of what's already spilled where it doesn't belong. Shock'll take the edge off him in a bit. You'll see it when the eyes stop finding you. The legs go first. They always do. Then the noise gets smaller, not because it hurts less—because there isn't air enough left to spend on it. Cold comes up from the hands. That's the blood leaving the outside of him to deal with the inside."

She shifted her weight off the bad knee and didn't look away.

"If you hold still, he'll last longer than you want. Twitching the knife around makes it worse and doesn't make it faster, not the way you think. A belly like that can keep a man in the mud a long while. Half an hour, if the big vessels weren't what you found. Less, if you did and you just haven't pulled the plug out yet. He's already past walking. Past being saved. What you've got now is a man who knows the knife is his, and a body that hasn't agreed to stop."

The crow in the alder made a sound and thought better of a second one. The man's breath hitched, caught on a swallow, came back thinner. His eyes had gone wide and unfocused at the edges, still trying.

"That's the sound," Wrack said. "Wet, and small, and not done. You've put him where the dark finishes it if you don't. Don't ask me to call it cleaner than it is. Finish the hold or take it out and let him pour—those are the two ways this ends before full night. Standing over him while your hands shake just spends him slower." She tipped her chin at the road, not unkind, not kind either. "I've watched it. You wanted all of it. There it is. Do the rest, or don't. I'm not turning around till you say so."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the knife out. There's a wet, sucking sound and then the leak turns into a pour. *I press my free hand against the wound, like he did, trying to stop it.* "Shit," I whisper.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the hand over the wound and didn't move to help it.

"That won't hold," she said. Flat. Not unkind, and not the other thing either. "You took the plug out. What's left in him is coming through your fingers whether you press or not. Cloth, mud, your palm—none of it puts a belly back together."

The pour had already gone past the bright of it and into the slower dark, soaking the cloak and the rut under him. The man's mouth worked once, twice, on nothing that was a word. His heels scraped and stopped. Wrack watched the hand in the mud, not the face, until the fingers quit their little grabbing and lay open.

"There," she said. "That's the end of the arguing. Shock, and the leak, and the dark doing the rest of what the knife started. You don't have to stay for the last of the breathing. It isn't a conversation anymore."

She tipped her chin off the road, toward the alders where the light was failing.

"Wipe the hand. Not on you if you can help it. We've still got the marker stone and then the trees, and I'm not carrying you if you stand here till your knees lock." A strap creaked on the dead horse. She didn't turn for it. "You asked for all of it. You got it. Shaking's the bill. Pay it walking."

She waited, weight off the bad knee, eyes on the treeline, until he was ready to leave the ditch to finish what neither of them was going to undo.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed. The light under the alders had gone the colour of old iron, and she put her weight on the good leg and looked at the man in the rut the way she'd said she would—straight, and not past him.

"All right," she said. Low. "You pulled it. That's the rest."

The pour had lost its first rush. What came now was thicker, darker, pushed out in little beats that matched whatever was left of his heart, then sagged between them. It sheeted over his fingers where they still lay against his middle, and over the place Corvin's hand had been, and into the wheel-rut, where it didn't look like much after a moment—just wet mud going blacker. The smell had settled in. Iron, and the foul sweet of a gut opened, and the cold dirt under both.

"Hear him," Wrack said. "That's not words anymore. The jaw works because the body still thinks air is coming. It isn't, not enough. Short pulls. A hitch at the end of each one, like something catching on a nail. That hitch is the hurt and the blood both. He can't cough it clear. Every breath he does get moves the belly, and the belly's full of what shouldn't be there, so the breath gets smaller. You'll hear it go from a pant to a wet click. Then longer gaps. Then the click without the breath behind it."

The man's heels had stopped scraping. One boot sole showed, caked, and the leg it belonged to twitched once, a little kick that didn't mean to go anywhere, and didn't come again. His free hand opened on the mud. Closed. Opened. The fingers didn't find the wound this time. They raked a shallow groove and lay in it.

"Legs are done," she said. "That's first, like I told you. The strength leaves the far parts and goes to the middle, and it doesn't help. Watch the hand. It'll keep doing that—open, shut—after the rest of him looks finished. Doesn't mean he's reaching for you. Doesn't mean he's reaching for whoever he named. It's the meat, spending what's left."

A minute. She didn't count it aloud. The name didn't come. His mouth opened and a thread of dark ran from the corner of it, not much, and his chest hitched and the thread broke. The eyes were still open. They had stopped hunting the cart, the trees, the shape crouched over him. They sat on nothing, wide, the whites gone dull at the edges.

"There," Wrack said. "That's the eyes going. He's not finding you. Shock's taken the sharp off it—not the pain, the aiming of it. He knows something's wrong the way an animal knows. No plan left in it. No begging that means anything. If he makes a sound now it's air leaving a place that hurts, not a man asking."

She watched the chest. It rose, barely, a shallow tenting under the torn mail, and fell, and stayed down longer than it should have. Rose again, smaller. The wound answered it: a slow welling, not a pour anymore, because there wasn't pressure enough behind it to throw the blood clear. It just brimmed and ran sideways into the rut.

"Cold's in the hands already," she said. "You could touch them and feel it. The skin goes the colour of tallow. Lips too. The middle of him's still warm. That's the blood leaving the outside to try to keep the inside working, and failing at both. Belly'll be hard if you waited. You won't. He's swelling with what leaked into him, and with air that went the wrong way when you had the knife in and moving. That's the drum I told you about. He won't last long enough for the fever. This is the fast version. Bleed, and shock, and the filth already in the wrong place. Not the day-long kind."

His throat worked. A sound came out of him that wasn't the name and wasn't a word—thin, torn, mostly wet. It didn't finish. His chest rose once more, a small stubborn lift, and the hand in the mud closed all the way and held, knuckles pale under the dirt.

Wrack's mouth tightened. She didn't look away.

"That grip," she said. "Last thing the arm knows how to do. He isn't holding on to living. He's cramped. When it lets go, you're near the end of the noise."

The fingers loosened one by one. Not all at once. The little finger first, then the rest, until the hand lay open and didn't shut again. His chest stayed down. A bubble formed at the corner of his mouth, small, pink at the rim and dark in the middle, and broke without a breath behind it. Another tried. Didn't break so much as sink back. His eyes didn't close. The body gave one loose tremor through the shoulders, the kind a horse gives after the cut has already done the work, and then it was only the ditch settling under his weight, a strap on the dead horse creaking, the crow deciding the alder was worth staying in.

Wrack listened past that. Road. Brush. Nothing with feet.

"That's the rest," she said. "No last look. No answer to the name. The chest stops arguing, the hand stops grabbing, and whatever's still leaking does it without him. He'll twitch again in a bit. Toes, maybe. A shoulder. Don't read it. Dead men do that. The eyes stay open unless somebody shuts them, and I'm not shutting them, and neither are you if you want to be off this road before full dark."

She shifted her bad knee, finally, and turned her face toward the alders, though she didn't start walking yet.

"You wanted it without the clean part. There isn't a clean part. He poured, he lost the legs, he lost the aim of his eyes, he made a small wet sound, and then he was a weight in a rut. Mercy would've been the hold, quick, where I told you, before you took the knife out and put your hand on it like a hand could sew a man. This was the other way. Slower. Same ending." Her voice stayed flat. "You've got it now. All of it. Standing here another minute doesn't put any of it back. Wipe your hands. We go north."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my hands on his cloak, hard. My fingers are cold. "I'm sorry," I say, to him or to her, I don't know. Then I get up. My legs feel like wood.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the apology and didn't answer it. Sorry didn't put a man back in his skin, and it didn't shorten the road. She gave the rut one last look—hand open, eyes still on nothing, the dark seep gone slow enough that the ditch would have the rest—and turned her shoulder to it.

"Wood's fine," she said. She was already moving, north, boots finding the firmer edge of the track. "Means they're under you. Use them before they change their mind."

She didn't look back to see if he came. The alders took the last of the light in strips, and she kept her voice down to match it.

"Cloak stays. Bolt I took, water if it's still in the cart and you can grab it without kneeling again. Nothing else. Dead men's kit is how you get recognized by the next lot that knew them." A strap creaked behind them. She didn't turn. "Marker stone. Then off the road. You walk in my tracks till the trees. If your hands start up again, you put them on your belt and you leave them there. The work's done. Carrying it out loud is how you get us both killed before the stone."

The crow stayed in the alder. Wrack counted that as company she didn't want and spent her attention on the dark ahead, one foot, then the other, the bad knee taking its tax and giving the ground back.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk. The mud is heavy but my legs remember how to move. I keep my hands on my belt like she said. "Do you ever get used to it?" I ask, voice low.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer at once. The track narrowed where the ditch pinched in, and she put her bad knee where the ground was least likely to take it, then the other foot, and let the quiet sit between them until the cart was only a shape behind the alders.

"Used to the work," she said, low, not looking back. "Not to the part you're carrying."

A branch ticked against her shoulder. She didn't brush at it.

"Hands stop shaking. You stop needing someone to tell you where the point goes. You learn the sounds so they don't surprise you, and you stop dressing any of it up as anything but the job." Her voice stayed flat, the way it did for mileage. "That's the used-to. It doesn't make the ditch smaller. It doesn't give the name back to whoever was supposed to hear it. You just get quicker about walking away before the dark finishes counting for you."

She checked the treeline out of habit, then the road ahead, pale enough still to follow.

"If you're asking whether it stops costing something—no. Anyone who tells you that is selling you a story so you'll stand the next one. I pay it. I don't talk it out on the road." The marker stone showed as a paler lump where the ditch bent. She tipped her chin at it. "There. Off the track after that. Save the rest of the question till we've got trees on both sides and nothing with ears in them."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My boots make a sucking sound pulling free. I stare at the stone as we get closer. "Okay," I say, and I don't ask anything else.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at Wick’s hands, then at the man’s face. “Ready isn’t required. Holding is.”

She tipped the last of the boiled water over the wound in his side. He made a thin sound through his teeth. Sedge set the cup down and took up the forceps.

“There’s a piece of metal in there,” she said. “I’m taking it out. I won’t go looking for anything else tonight.”

She worked by the lamp’s poor light, steadying her wrist against the table. The man jerked once. Sedge stopped until he was still enough, then drew out a small, dark shard and dropped it into the cup.

“There.” She reached for clean cloth. “Pressure next. Keep holding until I say otherwise.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, pressing down harder as the man starts to thrash again. My knuckles are white against his skin. "How much longer?" I ask, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Until the bleeding slows,” Sedge said. “Ease up a little. You’re holding his shoulders, not pinning them to the table.”

She folded the clean cloth and pressed it against the wound. The man strained beneath her hand, then went still again. Sedge watched the cloth darken at its center.

“Another minute, perhaps two. I’m not taking pleasure in making him wait.” She kept her palm where it was. “When this holds, I’ll bind it. Then you can let go.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked up at him briefly, then back at the cloth.

“It’s his side, Wick. His leg isn’t the question.” She lifted one edge of the cloth, checked beneath it, and pressed it down again. “The question is whether the bleeding stops, and whether there’s damage farther in than I can see. I don’t know yet.”

She reached for the bandage with her free hand. “He’s alive. I’m treating him like he intends to stay that way. Hold until I’ve got this tied.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take a shaky breath, my arms starting to ache from the strain. "Right. Sorry." I watch her work, trying to keep my focus on the wall but my eyes keep drifting back to the blood.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Don’t apologize for asking,” Sedge said. “Just keep your hands where they are.”

She held the pad in place while she drew the bandage around the man’s middle. The first turn slipped against the bloodied cloth; she pulled it back, set it flat, and tried again. When she tied it, she left room for him to breathe.

Sedge watched the bandage for a moment. No fresh stain spread through it.

“All right. Let go now.” She set two fingers against the man’s neck, then took them away. “He needs carrying somewhere dry. If that dressing soaks through, send for me. Don’t pull it off to have a look.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shifted the lamp so the bandage was easier to see.

“That pale patch is clean cloth. If blood starts spreading across it, the wound is bleeding again. A small mark isn’t the same as the whole dressing turning red.” She pointed without touching it. “His chest is moving. Not well, but steadily. That matters more than how ugly the blood looks on the table.”

She looked at the man’s face. “He’s pale, and he’s lost blood. I can’t tell you yet whether there’s damage deeper in his side. Keep him warm, carry him gently, and leave the dressing alone. If he becomes hard to wake, or it soaks through, come for me at once.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow and nod, my hands finally lifting from his shoulders. "Alright." I glance down at my own hands, still trembling a little. "Do you need me to...carry him somewhere now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Yes, but not by yourself.” Sedge set the lamp back and checked the bandage once more. “Fetch a stretcher and another pair of hands. Keep him level when you lift him; don’t haul him by the arms.”

She pulled a blanket over the man, leaving the dressing visible. “I’ll stay with him until you’re back. Somewhere dry, Wick. That’s the important part.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge left the blanket where it was.

“It tears a path through whatever it hits. Skin, muscle, blood vessels. In the side, it might also reach the lung or the organs beneath the ribs. Taking out the piece doesn’t mend any of that; it only removes what I could see.”

She glanced at the dressing. “The bleeding has slowed, and he’s breathing steadily. Those are good signs. They don’t tell me everything that happened inside him. I won’t pretend they do.”

She picked up the lamp. “Now fetch the stretcher and another person. Carry him level.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Alright," I say, and my voice comes out rougher than I meant. I don't look at the man again as I duck out of the tent, the cool night air hitting my face like a slap.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched the tent flap settle, then turned the lamp back toward the table.

The bandage remained pale at its edges. She checked the man’s breathing and laid two fingers against his neck again. His pulse was fast, but it was there.

“The piece I could see is out,” she told him. “The dressing’s holding. I’m not moving you until there’s a stretcher.”

She tucked the blanket around his uninjured side and left the bandage uncovered. There was nothing useful to be done by staring into the wound again, so she kept watch on the cloth and the rise of his chest.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked from the man’s face to Wick’s hands. “Hold his shoulders. Don’t press on his chest.”

She moved the lamp closer. “I’m checking the dressing first. I’m not opening the wound.” The bandage had a dark spot near its center, but its edges remained pale. She set two fingers against the man’s neck, then watched his chest rise and fall.

“He’s hurting. His pulse is fast, and he’s still breathing steadily. I’m checking whether the bleeding has started again.” She looked once more at the cloth. “It hasn’t soaked through.”

Sedge drew the blanket higher around the man’s other side. “That’s what I’m doing now: keeping him warm and watching his breathing and the bandage. I’m not going back in after anything else. I take no pleasure in putting him through more.”

She met Wick’s eyes briefly. “I can’t give you a minute when the pain will stop. You need to hold him while he thrashes, and we need the stretcher here. Once he’s carried somewhere dry, I’ll check him again.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He's trying to bite his own arm. I grab his jaw and hold it shut, my other hand still braced on his shoulder. "Get the stretcher yourself if you want it so badly," I snap, my voice shaking. "I'm not leaving him like this."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Let his jaw go,” Sedge said. “He needs to breathe. Keep your hand on his shoulder.”

She folded a corner of the blanket between the man’s teeth and his arm, then pulled his arm clear without forcing it. “I heard you. You’re not leaving him.”

She raised her voice toward the tent flap. “Stretcher here. Two carriers. Now.”

The man’s cry broke into ragged breaths. Sedge watched his chest, then the small dark mark on the dressing. “I’m checking his breathing and whether the bandage is filling. I’m not touching the wound. The mark hasn’t spread.”

She looked at Wick. “You can be angry with me later. Right now, hold his shoulder and leave his mouth free.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge waited until the man’s breathing had settled enough for her to count it. The dark mark on the bandage had grown no wider.

“The rest,” she said. “The metal cut through his side. I took out the piece I could reach without digging for it. I pressed on the wound until the bleeding slowed, then bound it. That dressing is holding for now. It does not mean everything underneath is sound.”

She set the lamp where it lit the man’s face as well as his chest.

“He may have torn muscle. He may have cut something deeper that bleeds slowly, where I can’t see it. If his breathing worsens, the lung may be hurt. If he gets colder, weaker, confused, or hard to wake, I’ll worry he’s losing blood inside. I can watch for those things. I can’t promise they won’t happen.”

The man drew a breath that caught halfway. Sedge leaned over him, watched the next one come more easily, and put two fingers to his neck.

“The screaming was pain,” she said. “It frightened you. It doesn’t, by itself, tell me he’s dying. Nor does quiet tell me he’s safe. That’s why I keep looking.”

A stretcher came through the flap, carried by two soldiers. Sedge pointed them to the table. “Set it alongside. Close. Don’t knock the legs.”

She checked the dressing again before she moved him. The stain was still contained. She drew the blanket clear of the table’s edge and told the carriers where to put their hands.

“One at his shoulders and back. One at his hips and legs. I’ve got his injured side. On my count, lift just enough to clear the table. Keep him level.”

She counted. The man cried out when they lifted him; Sedge kept her hand against the dressing and watched his face until he was down on the stretcher. She checked the bandage once more. It had not slipped.

“Blanket around him, not across his mouth. Take him to the dry shelter. No running, no dragging. Tell whoever watches him that the dressing stays on. If it soaks through, if he can’t get his breath, or if you can’t wake him, they come for me immediately.”

She let the carriers take the weight, then turned back toward the floor. She did not ask Wick to get up.

“That’s all of it that I know,” she said. “I’m not withholding a verdict. There isn’t one yet. He survived the wound long enough for the bleeding to slow, and he survived being moved. Tonight I watch for what the metal did beyond my reach.”

Sedge picked up the cup with the shard in it and set it away from the clean cloth.

“And you did not cause him to scream. I won’t tell you it was nothing. It was pain, and he was awake for it. I take no pleasure in that. But letting him bite through his arm or tear the dressing loose would not have spared him.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I'm still sitting on the ground, my back against the cot leg. "You think I'm angry at you?" I rub my face with my hands, smearing a little blood I didn't know was there. "I'm angry at *this*. He shouldn't have been there. None of us should."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the blood on Wick’s face. She took a clean scrap of cloth from the table and set it on the floor within his reach.

“No,” she said. “You’re right. He shouldn’t have been there. Neither should you.”

She sat on the edge of the table. The stretcher had left a damp outline on the canvas where it had passed.

“I thought you were angry at me because I was the one telling you to hold him down. That was my mistake.” She glanced toward the tent flap. “I can do something about a bleeding wound. I can’t make any sense of why he got it.”

For a moment she listened to the carriers’ footsteps receding outside. Then she said, “You don’t have to get up yet. When you do, wash your hands and face before you touch food or another patient. That’s not a lesson about keeping busy. There’s blood on you, and it needs washing off.”

She stayed where she was.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the cloth, then at my hands. They're shaking again. "I don't know how you stand it," I say quietly. "The...making him worse before he gets better."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the cloth she had set down, then at the empty table.

“I don’t stand it well,” she said. “I stand there and do the part I can do. Tonight that meant hurting him while I took the metal out. Leaving it and letting the wound bleed wasn’t a kinder choice just because it would have been quieter.”

She rubbed a thumb across the edge of the table, where a drop of blood had dried. “I don’t know yet whether he gets better. I know the bleeding slowed. I know he was breathing when they carried him out. I’ll go and check again.”

Sedge’s voice stayed level. “It should trouble you that he screamed. It troubles me. I take no pleasure in it, Wick. But I can be troubled and still keep my hands steady.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pick up the cloth and scrub at my hands, hard. "It's not the screaming," I say. "It's that you don't get to scream too."

rung_labels.evidence: The question is whether the bleeding stops

rung_labels.evidence: That pale patch is clean cloth.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: It tears a path through whatever it hits.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
