rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The metal cut through his side.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave Wick one brief look. “Good enough.”

She checked the man’s wrists for a pulse, then pressed two fingers into each hand and watched for a response. “Both hands still warm. I’m checking again after.” She leaned close to the patient. “I’m going to put your shoulders back. It’ll hurt. Don’t help me.”

He made a sound that might have been an answer.

Sedge took his left arm and eased it outward, slow and steady, keeping the joint aligned. “Hold his chest down. Not his neck.” She waited until the tension in the arm changed, then adjusted her grip and guided the joint home.

The man bucked against the table. Sedge kept hold of his arm until the hard resistance gave way. There was a dull shift under her hands.

“That one’s in,” she said, without looking up. She checked the man’s fingers again, then moved to the other side. “Now the right. Same as before. Don’t let him twist.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my hands firm on his chest, but I can feel the tremors running through him. My eyes flicker to Sedge's face, then back to the wall. "Right," I mutter, bracing myself for the next one.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge took the right arm just above the elbow and supported the wrist with her other hand. “Keep his chest down,” she said. “If he twists, the joint won’t go where I need it.”

The man’s breath hitched. Sedge waited for the arm to loosen, then drew it outward in a slow, controlled line. He jerked hard against the table. She held the alignment and kept moving, inch by inch, until the resistance softened.

The joint shifted back with a blunt clunk.

“That one’s in.” Sedge let the arm rest against the man’s side, then checked his fingers for warmth and pressed each nail bed, watching the color return. She checked his wrist pulse, then repeated the tests on the left. “Hands are warm. Pulse is there. Tell me if either hand goes numb or starts getting cold.”

She looked over the man’s shoulders, careful not to move them more than necessary. “No more pulling on them tonight. We’ll bind him close and get him somewhere he can be watched.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at him. “Neither. His shoulders were out. That wasn’t a leg, and I’m not cutting anything off.”

She checked the man’s hands once more, comparing their warmth and color. “The hands are warm and the pulses are there. That’s good. It isn’t a promise. If either goes cold, numb, or pale, you tell me at once.”

She reached for the bandages. “He’ll hurt. That’s the part we’re being kind about: keeping him still, watching the hands, and not pretending it won’t.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. My hands relax a little on his chest, but I don't move away yet. "Right," I say, glancing down at his hands. "Cold, numb, pale. Got it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Keep your hands there until I’ve got the wrap on,” Sedge said. “Then you can let him breathe.”

She folded a strip of cloth around the man’s upper chest and arms, securing them close to his sides without pulling the shoulders forward. She checked the fit with two fingers, then watched his hands again.

“Not tight enough to stop his breathing,” she said. “Tight enough to stop him trying to sit up and put them out again.”

The man gave a thin, exhausted groan. Sedge tucked the end of the bandage beneath the wrap and felt along both wrists for the pulse.

“Still there. Still warm.” She set the man’s arms where they rested easiest and pulled a blanket over him. “We’ll check again in a little while. If his hands change, call me. If he wakes up and tries to move, keep him flat and tell him I said no.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at Wick, then back at the man’s hands. “You’re seeing that both hands are still warm, and the color comes back after I press the nails. I can feel a pulse at each wrist. That means blood is getting through for now.”

She checked the fingers again, one hand and then the other. “You’re also seeing swelling and the start of bruising around the shoulders. That’ll get worse before it gets better. The joints are back in place; the hands tell me whether anything important got pinched or stretched in the process.”

She laid the man’s arms against his sides and watched his breathing beneath the wrap. “He’s breathing without the bandage fighting him. I’ll check his hands again soon. If one turns cold, pale, blue, or numb, that’s not something to wait on.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, trying to commit the details to memory. "Okay. So... warm good, cold bad." I finally lift my hands off his chest and step back, wiping my palms on my trousers. "You need me to stay with him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Sedge said. She wiped her hands and reached for the next strip of clean cloth. “Stay until I’m back. Watch his breathing. Check both hands in a few minutes—warmth, color, feeling. Don’t unwrap him or try to move his arms.”

She gave the bandage one last look to make sure it wasn’t riding up over his chest. “If he wakes and starts to sit up, keep him flat and call me. If either hand changes, call me louder.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused with the cloth in her hands. “Straight, then. A piece of shrapnel doesn’t make a neat hole. It tears through whatever’s in its way—skin, muscle, blood vessels, nerves. If it hits bone, it can break it and scatter smaller pieces. The metal and whatever filth it carries can leave an infection behind. Sometimes it stops where it lands. Sometimes it goes deeper than the wound makes you think.”

She set the cloth down and looked at the man’s shoulders. “I haven’t found a fragment in him. I’ve put his joints back and checked the hands. That tells me the arms are getting blood for now. It doesn’t tell me what a piece might have done elsewhere, or promise there’s no damage we haven’t seen.”

She reached for the man’s wrist again. “That’s why we watch him. If his breathing changes, he gets confused, goes cold, or starts bleeding, you call me. No guessing that he’s fine because he’s quiet.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let that settle in my gut, heavy. "Alright." My eyes stay on his chest rising and falling under the blanket. "I'll yell if anything changes."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Good,” Sedge said. “Watch his chest, not the blanket. If his breathing gets shallow, uneven, or stops, call me. Don’t wait for it to look dramatic.”

She checked the man’s pulse once more, then set the blanket clear of his face. “I’ll be just outside. Quiet isn’t the same as fine.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked up at the renewed screaming. “I’m not putting either shoulder back again. They’re in. More pulling would risk doing damage.”

She checked the wrap first, sliding two fingers beneath it to make sure it hadn’t tightened across his chest. Then she watched his ribs rise and fall. “I’m checking that he can breathe under this. I’m checking both hands again: warmth, color, feeling, and pulses at the wrists. If those have changed, I’ll deal with that. If they haven’t, I’m leaving the joints alone.”

The man strained against the table. Sedge kept one hand near his arm without forcing it down. “He’s hurting, and he may keep hurting. I’ll give him what pain medicine we have, if he’s alert enough to swallow and it’s safe. Then I’ll settle his arms where they’re easiest, secure the wrap again if it’s slipped, and keep watching his breathing and hands.”

She leaned toward the patient. “Don’t try to sit up. Don’t pull your arms. You can shout. You can breathe. You don’t need to help me.”

Sedge checked the first wrist, then the second, her fingers steady against his skin. “Both pulses are there. I’m checking the nails now.” She pressed and released each one, watching the color return. “Still warm. Color’s returning. That is what I’m seeing. It doesn’t tell me the whole injury is harmless.”

She looked toward Wick. “The hands need checking again in a few minutes. The breathing needs watching now. This part takes as long as it takes; I’m not going to give you a false number. I’ll stay until he’s settled enough to leave under watch.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her press his nails, the tiny white turning pink again. "Okay," I say, my voice lower than I mean it to be. I shift my grip, just keeping him flat, not pinning him. "You said pain medicine. When?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Now, if he can swallow safely,” Sedge said. “I’m not pouring anything into his mouth while he’s bucking. He could choke.”

She leaned close enough for the man to hear her. “Look at me. Can you tell me your name? Can you swallow?”

While she waited, Sedge kept an eye on his breathing and the wrap. “If he answers and can swallow, I’ll give him the dose by mouth. If he can’t, I won’t force it. I’ll check what else I have.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge waited until the man could take a breath without fighting it. His eyes were open, though unfocused. She kept the blanket clear of his face and watched his chest rise twice before speaking.

“Tell me your name.”

He managed it, hoarse and broken by the shouting.

“Good. Can you swallow?”

He nodded. Sedge gave him a little water first and watched his throat move. He swallowed without coughing.

“Now the pain dose,” she told Wick. “A measured amount by mouth. I’m not giving him enough to knock him senseless, and I’m not giving him anything while he can’t protect his own airway. It should take the edge off. It won’t make this painless.”

She measured it carefully, brought it to his lips, and waited while he swallowed. She watched him breathe afterward, then checked that he could answer her when she said his name again.

“Stay awake for me a little longer,” she told the man. “You can close your eyes after I’ve checked you.”

Sedge checked the wrap again, slipping two fingers beneath it at the center of his chest. “There’s room here for his ribs to move. I’m checking that because a tight bandage can turn a shoulder injury into a breathing problem.” She watched his chest rise and fall. “Still even. No obvious struggle.”

She moved the blanket aside enough to inspect the parts of him she could reach without shifting his arms. Her fingers traced the cloth near his shoulders, not pressing into the joints. She checked for fresh blood, then looked along his chest and upper arms for any visible wound she might have missed in the bad light.

“I don’t see a fragment sitting in the skin,” she said. “That is not the same as knowing there’s no fragment inside. I’m not going to dig blindly for metal. That makes a larger wound and can hit something important. If something is lodged deep, we leave it until there’s a way to see where it is and someone with the equipment to remove it.”

She drew the blanket back over him and returned to his wrists. “Now the hands again. I’m comparing them, not just looking at one and deciding it’s fine.” She checked warmth with the backs of her fingers, pressed each nail, and watched the color return. Then she felt both pulses. “Warm. Color returns. Pulses present.”

She looked at the man. “Can you feel this?”

She touched one fingertip, then another, asking him to name which one. His answers came slowly, but they came. Sedge repeated the check on the other hand.

“Feeling is there now. That’s useful. It still doesn’t tell me whether a nerve was stretched, and it doesn’t promise the swelling won’t change things later. That’s why we check again instead of deciding once and forgetting it.”

She adjusted the man’s arms by fractions, only enough to settle them close against his sides where the wrap supported them. When his face tightened, she stopped.

“That’s as far as I’m moving them. They stay supported. Nobody pulls him up by the arms, nobody tries to test how far he can lift them, and nobody puts either shoulder out again to see if it’ll go back in easier the second time.”

The man made a thin sound and shut his eyes.

“Not yet,” Sedge said. “Keep them open for me.”

He opened them.

Sedge checked his breathing once more, then his pulse. “Here’s the rest. The joints are back where they belong. His hands are getting blood, and he can feel my touch at the moment. That’s what I know. I don’t know whether he has a small fracture, whether there’s a deeper injury from the blast, or whether the swelling will press on a nerve later. I can’t tell you none of that will happen.”

She tucked the blanket around his ribs but left his face and chest unobstructed. “For tonight, he stays flat and warm. We keep the wrap in place, but we don’t cinch it tighter. We check his breathing and both hands again in a few minutes, then keep checking them. If a hand turns cold, pale or blue, if he loses feeling, or if the pulse changes, I want to know immediately. If his breathing gets shallow, uneven, or difficult, same answer. If he becomes hard to wake, starts bleeding, or gets confused, call me.”

She put the back of her fingers near his cheek, then watched him take another breath. “If he vomits, turn him onto his side as one piece. Don’t wrench one shoulder around by itself. If he tries to sit up, stop him and call me. The joints may be in now, but they can come out again.”

Sedge pulled a stool close enough to reach the man’s wrists without leaning over him. “The pain medicine needs time. I’ll watch him while it takes effect. I won’t give him another dose early because he’s still hurting. If he gets sleepier than he should, or his breathing changes, that matters more than the pain.”

She held the man’s wrist for a count, then released it and checked the other. “Still there,” she said. “I’m staying here until he’s settled and the next check is done. After that he needs someone beside him, watching—not someone deciding that quiet means cured.”

Sedge kept her eyes on the man’s chest, counting each rise before she looked back at his hands. “That’s the rest,” she said. “No clean ending. We keep him still, keep him warm, keep checking what we can, and we don’t lie to ourselves about what we can’t see.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I rub my face with my palms, still sitting on the floor. "So he's not safe," I say, more to myself than to her. "Even now. Even with all that."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept two fingers on the man’s wrist, counting the pulse before she answered.

“Not safe isn’t the same as dying,” she said. “His shoulders are back in place. His hands are warm, his pulses are there, and he’s breathing evenly. Those are good signs.”

She released his wrist and checked the other hand again. “But he’s hurt, and I can’t see everything that happened inside him. He could worsen. So we watch him. That’s the honest answer.”

The man’s chest rose beneath the blanket. Sedge watched it rise again before reaching for his fingers.

“He isn’t alone, and he isn’t being left to chance,” she said. “For now, that’s what we can do.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up off the floor, my knees stiff. "Alright." I look at the man, then at my own hands. "I'll watch. You tell me when to swap out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge nodded once. “I’ll tell you. Don’t wait until you’re shaking to say you need a break.”

She checked the man’s breathing again, watching his chest rise and fall before she took each wrist in turn. “For now, count his breaths now and then. Watch for the effort, not just the number. Check both hands for warmth and color. Ask if he can feel your touch, but don’t make him move his arms to prove it.”

She set the man’s wrists back against the blanket. “If anything changes, call me. If it doesn’t, keep watching. I’ll be close.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean against the tent pole, arms crossed. "He's got a name," I say, my voice rough. "Tell me it so I can use it when I talk to him."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack wiped the knife once more and stood. The dead man’s cloak slipped from her hand into the mud.

“Good,” she said. “Then we’ve both heard him.”

She went around the cart, keeping her blade low. The wounded man was on his side in the trampled grass, one hand pressed uselessly to his belly. His breath came in short, wet pulls.

Wrack crouched beside him and looked over the wound. “Still alive,” she said. “That’s inconvenient.”

She glanced back toward the ditch. “If you mean to do something, now’s the time. Otherwise I’ll make it quick.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, trying to keep my voice steady. "I'll... I'll do it." I walk over, my hand tightening on the hilt of my sword.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack shifted aside, leaving the space by the man clear. His breath hitched, then dragged wetly through his teeth.

“Under the jaw,” she said. “Up. One thrust. Don’t hack at him.”

She kept her eyes on the wounded man, not on Corvin. “Make it quick. That’s the only kindness left.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked down at the man’s hand, pressed hard against the wound. Blood kept working between his fingers.

“He’ll die,” she said. “Could take an hour. Could take less. He’ll spend it hurting.”

She glanced at Corvin’s sword, then back at the wounded man. “Mercy and easier can be the same thing. Doesn’t make either one a lie.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: (My hand's shaking. She can see it.) "An hour." I repeat the words, trying to anchor myself. I kneel down, my sword feeling heavy as stone. "Under the jaw," I whisper, mostly to myself.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack saw the tremor in his hand. She had seen it in plenty of hands. It didn’t make the blade any heavier.

“Don’t stop halfway,” she said. “That’s when it gets ugly.”

The wounded man pulled another ragged breath through his teeth. Wrack kept her eyes on him.

“If you can’t do it, say so. I will. No one’s keeping score.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack followed his gaze to the man’s hand.

“His belly’s opened. Deep enough that pressing on it won’t stop what’s happening inside.” She kept her voice level. “He’s lost blood. He’s cold, hurting, and still awake enough to know both.”

The wounded man’s breath caught, then scraped out of him.

“That wet sound’s his throat. Not the wound.” Wrack looked at Corvin’s sword. “He may go quiet on his own. He may not do it soon.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, and the movement feels mechanical. My grip on the sword tightens until my knuckles ache. I lean down, placing the tip just under the man's jawbone. His eyes find mine, wide with pain and fear. I look away as I shove the blade upward in one sharp, desperate motion.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched the man jerk once beneath the blade. The wet rasp stopped. For a moment, only the wind moved through the trampled grass.

She crouched and checked his eyes, then the pulse at his throat. Nothing.

“Done,” she said.

She wiped the blood from her fingers on the dead man’s shirt. “You put it where I told you. That’s better than most manage the first time.”

Her gaze shifted to the cart, then to the darkening road beyond it. “We should move before the rest of them come looking.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t soften it.

“Straight, then. The spear went through his belly and opened something it shouldn’t. Maybe bowel. Maybe a blood vessel. I didn’t see the angle, so I won’t pretend I know which.”

She looked down at the dead man. “The blood under his hand was only what you could see. The rest was going inside him. If it was bowel, its contents would leak into the wound and poison him over the next days—if the bleeding didn’t finish him first. He was cold, losing blood, and in pain. He wasn’t walking away from it.”

Wrack wiped her hand on the dead man’s shirt.

“That’s what a spear does. It makes a small hole outside and a larger mess where you can’t reach it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's hand, still pressed against his belly. "So my mercy was the only clean part of it." I stand up, my knees stiff and cold. "I'll check the cart. Then we move."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the dead man’s hand, still curled against his belly.

“Mercy isn’t clean,” she said. “It just ends the part that can still be ended.”

She bent to retrieve her knife and wiped it on the cloak before sheathing it. “Check the cart for food, water, anything that’ll keep. I’ll see what these six were carrying.”

She glanced once toward the road. The light was thinning fast.

“And don’t take anything you can’t carry at a run.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped and looked back. She stayed where she was, close enough to see his hands.

“He’s dead,” she said. “He won’t feel anything. He won’t take time. There’s no breath left to catch, no voice left to make a sound.”

Her gaze remained on the body. “If you’re searching him, you’ll hear cloth drag and buckles knock. If you’re doing something else, tell me what—and I’ll tell you what it does. I won’t make up the parts I can’t see.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I reach out and uncurl his hand from his belly. The skin is already going slack. "You'll see," I say, my voice low. "You'll watch me do it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed where she was.

The dead man’s fingers came loose without resistance. His palm left a dark smear across his shirt.

“You’ve got a witness,” she said. “But I won’t name what you’re doing before you do it.”

Her eyes stayed on his hands. “If you’re looking for something, say so. If you’re making a mess, at least know you’ll be the one cleaning it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stayed beside the body. The hand lay open now, fingers crooked where they had stopped.

“The rest,” she said. “His skin will cool. His blood will settle in the low places. In a few hours, the joints will start to stiffen. None of it means he’s coming back or that he can feel anything. It’s only the body changing after the person is gone.”

She paused, then added, “If you open him, you’ll find what the spear did. I can tell you what I see. I won’t guess at what’s hidden, and I won’t pretend there’s a lesson in it.”

Her gaze stayed on Corvin. “He was alive, and hurt, and afraid. Now he’s dead. That’s all the rest I know for certain.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at my own hand, the one that held the sword. "He didn't even try to stop the blade." My throat tightens. "That's the worst part."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the open hand, then at Corvin.

“He had one hand holding his belly shut and barely enough breath to keep making noise,” she said. “He may not have had the strength. He may have known what you were there to do. I can’t tell you which.”

She wiped her knife clean against the cloak and sheathed it.

“Don’t turn it into proof he wanted it. Don’t turn it into proof he didn’t. He was hurt and afraid. Then he wasn’t.” Her voice stayed flat. “That’s all we get to know.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: (My hand's still shaking.) I press my palm flat against the cool, damp ground. "It doesn't feel like mercy when you're the one holding the knife." I finally push myself up, looking toward the cart. "Let's see what they had."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the dark smear on the ground beneath Corvin’s hand.

“No,” she said. “It doesn’t.”

She turned toward the cart and lifted the loose edge of its canvas. Beneath it sat two sacks of grain, a cracked water barrel, and a wooden box bound with iron. She checked the barrel first, sniffed the water, then set it aside.

“Water’s sour. Grain might keep if we don’t mind weevils.” She tested the box’s latch with her knife. “They weren’t carrying anything worth dying for. That’s usually how it goes.”

The latch gave. Inside were a few spare bolts, a whetstone, and a purse with enough coin to matter if they lived long enough to spend it. Wrack took the whetstone and left the purse where it was.

“Take what you can carry,” she said. “Leave the rest for the crows.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my knife off on the grass before sheathing it. My eyes keep drifting back to the man's body. "You're not taking the coin?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No, you're not," Sedge said, not unkindly. "Nobody is. Do it anyway."

She tipped the lamp toward the man's thigh and cut the rest of the trouser leg away in two long strokes. The field dressing underneath had gone black at the center and bright at the edges, which meant it was still going. She peeled it back, and the smell came up to meet them both.

"Shell fragment. Went in here." She touched the edge of the wound with the back of a gloved knuckle, the way someone might point at a line on a map. "Didn't come out. It's sitting somewhere near the bone, and every time he moves it chews a little more. So it comes out, and then I tie off whatever it's been chewing on, and then we find out if he keeps the leg."

She picked up the forceps and held them where the light would catch them, checking the jaws. Her hands were steady. They had been steady for four years, and she no longer thought of that as a virtue, only as a fact about her hands.

"I'm not going to count down. Counting just gives him time to brace, and bracing makes it worse. When I go in, he's going to find a new sound. That's the nerve, not you, and not me, and it doesn't mean anything's going wrong." She glanced up once, not at the man but at Wick's hands on his shoulders. "Elbows locked. Put your weight through your arms, not your back, or you'll feel it tomorrow and be no use to me."

The man's eyes had drifted half open. He was looking at the tent roof, or through it. Sedge leaned down so her face was in his line of sight.

"This is the bad part," she told him plainly. "After this it's only sore."

Then she went in.

She was right about the sound. He came up off the table all at once, his whole body arching against Wick's weight, heels drumming the boards. Sedge kept her left palm flat on his hip and let the forceps follow the track of the wound down, slow, feeling rather than seeing.

"There. Touching it." Her voice didn't change. "It's turned sideways, the bastard. Hold. *Hold.*"

The table creaked. Something on the instrument tray rattled and went still.

"Nearly." A small twist of her wrist. "Keep him flat, Wick. Flat. If he comes up now, it tears on the way out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My elbows lock, my arms straining as I try to keep him pinned. I can feel him trembling under my palms. "He's slipping," I grunt through clenched teeth, sweat starting to bead on my forehead.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then lean," Sedge said. "Chest over him if you have to. He's not glass."

She didn't look up. Her eyes were on the wound, on the small dark mouth of it where the forceps disappeared, and her left hand moved from his hip to the top of his thigh and pressed down hard, pinning the leg from her side so that the whole of him was caught between the two of them.

"Good. Like that. Stay like that."

The man's sound had gone ragged and high, breath dragging in between. Sedge ignored it the way she ignored the lamp smoke and the wet cold coming through the tent floor. It was information, nothing more: he was still breathing, and still had enough in him to fight. Both were good.

"I've got the edge of it. It's small, it's jagged, and it's caught on something." Her wrist rolled a quarter turn and she waited. Waiting was most of the work, and nobody ever believed that until they watched. "Easy. Easy. There. It's coming."

She drew back steadily, not fast. Fast was how you left half of it inside. The forceps came up out of him slick and dark, and in their jaws was a curl of grey metal no bigger than a thumbnail, torn at every edge like the lid of a tin.

"That's it," she said. "That's the whole of it. That little thing."

She dropped it in the basin, where it rang once, and she already had a pad in her other hand, jamming it down into the wound as the blood came up to replace the metal. Bright now, and fast.

"Right. There's the thing it was chewing on. Don't let go yet. He'll think it's over and he'll try to sit up, and it isn't." She leaned her weight onto the pad with the heel of her hand and reached for the needle holder without looking, the way someone reaches for a cup they know is there. "Two minutes. Maybe three. The worst of it's done. Now it's just sewing."

She glanced up then, briefly, at Wick's face and the sweat standing on it. Her expression didn't soften much, but it moved.

"You held," she said. "Keep holding."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer straight away. She was threading the needle by feel, eyes on the pad, and she finished that first because it mattered more than the question.

"I don't do that kind," she said. "Kind like that just means he finds out later, from someone who doesn't have the time to sit with him. What I told him was true. This was the bad part. After this it's only sore." She peeled the pad back a finger's width, looked, and pressed it down again. "Whether it's sore with a leg or sore without one, I don't know yet. Nobody does. That's not me being careful. It's just where we are."

She took the pad away properly this time and went in with the needle before the blood could fill the space. Small bites, quick and close, her lips moving slightly, counting stitches rather than seconds.

"The vessel it was chewing on is the big one down the inside of the thigh. Not cut through. Nicked, ragged, and he's been leaking out of it since whenever he got hit, which is why he's the colour of that canvas." A knot, snugged down. Another bite. "If I'd found it cut clean in two, you and I would be having a different conversation. Nicked, I can close. The question is whether enough blood gets past my stitching to keep everything below it alive, and whether the rot's already started in the meat around it. That smell isn't nothing."

The man had stopped arching. He was shaking now, a fine hard tremor from his jaw down, and his breath came in short wet pulls. Sedge put the back of her wrist against his neck for a moment without breaking rhythm, then went back to the sewing.

"Cold, fast heart. He's lost a lot. Doesn't mean he's going." She tied off the last knot and cut the thread close, then sat back half an inch and looked at the wound. The fresh blood welling at the edge was slow now, dark, and it didn't come back when she dabbed it. "There. That'll hold, if he lets it."

She pulled her glove off her right hand with her teeth and reached past the wound, all the way down the leg to the foot, which was grey and bare where the boot had been cut away. She pressed two fingers in behind the knob of the ankle bone and went very still.

It went on a long time. Long enough that the tent seemed to get quieter around it.

"Come on," she said, low, to the foot and not to anyone in the room.

Then something in her shoulders let go by a fraction.

"There. Weak. But it's there." She kept her fingers where they were a moment longer, as if to make sure it didn't change its mind, then took them away. "That's the first answer, and it's the good one. Blood's getting through. If his toes are pink by morning and the smell isn't worse, he keeps it. If the smell's worse, I take it off above the knee and he lives. If it's worse and I wait too long, he doesn't. So tonight someone looks at that foot every hour."

She looked up at Wick, and this time held it.

"You can let go of him now. Slowly. Don't just drop your weight or he'll think he's falling." A pause. "And that's a straight answer, all of it. When I'm lying to make it easier on you, I'll tell you I'm doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I let go slow, like you said. My arms ache like hell. "Who's on the watch? I'll take a turn."

I look down at the man's face. He's not shouting anymore, just staring at nothing.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"You are," Sedge said. "First turn and third. I'll take second, and Merrow can have the last one when he comes off the ward. He'll complain. Let him."

She was already moving. She peeled the other glove off and dropped both into the bucket by the table leg, then wrapped the thigh in clean linen, firm but not tight. She tucked the end under rather than tying it, so it could come off fast.

"That's the wrong thing to be watching." She nodded at the man's face without looking at it. "The staring. That's just what they do after. The body's spent everything it had keeping him awake through that, and now there's nothing left to put behind the eyes for a while. It isn't damage and it isn't dying. Talk to him if you want. He won't answer and he probably won't remember it, but some of them say later they could hear a voice and it gave them something to hang on to. Doesn't matter what you say. The weather. Your mother. Anything but the leg."

She dragged a folded blanket off the shelf behind her, shook it out one-handed, and laid it over him from the chest down, leaving the foot bare. She pulled the lamp closer to the end of the table and turned the wick up until the grey skin of his toes caught the light.

"This is what you watch. Every hour, on the hour. Don't guess, look at your watch. Three things." She held up a finger for each. "Colour. It's grey now. If it goes pinker, good. If it goes mottled, blotchy purple like a bruise that can't decide, you come and get me. Second, press the big toenail. It'll go white. Count how long it takes the colour to come back. Right now it's slow, four, five. If it gets faster, good. If it stops coming back at all, you come and get me." She crouched and did it herself to show the way, thumb on the nail, lips moving as she counted, and then straightened. "Third is the smell. Get your face down near the dressing each time. I know. Do it anyway. You'll know it if it changes. It goes sweet, and it's a sweetness you won't mistake for anything else once you've had it in your nose. That's the one you run for."

She looked down the length of the table at him, the wrapped thigh, the bare grey foot.

"And if his breathing goes shallow and quick and doesn't settle, or he gets hot to the touch, or he wakes up and can't tell you where he is, same answer. You don't wait to be sure. I'd rather be woken for nothing ten times than once too late."

She wiped her hands on the rag at her belt, which did nothing much, and glanced at Wick's arms.

"Before your turn starts, eat something. Anything. Then get warm water from the stove and put your forearms in it for a few minutes. It'll help with the shaking. You'll have the shaking in about a quarter of an hour, when you stop thinking about him. Everyone does, the first several times. It doesn't mean you're soft. It means you held a grown man down with your arms for twenty minutes."

She picked up the basin with the metal in it, looked at the small torn curl in the bottom, and tipped it out into her palm. She turned it once in the lamplight.

"He'll want this," she said. "They usually do, when they come round. Something to hold that isn't inside them anymore." She wrapped it in a scrap of gauze and set it by his hand on the table. "Put it in his pocket if he wakes on your watch."

Then she sat down on the upturned crate by the tent pole for the first time in what might have been hours. She rested her elbows on her knees and let her hands hang. For a moment she only breathed.

"You did well tonight," she said to the floor. "I don't say that to be kind, either."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't lift her head right away. When she did, she saw where Wick's eyes had gone: down past her boots to the boards under the table, where the lamplight didn't quite reach and everything was the same dull black.

"All right," she said.

She got up off the crate, took the lamp from the end of the table, and set it on the floor, low, so the light ran flat across the planks. The black turned red at the edges. It lay in a long uneven sheet under the table, thickest beneath where the thigh had been, with a darker crust at the rim where it had started to dry.

"That's him. Most of what came out tonight, anyway. Some of it's in the dressings in the bucket, and some he left in the mud between wherever he got hit and here." She crouched beside it, forearms on her knees, and looked at it the way she'd looked at the wound, measuring. "Looks like a lot, doesn't it. It always looks like more than it is when it spreads. That's maybe two pints on the floor. The first ones I ever saw like this, I thought the man had to be empty. He wasn't. Neither is this one."

She pointed with one finger, not touching.

"See where it's gone thick, like jam, round the edge? That's clotting. That's his blood doing what it's meant to do. That's good. If it stayed thin and ran and never set, I'd worry his blood had given up trying, and then no amount of sewing helps." Her finger moved inward, to a brighter smear near the table leg. "That brighter bit's from when I had the pad off, right at the end. Fresh, straight from the vessel. It stopped. You watched it stop, even if you didn't know that's what you were seeing."

She picked up the lamp, stood, and carried it back to the table, setting it near the bandaged thigh without touching the linen.

"Under here, since you'll be wondering on your watch whether you should be. There's a hole about the length of my thumb, going in at a slant. Inside it, the meat's torn where the metal worked around. That's the stuff that smells. Some of it's already dying. I cut away what I could see was gone, but I can't see all of it by this light, and I won't know about the rest until it tells me. That's what the smell is for." She set her palm flat on the blanket above the knee, lightly. "Deeper than that there's the vessel, with eleven stitches in it, and they'll hold as long as nobody lets him thrash. Past that is the bone. The metal didn't break it. It only scraped it. If it had broken it, I'd have had to take the leg tonight."

She let her hand come away and looked at him for a moment, the whole length of him under the blanket: the grey foot, the slack face.

"That's all of it. There's nothing in there worse than what I've said. If there was, I'd say that too." She wiped her fingers on the rag again out of habit. "Imagining's worse, you're right about that. Imagining never knows where to stop."

Then she nudged the bucket of dressings under the table with her boot, out of the lamp's path.

"I'll scrub the boards in the morning," she said. "Not now. If I start now, I'll never get up again."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I take a long breath, the kind that makes my ribs ache. "If you're scrubbing in the morning, I'm scrubbing with you."

I look at the man's foot again, really look. "I'll get the water for my arms. And I'll talk to him. About the weather, maybe."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick a moment longer than she needed to, the way she'd looked at the foot, waiting for something to show itself.

"Fine," she said. "Two brushes, then. There's a second one under the stove if Merrow hasn't used it for his boots again." She sat back down on the crate, and it creaked under her. "Cold water for the boards, not hot. Hot sets it. You'll learn that the hard way otherwise, and then the boards stay that colour until they rot."

She reached over without getting up and turned the lamp wick down a quarter, enough to save oil, not enough to lose the foot. The light pulled in closer around the end of the table and left the rest of the tent to the dark.

"The weather's good," she said. "It's what I use. There's always weather, and it never upsets anybody." Something tugged at one corner of her mouth, briefly. "Though I'd leave out that it's been raining for eleven days. Tell him it's clearing. It might be. Nobody's checked."

She pulled her own watch out of her breast pocket, thumbed the case open, and squinted at it in the dim light. Then she unhooked the chain, leaned forward, and set it face-up on the table beside the little gauze bundle with the metal in it.

"Use that one. It keeps better time than anything else in this camp, and I'll want it back." She let her hands hang between her knees again. "Top of the hour's in about twenty minutes. Arms first, then eat, then the foot. In that order. If you do the foot first, you'll stand there staring at it for twenty minutes and never get to the other two."

The man on the table breathed, short and wet, but steadier than before. Sedge listened to it the way other people listen to rain on a roof, not really attending, just noticing it was still going.

"Wake me for the second turn," she said. "Kick the crate if I don't answer. Don't shake me. I come up swinging sometimes, and I don't mean anything by it."

She tipped her head back against the tent pole and closed her eyes. She wasn't asleep yet. Her fingers were still loosely curled, the right hand bare, and the dark under her nails was already dry.

"And Wick," she said, eyes still shut. "When you talk to him, use your ordinary voice. Not a sickroom one. They can hear the difference. Talk to him like he's already going to be fine, and you're just passing the time until he is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't open her eyes at first. Her head stayed tipped against the pole, and for a moment it seemed she might let the question go by. Then she breathed out through her nose, and her eyes opened.

"All right. Straight."

She held up her bare right hand and looked at it rather than at Wick, as if the explanation were written there.

"A bullet's a made thing. It's smooth and it's meant to go in a line. It makes a hole, and if you're lucky the hole's clean. Shell casing isn't made to go anywhere. It's just what's left when the shell tears itself apart, so every piece comes off ragged, like that one." She tipped her chin at the gauze bundle by the man's hand. "Edges all round. It comes in hot, spinning, going sideways as often as straight. It doesn't cut through meat. It rips through it, and it doesn't care what it drags along."

She closed her fingers slowly.

"That's the first thing. When it goes in, it goes through his trousers first, so it takes a bit of the cloth with it. Wool, and whatever's on the wool. Mud. Muck from the trench. Horse, sometimes, if there's been horses. It punches all of that in deep, where it's warm and dark and there's no air, and it leaves it there. I pulled two threads of his trouser leg out of that hole tonight before I ever reached the metal. You didn't see. You were looking at the canvas."

Her voice didn't change. It never did for this part.

"Second thing. It doesn't just break what it touches. It shoves. Everything around its path gets hit hard enough to bruise to the core, and bruised meat's got its blood supply knocked out of it. So there's the track you can see, and around it a sleeve of flesh that looks all right for a day or so and is already dying. That's what I was cutting away with the scissors. You cut until it bleeds, because meat that bleeds is still alive. Meat that doesn't bleed is just waiting to rot."

She let her hand drop back to her knee.

"Third thing's the one that kills them. Dead meat, no air, dirt packed in. There's a kind of rot that grows in exactly that, and it's fast. It makes gas as it goes. You can press the skin near a bad one and feel it crackle under your fingers, like stepping on frost. That's where the sweet smell comes from. Once it takes hold it runs up the limb about as fast as you can walk, and the only thing that stops it is getting ahead of it with a saw." She looked at the bare grey foot at the end of the table. "That's why I told you not to wait to be sure. With that one, by the time you're sure, you're late."

She was quiet a moment. The lamp hissed.

"And the metal itself, if you leave it in, keeps working. Every time he moves, the muscle drags across the edges. That's what I meant by chewing. Give it long enough near something important and it opens it. Some men carry a bit around for years and it never bothers them. Some bleed out in the night from a piece they got a week before." She shrugged, just barely. "You can't tell which from the outside, so you go and get it if you can reach it."

She settled her head back against the pole.

"That's the lot. It tears, it drags filth in, it kills the meat around it, and the dead meat feeds the rot. Everything I did tonight was about one of those four. Nothing mysterious about it. It's ugly, but it's simple, and simple is something you can fight." Her eyes closed again. "The fighting's the hour-by-hour part. That's you now. Arms in the water, Wick. Clock's running."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I nod and push off from the table. My arms feel like lead. I take the lamp over to the stove, check the pot. There's still some warm water left.

I pour it into the basin, roll up my sleeves, and sink my arms in. The heat feels like a shock. I lean over it, let the steam hit my face. "It's clearing," I say to the man on the table, voice rough. "Sky's clearing up."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't open her eyes, but the corner of her mouth moved again.

"Better," she said. "Rougher than you meant it, but that's all right. Rough sounds like a person. He'd take rough over sweet any day."

She shifted on the crate. The dark had come in close around the table now that the lamp was over by the stove, and the grey foot had gone to a pale shape at the edge of what little light was left. She turned her head a fraction toward it, then away.

"Leave the lamp where it is while you're soaking. He's got a quarter hour before anyone needs to see his toes, and you need to see what you're eating." A pause. "Bring it back with you when you come. Don't forget it on the stove. People do, and then they check the foot by feel and tell themselves it's fine."

The man on the table made a sound, not the one from before, low and without any shape to it. Something between a breath and a word. Sedge's eyes opened. She didn't move otherwise, only listened, head cocked, the way a person listens for a second knock at a door.

Nothing followed it. His breathing went on, short and wet, no quicker than before.

"That's not pain," she said, quieter now. "That's him hearing something and not knowing what it is yet. Keep going. Tell him more than the sky." She let her eyes close again. "Tell him the mud's drying out on the east road, and the cook's found onions. That last one's true, as it happens. Merrow saw the sack."

For a while there was only the hiss of the lamp and the tick of the stove cooling. When she spoke again, her voice had gone thick at the edges, heavier with sleep.

"The heat'll sting when you take your arms out," she said. "Dry them properly. Wet skin gets cold fast in here, and cold brings the shaking back." A long breath. "Top of the hour. Colour, nail, smell. Then wake me for second."

Her right hand, still bare, slid off her knee and hung loose. She didn't catch it.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came up off the crate before she was properly awake. One hand was already out in front of her and the other went to her belt where a knife wasn't. For half a second her eyes didn't know the tent. Then they did.

"I'm not doing anything to him yet," she said, and her voice was flat and clear, as if she'd never been asleep at all. "That's the first thing. Nobody's touching him but you. So now we find out why."

She snatched the lamp off the stove shelf on her way past and brought it down low over the thigh. Her bare hand went flat on the linen, not pressing, only feeling.

"Dressing first. If the vessel's let go, this is where it tells us." She lifted the edge of the bandage a finger's width and angled the light under it. "Dark. Wet, but dark, and no more than it was. No bright red coming through. So it isn't the stitches." She let the linen fall. "That's the worst thing it could have been, and it isn't that. Keep him flat anyway. If he gets that leg under him and kicks, it could still become that."

The man's scream broke in the middle and turned into words, or pieces of them. Something that might have been a name. Something that might have been *down*. His eyes were wide open now and looking at nothing in this tent.

Sedge went straight down the table to the foot and pressed the big toenail with her thumb. Her lips moved.

"Four. Same as before. Colour's the same." She bent and put her face close to the dressing, breathed in once through her nose, and straightened. "Smell's the same. Not sweet." She said it to herself as much as to Wick, ticking the list. "Leg's not going on us. Bleed's not open. So this is his head, not his leg."

She came back up to his shoulders, next to Wick's hands, and put her own palm flat on his breastbone.

"He's woken up somewhere else. Back wherever he was when it hit him, I'd guess. He can feel the leg, and his head's decided the shelling's still going. It happens when they come up out of the grey. The body remembers before the mind catches up." She kept her hand where it was, a steady weight. "It's loud and it's ugly, and it's the least dangerous thing that could be happening right now. The danger is him fighting you hard enough to tear what I sewed. So you keep doing exactly what you're doing, and I'm going to shorten it."

She reached under the table without looking and came up with a small tin box. She thumbed it open against her hip. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, were a glass syringe and three little ampoules. A fourth slot was empty.

"Morphia. That's the last three in this tent until the cart comes, and nobody knows when the cart comes." She snapped the neck off one ampoule with her thumb and drew it up, then held the syringe to the lamp and flicked it twice. "I'd hoped to save it for when the pain was worse than the fright. It's about even now, and even is enough. He can't lie still on his own, and he has to lie still."

She pushed the blanket off his upper arm and pinched up the meat of it between her finger and thumb.

"Into the muscle. Not the vein. The vein's quicker, but with the state his blood's in it could stop his breathing, and I'm not going to be the thing that kills him tonight. Hold that arm still. The rest of him can buck. That arm can't." She went in, straight down, and pressed the plunger slowly, not in one push. "There. That's all of it."

The needle came out. She held her thumb over the spot a moment, then pulled the blanket back up.

"How much longer. You asked, so here's the honest version. In the muscle, ten minutes before he feels it. Maybe fifteen, with his heart going the way it is. It won't knock him out. It'll pull the edges off. He'll still know it hurts, he just won't care as much." She leaned in close, her face in his line of sight the way she'd done before the forceps. "You're off the line," she told him, not loudly. "It's over. You're in a tent. There's a roof. Nothing's falling on you."

His eyes slid across her face without catching. She didn't seem to expect them to.

"He won't take that in yet. He will later." She straightened. "Meanwhile, you talk. Same voice as before. Say it's quiet. Say it's over. Say his name if we had it. We don't, so check his collar for a tag when he settles." She kept her hand on his chest and glanced once at the watch lying on the table. "I'll call the minutes. Two gone. Somewhere around eight, you'll feel him start to go loose under your hands before you hear it in his voice. That's how you'll know it's working."

Then she looked at the arm she'd injected, at the slack fingers on that side, and the gauze bundle lying next to them.

"Put the metal in his hand," she said. "Now, not later. Close his fingers on it. Sometimes it helps to be holding the thing that did it, and know it's out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean across and grab the gauze bundle, working it into his limp hand. I close his fingers around it and hold them there for a second. "You got it," I tell him. "It's out. It's just you in there now."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched the hand, not the face.

"That's good," she said. "*It's just you in there now.* Better than anything I'd have said. Keep that one."

For a while nothing changed. He was still shouting, though the words had fallen apart again into sound, and his shoulders still drove up against Wick's palms in long hard heaves that made the table legs knock on the boards. Sedge kept her hand flat on his breastbone and counted his breathing under it without seeming to.

"Four minutes."

Then his fingers moved. They didn't open. They tightened, slowly, the way a sleeping child's hand closes on whatever's put in it, until the gauze crumpled and the knuckles stood out pale.

"There," Sedge said quietly. "He's got it. Some part of him knows what that is."

She glanced at the watch.

"Six. Keep your weight on. It's not working yet, that's just him holding on. Don't mistake the one for the other and ease off too soon."

At seven the shouting caught in his throat and didn't start again straight away. At eight it came back, but lower, with gaps in it where he breathed. Somewhere just past that his heels stopped drumming. Sedge felt it through her palm before either of them could have heard it, and her hand pressed down a fraction more, as though it were holding something in place while it settled.

"Feel that?" she asked. "Under your hands. That's the edges coming off."

His head rolled to one side. His eyes were still open, but they had stopped searching and now only rested on the canvas wall where Wick had looked earlier. The sound he made now was barely a sound at all, a long uneven hum on each breath out.

Sedge took her hand off his chest. She reached up to his collar, folded it back with two fingers, and tilted the lamp. A thin cord ran around his neck. She drew it out, and on the end of it was a disc of pressed fibre, soft at the rim from sweat and wear. She turned it to the light and read it with her lips moving, as she did with stitches.

"Tollan," she said. "A. Tollan. Private." She let the disc lie on his chest where he could find it later. "There. Now you've got something better than the weather."

She leaned down to his line of sight again, though his eyes didn't come to her.

"Tollan. You're in a tent. The leg's sewn. You've got the bit that did it in your hand." Her voice was the same as it had been over the forceps, plain and unhurried. "Sleep if you want. Somebody's watching."

She straightened, and something in her back cracked audibly. She pressed a fist into the base of her spine and didn't comment on it.

"You can come off him a bit now. Not all the way. Keep one hand on his shoulder so he feels it if he surfaces again. He might. It's two hours of this, maybe three, before it wears thin, and when it does we've got two more ampoules and no cart." She shut the tin box and slid it back under the table, and her boot stayed against it a moment as though she were marking where it was. "So if he goes again before morning, we try your voice first and the needle second. I'm not saying that to be hard. I'm saying it because there'll be somebody else on this table before the cart comes, and he'll need it too."

She picked up the watch, looked at it, and set it back down facing Wick.

"And that's the top of the hour, near enough. He's made you late for your first check." She stepped back to give room at the foot of the table and held the lamp out, handle first. "Colour, nail, smell. Out loud this time. I want to hear you do it once before I go back to that crate."

Her hands were steady on the lamp. The left one, still gloved, had a thin crack of dried blood across the knuckles where the rubber had split, and she didn't seem to have noticed.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked down at Wick on the boards for a moment. Then she turned back to the table with the lamp still in her hand, since nobody else was going to take it.

"Check first. Then the rest."

She bent over the foot. "Colour. Grey, a shade warmer than it was. Could be the lamp. I'll call it no worse." Her thumb went to the big toenail and her lips moved. "Four. Same." She put her face down to the dressing and breathed in. "Smell's the same. Not sweet." She straightened. "That's the hour. You'll do the next one out loud, and I'll lie on that crate and listen, and you won't know if I'm asleep."

She set the lamp on the table where it would keep the foot in its light. Then she lowered herself onto the floor across from Wick with her back against the crate, slowly, one hand on the boards, the way a person does when their knees have opinions. She stretched her legs out. The toe of one boot came to rest a hand's width from the edge of the dried black on the planks, and she didn't move it.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She pulled the split glove off her left hand. It stuck at the knuckles where the blood had dried, and she worked it free with small tugs, looking at that while she talked.

"You've had the leg. You've had the metal and what it does. The part I haven't said is what comes after tonight, and the part where I tell you what I'm not sure of. So here it is.

"Tonight's the bleed and the head. We've done the bleed. The head's quiet for now. If he's still breathing like that at first light, he's through tonight, and tonight's the one that takes most of them who are going to go fast. So that's one door shut.

"Then comes the second night, and the third, and the fourth. That's the rot, or the fever, or both, and it doesn't care how well anyone sewed. He'll get hot. They all get a bit hot. What I'm watching for is whether it breaks and comes back lower each time, or climbs and stays. If it climbs, he'll start talking to people who aren't here. His heart will go fast and light like a bird's, and the skin round the wound will go tight and shiny and red, spreading up the thigh. I'll draw a line in ink at the edge of the red, and every few hours I'll look to see whether it's crossed the line. That's how I decide. Not by how he looks. By the ink."

She dropped the glove into her lap.

"If it crosses, the leg comes off. I told you above the knee and I meant it. People think you take off only what's bad, as little as you can. You don't. You go where the meat's still clean, because if you cut through rot you just have to do it again, higher, on a man who's weaker. So above the knee, a hand's width or more.

"How it goes. There's a bottle of chloroform in the other tent, and it's a third full. If it's still a third full when I need it, he gets it on a cloth and he's under. If somebody else needed it first, he doesn't, and you and Merrow hold him the way you held him tonight, only longer and worse. I'll tell you which it is before we start. I won't let you find out halfway.

"Strap round the top of the thigh, tight, to stop the blood. I cut the skin and I leave a flap long enough to fold over the end, the way you'd leave paper to wrap a parcel. Then I cut the muscle straight down to the bone, all the way round, fast, because fast is kinder here. It's the one place fast is kinder. Then the saw. That takes less time than you'd think and sounds like exactly what it is. I've seen grown soldiers go down on the floor at that sound who didn't go down for anything else. If you do, you do. Just fall away from the table.

"Then I tie off the vessels, one by one. There's the big one I stitched tonight, and a dozen smaller ones that have been quiet all along and will suddenly have a great deal to say. Fold the flap, sew it, and it's done. Twenty minutes if it goes right. The leg goes in a sack and out of the tent before he wakes, because some of them ask to see it, and nobody's ever been glad they did."

She said it at the same pace as everything else, and when she stopped it wasn't for effect. She was finding the next part.

"Now, the odds, since you'll want them. I don't have real numbers. Nobody out here keeps them, and anyone who gives you one is guessing louder than I am. What I've got is what I've seen. If the foot pinks up and the smell stays honest, he walks out of here on his own leg with a limp, most likely, and aches when it rains. That's more than half of them, the ones who look like him tonight. Not a lot more. If it goes to the saw, most live, as long as I don't wait. Some don't, even when I don't wait, and I've never known for certain why. Their hearts just stop, a day or two after, as if they'd been holding their breath for the whole business and let it all go at once."

She turned the glove over in her lap.

"And some of them look better than he does and die anyway. I've had men sitting up and eating and asking for their letters, and gone by the next morning. I'll not pretend otherwise. If that happens to this one, it won't be because you checked the foot wrong. There's a lot that goes on inside them that neither of us can reach, and the ink and the nail and the smell are only the parts we can.

"If he keeps it, there's a man somewhere who gets a letter from him in a month. If he loses it, he goes home on a hospital train, and some nights for the rest of his life he'll feel the foot that isn't there. It itches. It cramps. They reach down to rub it. That's real, it happens to nearly all of them, and nobody tells them before, so they think they're going mad. If it comes to that, one of us tells him before he wakes up to it. That's on the list too."

She stopped and looked across at Wick then, properly, in the low light.

"That's him. The last part's you, since you're sitting on the floor and not getting up.

"You'll have the shaking soon. I said that. Tonight you'll sleep like you've been hit with a spade, and tomorrow you won't be able to eat. Then for a while you'll hear that sound he made when I went in, at odd times. Washing, mostly. It'll come in water noise. After enough of them it gets quieter, and the voices start to run together, and I'll be honest with you, that's worse in its way, but it's the way you keep doing it." She paused. "I remember the first one's name. Only his. I don't remember any of the others from that year."

She folded the glove in half and set it on the boards beside her.

"That's all of it. There isn't another piece I'm keeping back. If one turns up, it'll be because it's happened and not because I hid it."

Tollan breathed on the table above them, long and uneven, the hum gone out of it now. Sedge listened for a few breaths with her head tipped back against the crate.

"Stay down there as long as you like," she said. "The floor's no worse than the crate. But at the top of the hour you're up, and you're doing it out loud." She reached up without looking, found the watch on the table's edge, and set it on the boards between them, face up, where both of them could see it. "Fifty-one minutes."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay on the floor, elbows on my knees. I watch his breathing. “What was his name? The first one.”

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer at once. She wasn't deciding whether to. She was going back for it, the way someone goes into a cellar they know well in the dark.

"Pask," she said. "Jory Pask. Corporal. He'd have been about twenty-two, though he told me nineteen, because he thought it would make me gentler with him." Something moved at the corner of her mouth and went away again. "It didn't. I didn't know how to be anything with him. I was on the floor where you are. Not the one with the forceps. There was a surgeon then, Adair, with a proper bag and a proper apron, and I was the one holding the shoulders."

She looked at the watch between them, not at Wick.

"Shoulder wound. Shell, same as this. Adair got the metal out, and it was bigger than Tollan's. Pask kept it in his breast pocket and showed it to anybody who came past, the way you'd show a coin you'd found. Second night he was sitting up. Third night he was hot, and by the fourth the red had gone right down his arm and across his chest, where you can't take anything off to get ahead of it." She said it at the same pace as the rest. "Nobody drew a line. Adair had forty men and no time, and I didn't know there was such a thing as a line. I thought he was just fevered and would come down. I sat with him and told him about the weather."

She was quiet for a breath or two. Tollan's breathing went on above them, slow and uneven.

"That's where the ink comes from. I didn't read it anywhere. I made it up the next winter, because I wanted something I could look at that wouldn't lie to me the way his face did. He looked all right, you see. Right up until he didn't." She turned her bare hand over on her knee and looked at the dark under the nails. "So when I tell you not by how he looks, that's Pask telling you. Not me."

She lifted her eyes to Wick then, level and plain.

"You asked, so I'll say the rest of it too. I don't keep his name out of guilt, or not mostly. It wasn't my fault, and I was right not to blame myself even then. I keep it because it's the only one I've got with the whole shape still on it. The rest are only pieces. I'd like one of them to stay whole." She tipped her head a fraction toward the table. "You'll likely get Tollan. Whichever way it goes, that's the one you'll carry. So you might as well learn the right things from him."

She reached out and turned the watch a quarter so it faced Wick squarely.

"Forty-six minutes." She let her head go back against the crate. "If you want to talk to him in the meantime, you've got a name now. And the onions. Don't forget the onions."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Tollan," I say to the table. "Cook's got onions. Jory Pask kept his shrapnel in his pocket." My voice is low, raw. "You're allowed to keep yours."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's head came off the crate an inch at the sound of the name. It wasn't sharp. It was the way a person looks up when they hear their own door open in another part of the house.

She didn't say anything for a moment. She looked at the table, at the pale shape of the hand on the blanket with the crumpled gauze still in it, and then at nothing in particular.

"Nobody's said that out loud in three years," she said at last. "Pask. I'd stopped saying it myself. You start to think it'll wear thin if you use it too much." She let her head go back against the crate. "It didn't. That's good to know."

On the table, Tollan's fingers moved. They didn't open. They shifted their grip on the gauze the way a sleeper turns over, and settled again, tighter. His breath caught once, came out long, and went on.

Sedge watched it happen and didn't comment on it for a while.

"That's not him hearing you," she said eventually. "Not the words. I'd like to tell you it was, and it might be, but I don't know that, so I won't say it." A pause. "What it is, is a man holding on to something in his sleep. That's worth having, whatever did it."

She reached out and tapped the watch face with one finger, not moving it.

"Forty-one."

She drew her legs in a little, knees up, and folded her arms across them. In the low light her face looked older than it had over the forceps, or perhaps only more tired, the lines left where they were because there was no work for them now.

"He will want to keep it," she said. "They nearly all do. Some of them put it on a string. One I had drilled a hole through his and wore it on his tag cord, next to his name, and said it was the only thing in the whole war that had ever been honest with him." She breathed out through her nose, something close to a laugh without the sound. "I thought about that for a long time afterwards. I still don't know whether he meant it kindly."

The stove ticked. Somewhere outside, a long way off, a cart creaked through the mud, and it wasn't theirs. Sedge listened until it was gone, and then her eyes began to close on their own, and she let them.

"Keep talking to him if you want," she said, slower now. "You've got a good voice for it. Plain. He'll like it better than mine." Her arms loosened across her knees. "Forty minutes. Out loud. I'll hear you."

Her breathing changed, not all at once, until it matched the uneven rhythm coming from the table above them nearly stroke for stroke. Her bare hand had come to rest on the boards beside the watch, palm down, a finger's width from it, as if she meant to know if it moved.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I watch her breathe for a minute. "Alright, Tollan," I say, voice low. "It's the quiet part of the night. I'm supposed to tell you the mud's drying on the east road, but it isn't. And your toes are still grey."

I glance at the watch. Thirty-nine minutes.
