dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced at Wick’s hands, then at the man’s leg. “Ready’s not a requirement. Staying put is.”

She poured the last of the clean water over the wound. The man went rigid. “That’s me cleaning it,” she told him. “There’s a piece of metal near the surface. I’m taking that out, then I’ll dress it. I don’t enjoy this, and I won’t make it last.”

She picked up the forceps. “Hold.”

The lamp guttered as she leaned in. She caught the edge of the fragment and drew it free in one steady pull, then dropped it into the basin with a small, hard sound. “Out,” she said. “Keep holding. I need to check the bleeding.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel him tense up under my hands and I almost flinch away. "How much more?" I ask, voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Two minutes, if the bleeding behaves,” Sedge said. “Longer if it doesn’t.”

She pressed a folded pad against the wound and watched for blood seeping through. “That’s pressure. I’m making sure it’s stopped before I wrap it.” After a moment, she lifted one edge, checked, and set the pad back down.

“It’s slowing. Keep his shoulders down until I say otherwise.” She reached for the bandage.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Neither, as it stands,” Sedge said. “The bleeding’s slowing, and I haven’t found anything that says the leg has to come off. Infection could change that. So could bleeding I can’t see yet. I’m not calling either one before it happens.”

She wound the bandage around the leg, firm enough to hold the pad in place. “Keep holding. I’m checking his foot next. Then you can let go.”

She glanced up once. “Being kind right now means finishing the job.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I shift my grip a little, trying to ignore how my fingers are cramping. "Right," I mutter, then nod toward the guy's foot. "So it's still...attached, then?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Attached was never the question,” Sedge said. “Whether blood’s reaching it is.”

She pressed two fingers against the top of the man’s foot, then pinched one toenail and watched the color return. “Warm. Pulse is there. Color comes back.” She eased the bandage a fraction and checked again. “Good.”

She looked up. “You can let go. Slowly. If he starts bleeding through that dressing, you tell me at once.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge held the lamp closer to the foot. “Skin’s warm. That matters because a foot without enough blood turns cold. Press here—see how the nail goes pale? The color comes back quickly. That means blood is getting down the leg. I can feel a pulse here, too.”

She moved the light to the bandage. “That darker patch is blood already in the pad. If it spreads past the edge, or the foot goes cold or pale, you tell me. Same if he stops answering when someone speaks to him.”

She set the lamp down. “What you’re seeing now is a wound that’s dressed and a leg that’s still getting blood. That’s enough for tonight. It isn’t a promise about tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I ease my hands off his shoulders and step back, rolling my shoulders out. "So he might just... keep it?" I wipe my palms on my pants. "Never seen that before."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“He might,” Sedge said. She checked the dressing once more, then pulled the blanket over the man’s uninjured leg. “Metal came out cleanly. Bleeding’s under control. His foot’s getting blood. Those are good signs, not a guarantee.”

She put the bloodied forceps in the basin. “I’ve seen men lose legs to smaller wounds because they went foul. I’ve seen worse wounds heal. Tonight we keep him warm, give him water when he can swallow it, and watch the dressing.”

Sedge glanced toward the foot. “And tomorrow, we check it again.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the basin aside. “It tears. A bullet tends to make a track; shrapnel can tumble and cut whatever it meets. Skin, muscle, blood vessels, nerves, bone. It can carry dirt and cloth in with it, too. Pulling the metal out doesn’t pull all that back out.”

She nodded toward the bandaged leg. “In his case, I found one piece near the surface. The bleeding slowed under pressure, and his foot is warm and getting blood. That tells me no major vessel to the foot is cut clean through. It doesn’t tell me every bit of muscle is sound, or that the wound won’t turn foul.”

“That’s the straight answer. The metal did damage on its way in. I dealt with what I could see tonight. Now we watch for what I couldn’t.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "Right. Straight enough." I glance at the man, still out cold. "What're the odds? Tell me that straight, too."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the man’s face, then checked his breathing and pressed two fingers to his neck. “I can’t give you odds worth trusting. He’s breathing, his pulse is there, the bleeding’s slowed, and blood’s reaching his foot. Those are reasons to think he could keep the leg.”

She touched his shoulder and called to him. “I don’t like that he’s stopped answering. Could be exhaustion. Could be blood loss. I’m not guessing which.”

She looked back at the dressing. “We keep him warm and watch his breathing and the blood on that bandage. No water until he’s awake enough to swallow. If he worsens, you get me. That’s the straight answer.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hand on the blanket. “I’m not doing anything to the wound now,” she said. “The metal’s out. The dressing’s on. I’m checking why he’s shouting again.”

She brought the lamp close enough to see his face. “I’m calling to him. If he can answer, that tells me more than the shouting does.” She said the man’s name, then asked him where he hurt. She waited a beat before checking his breathing and pulse.

“Now the bandage.” She held the light over it without lifting the pad. “The stain hasn’t reached the edge. Pulling the dressing off just to look underneath would start the bleeding again, so I’m leaving it alone.” She felt the man’s foot. “Still warm. Pulse is still there.”

Sedge set the lamp back. “That check’s done. Less than a minute. If he can tell us where the pain is, I’ll listen; if he can’t, I’ll keep checking him. I won’t put the forceps back in him because he screamed.”

She glanced at the man’s face again. “He’s going to need watching through the night. Breathing, whether he answers, blood through the bandage, warmth in the foot. I can tell you each time I check. I can’t give you an hour when he’ll stop hurting.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wipe sweat off my forehead with the back of my hand. "Alright, alright." I look at her, not the bandage. "You stay, or me? Tell me exactly what to look for, not just... warm."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“You stay with him,” Sedge said. “I’ll be in this tent unless they carry me out of it. I’ll check him again in a quarter hour. Between checks, you watch.”

She took a stub of charcoal and marked the edge of the bloodstain on the bandage. “If fresh blood goes past that line, call me. If it soaks through, call me before you touch the dressing. Don’t peel it back.”

She lifted the blanket just enough to show his feet. “Compare this foot with the other one. Feel the tops with the back of your fingers. If the injured one turns noticeably colder, pale, or blue, call me. Press a toenail until it goes white; the pink should come back in a couple of seconds. If it doesn’t, call me.”

Sedge looked at the man’s face. “Speak to him now and then. He doesn’t have to make sense, but if he stops responding when he was responding before, or his breathing turns slow, ragged, or hard to see, get me immediately. Same if he becomes clammy and weak, or the pain suddenly changes.”

She set the blanket back over his legs. “That’s the list. Don’t give him water while he’s shouting or too dazed to swallow. You aren’t treating the wound. You’re noticing a change soon enough for me to do something about it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him for a moment. The man on the table had gone quiet again, but his chest still rose and fell. She checked the charcoal line on the bandage. The stain had not crossed it.

“The rest,” she said. “All right.”

She pulled a stool beside the table, where she could see the man’s face and his injured foot without moving the lamp.

“He may shout like that again. Pain comes in waves, and he’s got a torn leg. Shouting by itself doesn’t tell me he’s dying. Going quiet doesn’t tell me he’s safe, either. I need to know whether he can be roused, how he’s breathing, whether he’s bleeding, and whether blood still reaches the foot. That’s why I keep checking the same things. It isn’t because I’ve forgotten the answers.”

She laid two fingers against the man’s wrist and counted under her breath before she went on.

“Tonight, bleeding is the danger I can do the most about. If that line starts moving, you call me. If blood comes through fast, I’ll put pressure on it and see whether I can stop it. If his foot changes, I’ll check whether the bandage is too tight or whether something deeper has gone wrong. I can’t tell which by looking at him from across the tent.”

She released his wrist. “Tomorrow and the days after, infection becomes the thing to watch. The wound might swell, turn hotter and redder, start draining, or smell foul. He might run a fever. He might grow confused or weak. If that happens, I open the dressing and clean what I can. I may have to cut away tissue that’s died. I’ll tell him what I’m doing if he can hear me. I won’t pretend it won’t hurt.”

Sedge glanced at the basin, at the small piece of metal lying in its bottom.

“I got that out. I did not put the muscle back the way it was, and I did not make the wound clean all the way through. He’ll need dressing changes. He’ll need rest, food, and water when he’s awake enough to take them. Even if the wound stays clean, he may not walk properly for a long time. If a nerve was cut, he may always have a numb patch or a weak foot. I won’t know tonight.”

She checked the man’s breathing again. It remained steady enough for her to leave him undisturbed.

“And yes,” she said, her voice still level, “he could lose the leg. He could die. Not because I’ve seen that coming, but because wounds do turn, and men who look better in the evening sometimes look worse by morning. I won’t call either outcome inevitable to make you ready for it. That would be a lie.”

Sedge shifted the lamp so its light fell on the bandage. “What I can say is this: when I took the metal out, the bleeding answered to pressure. His foot had a pulse. It was warm. The color came back when I pressed the nail. I checked again after he shouted, and those things were still true. That is better than the other sort of answer.”

She sat back, keeping her eyes on the man.

“If he wakes enough to speak, ask his name. Tell him where he is. Don’t demand that he be brave, and don’t tell him the leg’s fine. If he asks, tell him the metal is out and I’m watching for bleeding and infection. That’s true. If he wants water, get me first so I can see whether he can swallow. If he sleeps, let him sleep, but make sure you can wake him.”

For a few breaths, Sedge listened to the man breathe.

“That’s the rest I know,” she said. “There isn’t a hidden verdict I’m keeping from you. There’s a wound, a dressing, a man still breathing, and a night we have to get through one check at a time. I’ll be here for the next one.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I sit there for a minute, listening to his breathing too. "Okay," I say finally, and push myself up off the ground. "I've got the list." I drag a crate over near the foot of the table so I can see it better. "Check now—foot's same color, breathing's same."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked from the man’s face to the two feet showing beneath the blanket. “Good. Same is what we want.”

She touched the injured foot with the back of her fingers, then the other. “Same warmth, too.” Her eyes moved to the charcoal mark. “No fresh blood past the line.”

She shifted the lamp so it lit the bandage without shining in the man’s face. “Next check in a quarter hour. You don’t have to stare at him every second. Listen for his breathing, look at the dressing now and then, and call me if something changes. If you’re unsure whether it changed, call me anyway.”

Sedge settled onto the stool beside the table. “You’ve got the list. I’ve got him too.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, not looking away from the man's face. "His name's Kael, if he wakes up and you need to ask." I lean forward, elbows on my knees. "Quarter hour," I repeat, like I'm setting a timer in my head.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Kael,” Sedge repeated. “Good. A name’s easier to answer than ‘you.’”

She looked at the man’s face. “Kael. You’re in the aid tent. The metal’s out of your leg. You don’t have to answer me now.”

His breathing continued, rough but regular. Sedge kept her fingers near his wrist for a few beats, then let go.

“Quarter hour,” she said. “And sooner if anything changes. I’ll tell you when I make the next check.” She glanced at the charcoal line once more. “For now, the stain’s where I left it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the way his chest rises and falls, counting breaths without meaning to. The silence in the tent feels heavier than the shouting did. "You've done this before," I say, not as a question.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the knife and rose. She gave Corvin a once-over, quick, the way you check a rope for frays before you trust it with weight.

"Whose it is doesn't matter. Question is whether any of it's coming out of you. I don't see you leaking anywhere important, so I'll say you're fine."

The noise past the cart swelled and thinned. A man's voice worn down to one note, over and over.

"That's a gut wound talking," she said. "You can hear it, if you listen. Lung noise is wet and fast and it finishes quick. That one's got hours in him still, and sound carries at dusk. Anything with ears and an opinion — wolves, his friends, whoever sent him — walks toward that noise."

She crouched by the nearest body and started going through its belt, unhurried, like she had all the time the day wasn't going to give her.

"You can go do it, or I can. No score in either. If it'd be your first, I'll tell you the one thing worth knowing: it's not the same as the fight. Everyone finds that out once. After that it's just the last part of the job." She worked a knife free of its sheath and added it to her own hip. "But decide before the light does. Then we go through that cart. Six men don't guard an empty wagon."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I push off from the tree I was leaning on. "I'll do it." My voice sounds steadier than I feel. "Might as well be me."

I start walking toward the cart, but I look back at her. "What's the one thing?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't look up. She was working a boot off the second body, methodical about it.

"The one thing." She said it like he'd asked her the time. "A fight's loud, and the other man's busy trying to kill you, so there's no room to notice anything. This is the other kind. Quiet. He'll look right at you. Maybe hold your wrist. Odds are good he thanks you for it."

The boot came free. Nothing in it. She reached for the next.

"The blood's not what keeps you up after. The thank-you is. So don't stand over him working up your nerve. That's spending what's left of his time on your comfort. Walk over, be quick, be done."

She rose, knees cracking, and weighed a small coin purse against her palm before it went in her pocket.

"And leave the sword. Too long, wrong angle, you'll botch it and he'll know. Knife, low, lean your weight in. It's butchery, same as anything. The thinking's already finished — leave it finished."

She turned back to the bodies, already done with the conversation.

"Light's going. I'll listen for the quiet."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped with her hand in a dead man's coat and considered the question, which was more than she gave most questions.

"Both," she said. "That's the part nobody tells you at the fire. It's almost always both at once, and you don't get to pick which one you're doing. Anybody who tells you it's pure mercy is selling something. Anybody who says it's just easier has never listened to a gut wound for a night."

She pulled her hand out. Nothing worth having.

"Out here he's dead anyway. Question's whether it costs him two days or ten seconds. Two days is screaming, and the flies come before the cold does, and by the end he's begging anything with ears. So yes — mercy. And yes, it's easier for us, because we don't spend the night listening and don't wake up to wolves on the picket line. The two things ride in the same saddle. Always have."

She nodded past him, toward the cart and the sound.

"So go. It's a good question and it'll keep. It's got no bearing on the knife."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I nod, even though she's not looking, and walk toward the cart. The noise gets clearer with each step—a low, guttural moan that rises and falls. I leave my sword against a wheel.

When I get around the cart, I see him. He's propped against a broken crate, clutching his stomach. His eyes are wide and fixed on me.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't follow him in. She'd said her piece, and a man doing his first one doesn't need the company standing behind him counting his blinks.

She went to the horse

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came around the cart, wiping her hands on her thighs, and crouched an arm's length off. The man shied from her, scraping against the crate, which got him nowhere.

"Belly," she said. "Went in under the edge of his jerkin and up. Missed the lungs — that's why it's one note instead of two. Missed the heart, or he'd be done already. So what he's got left is the middle of him, opened, and everything that lives in there." She nodded at his hands, pressed flat and slick to the knuckle. "See how the blood's not jumping? That's the heart telling you it's in no hurry. It'll bloat him before it kills him. By morning the smell isn't blood — it's the rest of him. And the flies find it before the cold does. You're looking at six hours. Eight, if he's stubborn."

The man spoke. Not much left of his voice — two words, or one said twice.

"He's asking if it'll be quick," Wrack said. "They all ask that. Or it's a brother, or a name. Half of it's true."

She looked at the wound, then at Corvin, and gave the numbers like a mason giving measurements.

"Under the breastbone, angled up toward his shoulder. Your knife's short enough — lean your weight through it, one motion, no poking. You'll feel it stop arguing."

She stayed crouched, forearms on her knees.

"Well. He's waiting on the answer."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down beside him, my knife in hand. "Yeah," I say, my voice low. "It'll be quick." His eyes don't leave mine as I do what she said.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack watched, and didn't look away, and didn't let him think she might.

"Keep the weight on it," she said, quiet. "Don't pull until he's pulled his last breath past your hand. He'll take a few more after you'd think he's done. That's not him changing his mind. That's just the bellows emptying."

She was right about the timing. The grip on Corvin's wrist came and went in stages, like a hand letting go of a rope one finger at a time, and then it was only weight, and then it was only a man against a crate.

"That's the whole of it," she said. "Quicker than I'd have bet, first try."

She waited while Corvin drew the knife, and nodded at the dead man's cloak.

"Wipe it on him, not on the ground. Blood in the dirt draws things. Blood on a dead man draws nothing that matters."

She rose and looked him over again — the same fraying-rope check as before, but slower this time, and she let it be seen that she was doing it.

"He say anything? Before?"

She didn't wait long for the answer either way.

"Doesn't weigh anything, whatever it was. First ones feel like they should. They don't." She turned to the cart, boots crunching on the rutted ground. "Now come spend your shake on something useful. Six men and a wagon. I want to know what's worth six men."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a moment, and something that might have been approval crossed her face and left again.

"Good. That's the right way to ask."

She crossed to the nearest of the six and rolled him over with her boot. Spear hole under the ribs, this one. She crouched beside it.

"Look at that. In is smaller than you'd think — two fingers wide, no more. That's the lie of a spear. The point makes the hole and the shaft does the work behind it. It doesn't slide clean. It goes in and whatever's in the road, it shoves aside. Liver. Gut. Doesn't care which."

She traced a line in the air near the wound, not touching it.

"The belly's a bag. Everything inside stays put because it's sealed. Open the bag and the blood's not what kills him — the spill is. Man can take a spear in the gut and walk a mile before he knows how bad it is. Fever comes on the second day, the wound goes bad, and by the fourth he's dead or wishing. Slowest I ever saw was a week."

She tugged her collar down. A knot of scar sat low on her left side, old and ugly.

"Mine. I was twenty-three. Packed it with moss and honey and spent day four learning why he told me what day four looked like. He was right about all of it."

She stood and pulled the collar straight.

"Now you know. Not for them." A nod at the bodies. "For ours. When it's one of ours down, you'll look, and inside ten seconds you'll know if it's bind-it-and-he-walks or six-hours-and-you-owe-him-ten-seconds. First kind, you do medicine. Second kind, you do what you just did. Standing there not knowing is the worst thing a man can be."

She walked to the wagon and threw back the canvas. Crates. She pried one lid with her knife and went still a moment.

"Six men don't guard grain. And nobody ships spearheads with the maker's mark chiseled off unless he doesn't want them traced."

She looked back at Corvin.

"So. Now it's a question of who's arming men and hiding it. Light's going. Decide what you want to carry and what you want to leave."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my knife on the dead man's cloak and stand up, my legs a little steadier now. "Let's see what else they're hiding." I move to the wagon, pulling open another crate. "Six men... and a wagonload of unmarked steel."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came up beside him and hooked the lid wider with her knife.

"Spearheads. Greased and wrapped like a winter store, not a shipment. Somebody's not arming men yet — somebody's filing steel against a day. Men you can count. Patience you can't."

She worked down the wagon, prying as she went. Third crate: rolled sacking, and she hauled a bundle out and let it drip grease into the straw. She thumbed the rings.

"Mail. Garrison pattern — and look. Mended rings. New straps on old holes. This came off men who stopped needing it. Somebody's been walking battlefields behind us, picking the dead clean. Ten years of war and the only trade that's grown is us."

She stepped down, crossed to the team, and pushed the near ox's flank aside to show the brand on its hip. Burned deep, burned over, half-hidden under a hair crop.

"Fortress mark, doctored. Same as the chisel on the steel. It's not the mark that matters — it's that somebody hid it twice. Honest people hide things once."

Back at the wagon she flipped open the last crate and pulled out a flat piece of board scored with notches, wrapped in oilcloth.

"Tally. Five notches. Four wagons came down this road before this one, and I've not heard of one new spear company raised on this border all year. Which means somebody's steel is going somewhere quiet, and quiet costs more than loud."

She weighed the tally in her hand, then held it out to him.

"Carry that. Here's the sum as I make it: the steel's too heavy to take and too telling to rob, so it goes in the flooded quarry past the ford, and the scene stays honest — six men dead at their own cargo, which on this road is weather, nothing to hunt. The coin and the papers come with us, because the papers are worth more. Every lord on this border would pay for that tally. Two of them would pay more to burn it."

She glanced at the sky, then at his hands.

"And there's your real question, so carry it with the board: who do we sell the knowing to? Because if it turns out our own paymaster's the one buying steel with the marks chiseled off, we've just spent today handing him our rope. Ten years teaches one sum — nobody's honest just because you eat with them."

She shouldered a bundle of mail, unhurried, like the night wasn't already leaning on the hills.

"Light's gone. Oxen come with us — meat and muscle either way. And if your hands are still shaking, good. Carrying cures it faster than standing."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the knife on his cloak, my hand finally steady. "So who's buying unmarked steel?" I take the tally board, tucking it into my belt. "You think our own paymaster's the type?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got the oxen moving first — a hand on the near one's shoulder, a word in the low voice people keep for animals and the dying — and let the wagon creak twice before she answered.

"The type." She chewed on it a moment. "There's no type. That's a horse word — a horse bites or it doesn't, and it's still biting in ten years. Men are sums. Put a man where the honest road pays worse than the crooked one, he'll take the crooked one nine times of ten, and the tenth man is only slower about it. So don't ask if he's the type. Ask what he's paid, who pays him, and whether he's ever once asked us a question he didn't need the answer to."

She walked with one hand on the mail bundle, eyes on the dark coming down out of the hills.

"Now the buying. Three customers for chiseled steel. A lord raising men he can't be seen raising — that's the big one, that's a war getting born. A garrison captain selling his own issue to cover a theft — that's the common one, that's rent money, and rent doesn't want four wagons. Or somebody over the border seeding trouble on our side of it, which is the oldest game on this line and never went out of fashion. The tally's the tell. Four wagons before this one. That's not greed. Greed is one wagon and a good dinner. Four wagons is an army in its first month."

"As for ours — I don't know him well enough to swear, and that's already half the answer." She shrugged. "So we don't ride to him with it. What he asks first tells you everything. An honest man asks what was in the wagon, so he can sell it. A guilty one asks whether anyone followed us. Or offers coin for your silence before you've named a price."

She glanced sideways at him.

"Either way, we sell to his rival first. Every paymaster's got one man who'd pay double just to watch him swing. If ours is clean, the rival still pays. If he's not, we've sold the rope and kept a length of it for ourselves. That's the whole trick of knowing things — never sell it where it costs you."

The quarry fork came up and she turned the team toward it.

"Steel in the water. Papers under my shirt. And your hand's steady now — that's the day's other wage. Most men pay good money for theirs."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the knife on his cloak, my hand finally steady. "So who's buying unmarked steel?" I take the tally board, tucking it into my belt. "You think our own paymaster's the type?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the tally board in my hand. "You're saying we walk in and watch his face." I fall into step beside the oxen. "What if he's the rival's man too?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The quarry showed as a paler dark ahead, a hole cut into the hills with water standing in it, black and patient. Wrack brought the wagon along the lip until the near wheel was a hand's width from the edge, then chocked it with a stone, unhurried, like the oxen could be trusted with a grade, which they couldn't.

"Then he's sold us his own secret twice," she said, "and the only ones richer are us. It happens. Men who play both ends get careless about which hand they're holding out." She hauled the first crate of spearheads up and set it rocking at the lip. "But if it turns out both ends of this trade are the same coat turned twice, we don't sell at all. We salt it. Word goes into three taverns that a tally exists, and where it surfaces if we stop breathing. A live witness gets bought. A letter that opens when you don't — that's the only kind a lord reads twice."

The crate went over. The water took it with less noise than a thing that size had any right to make, and grease came up after it, spreading silver across the black.

"And nobody walks in and watches a face. Faces are what a man keeps clean — it's his hands that go to the purse or the hilt before his tongue's made up its mind. You walk in hungry and stupid-looking. Stupid men get told things. It's the one wage of being stupid, so spend it."

She levered the second crate to the edge and stopped, and looked at him.

"Now the tally. Five notches, and the third is cut deeper with a cross — somebody counted a wagon twice, or marked one paid. Learn that out of your head, not off the board. The board sinks here tonight. The count walks with us." She tipped the crate and watched the water close. "Say it back to me once we're loaded. You sleep with the numbers, I sleep with the papers, and between the two of us we're harder to burn than either."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I lean against the wagon and close my eyes for a second, repeating the pattern in my head. "Five notches. Third one's deep with a cross." I open my eyes again. "So what's the first thing you ask when we're stupid and hungry?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up to see whether the lie showed. She set her knee against the table edge, got both hands on the nearer arm, and spoke to the canvas and the bad light like they were the ones who needed the briefing.

"Left one's out of the socket. I'm putting it back. On three he comes up off this table whether he wants to or not." She shifted her grip, one hand high on the arm, the other braced at the elbow, and counted without hurry. "One. Two."

On three she pulled, steady and ugly, and the joint went with a wet click she felt more than heard. The man made a sound that wasn't a word. She didn't let the arm drop. She laid it down along his side, checked the pulse at the wrist with two fingers, and only then moved to the other shoulder.

"That one took. This one's worse — broken through, not just out. I'm lining the bone up so it doesn't grind while we get him somewhere with a real saw." Her mouth was a flat line. No pleasure in it. "Hold him. Don't watch my hands if you don't want to. Watch his."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look down at his hands, the knuckles white where they're gripping the table. I can feel the muscles in his shoulders twitching under my palms. "Just get it done," I mutter, my own voice sounding tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set her jaw and got both hands on the broken arm, one above the break and one below, and didn't bother with a count this time.

"He's going to scream," she said, flat, to the canvas. "Let him. Don't let him roll."

She pulled along the line of the bone, slow, feeling for the ends to meet instead of grind. The man came up under Wick's weight with a sound that tore itself in half. Something shifted under her palms — not clean, not the click of the other one, just the sick give of bone finding bone where it had no business being. She held it there, breathing through her teeth, until it stopped trying to slip.

"There." She eased the arm down against his ribs, not letting go until it was lying where she wanted it. Two fingers at the wrist again. Pulse, thin and fast, still there. She bound the arm in against his side with whatever strips she had left, tight enough to keep the ends from walking apart, and tied it off without looking at either of them.

"That's all I can do for it here." She wiped her hands on her trousers and finally glanced at the man's face, gray and wet and gone somewhere else. "He'll live the night if the bleeding stays where it is. Get him water if he'll take it. Don't let him move that arm."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge wiped her hands again, though they were as clean as they were going to get, and looked at the arm she'd just tied in, not at Wick.

"It's an arm," she said. "Not a leg. And it's not the kind of bad you're asking about." She checked the fingers again — color, warmth, the thin pulse at the wrist — and let the hand lie where it was. "Bone's lined up well enough that it won't chew itself to pieces before someone with a saw and a light gets to it. If the pulse holds and he doesn't start pouring blood, he keeps it. He won't use it right for a long time. Maybe never right. That's the damage. That's all the damage is."

She straightened, one hand braced on the table edge, and finally met Wick's eye for half a second.

"We're not being kind. We're keeping him until morning. Water, if he'll take it. Don't let him roll onto that side."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go of his shoulders slowly, my hands stiff. "Got it," I say, and I look away from the man's face, because I can't stand the gray stillness of it. "I'll get the water."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stayed where she was until the canvas shifted and Wick was gone with it. Then she put two fingers back on the man's wrist, counting under her breath, and moved them to the hollow of his throat when the arm didn't give her enough.

Still there. Fast, thin, stubborn.

"You're not done," she told him, not unkind and not kind either. She pulled the blanket up over the good shoulder and left the bound arm out where she could see the fingers. Color was poor. Not dead-poor. She pressed a nail and watched the blood creep back, slow, and let the hand go.

The lamp smoked. She turned the wick down a fraction, checked the strips at his side once more — not tight enough to kill the hand, not loose enough to let the bone walk — and set the basin where a reaching man couldn't knock it. His eyes were half open and not on anything.

"Water's coming," she said to the bad light. "You swallow it or you don't. Either way you stay on your back."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't make him wait for it. She tipped the lamp a fraction so the bad light fell on the hand and not on the man's face, and put two fingers where the pulse had been thin and fast.

"You're seeing a hand that's still being fed," she said. "Nail beds are gray, not blue. I press and the color comes back. Slow, but it comes. That means the vessel I was worried about isn't shut. If it shuts, this hand goes cold and white from here down and we start talking about losing it. It hasn't."

She moved her hand up, not gentle, to the strips binding the arm in against the ribs.

"Break's under there. I don't open it again to show you. Ends are meeting well enough that they aren't grinding every time he breathes. Binding's to keep them there. Too tight and I kill the hand I just saved the pulse in. Too loose and the bone walks and we're back where we started, only worse." She checked the knot with her thumb and left it. "It's right. Leave it."

Her eyes went to the other shoulder, the one she'd put back, lying quiet along his side.

"That one took. Socket's holding. He'll hurt like hell when he wakes enough to know it, and he won't lift it for a while, but it isn't the one that kills him."

She looked at the rest of him then, the part Wick had been trying not to imagine — the gray of the face, the sweat gone cold, the chest moving shallow and quick.

"This is the part that does, if anything does. He's bled into himself and he's cold and his heart's running hard for not enough blood. Shock. Not the screaming kind. The quiet kind." She set the blanket higher over the good shoulder and left the bound fingers out in the light. "Water if he'll swallow. On his back. You watch those fingers. If they go white and stay white, you come get me. You don't wait to be sure."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing hard. "White fingers. Got it." I glance back at the tent flap. "Water's taking too long. I should've been quicker."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look at the flap. She looked at the man's mouth, open a little, dry at the corners, and at the chest still doing its shallow work.

"Water doesn't put the blood back," she said. "It keeps his mouth from splitting and it tells me his throat still works if he swallows. You being quicker wouldn't have changed the arm or the shock." Two fingers at the wrist again. Thin. Fast. Still there. She let the hand lie where the lamp could find the nails. "Go get it. Don't run. You run, you spill it, and then we're waiting twice."

She pulled the blanket a fraction higher over the good shoulder and left the bound fingers out in the bad light, gray and not white.

"I'll be here. He isn't going anywhere you have to hurry for."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the arm she'd bound, then at the gray face, and didn't dress it.

"Not in him," she said. "If it was in him I'd have holes, and cloth punched in with the metal, and I wouldn't be standing here telling you the bone's lined up. His came apart from the blast throwing him, or from the blast itself. That's a different bad."

She set two fingers on the thin pulse and left them there while she said the rest, flat, to the lamp.

"Shrapnel's iron that's already been broken once. It doesn't slice. It tumbles. It goes in hot and ragged and it drags dirt and uniform and whatever it hit on the way in with it, and it doesn't stop where a bullet stops. It tears muscle instead of parting it. It nicks a vessel you can't see until the blood's already somewhere it shouldn't be — in the chest, in the belly, pooling where you can't put a hand on it. Hit bone and it doesn't break clean. It shatters. Little edges left in the meat that keep cutting every time he breathes, every time somebody moves him. You don't always find all of it. Some of it you leave, because digging for every scrap kills him faster than the iron will."

She took her fingers off the wrist. Still there. Still fast.

"What kills them isn't the piece you can see. It's the bleeding you can't, and the dirt, and the shock after. Quiet, like him." She nodded at the bound fingers, gray in the bad light, not white. "This one isn't that. Don't go looking for metal that isn't here. Watch the hand. Get the water."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the bound arm, then back at her. "So he got lucky." It doesn't feel like the right word. I duck out of the tent, walking fast but not running, the canteen heavy in my hand.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let the canvas fall and didn't spend the word luck on him. Luck was what people called it when the iron missed the big vessels and the man was still making noise in the morning. She put two fingers back on the thin wrist, counted, and moved them to the throat when the arm stayed stingy.

Still there. Fast. The chest kept its shallow bargain with the air.

"Not lucky," she told the bad light, and the gray face that wasn't listening. "Not dead. That's the whole list."

She checked the strips once more — knot sitting where she'd left it, fingers gray and not white, nail beds slow to pink when she pressed — and pulled the blanket higher over the good shoulder. The bound arm stayed out where the lamp could find it. His mouth was open a little. She wet a rag from the basin and wiped the corners without asking him to swallow yet. Water was coming. Running wouldn't have put the blood back either.

The lamp smoked. She turned it down a hair and stayed on her feet, one hand on the table edge, listening to the tent and the breathing and nothing else that mattered.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge got a hand on the man's chest and the other on the bound arm before the scream had finished climbing, and she did not flinch from it.

"He's not coming apart," she said, over him, to Wick and to the canvas. "Pain. The socket's telling him it's back in a place it doesn't trust, and the break's telling him somebody moved it. Let him yell. You keep the shoulders down. I keep the arm from walking."

She checked the strips with her thumb while he bucked — knot still sitting, not slipped, not cutting in. The fingers stayed out in the lamp. Gray. Not white. She pressed a nail anyway, watched the color crawl back, slow, and let the hand go.

"What I'm doing is nothing heroic. I'm holding what I already set so he doesn't undo it by thrashing. I'm not cutting. I'm not pulling again. Pulling's done." She shifted her weight so the bound arm stayed against his ribs and spoke without looking up. "If the binding holds and the pulse holds, this part is five minutes of him fighting us and then the fight goes out of him. Shock does that. He'll drop quieter than he came up. That's not me finishing him. That's the blood he doesn't have."

The scream broke into something wet and shorter. She put two fingers at the throat, counted under it, and left them there.

"Still there. Fast. After he drops I check the hand again, I check he can swallow, and then we wait. Water when his mouth will take it. Blanket. On his back. No more setting tonight unless the bone slips or the fingers go dead." Her mouth stayed a flat line. No pleasure in any of it. "That's the whole of it. You hold until he stops trying to sit up. I don't leave this arm until he does."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my weight on him, my arms starting to shake. "I've got him," I say through gritted teeth. The screaming cuts off abruptly, leaving a ringing silence. I can feel him go limp beneath my hands.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stayed on the arm until the last of the fight left it, then didn't trust the quiet.

"Don't let go yet," she said. Two fingers went to the hollow of his throat and stayed there, counting past the place where a faint pulse could be wished into being. It was there. Thin. Faster than it had any right to be, and weaker than it had been before he screamed. She moved to the wrist of the bound arm, pressed a nail, and watched the color crawl back — slow, gray going a little pink, not the dead white she'd told Wick to fear.

"He's not gone. Shock took the scream. That's what I said it would do." She checked the knot with her thumb. Still sitting. The bone hadn't walked. She laid the arm back against his ribs and only then took her hand off it. "You can ease up. Not all at once. If he starts up again you put him back down the same way."

She pulled the blanket higher over the good shoulder and left the fingers out in the lamp where both of them could see them. His mouth was open. Breath shallow, still making its bargain. She wet the rag and touched it to his lips, not pouring, not asking him to be brave about it.

"Water when he swallows on his own. Until then this is enough." She didn't look at Wick's shaking arms. She looked at the hand. "Five minutes of that, maybe less next time. You held. That's the job. Now we wait, and you watch those fingers."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stayed on her feet a moment longer, one hand on the table edge, listening to the shallow breathing until she was sure it meant to keep its bargain. Then she lowered herself onto the overturned crate by the basin, close enough to reach the wrist, and didn't tidy any of it.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She nodded at the bound arm without touching it.

"The bone's in two. Not three, not a bag of gravel — two ends, and I felt them meet. That doesn't mean they're friends. There's a gap in the meat where the ends tore through on their way out of line, and that gap is full of blood that has nowhere useful to go. It'll swell. By morning the arm'll be fat and hot and the skin'll shine, and that's the swelling doing its job and also threatening the hand. The strips are tight enough to keep the ends from walking and loose enough that I can still get a finger under them at the knot. If the arm swells into the binding, the knot becomes a tourniquet I didn't mean to set. That's why you watch the fingers. White and cold and staying that way means the binding is winning and the hand is losing, and you cut the strips. Not the skin. The strips. Then you come get me even if you think you've already fixed it."

She put two fingers on the thin wrist, counted, and left them there while she went on.

"The shoulder I put back is a socket that got levered apart and a ball that went back in angry. The muscles around it are torn enough that they won't hold it if he rolls, or if he tries to push himself up, or if somebody grabs him under the arms to move him. It can come out again. If it does, you don't put it back. You hold him still and you wait for me. Doing it twice in one night on a man this empty is how you tear the vessel I just proved is still open."

Her eyes went to the chest, still quick, still shallow.

"Shock is the part that takes them when the iron didn't. He's lost blood into the arm and into the shoulder and into the places I can't see, and what's left is doing the work of a full load. Heart's fast because it's trying to push too little around a body that wants more. Skin's cold because the body's given up on the outside and is spending what it has on the middle. That's why the face is that color. That's why he went quiet. It isn't peace. It's the body choosing. Breathing like that — short, high, not using the bottom of the lungs — means he isn't getting ahead of it. If the breaths get further apart, or if he starts a wet sound in the throat that isn't swallowing, or if the pulse at the neck goes from fast to a flutter you can barely find, you put your hand here." She tapped the hollow of her own throat. "And you shout. You don't wait to see if it comes back on its own. It sometimes does. It sometimes doesn't, and the difference is minutes."

She took her fingers off the wrist. Still there. She wiped them on her trousers out of habit.

"Water. When he swallows on his own, small amounts, sitting him up no more than a hand's width. Too much and he brings it back up and chokes, and choking on a man who can't roll is how a night's work ends in a basin. If he won't swallow, you stop. A dry mouth won't kill him before morning. Water in the lungs will."

The lamp smoked. She didn't turn it down this time. She wanted the fingers where she could see them.

"Pain will come back when the shock loosens its grip. He'll start up again. Not as long as the last time, if we're lucky in the only way that word applies, which is that his body runs out of the strength to fight us. You hold the shoulders. I hold the arm. We don't talk him out of it. There isn't a sentence that makes a broken bone polite."

She looked at the gray face, half-open eyes on nothing, and her mouth stayed a flat line.

"What I can't do here is open the arm, wash the ends, and put them together under a light with something cleaner than my hands. I can't replace the blood. I can't promise the hand. I can keep the bone from grinding itself to splinters overnight, I can keep the socket in, and I can keep him on his back until somebody with a saw and a morning gets here. If the bleeding stays where it is and the fingers stay gray instead of white and the breathing doesn't quit, he sees that morning. He won't thank anybody for the arm. He may never lift it over his head again. That's the damage. That's the rest of it."

She leaned back on the crate, eyes on the hand in the bad light, and didn't look at the floor.

"I'm not leaving. You don't have to get up. You watch the fingers. I'll watch the throat."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press my hands against my eyes. "And if he doesn't see the morning?" My voice is quiet. "What do we do then?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was quiet long enough that the lamp crack made a sound of its own. She didn't look at Wick's hands over his eyes. She looked at the throat, then the fingers, gray and not white, and answered the floor of the question instead of the softness in it.

"Then he doesn't," she said. "And we stop pretending the night has a job left for him."

She put two fingers in the hollow of the man's throat and left them there while she said the rest, the same way she'd counted a pulse that was still being stubborn.

"You don't shake him. You don't pour water in a mouth that isn't swallowing. You don't set the arm again because it feels unfinished. If the breaths stop and the pulse at the neck is gone — not thin, gone, and it stays gone while you count slow to thirty — that's the end of it. I listen at the chest once, because I've been wrong in bad light before. If there's nothing, I say so. Out loud. So neither of us spends the rest of the night bargaining with a body that's already done."

Her mouth stayed flat. No ceremony in it, and no cruelty either.

"We close his eyes if they'll stay closed. We straighten him on his back, bound arm where it is, blanket over him including the hand. The binding comes off only if someone after us needs the strips. Not for him. He doesn't feel it. We don't wash him unless there's time and water to spare, and there usually isn't. Tag if we've got one — name, if we know it, and what took him. Shock, blood loss, the arm. Honest. Not a story."

She took her fingers off the throat. Still there, this minute. Fast. She wiped them on her trousers.

"Then we move him out of the light so the next one can have the table, if there is a next one. If there isn't, he stays until the detail comes. You don't sit with him till morning out of manners. Manners don't put blood back in the living. You drink what's left in the canteen. You sleep if your hands will let you. I write it down so I don't have to remember the color of his face later and get it wrong."

The lamp smoked. She didn't turn it down.

"That's if. It isn't yet." She nodded at the fingers in the bad light. "He's still spending what he has. You asked what we do if he doesn't see morning. We do the small things right, and we don't make a speech over him. Watch the hand. I'll tell you if the throat quits. You won't have to guess."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at the man's hand, really look at it, the dirt under the nails and the fine hairs on the knuckles. "I'm going to remember the color of his face anyway," I say, and my voice sounds tired even to me. "Even if you write it down."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't argue with it. She looked at the gray face once, the way she looked at a dressing she already knew was as good as it was going to get, and then back at the hand in the lamp.

"You will," she said. "Writing it down isn't so you forget. It's so the record isn't whatever your head does to it at three in the morning a year from now. Color, pulse, what the arm did, what it didn't. Facts. Your remembering is your business. The page is mine."

She put two fingers at the throat again, counted past a wish, and took them away. Still there. Fast. The chest kept its short bargain.

"Dirt under the nails means he was working when it hit him. Hairs on the knuckles mean the hand's still a hand and not a thing we're done with." She nodded at it, not gentle. "That's what you're looking at. Not a keepsake. If they stay gray and the nail comes back when you press, he's still spending. If they go white and stay white, you cut the strips and you shout. You already know that. Knowing it again won't make the face any less gray when you shut your eyes."

The lamp smoked. She left it.

"Sit there if you're going to sit. Drink if the canteen's still in your hand. I'm not going to tell you it gets easier to look at, and I'm not going to tell you to stop looking." Her mouth stayed a flat line. "He's not dead. That's the list. Watch the fingers."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pick up the canteen from where I dropped it and take a swallow, the water warm and flat. "You write everything down? Every one?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood, rolling her shoulders until something in her back cracked. She walked to the nearest body — big man, badly surprised — crouched, and started going through his coat.

"Hearing him isn't doing anything about him," she said. Somewhere past the cart the noise kept on: wet, unhurried, a little slower than it had been. She didn't look

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Let him wear himself out." I say, forcing a calm I don't feel into my voice. I try to focus on cleaning my sword, but my hands aren't steady. "Waste of effort to go finish it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "He's gutted," I mutter, finally looking toward the cart. "I saw him go down." The sound from over there *is* getting weaker. I rub at my face again, smearing the blood. "Fine. I'll... I'll go check."

dialogue.name: Wrack

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came over last, wiping her hands on her trousers. The big man's coat had held nothing but lint and a pipe she didn't want. She crouched on the far side of the dying man — he was laid out by the cart wheel, knees drawn up, both hands pressed to his middle like he could hold himself shut — and looked him over the way she'd look at a horse somebody was trying to sell her.

"Gut wound, low, left side. See how the belly's gone round and tight? That's blood filling him up where blood shouldn't be. Blade went in under the ribs and did its work on the way out." She nodded at his hands, dark and shining. "And the gut's opened, so what's in there is spilling where it doesn't belong. That's poison once it's loose. The bleeding might not kill him. That will."

The man's eyes found them and stayed. He made a sound that had given up on being words.

"He can hear us," she said. "Hearing's the last thing to go. He'll be cold soon, then warm again, and he'll think he's fine — that part fools people. Then it's a long bad night and he's dead by dawn, or noon if he's stubborn. Nobody hauls a belly like this forty miles to a barber, and if they did he'd die anyway. Just more expensive."

She stood and rolled

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "He can hear us?" I swallow hard, looking down at the man's fixed stare. "Right. Okay." I grip the hilt of my sword tighter. "So... so it's a mercy, then."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: "It

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Then I won't." She settled back on her heels. "He hears it too. Nothing I'm telling him he doesn't know better than I do."

"Spear went in under the ribs, left side, angled down. That's not bad luck — that's where the wall of a man is thinnest. A point goes in there like it's been invited. The head opens him going in and opens him wider coming out, and the gut isn't built for holes. It's twenty feet of coiled tube, and everything inside it — half-worked bread, bile, the stuff that makes a corpse smell like a corpse — belongs in the tube and nowhere else. He's got at least two leaks. It's been running into his belly since he sat down, which is why it's gone tight and round. He's filling up like a wineskin.

"By full dark he'll be swollen drum-hard and the pain will climb past the point where a man can scream. He'll just lie there and shake. He'll be thirsty in a way you've never been thirsty — gut-shot men always are — and drinking only gives the leak more to run. Fever comes with the night, and by then the poison's in his blood, and the blood takes it everywhere. Then the smell comes. You'll know that smell the rest of your life. Somewhere near dawn his heart loses count and quits. That's the whole road. No shortcuts on it except the one you're holding."

The man's breath had gone quick and shallow. His eyes moved between them and stayed.

"Now the part you actually want. Don't put steel in his belly again — he's paid enough there. Heart's here." She leaned over and set two fingers on his chest, just under the breastbone. "Point there, angled up toward the back of his neck, and lean. Don't jab. Jabbing's hope; leaning's work. He'll go quick. Sometimes the body takes a breath or two after the heart's done — don't let it frighten you. That's just meat settling. Or open his throat if you'd rather be certain. Slower to be sure of, messier to wear."

She stood and stepped back a pace, arms crossed, out of the way.

"You asked me before — mercy or just easier. It's both. That's more common out here than you'd think, and sorting the two apart takes longer than he's got." A beat. "I'll do it if you say the word. It's nothing to me anymore. But it's your blade in your hand, and you'll be doing this again someday whether you practice now or not. Either way — before the light goes."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My knuckles are white around the hilt. I nod, just once. "I'll do it." I kneel down, trying to block out the sound of his breathing. "Hey," I say, and his eyes flick to mine. "It's over." I place the tip where she showed me, and lean in.
