dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wr

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "She's not coming," Wrack says, and her voice is flat. "And if she was, it's been four hours. One more won't change anything except the light you'll have to walk back by."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wr

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath, let it out slow. My sword's still in my hand, point down in the dirt. "Alright," I say, finally pushing myself to my feet. "Lead on then."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content: Wr

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I scrub my bloody hand through my hair, leaving a smear I can’t see. “So where are you leading us?” I ask, forcing my voice not to shake. “I’m not spending the night in a ditch.”

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Ready enough,” Sedge said. It wasn’t reassurance. “Right side first. Don’t let his chest roll.”

She checked the man’s wrist for a pulse, then pressed two fingers briefly to his fingertips. “Tell me if you can feel that,” she said to him, though he was already sucking air through his teeth.

He managed a ragged nod.

Sedge took his forearm and supported the elbow, keeping the arm close to the angle it had settled at. “I’m going to pull slowly. It’ll hurt. I’m not doing it to punish you.”

She leaned her weight back by careful degrees, watching his face and the line of his arm. The man made a hoarse, broken sound and tried to twist. The table creaked.

“Hold,” Sedge said, flat and immediate. “Keep his shoulders down.”

She eased the pull, adjusted her grip, and tried again—steady traction, no jerking. Her eyes stayed on the joint, her hands patient despite the noise. “That’s it. Breathe if you can. I need the muscle to stop fighting me.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press down harder, feeling the soldier's muscles straining against me. "He's shaking bad," I say through gritted teeth, trying to keep my voice steady. I can't look at his face anymore.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Shaking is expected,” Sedge said. “It isn’t a reason to let go.”

She eased the pull by a fraction, not stopping it. The soldier’s muscles clenched against her hands. Sedge waited, watching the joint and the color in his fingers.

“Keep his chest square,” she said. “I have the arm.”

The man gave another hoarse cry. Sedge adjusted the angle, then drew the forearm outward with slow, even traction. A small shift passed under her palm. The soldier’s arm slackened.

“There,” she said. “That one’s back.”

She supported his elbow and checked his wrist pulse, then pressed each fingertip in turn. “Can you feel this?”

The soldier nodded, shuddering.

Sedge secured the arm against his body with a folded blanket. “Don’t move it yet. The other side still needs doing.” She glanced at Wick. “Keep your hold. I’ll tell you when to change.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Neither,” Sedge said. “His legs aren’t the problem. I’ve seen no sign they’re involved.”

She kept one hand steady beneath the soldier’s elbow, checking the warmth in his fingers again. “Both shoulders were out. One’s back in. The other still needs doing. It’ll hurt, and I won’t pretend otherwise. Leaving it out would hurt longer and do more damage.”

Her eyes stayed on the soldier. “That’s what kindness looks like here. Hold him steady.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, shifting my hands to brace him for the other side. "He's starting to fade," I mutter, keeping pressure on the good shoulder. "You want me to keep talking to him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Sedge said. “Keep him answering. Ask his name. Ask where he is. Short questions.”

She set the second arm in a supported position and checked the soldier’s pulse at his neck, then watched the rise and fall of his chest. “Don’t press harder. Keep him square.”

Her fingers stayed at his throat as she leaned into his line of sight. “Can you hear me? Keep your eyes open.”

She looked to Wick. “If he stops answering, or his breathing changes, tell me at once. The shoulder can wait a few seconds.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept two fingers at the soldier’s neck. “His face has gone gray. He’s sweating, and his eyes aren’t holding focus. His pulse is fast. He’s still breathing, but I’m watching to see if it gets shallow or uneven.”

She shifted her hand to his jaw, keeping his head turned enough to see his mouth and chest. “That can be pain and exhaustion. It can also be shock. I can’t tell you which from his color alone.”

Her gaze stayed on the soldier. “What’s your name? Where are you?”

She watched for his answer, then said, “If he stops responding, that matters. If his breathing changes, that matters. The arm can wait while I deal with either.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean closer, my own sweat dripping onto the canvas. "Hey, soldier. Your name. What is it?" I watch his eyes flicker, waiting for any sign he's still in there.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The soldier’s eyes moved without settling. His mouth worked once before a thin, breathless “Marek” came out.

“Good,” Sedge said. She kept two fingers at his neck, counting beneath the skin. “Where are you, Marek?”

His brow pinched. No answer came. His next breath was shallow, with a pause before the one after it.

Sedge stopped preparing the arm. “That’s enough. I’m not putting the shoulder back while he’s fading.”

She checked his airway and the pulse at his wrist, then looked at his face again. “Marek, stay with me. Keep breathing. You’re under canvas. You’re not alone.”

Her voice remained level, but her hands moved faster now, checking for blood and feeling along his ribs and abdomen. “The shoulder can wait. His breathing can’t.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge kept one hand at Marek’s jaw and watched his chest. “A fragment can cut a vessel and let him bleed inside where we can’t see it. It can break a rib, tear the lung, and make each breath harder. It can pass through muscle and leave a ragged channel behind it. Or it can lodge without hitting anything vital. The size doesn’t tell me what it struck.”

She pressed carefully along his ribs and abdomen, watching his face for a change. “I haven’t found a wound yet. That doesn’t prove there isn’t one. I don’t know what’s happening inside him. His breathing is getting shallow, and that’s what I know.”

Her fingers returned to his neck. “Keep him answering if he can. I’m checking for blood and making sure he can breathe. The shoulder waits.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my hands on his shoulders but lift my head to look at you properly. "You're checking for things you can't fix here, aren't you?" My voice is quieter than I meant it to be.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Sedge said. “Some of what I’m checking, I can’t fix in this tent. If he’s bleeding inside, I can’t clamp it from here. If his lung’s torn, I can’t stitch it shut.”

She kept her fingers at Marek’s neck and watched his chest rise. “But I can keep his airway clear, stop what bleeding I can reach, and get him moved. And knowing what’s wrong tells me what not to do. I won’t put his shoulder back while he’s struggling to breathe.”

Her gaze stayed on Marek. “Keep him answering if he can. Tell me at once if his breathing changes again.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with her hands off the second arm. “I’m not putting that shoulder back now.”

Marek’s scream broke into a ragged gasp. Sedge watched his chest through the next two breaths, then put two fingers to his neck again.

“Keep his shoulders square. Don’t squeeze his chest.”

She leaned close to Marek’s mouth, checking that nothing blocked it, then watched his ribs rise. “The scream means air is moving right now. It doesn’t tell me why his breathing went shallow, and it doesn’t mean he’s safe.”

She cut open the front of his shirt and searched the skin for blood, punctures, or swelling, working from his collarbones down across his ribs and abdomen. “I’m looking for wounds I can reach and bleeding I can stop. I haven’t found one yet. That does not rule out a fragment inside him.”

Her hand returned to his neck. She counted his pulse, then checked his fingers for warmth and color. “His pulse is still fast. I’m checking whether it’s getting weaker, and whether his breathing changes again.”

Sedge looked toward Wick. “You asked how much longer. I can’t give you a safe number. I’m not spending another minute on the shoulder while his breathing is like this. I’m checking him now, then he needs transport to someone who can treat what I can’t reach here.”

She kept one hand near Marek’s jaw and watched his chest. “I’m not hiding anything. I don’t know yet whether he’s bleeding inside or whether pain and exhaustion are making him fade. I do know the next job is keeping his airway clear and getting him out.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look down at Marek's face, gray and damp. "Then get him out." My hands are still pressed into his shoulders, holding him against the table. "You want me to carry him, or do we wait for a cart?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Get the litter,” Sedge said. “If it’s at the entrance, bring it here. If it isn’t, send someone for it. We don’t wait on a cart while he’s breathing like that, and we don’t carry him in our arms.”

She kept Marek’s jaw clear and watched his chest through another breath. “Keep his shoulders square, but leave his chest free. I’ll keep his head and neck steady while we move him. No twisting, no pulling on either arm.”

She glanced toward the tent flap. “We move as soon as the litter’s here. If his breathing worsens before then, tell me at once.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The litter came in with two orderlies carrying it, one at each end. Sedge told them to put it alongside the table, not across the tent.

“Head first. Keep it level. No one pulls on his arms.”

She kept Marek’s jaw clear and watched his chest. His breaths came thin and uneven, with a longer pause after each one. She counted his pulse again. Fast, and weaker beneath her fingers.

“I’m moving him now,” she said. “If he stops breathing, I’ll tell you. Don’t try to sit him up.”

The orderlies slid the litter close. Sedge supported Marek’s head and neck while they worked the blanket beneath him. When they rolled him just enough to free it, her hand came away wet.

“Stop.”

She turned him no farther than she had to. Blood had soaked the blanket beneath his right side, dark and spread wide. The wound was tucked under his arm, where the table and his body had hidden it. Sedge pressed a folded dressing against it.

“Here. Hold pressure. Don’t lift it to look.”

The orderly put both hands over the dressing. Sedge checked Marek’s mouth, then his chest. One breath. A pause. Another, shallow enough that his ribs barely moved.

“Move,” she said. “Slowly. Keep him level.”

They lifted the litter. Sedge walked at Marek’s head, one hand steadying his jaw, her eyes on his breathing. The orderlies moved carefully around the tent stakes and out through the flap. The air outside was cold against the sweat on her hands. She kept watching his chest.

At the entrance to the aid station, Marek’s next breath did not come.

Sedge stopped the litter. “Set him down. Now.”

She opened his mouth and checked for an obstruction. There was none. She tipped his jaw forward and watched his chest. Nothing moved. She put her fingers to his neck, counted, shifted her hand, and checked again.

“No pulse.”

She started compressions. Her hands went to the center of his chest. She pressed hard and kept the rhythm. The litter frame creaked beneath him.

“Get the airway kit. Tell the surgeon we have penetrating trauma and no pulse.”

One orderly ran. The other stood at the head of the litter and held the mask while Sedge gave breaths between sets of compressions. She watched for the chest to rise. It did, unevenly. She continued.

She checked his pulse again. Nothing.

Sedge went back to compressions. Her shoulders worked. Her face did not change. She counted under her breath, stopped to give breaths, then pressed again. She kept at it until the surgeon arrived, until he checked Marek himself and told her to stop.

She stopped.

For a moment, she kept her hands on Marek’s chest. Then she took them away and looked at the blood on her palms. She covered the wound, pulled the blanket up over him, and gave the surgeon the facts: when his breathing had changed, where the blood had been found, how long they had worked. She did not say that the shoulder would have been fixable. It was not the part that had killed him.

Later, in the tent, Wick sat on the floor and told her to say the rest.

Sedge set the bloodied dressing aside. She did not soften her voice.

“Marek died before we got him to the aid station. He had a wound under his right arm. There was blood beneath him, but not enough outside him to tell me how much he’d lost inside. His breathing failed, then his pulse stopped. We tried to bring him back. We couldn’t.”

She rinsed her hands in the basin. The water clouded red, then pink.

“I don’t know whether the fragment tore a vessel, damaged his lung, or did both. I can’t tell you the exact path it took. I can tell you the shallow breathing was a warning, and I can tell you I stopped the shoulder because of it. His shoulder wasn’t what killed him.”

She dried her hands on a rag that was already stained.

“You held him steady while I checked him. That was useful. It didn’t make you responsible for what was inside his chest.” Sedge folded the rag once and set it down. “That’s the rest.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at my own hands, still pressed into the canvas floor. "He said his name," I say quietly. "That's all he gave us."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Sedge said. “Marek. I’ll put his name on the tag and in the ledger. He won’t go down as unidentified.”

She folded the stained dressing in on itself and set it aside.

“You asked him to answer. He did, while he could. I can’t tell you it changed what happened.” Her voice stayed level. “It was still worth asking.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my legs unsteady. "I'm going to need a minute before I hold anyone else down." My voice sounds rough to my own ears.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
“Then take it,” Sedge said. “Sit before your legs give out. There’s water by the basin.”

She set the ledger beside Marek’s tag. “You’re off restraint duty until you tell me you’re steady. I need hands that can hold properly, not someone falling onto a patient.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I sink back down against the cot pole, my hands shaking. "Don't suppose there's anything stronger than water in here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway raised the lamp another inch. The light caught a pale curve above the water, then a second curve beneath it.

“The shoulders,” she said. “Too narrow for the length of the arms. And the left arm has an extra joint between the elbow and wrist.”

She watched the far end of the cellar. Nothing moved. That was not the same as dead.

“Also, it stopped where the water gets deeper. Convenient place to disappear if it wants us closer.” She hooked the toe of her boot beneath a loose brick and pushed it out across the water. “Watch the surface around it. Not the thing.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I watch the brick skip, sending ripples out towards those pale curves. My stomach twists. "The ripples...they're not going around it. They're going *through* it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady. The brick struck the far wall and sank; its ripples crossed both pale curves without breaking.

“Good. It isn’t occupying that space.”

She lowered the lamp toward the water. The curves slid with the change in angle, keeping their distance from the light. “Reflection, then. Not of anything behind us that I can see.”

Something tapped the underside of the stair on which they stood. Once, then twice, with a pause between taps.

Halloway did not look down. “It wants us watching the far end,” she said. “That does narrow down where the rest of it is.”

She drew her knife slowly, keeping the lamp trained on the false shoulders. “Stay on the stairs. If the wood shifts, tell me before it breaks.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway studied the pale curves a moment longer.

“Possibly. Those could be human shoulder blades. I can’t tell whether they’re attached to anything, and I can’t tell how recently they belonged to someone until I see them out of the water.”

A third tap came from beneath the stair, closer to her boot. Halloway shifted her weight onto the stone threshold without lowering the lamp.

“Whatever’s under us knows we’re discussing it. Poor manners, if it used to be a person.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my own heartbeat loud in my ears. "If it's not behind us...and it's not over there...where's its head?" I whisper. The question feels stupid as soon as I say it.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not turn the lamp. “That isn’t a stupid question. We haven’t seen a head.”

She looked at the gap between the lowest stair and the water. A thin line of bubbles collected there. They rose, burst, and were replaced.

“Something’s breathing under the stairs,” she said. “Or letting air out. I’d prefer the first; it means it has a reason to keep its face above water.”

She eased the tip of her knife beneath the edge of the step. “I’m going to lift the board. Watch the water beside my boot, not the pale shapes.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway caught the edge of the board with her knife and lifted it an inch. Water drained from the gap. Beneath it lay a human face, pressed sideways against the stair support. Its eyes were open. A narrow stream of bubbles escaped its mouth.

“I don’t know what happened to it yet,” she said. “That is a person’s head. There’s no visible wound to the face, and bubbles don’t prove it’s breathing. Air can come out of a body after death.”

She let the board settle without taking her eyes off the gap. Beneath the water, something pale tightened around the support beside the face. It bent once, then again, at joints too close together.

“But that arm is moving on its own. And if you’re close enough to hand me the lamp, you’re close enough for it to reach you.”

Halloway drew her knife free. “Back to the stone threshold. We’ll find out what happened without offering it another person.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I scramble back, my boots slipping on the wet stone. "It's *under* the stairs? All of it?" The thought makes my skin crawl. "How did it even get there?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her knife against the edge of the step.

“Not all of it. I’ve seen a head and part of an arm. The rest could be under the stairs, or through the wall behind them.”

She crouched far enough to inspect the stair support without putting her hand in the water. The wood around the face was splintered inward. Two nails had been pulled halfway out of the beam.

“It didn’t crawl in through that gap,” she said. “The stairs were forced up, and it was put beneath them. Whether it was like this before that happened, I can’t tell.”

The pale arm loosened its grip on the support. Water stirred along the underside of the lowest step, travelling toward the threshold.

Halloway stood. “That’s enough inspection. Keep the lamp on the water between us and the stairs. If we can see which way the arm goes, we may get to keep our ankles.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched the stirring water. It advanced along the lowest step, too steady to be a ripple.

“Exactly? I can’t. I haven’t seen beneath his skin, and I don’t know whether he’s dead. What I can tell you is that his face looks human, the arm beside it has more joints than a human arm, and that arm moved while his head didn’t.”

She shifted back onto the stone, keeping her knife low. “The stairs were forced up to put him there. Whatever did it has reached at least this far.” She pointed to the moving water with the knife. “If you meet another one, don’t assume the part you can see is the part that can reach you.”

The water beside the step bulged. Halloway raised the lamp higher, searching for the arm beneath it.

“As for what it took from him,” she said, “we find that out after we get him clear. Not by putting our hands under the stairs.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a shaky breath. "Alright. So we get him out. How?" I glance at the rippling water. "You lift, I pull?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“No,” Halloway said. “You pull, it gets two hands within reach of one arm. That’s a poor exchange.”

The bulge reached the foot of the stairs. Halloway drove her knife through the water beside it and into the soft wood of the bottom step. Something struck the blade from below. The step shuddered, but held.

“We take the stairs apart from above,” she said. “Then we use the rope in my pack to bring him toward the threshold. If he’s alive, we keep his face clear of the water. If that arm is attached to him, we don’t yank it loose trying to be helpful.”

A scraping sound travelled beneath the step, away from the pinned blade. Halloway watched the water on the other side.

“First, though, we learn whether that’s the only arm.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway worked the knife along the split beside the bottom step. “The wood smells of rot. There’s something else under it—sweet, like meat left in a warm room. I can’t tell whether that’s coming from him.”

A strip of wood came free. Beneath it, the pale arm lay folded twice around the stair support. Dark threads ran along its surface, visible under the skin. Its hand had five fingers. Each finger ended in a blunt, human nail.

“The extra joints are in the forearm,” Halloway said. “Two bends between elbow and wrist. The skin hasn’t split over either one. Whatever changed it happened slowly enough for the skin to grow with it, or it was never an ordinary arm.”

She cut another strip away. The arm contracted, drawing the face harder against the beam. Water spilled from the open mouth, followed by a fresh stream of bubbles.

“It can move his head by pulling on that support,” she said. “That still doesn’t tell me whether he can move it himself.”

She paused with the knife against the next board. “That’s everything I can see. I’ll keep telling you as it changes.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow the sour taste in my mouth. "Those threads in its arm. Are they moving?" I ask. My voice sounds too loud. I pull the lamp back a little, so she can see the shadows.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway waited for the water to settle. With the lamp drawn back, the threads showed more clearly beneath the skin.

“Yes. They’re sliding toward the wrist when the arm contracts. Not pulsing with a heartbeat.”

She touched the flat of her knife to the exposed forearm. The fingers closed around the stair support. A dark thread slipped past the wrist and continued beneath the skin of the palm.

“Could be tendons. Could be something using the tendons. I’m not cutting it open while his face is underwater.”

A knock sounded from inside the wall behind the stairs. Halloway took the knife off the arm and looked at the plaster above the waterline.

“And that wasn’t the arm.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked from the lamp to the plaster behind the stairs. Another knock came from inside the wall, level with the trapped face.

“I will,” she said. “But I’m not putting a knife through that head to save time.”

She drove the blade into the split step and levered up a length of board. It cracked free. The arm beneath it folded sharply and struck at her wrist. Halloway withdrew her hand; its nails scraped the wood instead.

The opening showed a shoulder, then a chest wedged against the wall. The chest did not rise. Dark threads crossed it beneath the skin and disappeared into a hole in the plaster.

Halloway held still long enough to watch. The arm flexed. The threads drew taut. The face shifted against the beam, but the chest remained motionless.

“His body’s in there,” she said. “The arm is attached. Those threads run into the wall.”

She took the rope from her pack and dropped a loop over the exposed forearm. When the fingers reached for it, she pulled the loop tight against the stair support. The arm bent at all three joints and strained, but could not reach past the wood.

Halloway broke away another piece of plaster with the loose brick. Inside the wall was a dark mass the size of a fist. Threads entered it from the man’s shoulder and ran upward through a gap between the stones. It contracted when the brick struck beside it. The arm contracted with it.

“There you are.”

She put two fingers against the man’s neck. She waited, shifted them, and waited again. The stream of bubbles at his mouth had stopped. She checked once more before taking her hand away.

“No pulse.”

Halloway set the brick against the exposed mass to keep it from retreating into the wall. It pressed back hard enough to move the brick. She drove her knife through it and into the mortar behind. The arm jerked against the rope. She cut downward, separating the mass from the threads that ran up between the stones.

The knocking stopped. The arm gave one last pull and went slack.

Halloway left the knife where it was. She watched the hand until the water around it settled, then pressed the brick against the severed threads. Neither the hand nor the mass moved.

“He was dead before I cut it,” she said. “I couldn’t tell you when. This part is finished.”

She looked up at the gap between the stones, where the cut threads disappeared into darkness.

“We’ll get him out now. After that, we open the wall.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content:
I stare at the limp hand, still caught in the rope. "No pulse," I repeat, my own throat tight. "But it kept moving."

I wade back over, my boots sloshing. "Let me see that... that mass." I take the lamp from her and hold it up to the hole in the wall.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stepped aside so the light reached the hole. She kept one hand on the brick pinning the severed threads.

The mass was dark red, with a thin, clear membrane torn where her knife had passed through it. Its cut surface showed layers of muscle around a hollow centre. Small white strands ran from it toward the shoulder; thicker, blackened strands had run up between the stones.

“It contracted. When it did, the arm moved,” she said. “That’s what I know. I don’t know whether it grew inside him or was put there.”

She eased the brick back a fraction. The cut ends stayed still. She set it down again and angled her head to see past the mass. The gap above it was narrow, but the plaster around it had cracked in a line extending beyond the stairs.

“The part I cut was no bigger than my fist. Those strands go farther.” She glanced at the limp hand caught in the rope. “Enough of it was in him to move his arm after his heart stopped.”

Halloway withdrew her knife from the mortar. Its blade came free with a strip of membrane attached. She laid the strip on the exposed step, where it showed no movement.

“Hold the light there,” she said. “I want to see where the strands enter the wall before we break any more of it. I’d rather not find out what’s on the other side by standing in its way.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean in closer, the lamplight catching the gleam of the wet, severed threads. "It's like... a root system," I whisper. "But it was inside him." My stomach turns. "Did it replace his heart?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“No evidence of that,” Halloway said. “I can see the mass in the wall and strands entering his shoulder. His heart is inside his chest. We haven’t opened it.”

She leaned toward the exposed torso, keeping clear of the limp arm. The water obscured most of the ribs. Above it, the skin over the left side of the chest was intact, though a dark strand showed beneath it and ran toward the collarbone.

“It may have stopped his heart. It may have kept moving after his heart stopped for some other reason.” She pointed with the knife to the strands between the stones. “Those are cut, but we don’t know where they lead. Give the wall a little room.”

Halloway set the knife tip against the cracked plaster above the hole and lifted away a small piece. Behind it, the blackened strands divided and passed into three separate joints in the stonework.

“Roots are a fair comparison,” she said. “Not a diagnosis. Roots generally have the decency to stay out of people.”

She left the plaster alone and watched the exposed strands. None moved.

“First we get him free. Then we check what’s in his chest. We don’t break open the rest of that wall while he’s still pinned against it.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my hands cold around the lamp. "Alright. We get him free." I don't look away from the mass, the roots. "What do you need me to do?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Those could be human shoulder blades.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Beneath it lay a human face, pressed sideways against the stair support.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Exactly? I can’t.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Dark threads ran along its surface, visible under the skin.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She drove her knife through it and into the mortar behind.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady. The shape at the far end lay low in the water, its outline broken by ripples and shadow. She did not move closer.

“Wrong how?” she asked. “Don’t guess what it is. Tell me what doesn’t fit.” Her eyes tracked the visible silhouette. “Limbs. Joints. Which end you’d call the head. The water’s already doing enough to confuse the evidence.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean forward, squinting. "It's...too symmetrical. Like a person laid out straight, but the shoulders are wrong." I point a little. "That shouldn't bend like that."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway followed the line of Pike’s finger without lowering the lamp. The shoulders did look too even—two blunt rises at the same angle, as if they’d been set there deliberately. One bent inward beneath the surface. The other did not.

“Good. Don’t go nearer.” She shifted the lamp a fraction, watching the light slide over the water. “Could be the arms are folded under it. Could be the shoulders aren’t shoulders.”

She let the beam settle on the nearer bend. “Does it move when the water moves?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp trained on the shape.

“It might have been,” she said. “From here, I couldn’t call it one. The proportions are close enough to make the question sensible. The shoulders aren’t.”

She watched the water around the nearer bend. “And ‘recently’ is harder to judge while it’s submerged. Look for clothing, hair, skin—anything that belongs to a person and not just a shape that’s learned to imitate one.” A pause. “Don’t lean farther over. The cellar’s already given us one surprise.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold my breath, trying to see past the surface. "There's...a patch. Darker than the rest. Like wet cloth." I look at Halloway. "Should we get something to pull it closer?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp on the dark patch. “A pole with a hook, yes. Not a rope around it, and nobody gets in the water.”

She glanced along the cellar wall for anything long enough to reach. “We’ll catch the cloth and draw it only far enough to see what’s attached. If it pulls back, or the water moves against us, we let go. I’m fond of evidence. Less fond of being dragged under by it.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s jaw tightened when Pike entered the water. “Hold there. Don’t come any farther.”

She found an iron rake against the cellar wall and tested its length before lowering the hooked end toward the dark patch. The cloth caught. She drew it in by inches, careful not to put her weight over the water.

The shape rolled onto its side. A sleeve surfaced, then a pale hand, the fingers swollen and curled. Beneath the wet coat, both arms had been forced behind the body and folded at the shoulders. The joints sat at angles a living person could not manage.

“Plainly?” Halloway said. “It was a person. Someone put both arms out of place and left it in the water.” She kept the rake taut, watching for movement. “I can’t tell you whether that killed it. Not from here.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the bent arms, my stomach turning. "Who could bend them like that?" I ask, voice tight. "Not a person. Not a normal one."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the rake hooked in the sleeve and watched the hand for any change.

“Leverage,” she said. “A bar, a rope, enough time. People have managed worse with less.” Her gaze stayed on the shoulders. “That doesn’t tell us who did it, or whether the thing that did it was human.”

She eased the body another inch, then stopped. “We don’t settle that question by putting ourselves in the water.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the rake hooked in the sleeve and angled the lamp across the exposed shoulder. She did not draw the body any farther.

“From what I can see, both arms were forced behind him. The shoulders are displaced; the left side sits lower, and the right is turned inward. The coat’s twisted tight across his back. I can’t see through the skin, and I won’t pretend I can tell you what tore underneath without examining him.”

The pale hand remained still at the surface. Halloway watched it as she spoke.

“I see no missing limb, no obvious bite, nothing that tells me it took anything. I can’t tell how far the damage went, or whether it killed him. Water and clothing hide too much.” Her mouth tightened. “If you meet something that can do this, don’t let it get hold of your arms. That’s the useful part. The rest is a postmortem, and we’re not conducting one in four feet of cellar water.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my knuckles white where I'm holding the lamp. "I can't just leave him here like this," I say, looking at the pale hand. "We should pull him out. For the record."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked from the hand to the waterline. “For the record, we document him where he is first. Position, clothing, visible injuries, anything around him. Moving him will disturb the scene, and the water may have concealed what put him there.”

She eased the rake’s hook free of the sleeve without letting the body roll. “Then we get him out with a line and two people on dry ground. No one wades deeper, and no one grabs him by the arms. If there’s something in this cellar, I’d rather not give it a second chance at the same joints.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway cut the coat along its side seam, keeping the blade clear of the skin. The fabric parted reluctantly, heavy with water.

“Clothing first,” she said. “I’m not opening the body in a flooded cellar.”

Beneath it, the back was pale and water-swollen. Dark bruising spread over both shoulder blades, broader on the right, with smaller blue-black marks along the ribs. The skin was unbroken where she could see it. The arms remained trapped behind him at the unnatural angles; the coat had concealed how tightly they were pinned.

“The damage I can confirm is to the shoulders and whatever structures hold those joints in place. The bruising says force. It doesn’t tell me whether tendons tore, bones broke, or how far the injury extends. I can’t see that without examination on dry ground.”

A sour, stagnant smell rose from the disturbed water, with a faint organic sweetness beneath it. Halloway’s expression did not change.

“That’s cellar water and a body that’s been submerged. I can’t separate the smells well enough to tell you how long he’s been here.” She stopped cutting and studied the exposed skin. “No visible bite marks. No missing flesh. No sign, so far, that anything fed on him. We don’t know what happened under the skin, and we don’t know whether the arms killed him.”

She lowered the knife but kept the lamp trained on the body. “That’s the honest record. Anything more would be guesswork dressed up as confidence.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, the smell getting to me now. "So we still don't know if whatever did this was *trying* to get inside him or just...wanted him broken." I look away from the bruises finally. "Do you think he was alive when it put him in the water?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp on the bruising. “I can’t tell from what’s exposed. The injuries could have been made before death or after it. Water can hide signs of breathing, and I haven’t examined his lungs or airways.”

She glanced toward the still surface. “If he was alive when he went in, drowning may have killed him. If he wasn’t, the water may only have finished the work of concealing when.” Her mouth tightened. “We’ll know more on dry ground, if the evidence hasn’t washed away.”

She set the knife aside. “So we record both possibilities. We don’t choose the one that makes the culprit easier to understand.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the body, then at Pike. “I’ll finish the field examination,” she said. “I won’t cut into him here. We’d contaminate what’s left of the evidence, and the cellar water is not a sterile instrument.”

She returned to the torn coat. With the blade, she opened the remaining seam a little at a time, keeping its edge turned away from the skin. The soaked fabric sagged apart. Beneath it, the bruising continued across the back in irregular dark bands, strongest over the shoulder blades and fading along the ribs. There were no open wounds in the areas she could see. No punctures. No torn flesh.

Halloway paused at the right shoulder and adjusted the lamp’s angle with a small turn of the rake. The joint sat lower than the left, and the upper arm turned inward beneath the body. The skin there was stretched and discolored, but the water and position concealed the joint itself.

“Visible findings,” she said, as if dictating to a recorder. “Bruising over both shoulder blades, greater on the right. Right shoulder displaced or severely misaligned. Left shoulder also abnormal. Arms remain behind the back. No visible bite marks. No visible loss of tissue.”

She checked the wrists and hands without pulling at them. The fingers were swollen, pale, and curled. The cuffs covered most of the wrists; she cut them open rather than tugging the sleeves. Beneath each cuff, the skin showed a narrow red-brown band. Halloway studied the marks, then looked at the waterlogged cloth.

“Could be pressure from the sleeves,” she said. “Could be restraint. I can’t distinguish that here.” She lowered the knife. “And I can’t tell whether the shoulders were dislocated before death, after death, or both. That requires a proper examination.”

The cellar water shifted against the body and lapped over one hand. Halloway held still until the ripples passed. Nothing beneath the surface moved against them.

She leaned close enough to inspect the exposed neck and jaw, but did not turn the head. There was no obvious wound from that angle. The face remained mostly submerged. She did not try to raise it.

“No reliable time of death,” she said. “No reliable cause of death. We have a body submerged in stagnant water, with severe shoulder injuries and bruising. We have no proof he was alive when he entered it, and no proof he was dead.”

Halloway eased the knife shut and set it beyond the waterline. “That’s the examination I can finish without making the scene worse.” Her voice stayed level. “The rest needs dry ground, clean light, and someone whose job permits them to be wrong in a room with a sink.”

She kept watch on the body another few seconds, then looked toward the cellar entrance. “We’ll mark its position, get help, and recover it with a line. No one pulls on the arms. No one enters the water again.” A pause. “If it starts moving, we leave the room. The record can survive our absence.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Alright," I say, standing up. My legs feel shaky. "Let's get the line."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway nodded once. She gathered the cut coat away from the body, careful not to let it drag through more water, and set it on the cellar steps.

“Good. Keep to the steps. If your legs are shaking, let them shake somewhere dry.”

She took a coil of line from her kit and checked it for frays, running it through her gloved hands. Then she tied one end around the iron post at the foot of the stairs and tested the knot with a hard pull.

“We’ll make a loop under the torso, not around the neck or arms. I’ll guide it with the rake. You keep the lamp on the body and tell me if the water moves anywhere it shouldn’t.”

Halloway fed the loose end of the line toward the corpse, keeping her weight back from the edge. The loop touched the water and sank. She eased it along the body, the line brushing beneath the coat.

“Slowly,” she said, watching the dark surface. “If it catches on something, don’t haul. We stop and see what it’s caught on. I’d rather lose ten minutes than discover the cellar has a second occupant.”

The loop slid beneath the body’s middle. Halloway drew both ends through and secured them with a bowline, then tugged lightly to check the hold. The torso shifted a few inches. The arms remained folded behind it.

She stopped at once and watched for a response. The water settled. Nothing else moved.

“Secure enough to recover,” she said. “Not enough to drag it across the floor. We lift on the line and guide it to the steps. No one takes hold of the shoulders.”

Halloway looked toward Pike, then back to the body. “When I say pull, take the line steadily. If the body catches or the rope tightens suddenly, stop. We don’t win anything by being brave at a knot.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I grab the line, my hands still unsteady. "Alright," I say, bracing myself against the post. "On your count."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway planted one boot on the lowest dry step and wrapped the line once around her gloved palm—not enough to trap her hand if it slipped. With the other, she held the rake ready to keep the body from turning.

“Keep the pull low and steady,” she said. “Don’t jerk it. I’ll guide the shoulders clear of the step.”

She watched the loop beneath the torso, then the dark water around the body. Nothing disturbed the surface.

“On three. One… two… three.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean into the pull, the weight heavier than I expected. The line groans taut, and the body begins to slide through the water towards us.

rung_labels.evidence: I can’t see through the skin
