dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Good,” Halloway said. “Wrong was worth noticing. Now tell me where.”

She angled the lamp. The shape at the far wall had a head above the waterline, or something arranged to resemble one. Below it, two narrow ridges broke the surface. They were too far apart to be shoulders.

“Don’t step forward. The water hides the rest of it, and four feet is plenty of room for bad news.” She held the light steady. “Look at those ridges. If those are arms, where ought the elbows to be?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, trying to focus past the wrongness. "They're too straight, aren't they? Elbows would... bend. These don't."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp on the ridges. “And they run all the way to the wall. Arms don’t usually do that unless the owner’s having a very bad day.”

She lowered the light an inch. A thin line of water moved between the ridges, though nothing else did.

“Could be spines. Could be a second body under the surface. Either way, it’s still moving water.” She eased one hand toward the knife at her belt. “Tell me what you see at the wall. Don’t look at the head.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp on the far wall. “I couldn’t tell you yet. A head above water isn’t proof of a person, and I won’t call it remains while the water’s moving.”

The light caught a pale hand against the mortar. Its fingers were splayed, but no arm led back from the wrist. One of the ridges ran past it and disappeared into a crack between the stones.

“That hand may have belonged to someone recently,” she said. “The rest of the arrangement didn’t.” She shifted the lamp just enough to keep the hand and the crack in view. “Look there. Is the ridge coming out of the wall, or going into it?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean closer, squinting. "It's... going in. Like something grew out of the wall and wrapped around that wrist."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Into the wall, yes,” Halloway said. “Grew out of it, no. Don’t give it a history we haven’t earned.”

She raised the lamp. The ridge narrowed where it entered the mortar. Around the trapped wrist, the skin had puckered into a tight ring; above it, the fingers were still pale and intact.

“That hand was attached recently. Whether it still is, I can’t see.” She drew her knife but kept her feet planted. “The crack’s wider than it looked. If the ridge can pass through, something on the other side may be pulling it.”

A faint tap came from behind the wall.

“Excellent,” she said. “The cellar has a cellar.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Stop there,” Halloway said. “Closer won’t make it clearer. It’ll only put you within reach.”

She studied the wrist in the lamplight. “Plainly: something caught a person by the hand and pulled the wrist against that crack. The skin’s compressed where the ridge crosses it. I can’t see whether the arm is still attached, or whether the shape above the water belongs to the same person.”

The tap came again. This time the ridge tightened. The fingers flattened against the stone.

“That part I can tell you,” Halloway said. “Whatever holds the hand is still pulling.”

She set the edge of her knife against the ridge, well short of the wrist. “Keep the light on the crack. If the head turns, tell me. I’d hate to be rude and miss an introduction.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod and hold the lamp steady, my hand shaking a little. "It's not turning," I whisper. "But the head... it's leaning forward now."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Forward how far?” Halloway asked. She did not look away from the ridge. “No—keep the light where it is. I can see enough.”

The ridge tightened beneath her knife. At the far end of the cellar, the head dipped until its chin touched the water. A small wave spread from it, moving against the ripples at the wall.

“That isn’t being pulled by the wrist,” she said. “It’s moving on its own.”

She lifted the knife clear. Cutting the ridge now might free the hand, or it might give whatever waited behind the stones one less thing to hold. Neither was a useful experiment with Pike within reach.

“Back toward the stairs. Slowly. Leave the lamp on the crack.” Halloway moved beside Pike, watching the head. “If it follows us, we learn something. If it doesn’t, we still get out of this bloody water.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway held her position. “Then learn the useful detail: I don’t know what it took.”

She kept the lamp’s edge on the wrist and the crack. “One ridge crossed the outside of the wrist. The skin was puckered beneath it, not split. I saw nothing moving under the skin. I couldn’t see past the waterline, so I couldn’t tell you whether the arm was attached, how far the thing reached, or whether that head belonged to the person with the hand.”

The head lifted an inch. Water ran from its chin.

“What I did see was the ridge tighten when something tapped behind the wall. The fingers pressed flat. Then the head moved without the ridge pulling it. Those may be two parts of one creature, or two creatures. Assuming either would be a fine way to die.”

Halloway eased a step toward the stairs, knife ready. “If you meet another one, watch the wall as well as the shape in front of you. Don’t put your hand near a crack. And don’t cut anything holding a victim until you know what happens when it lets go.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take another step back, my eyes still locked on the head. "But you'd still try to cut them loose, wouldn't you?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“I’d try to get them out,” Halloway said. “That’s not the same as cutting the first thing I can reach.”

She backed toward the stairs, keeping the knife low. “If there’s a person attached to that hand, cutting the ridge might free them. It might also let whatever’s behind the wall pull them through. I’d want to see what holds the rest of them first.”

The head lifted another inch. Its mouth stayed below the water.

“And I’d rather make that decision from the stairs,” she said. “The water’s giving it too many places to hide.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set the knife against the ridge and drew it across, shallowly. The outer surface parted. Beneath it lay pale fibres packed around a darker cord; no blood came from the cut.

“Outside the wrist,” she said. “Not under the skin. It smells of wet mortar and old pond water. I can’t tell how far it goes beyond that crack.”

The cord drew tight. The trapped fingers curled, and a tap sounded from behind the stones. Halloway stopped cutting. At the far end of the cellar, the head rose clear of the water to the mouth. It was open.

“The cut made it pull,” she said. “The head rose with it. That’s what happened; I won’t guess whether they’re joined.”

She slipped the knife from the ridge without cutting deeper. “I haven’t freed the hand. I haven’t seen an arm. That is everything I know.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I see the open mouth. "It's not breathing," I say, my voice low. "But the head's keeping time with the pulls."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Keeping time, yes. Not breathing, I couldn’t swear to.” Halloway watched the open mouth through one more tap behind the wall. The ridge tightened; the head rose a fraction. When the ridge slackened, the head settled.

“That’s three pulls and three movements. Good thing to remember.” She withdrew the knife and held its cut edge toward the light. Pale fibres clung to it, with no blood. “Bad thing to mistake for proof they’re one body.”

She took another step toward the stairs. “We know it responds to a cut by pulling harder. We don’t know what happens if I finish. So we get above the water, find the other side of that wall, and look before we cut again.”

The mouth remained open. Halloway kept her knife ready. “If it starts keeping a different time, tell me.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked from the steps to the hand against the far wall. “I will. But I’m finishing the thing I can see, not cutting through a wrist and hoping for the best.”

She went back into the water. The lamp from the steps gave her enough light to find the shallow cut she had made in the ridge. The pale fibres had drawn together around it. The darker cord beneath them was still taut.

The head rose when she touched the ridge. Its mouth opened wider. She stopped with the knife poised and watched the hand. The fingers were curled now, but the wrist had not shifted against the stone.

“Still held at the crack,” she said. “If it moves when I cut, I leave the hand alone.”

She drove the knife through the ridge on the wall side of the wrist. The fibres parted first. The cord resisted, then gave with a hard snap. The severed length whipped across her sleeve. She pulled her arm clear.

The hand stayed against the mortar. The cut end leading into the wall slid through the crack and vanished.

At the far end, the head dropped beneath the surface. Water pushed outward in a broad swell.

Halloway backed a pace. “That didn’t finish it.”

A pale shape came up under the water between her and the far wall. She could make out the head at its front and the two ridges running back from it. Where they met was submerged. She waited until the head broke the surface, then put her knife into the joint beneath its jaw. It struck something firm. The mouth shut on the blade’s guard.

“That,” she said, bracing her wrist, “is a poor place for teeth.”

She forced the knife sideways. The mouth tore open at one corner. The ridges beat against the water, sending spray up the wall. Halloway pulled the blade free and struck again, lower, where the ridges joined the neck. Once. Twice. On the second cut, the darker cord showed through.

The tapping behind the wall stopped.

Halloway kept her distance while the water settled. The head floated against the stones, mouth open. Neither ridge moved. She watched through several breaths of her own before lowering the knife.

“The part in the water has stopped,” she said. “I won’t call the part behind the wall dead. And that hand is still there.”

She turned the blade toward the lamplight to check its edge. “We finish the rest when we can see it.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the hand, still pinned to the wall. "It'll dry out," I say, my voice flat. "It'll start to smell different than the rest."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“Yes,” Halloway said. “If we leave it here, it’ll dry at the waterline first. The submerged part will rot. You’ll smell the change before you see much of it.”

She studied the wrist from where she stood. The skin was still drawn tight beneath the severed ridge. She did not touch it.

“But smell won’t tell us whose hand it was, or what’s holding it now. We need the other side of that wall open.” She glanced at the crack, then at the head floating against the stones. “And we need to keep this cellar shut until we’ve done it. That thing stopped moving. I haven’t established that it was alone.”

Halloway backed toward the stairs, knife held clear of the water. “We’ll bring a hook down for the head. We won’t use a hand to find out whether its mouth still works.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I set the lamp down on the step and stand up, my legs feeling shaky. "What if it's waiting for us to get close again? It left the hand there like a... like a sign."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“It might be waiting,” Halloway said. “The hand’s visible from the stairs, and we’ve already gone back for it once. That’s reason enough not to do it again.”

She reached the bottom step and stopped, watching the crack. No ridge emerged. The hand remained pressed to the mortar.

“A sign would mean it wanted to tell us something. A trap only needs us to come close.” She wiped the knife on her sleeve. “We’ll treat it as the latter until we open the other side of the wall.”

She climbed out of the water and picked up the lamp. “First we shut this door. Then we find out what room shares that wall. If it has another way into the house, I’d prefer to learn that before it introduces itself.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the hand for another second. "It's not rotting yet," I say, like that matters. Then I turn and follow her up the steps, my wet clothes clinging and heavy. "I'll watch the door while you find the other side."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Its fingers were splayed, but no arm led back from the wrist.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The skin’s compressed where the ridge crosses it.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: I don’t know what it took.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: She slipped the knife from the ridge without cutting deeper.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The mouth tore open at one corner.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway made a small sound that might have been approval. "Good. 'Something wrong' is where it starts. Now make it specific. Wrong how?"

She didn't wait long for an answer. She rarely did the first time. She lifted the lamp higher, and the light slid across the black water and caught on the thing slumped against the far wall.

"Count the joints," she said. "Left arm. Shoulder, elbow, wrist. Then there's a fourth bend, halfway down the forearm, going the wrong way. That's not a break. A break swells. That one's clean, and the skin's folded over it like it grew there." She tipped the light a fraction. "Now the head. It's sitting too low. There's no neck to speak of, just the jaw resting on the collarbone. And see the waterline on the chest? It's not breathing, but the water's still moving against it. Small ripples, coming *out*."

She was quiet a moment. The drip from the ceiling beams filled the silence.

"So either it's got something living inside it," Halloway said, "or it's not as dead as I'd like and it's being patient about it. Neither option is the one where we walk over and give it a poke."

She shifted her weight. The water sloshed around her thighs, cold enough that she'd stopped feeling her feet a while ago. Behind her the cellar steps were a pale smudge in the dark. She'd counted them on the way down: eleven. She always counted the way out.

"Here's the other thing," she went on, in the same even voice. "It stopped moving about a minute ago. I didn't hit it. You didn't hit it. Nothing in here hit it." The lamp didn't waver. "Things don't just stop, Pike. They die, or they finish what they were doing, or they wait. I want you to tell me which one you think this is. And while you're thinking about it, keep an eye on the water between us and it. Tell me if it goes still when it shouldn't."

A beat.

"And if it does," she added, "you're going up those stairs first. That isn't chivalry. You're faster, and I'm heavier to drag."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on the water, watching the ripples. "It stopped when we came in. Like it heard us." My voice sounds thin in the damp dark. "I think it's waiting."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer straight away. She was watching the ripples too, and she'd started counting them without meaning to, the way she counted stairs.

"Yes," she said at last. "I think so too. I'd have liked you to be wrong."

She didn't lower the lamp. Lowering the lamp would be a change, and changes were information, and she didn't want to give the thing in the corner any more information than it already had.

"Here's what bothers me about waiting," she said, quiet and level. "Things that wait have a reason. They're hurt and hoping we'll leave. Or they're hungry and hoping we won't. Or," and she let the pause sit, "they're waiting for something else to arrive first." Her eyes went, briefly, to the dark water on either side of them. Then they came back. "Ripples are coming out of its chest in pulses. Roughly every four seconds. That's slower than a heartbeat and faster than breathing. I don't know what keeps that rhythm. I've been doing this thirty years, and I don't know, and I'd like you to remember that the next time someone in a tavern tells you they've seen everything."

The drip from the beams landed somewhere to her left. She didn't look.

"Four seconds," she murmured. "Three. Two." A ripple slid out across the black surface, lamplight trembling on it. She followed it with her eyes as it came toward them. It thinned and flattened, and it did not quite reach her.

"Right," Halloway said. "That one stopped short. About a yard from my knees. Water doesn't do that on its own, Pike. Something under the surface broke it up."

She breathed out slowly through her nose, and her voice turned almost conversational, the way it always did when things got bad.

"So. It's not the only thing in here, and the one in the corner is the one we're meant to be looking at. I've been properly insulted. Somebody thinks I'm an amateur."

Her free hand drifted down to her belt, to the short, heavy knife she kept for close work. She didn't draw it. She just rested her fingers on the grip.

"Don't move your feet yet. Movement travels in water. Here's what I need from you." The lamp stayed fixed on the slumped shape against the wall, steady as a nail. "I'm going to keep the light on the one in front. I want you to look at the water *behind* us, between us and the steps. Don't turn your whole body. Just your head, slowly. Tell me if there's anything there that doesn't match the ripples from the drip."

A beat. The corner thing's chest pulsed. Four seconds.

"And Pike," she said, without any change in tone, "if you see something, don't shout. Just say the word 'stairs,' and say it like you're telling me the time."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer at once. She took the question seriously, because it was a serious question, and because Pike deserved better than a lie told to keep him steady.

"Yes," she said. "I think so."

The lamp moved a fraction, no more than a finger's width, and settled on the thing's lower half where it disappeared into the water.

"There's a boot on the right foot. Hobnailed, good leather, resoled at least once. Someone who walked for a living. The left foot's gone, or it's under the surface where I can't see it. There's cloth at the waist. Wool, dark, sodden through. It's been torn open down the front, not cut. Pulled apart from the inside." She let that sit, then went on in the same flat, careful voice. "Hair on the scalp, what there is. Grey at the temples. The skin's that waxy colour you get in cold water, but it hasn't started to bloat. In water this cold, that gives you days, not weeks. Three, maybe four."

The chest pulsed. Four seconds. Another ripple slid out across the black and died a yard short of them, as the last one had.

"So it was a man," Halloway said. "Middle-aged, on his feet a lot, and dead less than a week. Whatever did the business with the arm and the neck came afterward. Or during, and I'd rather not think about during." Her mouth twitched, not quite a smile. "He's got a wedding ring on, if that's what you're really asking. Left hand, the bad arm. Someone's probably wondering where he's got to. We'll tell them, if we're the sort of people who get out of cellars."

She breathed out.

"Here's the thing, Pike, and I'm not saying it to be hard." Her eyes never left the corner. "Whatever's wearing him now doesn't care who he was. If you're thinking about his wife while you're standing in the water, you're not thinking about what's in the water, and that's how people end up as the next thing in the corner with somebody's lamp on them. You can grieve him on the stairs. I'll help. I'm good at it by now."

The drip landed to her left again. The pulse came. Four seconds.

Then the next one came in three.

Halloway didn't move, but her fingers tightened on the knife grip until the knuckles showed pale in the lamplight.

"That was quicker," she said softly. "It noticed we've stopped being interesting and started talking." A pause. "You still haven't looked behind us. Do it now, please. Slowly. And remember the word."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I tilt my head just enough to glance toward the stairs. My throat feels tight. "Stairs," I say, flat as I can. "There's...something hanging off the third step. Like wet yarn, but it's moving."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good," Halloway said, in exactly the tone of someone told it was half past four. "Well done."

She did not turn. The lamp stayed on the corner, and the corner stayed still. The pulse came again. Three seconds.

"Third from the bottom or third from the top?" she asked. "Don't point. Just tell me. It matters. One's in the water with us and one isn't."

She tilted her own head, a fraction, and looked down at the water beside her left thigh instead of behind her. It took her a moment to find it, because it was the same colour as the dark. Then the lamplight caught it: a single pale strand lying just under the surface, thinner than a bootlace, running dead straight from somewhere behind her toward the corner. It rose and settled with the pulse. Three seconds.

"Ah," Halloway said. "There's our ripple-breaker."

She let her eyes travel along it. A yard to her right there was another, and past that, a third. They weren't floating. They were taut, strung under the surface like washing lines, and every one of them ran to the thing slumped against the wall.

"Right. Here's what we're standing in, Pike, and I want you to hear it without doing anything clever. There are strands under the water. Fine ones, pale, pulled tight. They run from the corner out past us, and I'd bet my good boots they run up to your wet yarn on the step. That's why the ripples die short. They're hitting the lines." A breath. "The body isn't the animal. It's the middle of the web. The poor sod's been hollowed out and strung up so it's got somewhere to sit and feel for flies."

The pulse came. Three seconds.

"And we walked in down the only way out," she added, "which is the part where I'm insulted again, because I counted those steps and never once looked at them."

Her fingers came off the knife. She had decided against it. Cutting a line would be as good as ringing a bell.

"We're not touched yet. I'd know. You'd know. So this is what we do." Her voice stayed low and even, the way you'd talk a horse through a narrow gate. "I'm going to bring the lamp round, slowly, and put it on the stairs. The moment I do, the one in the corner's in the dark, and I'm trusting the web to tell it we're still standing here. Meanwhile you look at the water between you and the steps and find me a path. Look for the lines. Anywhere they're not, that's where your feet go. Step high, set down slow, no splashing. You go first. I'll be right behind you, stepping where you stepped."

She shifted her grip on the lamp handle. Cold had got into her fingers and she flexed them once, carefully, above the water.

"When you get to the steps, whatever's hanging off that third one, you do not brush it. You don't climb past it. You tell me what it's doing and we deal with it together." A pause, and a dry edge crept in. "If it turns out to be yarn, I'll knit you a scarf out of it for the ride home."

The chest in the corner pulsed.

Two seconds.

"Third from the top or the bottom, Pike," Halloway said quietly. "Then tell me when you're ready for the light."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The water moved when Pike did. Halloway felt it before she saw it: a slow swell against her thighs, then the lamplight wobbling on the surface as the wake rolled past her toward the corner.

She didn't flinch. She watched the pale line beside her left leg. It lifted with the swell, trembled, and settled.

The pulse in the corner didn't come.

Two seconds went by. Four. Six. Nothing.

"Well," Halloway said, very softly. "You've either gone clean between the lines, or you've told it exactly where you're standing and it's having a think about that." She finally let her eyes flick sideways to him, to the second lamp and the steady hand holding it. "I'd have liked to be asked first. But the light's good. Keep it there, and keep your feet where they are. Don't shuffle. Don't shift your weight."

She looked back at the corner. With two lamps on it the thing was worse. Every fold and seam showed.

"Plainly, then."

She took a breath and let it out through her nose.

"Something got into him while he was alive. I can't tell you how yet. The mouth, most likely. The jaw's hanging open further than a jaw should, and the corners of it are split back toward the ears. Split, not cut. Stretched past what the skin would take." Her voice didn't change. It was the voice she used for weather, and for invoices. "Once it was in, it ate. Not the way a dog eats. From the middle outward, like a grub in an apple. It kept the skin because it needed the skin. That's why he hasn't bloated. There's nothing left in him to rot and swell."

The lamplight moved over the ruined forearm.

"That fourth joint is where it went through the bone. Both bones in the forearm, snapped and pulled apart. Then the skin healed over the gap, or was made to. I don't think it was trying to hurt him by then. I think it was making room. Something that big has to come out somewhere, and it prefers to use the arms." She tipped her chin a fraction. "The neck is the spine. It's gone, or most of it. Pulled down into the chest, so the head just rests on whatever's holding it up. The front of the shirt is torn outward because that's the way it was going when it finished. That's where the lines start. Look at the ribs, just under the waterline. You'll see them coming out between the bones like threads out of a split seam."

She paused. The drip from the beams landed, loud in the silence.

"That's the plain version. It hollowed him out, moved in, and strung him up for a front door." Her mouth made its not-quite-smile. "There's a less plain version with more words in it. You can have that one on the stairs if you still want it."

The corner stayed dark and still. No pulse at all now.

That was worse, and she didn't pretend otherwise.

"It's stopped," Halloway said. "Which means it isn't feeling for us anymore. It's listening." Her fingers found the knife grip again, and this time they stayed there. "You still haven't told me third from the top or third from the bottom, Pike. I need that now. And I need you to look down at the water round your own legs and tell me, honestly, whether any of those lines are touching you. Don't guess. Look."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Third from the bottom," I whisper. I don't look away from the corner, from the stillness. "And there's one. Against my shin. It wasn't there before."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look at his shin. She looked at the water beside it, where the lamplight caught the line as it rose from the dark and bent, very slightly, around the shape of his leg.

It was bending. It hadn't been a moment ago.

"Right," she said. "Third from the bottom. That's the waterline, near enough, so whatever's on that step has its feet in the water with us. And now you've got a line leaning on you." She said it the way she might have told him he had mud on his sleeve. "Leaning isn't holding. Not yet. Is it wrapped round you, or only lying against you? Don't reach down. Just feel for it. Wrapped is tight all the way round. Lying is one side only."

The corner stayed dark and still. No pulse. The drip landed to her left, and she felt the line by her own thigh tick faintly in answer, the way a fishing line ticks when something noses the bait.

"It's warm-seeking, I think," Halloway went on, quiet and fast now, without hurrying the words. "It went still to listen, and it heard you move, and it sent a line to see what you were. It's tasting you. So here's what we're going to do, and you are not going to argue, because arguing makes noise."

She shifted the knife in its sheath. She didn't draw it. She took her left hand off the grip, flexed the cold out of her fingers once, and lowered it slowly toward the pale line beside her thigh.

"I'm going to give it something more interesting to think about," she said. "Bigger. Heavier. Warmer, God help me, for all I can't feel my feet." Her mouth made its not-quite-smile. "Better meat, from where it's sitting. It can't know I'm fifty and mostly gristle."

Her hand hovered an inch above the surface.

"When I take hold of this, every line in here is going to sing, and whatever's at the other end of them is going to turn its head my way. That's your moment. You don't pull your leg free. Pulling tells it you're prey. You let your knee go soft and you slide your leg down and back, out from under the line, the way you'd take your foot out of a sleeping dog's bed. Then you step for the stairs. Left of centre. The lines are thinner on the left; I've been counting them." A breath. "Don't touch whatever's on that third step. Stop on the second and tell me what it does."

She looked at him then, properly, for the first time since they'd come down. Just for a second.

"You'll be fine," she said. "I've done this before."

She hadn't. Not this. But she'd said it before, and it had been true often enough to be worth saying.

Then she looked back at the corner, put her hand into the black water, and closed it around the line.

It was cold and smooth and much stronger than it looked, like gut string, and the moment her fingers tightened it went taut as wire. She felt the whole web answer through it, a hum that ran up her arm and into her teeth.

In the corner, under two lamps, the dead man's head lifted off his collarbone.

It came up slowly, with nothing holding it but whatever was inside. The split jaw hung open. It turned, a quarter inch at a time, until the ruined face was looking straight at Halloway.

"There you are," she said pleasantly. "Hello."

The line in her fist began to pull.

"Now, Pike," Halloway said, without taking her eyes off it. "Knee soft. Down and back. Tell me the moment you're clear."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
For one moment Halloway was genuinely lost for words. It didn't happen often, and it annoyed her.

"*Now?*" she said.

The line pulled. Her boots slid an inch on the silt, and she set her weight back against it the way she'd once held a mule on a riverbank. The cold string bit into her palm. The dead man's face stayed fixed on her, split jaw hanging.

"All right," she said. "All right. You're not wrong. If you meet another you'll want it, and I might not be there to give it you." She breathed in through her teeth. "So here's the bargain. I talk, you move. Every word out of me from here on is one you're buying with a step. Stand there listening and I'll stop mid-sentence out of spite. Understood? Good."

She didn't wait for an answer. She rarely did.

"Under the skin." The lamplight was steadier than her grip, and she used it. "Look in the mouth. Past the teeth, where the throat should be. See that pale ridge? Ringed, like a finger joint, over and over. That's the body of it. It fills the chest cavity the way your hand fills a glove. It's using his ribs for a frame. The ribs aren't holding him up anymore; they're holding *it* in. That's why the chest pulses. Not lungs. It's the thing flexing against the bones, pumping water through itself. It breathes water, Pike. Remember that. Smoke won't touch it and drowning's no threat."

The line jerked. Her arm went out straight, and she leaned back hard, heels digging in.

"What it took." Her voice came a little shorter now, but it stayed level. "Everything soft. Heart, lungs, gut, the lot, eaten from the centre outward. Then the muscle, from the inside of the skin. That's why the skin's still whole except where it came through. Then the marrow. It went up the long bones like a worm up a straw; that's what the fourth joint is. It hollowed the forearm, got too fat for the tube, and broke out sideways. The spine went the same way. Once the marrow's gone the vertebrae are just beads on a string, and it pulled the string down into the chest to make room. That's your missing neck."

The dead man's head tilted, the way a dog's does at a strange noise. The eyes had been clouded grey a moment ago. They weren't grey now. Behind the milk of them something shifted, pale and slow.

"How far it got," Halloway said, and for the first time a thread of real dislike showed in her voice. "All the way up. Look at the eyes. It's in the skull. It'll have eaten the brain last, because that's the sweetest, and then it'll have kept the eyes." She swallowed. "Not to see with. I'd guess it's blind. It keeps them because they're wet and they catch light, and the next poor bastard who comes down those stairs with a lamp sees a face looking back at him and walks closer to check if it's alive. It's bait. The whole man is bait. It's not wearing him. It's *fishing* with him."

The line hauled. She went forward a full step, water surging up to her waist, and swore once, precisely and without heat.

"The lesson," she said through her teeth, "if you're still listening, and you'd better be walking while you do it. A body that doesn't bloat in cold water is a body that's got nothing left inside to bloat. Wrong joints mean it's been hollowed. Face turned your way means you've already been noticed. Any one of those, and you don't go closer. You go *out*, and you come back in daylight with lamp oil and a long hook and someone you trust holding the rope."

Behind her, low down by the steps, she heard a soft wet sound. Something heavy was shifting its weight on stone.

Halloway did not turn. She kept the dead man's borrowed eyes on her, and the line kept pulling, and her hand was starting to go numb around it.

"That's all of it," she said. "That's the long version. I hope it was worth what it cost." A breath. "Pike. Your wet yarn's just moved. I can hear it. Tell me where you are, and tell me what it's doing."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I ease my leg out slow, my boot sliding free of the line. It drops back into the water without a sound. I'm on the second step now. My voice comes out tight. "It's...breathing, Halloway. It's got a mouth, or a gill, something slick opening and closing on the stone."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Breathing," Halloway repeated, the way she might have repeated a price she didn't care for.

She thought about it for the length of one hard pull on the line. Her boots skidded again. The water was at her ribs now, and the dead man's head had tilted the other way, as if the thing inside was trying to work out why the warm heavy one wasn't coming closer faster.

"Right. Listen, because this is good news dressed up as bad." Her voice stayed low and very even. "I told you they breathe water. That one's sitting out of it. If it's working a gill on dry stone, it's gasping. It's a fish on a jetty, Pike. It came up to hold the door, and it's been holding its breath to do it, and it's not enjoying itself." Her mouth made the not-quite-smile. "Which makes two of us."

The line hauled. She let it take her half a step, deliberately, and didn't fight it this time. Fighting was costing her hands, and she needed her hands.

"Three questions. Short answers. Is the lines' end in it? Pale strings running from it into the water. Yes or no. How big is it? Compare it to something. A cat, a dog, a sack of grain. And is it between you and the top of the stairs, or off to one side where you could get past without brushing it?"

The dead man's jaw worked. Nothing came out of it but water, a thin black trickle over the split lip, but it moved as though it wanted to speak. Halloway found she'd rather it didn't.

"While you're answering," she went on, "get the lamp in your off hand and find the filler cap with your thumb. Don't open it yet. That's oil in there, and oil sits on a wet thing the way it sits on a wet road. It won't be able to shake it off, and it can't duck under the water to put it out without leaving the step. If it leaves the step, the door's open." She took a breath. "I'd rather you didn't set fire to it with me still down here, mind. It's a small cellar and I'm fond of my eyebrows."

Her numb fingers shifted on the line. She'd made her decision. She didn't much like it, but she'd made worse in better company.

"Here's my part. I'm going to let go. The moment I do, the one in the corner loses its grip on me, and it'll want to know where I've gone. It's blind, it's got a hundred feet of string for ears, and I'll be moving. So I'll be quick about it. Eleven steps, and I'm six yards from the bottom one. I can do six yards in water in about the time it takes a man to say his prayers, if he doesn't know many."

The pull came again. Stronger. Behind the milk of the dead man's eyes, something pale turned over.

"You don't open that oil until I say. You don't throw it until I say." Her eyes stayed fixed on the corner, but her voice went to him, flat and certain as a nail going in. "Now answer me, Pike. Lines, size, and can you get past it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The knife came out of its sheath in one movement. So much for letting go. Letting go meant the line would snap back slack, and slack would tell the thing she'd gone. A cut end would at least tell it something had bitten.

She drew the blade across the string under the water. It didn't part at once. It was like sawing wet rope, and on the third stroke it went with a sound she felt more than heard, a low twang that ran out through every line in the cellar at once.

The dead man's head snapped upright.

"You're a menace, Pike," Halloway said, already moving. "You'll either make a very good hunter or a very short story."

She waded. Not fast. Fast meant splashing. She went long and low, the way you'd walk into surf, her free hand out flat above the water to feel for lines before her body found them.

"Smell," she said. "You've got it yourself if you'd breathe through your nose. Under the cellar damp, under the rot you'd expect and aren't getting. Cut grass. Cucumber. That's the water-breathers, most of them. The ones that live in wells and cisterns. If you walk into a cold room and it smells like somebody's been slicing salad, you walk back out. Remember that one. It's the only warning some of them give."

Four yards. Behind her, something in the corner made a noise like a boot pulled out of deep mud.

She didn't look. She didn't need to. The lamplight from Pike's hand threw her own shadow ahead of her across the water, and beside it, at the edge of the light, the corner's shadow was changing shape.

"Underneath," she said, and her breath was going now, but the words came out whole. "It's coming out to see me. So you get the rest of the lesson free. Look past me, not at me. At the mouth. That pale ridge I showed you. It's coming out between the teeth. Ringed, like I said, and thicker than a man's arm, and every ring's got a fringe of those threads coming off it, fine as hair. That's where the lines are grown. It spins them out of itself, the way a spider does. So cutting them doesn't hurt it. It's like cutting my hair. It'll just make more."

Three yards. Her knee found a line under the surface and she stopped dead, lifted her leg over it with a slow care that cost her, and set it down again.

"How far it got. I told you. All the way. But here's what I didn't tell you, because I hadn't seen it yet." She took another step. "It's leaving him behind. Look at the face. See how it's gone slack? The eyes have gone flat. It's not wearing him anymore. It doesn't need the bait now it's got a bite. So when you see one of these again, and the corpse suddenly goes limp and ordinary, like a sack, that doesn't mean it's died. It means the thing inside has decided you're worth coming out for."

Two yards. The water was dropping, waist to thigh, the floor rising toward the steps. She could see the bottom stair now, pale in the lamp, and the third above it.

And on the third, the thing Pike had called yarn.

It was about the size of a folded coat. A wet heap, grey-green, fringed with strands that trailed down into the water, and in the middle of it, facing her, a slit that opened and closed with a sound like someone smacking their lips.

"Ah," Halloway said. "Hello to you as well."

She stopped at the bottom step, water to her knees, knife low. Close enough now that she could see the lines running out of the heap and into the dark behind her. Taut. Humming.

"Pike." Her voice dropped back to that calm, time-of-day flatness, but there was iron under it now. "I've answered everything you've asked. Every single thing. You've answered nothing I've asked, and I'm standing two feet from a gasping fish with a friend coming up behind me. So. Is it between you and the top, or can you get past? And have you got your thumb on that cap?"

Behind her, the mud-and-boot sound came again. Closer. Then came a soft rushing, like a rope paying out fast through water.

"Short answers," Halloway said. "Now would be lovely."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: (It's on the left side. I can get past.) "Dog-sized. Lines going into it from the water, yes." My thumb's on the cap. "What do you want me to do?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good lad," Halloway said, and meant it.

She could see it herself now, from the bottom step. The heap sat hunched against the left-hand wall where the stone was wettest, its fringe spilling over the edge of the tread and down into the water. The right side of the third step was bare, wet stone. There was room for one person to pass it if they kept to the wall and didn't dawdle, perhaps a foot and a half.

"Here's what I want," she said. The flatness was back in her voice, the time-of-day voice. "You go up. Right-hand side, shoulder to the wall. Step long over the third, don't set your foot on it at all if your legs will take you. Mind the fringe. It'll reach for warmth, and you're warm, so don't give it time to find you. Keep going to the top. Don't stop halfway to see how I'm getting on. I'll be getting on badly. That's normal."

The slit on the heap opened and closed. The sound was wet and eager. Its fringe was lifting now, a few strands at a time, turning toward her like grass bending toward the wind.

"When you're at the top, turn round, open the cap, and wait. Don't throw anything until I'm past the third step. When I'm past, pour it straight down on that thing, as much as you've got, then drop the lamp on it after." A breath. "Drop it. Don't throw it. Throwing is how you miss, and missing is how you set fire to the stairs I'm standing on."

Behind her the rushing sound stopped.

That was worse than the rushing. Halloway had thirty years of knowing what stopped meant.

She didn't turn. She set her right boot on the first step, slowly, and felt the stone take her weight. Water ran off her in sheets. Her legs were so cold they felt borrowed.

"And Pike." The dry edge crept in, and she let it, because it helped. "If I don't make it past, you pour anyway. Don't wait for me. Don't come down for me. You go and find whoever that man's wife is and tell her he's dead and not to go into the cellar, and then you go to the Anchor in Tollbridge and you ask for Maud, and you tell her Halloway owes her eleven shillings and she's not getting them."

Something touched the back of her left ankle, under the water. It was light and cold and exploratory, like a fingertip.

Halloway's face didn't change.

"Go," she said. "Now. Right side. Long step."

She lifted her left foot out of the water. The touch came with it. A line had curled once around the leather of her boot, lazily, the way a cat's tail curls round a table leg.

It wasn't tight yet.

The heap on the third step opened its slit wide. Every strand of its fringe had turned toward her.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't pull her foot. She had told Pike not to, and she wasn't going to be a hypocrite in front of him on what might be her last step.

She let her left knee go soft instead. The line around her boot lay slack for a heartbeat while the thing at the other end made up its mind. She used that heartbeat to turn her ankle a quarter-turn inward and slide the heel down out of the loop, the way you'd step out of a stirrup when the horse is going over. The line tightened on nothing and snapped back into the water with a small, sulky splash.

"Hah," she said.

Then she moved.

Second step. Her legs felt like sacks of wet sand, but they worked. On the third step the heap's fringe was already lifting toward her, dozens of strands rising off the stone. They reached out and swayed, like weed in a current, except there was no current. The slit in the middle gaped. Inside it was pale pink and ridged like the roof of a mouth, and a smell came off it that was all cut cucumber and something sweeter underneath.

She didn't step on the third. She took it long, her right boot landing on the fourth and her left trailing. Three strands brushed her calf through the wool. They didn't grip. They tasted her, and she felt them decide, and she was already past.

Fifth step. Sixth. She turned on the seventh with her back against the wall and her lamp still in her fist. It was the one she'd been holding since she came down, the one she'd kept fixed on the corner like a nail.

Below her the heap had turned. It moved in a slow, humping slide, the whole wet mass dragging itself round on the step to follow the warm thing that had got away. Its fringe hung toward her, quivering.

Behind it, the water at the foot of the stairs bulged.

It came up out of the black a yard from the bottom step. First the dead man's head, lolling on nothing, the face slack as a dropped glove. Then under it, shoving it up and aside, the thing itself. It was pale as a peeled root, thick as her thigh where it came out of the ruined chest, and ringed all along its length, with every ring bristling fine threads. The front of it had no face at all. It had a blunt, rounded end that split into four as she watched, opening like fingers uncurling, and every one of the four was lined with small backward-pointing hooks.

It lifted itself onto the first step. The dead man came with it, dragged along like a coat caught on a nail.

"No," Halloway said pleasantly. "I don't think so."

She thumbed the cap off her lamp. Oil slopped over her knuckles, cold and slick. She held the lamp out over the edge of the step, over the heap, and tipped it.

The oil went down in a thin gold rope and spread across the heap's back, beading on the wet grey-green and running into every fold. The heap flinched. The slit clenched shut. The fringe whipped back in on itself like a hand snatched from a stove.

She poured until the reservoir sputtered. Oil ran off the heap, down the third step and the second, and slid out across the surface of the water at the bottom in a widening, rainbow-sheened skin. It spread around the pale thing's body where it rose out of the water, and around the floating legs of the dead man.

The big one stopped on the first step. Its four-fingered end turned slowly, feeling the air. It could taste the oil, Halloway thought. It didn't know what it was. Things that lived in cold dark water hadn't much reason to learn.

"Right," she said. "That's the lesson where you learn what fire is."

She didn't throw the lamp. She'd told Pike that and she held herself to it. She crouched, leaned out as far as her knees would let her, and set it down, glass and wick and flame, gently on the heap's oil-soaked back, the way you'd put a candle on a cake.

For a moment nothing happened.

Then the flame went sideways, found the oil, and the heap lit up like a haystack.

It didn't scream. It had nothing to scream with. It made a sound like a kettle, high and thin, the wet in it boiling off. The whole mass humped and convulsed, and the slit tore open wide, and the fringe flailed. Every strand of it was burning now, lines of fire lashing off the step and down into the water.

And the lines carried it. Halloway watched it happen, and even thirty years in some cold part of her mind took notes. The fire ran down each thread the way a fuse burns, quick and bright, out across the oil-slicked water. It met the sheen and the sheen went up with a soft *whump* that she felt in her chest. A sheet of low blue-and-yellow flame rolled out across the flooded cellar, and the pale thing on the bottom step was standing in the middle of it.

It went up the stairs at her.

She'd half expected that. Burning things ran toward air, and she was between it and the door. It came in a surge, dragging the dead man bumping over the stone, and its four-fingered end snapped open and shut a yard below her boots. The oil on its rings had caught. The fringe of threads along its body flared and shrivelled, one after another, like hair held in a candle, and the smell went from cucumber to something like a burnt roast left on too long.

Halloway stood up on the seventh step with her knife in her hand and her back to the wall, and she waited for it to come the last yard.

It didn't.

It reached the third step, where the heap was still burning, and there was simply too much fire. It hesitated. She saw the hesitation, a stall in the pale ringed body, the blunt end swinging blindly from side to side. Then it recoiled, and the whole length of it slid backward down the steps and into the water. It went under the burning surface with the dead man's legs trailing after it, and the flame closed over the place where it had gone.

The surface churned. Once. Twice. Something big rolled beneath the fire, and a humped pale back broke through it for a heartbeat, blackened now and splitting along the rings. Then it went down again.

The churning slowed.

It stopped.

Halloway stayed on the seventh step for a long time, watching the fire burn itself down to little blue tongues on the water, and she didn't sit until the last of them went out.

---

Afterwards the cellar was dark except for Pike's lamp, and it stank.

Halloway sat three steps below him with her boots in a puddle and her back against the wall, and she had stopped shivering only because shivering took more than she had left. Her palm had a red welt across it where the line had bitten. She'd looked at it once and decided to worry about it tomorrow.

"Finish it," Pike had said.

She was quiet for a while before she answered. It wasn't reluctance. She was putting it in order.

"All right," she said. "All of it. You've earned it and I've paid for it, so we'll both get our money's worth."

She tipped her head toward the step below her. The third step.

"Start there, because it's closest. That's the door-warden, or that's what I'll call it in the book, since nobody's given me a better name. It's done. Look at it. What's left is about the size of a loaf, black, cracked like a burnt pie crust. The outside's charred through. Under the crust it's gone to a grey paste. That's what happens to a soft thing with no bones when you cook it. The slit's fused shut. You can still see where it was, a seam down the middle, puckered like an old scar." She sniffed. "The smell's the fringe. Burnt hair and seawater. You'll dream about that smell for a week. So will I, and I've had longer to get used to it."

She nodded at the stone beneath it, black with soot, scattered with small curled things like the ends of spent matches.

"Those are the lines. The bits that were on the step. They burn right down to the root, so nothing's left but a little knot of ash where each one grew out of it. Count them if you want. I got to forty and stopped." A breath. "It was holding the door, Pike. That's all. It was a wedge. It sat there gasping on dry stone for however long it had to, so that anything that came in couldn't leave without brushing it. And if you brushed it, the whole web would know. It wasn't a hunter. It was a doorbell."

She looked down past her boots at the water. It had gone flat and black again, and a scum of soot and burnt oil lay on it, and here and there bits of pale drifted.

"Now him."

The dead man had come back up. Halloway had known he would. Bodies with nothing inside them float. He lay face-down a yard off the bottom step, turning slowly in the water, spread out like a wet blanket.

"He's flat now," she said. "Flat as a sack. Whatever was holding his shape has gone out of him, so there's nothing but skin and the bits of bone it didn't want. The ribs are showing through at the back where the skin's split. You can count them from here if you've got the stomach. He's burnt along one side where he was lying in the oil, and the hair's gone from the back of his head. The boot's still on. The ring's still on." She paused. "I'll get the ring off him before we go. His wife will want it. She won't want anything else, and I won't be telling her the rest."

Her eyes went past him to the middle of the cellar, where the water was darkest.

"And that one."

She was quiet a moment.

"It's under there. I watched it go down and I watched it stop. It's not come up and I don't expect it will, because it had lungs full of water and it went into fire, and it doesn't know what fire is. Or it didn't." The dry edge crept into her voice. "It'll have learned in a hurry. I'll tell you what I think happened and you can argue with me in daylight. The oil caught on its rings. It went under to put itself out, because that's what water-breathers do when something hurts: they dive. But the oil was on the surface, and the fire was on the surface, and it had to come up to get away from us, and every time it came up it was coming up into flame. It was cooking from the outside in while it was hiding from the fire under the fire."

She let that sit.

"I want to see it. Not tonight. Tomorrow, with the shutters open and a long hook and somebody holding the rope, like I told you. Because I've been at this thirty years, and I don't know what it is, and I'm not having a thing that big in my book with nothing written under

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean forward, resting my elbows on my knees. "Are we done?" My voice is too tired to sound scared anymore. "Or do you want me to watch it until morning?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"...under it," Halloway finished, "except a question mark and a burn."

She looked at Pike then. He was hunched over his knees with the lamp between his hands, and his face in the light had the grey, scraped look people got after the first real one. She'd seen it on a lot of faces. She'd probably worn it herself once, though nobody had been there to tell her so.

"No," she said. "You're not watching it until morning."

She didn't get up yet. Instead she looked down at the black water and counted under her breath without meaning to. Four seconds. Three. Two. The soot scum lay flat. A pale scrap turned slowly by the dead man's shoulder and didn't go anywhere. There was no ripple coming out, and no ripple dying short.

"Nothing's feeling for us," she said. "Nothing's listening. I'll take that for tonight. It's not proof. It's a decent guess, and I've lived on decent guesses longer than you've been alive."

She flexed her hand, the one with the welt across it, and winced.

"Here's why you're not staying, since you'll ask. If it's dead, there's nothing to watch. If it isn't, then it's hurt, and it's in the dark, and it knows the shape of you now. A lad on his own on a cold step at three in the morning, nodding off over a lamp, is not a sentry, Pike. He's the next thing in the corner." The not-quite-smile came and went. "I didn't burn my good eyebrows off to hand it a second helping."

She got up slowly, one hand on the wall. Her knees told her about it at length. She stood a moment looking down at the dead man, turning in the water a yard off the bottom step.

"The ring," she said, mostly to herself. Then she shook her head. "No. Tomorrow. I said I'd get it and I will. But I'm not wading back in there in the dark to fish for a wedding band with a thing like that under the oil. His wife's waited this long. She can wait until there's daylight and a rope." A pause. "She'll never know it was a close thing. That's the job, mostly. Doing the part nobody sees so they don't have to."

She turned and put her boot on the next step up. Then she stopped.

"There's one more thing. We drop the trapdoor behind us, and we weight it. Anything heavy in the kitchen. Then we chalk it. A line across the boards, and my mark on top. If there's a smudge in that chalk in the morning, we don't come down with a hook. We come down with a great deal more lamp oil and a priest, and the priest isn't for it."

She climbed past him, a hand briefly on his shoulder as she went. It wasn't comfort, exactly. It was more like checking a rope was still tied.

"Come on. Up." She'd reached the top step, a darker shape against the dark. "You did well. You asked too many questions at the worst possible moments and you'll be the death of me, but you did well."

Then, quieter, as she stepped out into the kitchen:

"Eleven."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I blink up at her silhouette. "You still counted?" My throat's dry. I push myself up, legs shaking.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway was already in the kitchen by the time he said it. She'd found a chair by feel and was leaning on its back with both hands, the way old men lean on gates.

"Always," she said. "Every time. Down and up."

She straightened with a small grunt and went looking for something heavy. The kitchen was a cold, ordinary room. There was a scrubbed table, a dresser with the plates still on it, and a loaf gone green on the board. Someone had been meaning to come back to that. She didn't look at it long.

"The day you stop counting is the day you come up in the dark and put your foot on a twelfth step." She got her hands under the end of a flour barrel and tested it. Half full. Good. "Stairs don't grow new ones, before you ask. But things sit on them. Things that are the same colour as stone, and patient, and very fond of ankles. If I count eleven going down and I feel twelve coming up, I stop. I don't wonder about it. I stop, and I find out what I'm standing on."

She rocked the barrel onto its rim and walked it across the flagstones in short, grinding half-turns.

"Tonight it was eleven both ways. So either nothing's sitting on them, or it's sitting very still and waiting for somebody who doesn't count." She set the barrel down beside the trapdoor and straightened, breathing hard. "I'd rather it was the first. Mind your feet, I'm going to shut it."

She waited until he was clear. Then she took hold of the ring and let the door down slowly, so it didn't bang. She'd no particular wish to announce to anything below that they'd gone. The cellar smell came up in one last sour breath of burnt hair and cucumber and seawater, and the boards closed on it.

She walked the barrel onto the middle of the door and leaned on it until it settled.

"Chalk," she said, and patted her coat. She found it in the inside pocket, a stub worn down to the size of a knucklebone, and went down on one knee with a sound that wasn't quite a groan. She drew a line across the seam of the trapdoor, both edges, board to flagstone, steady and unbroken. Then she drew her mark over the top: a circle with a single stroke through it, like a door with the bar down.

She looked at it a moment in the light of Pike's lamp.

"There," she said. "Now it's a letter. If anything opens it in the night, it'll have to tear the envelope to do it, and we'll know."

She got up, one hand on the barrel, and stood swaying slightly. Now that she had stopped there was nothing left to hold her up, and she seemed to notice that all at once.

"You're shaking," she said, without looking round. "So am I. That's the cold, mostly, and the rest is the other thing, and it passes. Sit by the grate. There'll be kindling in that box if the poor man was the tidy sort, and his boots say he was." A pause. "Get a fire going and don't put the lamp out until it's caught. I've had enough of the dark for one night, and I'm told I'm the brave one."

She lowered herself onto the chair she'd leaned on and looked at the chalk line on the floor. Her hands lay open on her knees, the welt dark across one palm.

"You asked me if I still counted," she said after a while, more quietly. "I'll tell you something I don't put in the book. The first cellar I ever came out of, I didn't. I was too frightened to think of it. My old master was with me, and he came up behind me, and at the top he said, 'Nine,' just like that. I asked him why, and he said..."

She stopped. The not-quite-smile came, and this time it stayed a little longer.

"He said, 'So one of us knows how many there were, if the other one has to go back down for the body.'"

She let her head rest against the wall.

"Get the fire lit, Pike. I'll take first watch on that chalk. You can take second, and you'll wake me if the line so much as blurs." Her eyes were already half-closed. "And you'll wake me at dawn regardless. We've a ring to fetch."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I kneel by the grate, stacking the kindling with clumsy fingers. "I'll wake you," I say. My voice is still thin. "If the line blurs... what then?"
