dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Nobody's ready," Sedge said. "Ready's for inspections. Hold anyway."

Two fingers under the man's jaw. She counted against her own pulse, then pulled his eyelid up; the eye rolled after the lamp, slow, like it had to think about it first.

"That's the part I don't like," she said. "Shouters who stop. Noise means there's fight left. Quiet means the body's started settling its accounts." She smacked his cheek, twice, not hard. "Corporal. You keep making noise for me. Silence is a liar."

He produced something low and torn, not a word. She nodded as if it were a signed order and turned back to the row of instruments.

"Here's what we've got. Shell fragment, left thigh, deep. It's parked a thumb's width off the femoral, and every time he tenses, it leans on the artery. It stays in, the leg rots by Friday and he follows it. So it comes out now." She held the probe up to the bad light, squinted, dipped it in the carbolic. "Wound's three days old. You'll smell it in a minute — sweet, wrong. That's rot starting. I'll be cutting that back too, so this is a long job, not a clean one. You should know that going in."

She rolled the belt and worked it between his teeth. "Bite. Your tongue is the last thing I need to fix tonight."

She trapped his leg between her forearm and her ribs, braced her hip against the table, and set the probe at the mouth of the wound.

"For the record — I don't enjoy this. People who enjoy it get marched away from tables. I do it because it's Tuesday and he'd like to keep the leg."

The probe went in along the tract. The smell rose up, sweet and wrong, right on schedule, and the man's whole body came off the canvas — not shouting anymore, convulsing, everything he had left arriving at once, all of it driving up through his shoulders. The table legs skidded an inch in the dirt.

"There it is," Sedge said, level, elbow-deep, eyes on the wound. "That's the wanting-to-let-go. Don't. I've got the fragment — it's slippery and it's a coward and I'm not letting it win. Ninety seconds. Then you can hate me."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The man's shoulders surge under my hands, slick with sweat. I plant my feet and lean harder, my own teeth gritting. "I've got him," I grunt, voice tight. I can smell the rot now, cloying and awful.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: The table shifts again, dirt scraping. I can feel the muscles in his shoulders bunching, trying to tear free. "Is it always this much fight?" I ask, breathless.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My eyes stick on the dark, wet mess of the wound. The smell is worse up close. "Just tell me," I repeat, my voice steadier than I feel.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then look," Sedge said. "Eyes are free. It's the hands that cost."

The probe walked deeper, following the tract. She talked the way she worked — level, unhurried, because hurry on a table was just dying with extra steps.

"Top to bottom, since you asked. Red at the rim — that's him. Live muscle. Hurts, bleeds, works. Good. Under that, the grey-yellow, the stuff that looks like cheese left in the sun — that's not him anymore. That's the rot. It doesn't bleed because there's nothing left in it that remembers how. It just spreads. An inch a day, and it turns the wound into a boarding house for everything that kills him by Friday. I cut it out because you can't argue with it. You can only evict it."

The probe tip touched something. A small hard click, metal on metal, and the corporal's whole leg tried to leave without him.

"There's our tenant. Thumb-sized, jagged, parked a thumb's width off the femoral like a drunk on a railing. So — your question. He keeps the leg. The rot's shallow yet, it hasn't eaten through the fascia. I've seen this leg live. The kind version of tonight is a sheet over his face and me walking to the next cot.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Straight, then." She traded the probe for the forceps and dipped them without looking at the dish. "A bullet's honest. In one side, out the other — a drilled hole, drains itself, heals like a letter slot. Shrapnel's a liar. It's torn metal, and it doesn't cut, it crushes. The path it leaves isn't a path. It's a bruise with a tunnel in it, full of meat that's dead and hasn't been told yet."

Two strokes of the scalpel widened the mouth of the wound. The corporal's roar came a half-second behind the blade, muffled by the belt to something more felt than heard.

"Keep him flat. He twists, I slip, and this thing does my cutting for me. Straight shoulders — I'll settle for straight, I don't need still."

The forceps went in along the tract, following the path the probe had mapped. Her voice stayed level, unhurried.

"It travels dirty, that's the second thing. Goes in carrying his trousers, the field he fell on, whatever the shell picked up before it picked up him. That stink you're fighting — rot didn't find this wound. It was delivered with it. Seeded the first second." The forceps eased deeper. "Third thing, and this is the one that matters tonight: it doesn't have to cut the femoral to kill him. It only has to lean. Every time he tenses — like now — metal rubs the artery wall, and the wall wears the way rope wears over a stone edge. Thin, thinner. Then some night next week, asleep, it lets go, and he's emptied out before anyone thinks to shout for me. That's why tonight. And why I don't yank." The forceps closed. Something in there held. "Every edge on it is a hook. Going out does the same damage as going in, unless you open the door and back it out the way it came. Politely."

She braced her hip against the table, clamped the leg against her ribs, and drew back. The corporal's spine came up off the canvas, held, held — and then it was out. A thumb-sized piece of shell casing, black and jagged, sitting wet in the forceps with a grey thread of trouser still snagged on its edge.

She held it up where it could be seen, since eyes were free.

"Three days a tenant." It went into the basin with a small tin clatter, and she pressed her palm flat over the wound, counting against her own pulse. Under her hand the beat pushed back at her, steady, even. No jet. "A nicked artery spouts like a kicked pump. This one's telling the truth. He keeps the leg."

She looked down at the wound, then at what was left of the night's work.

"Only part of this I enjoy is that part being over. Now the long half — the rot comes out, and it comes out by the inch. Get your grip back. Quieter, but it goes on for a while."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding, my hands loosening slightly on his shoulders. "Hell," I mutter, staring at the bloody piece of metal in the basin. "So it's out. That's good, right?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good's a strong word for a table," Sedge said. "It's better. Better has a shape to it. That thing in the basin was the half that kills him quick — no warning, middle of the night, done. That half's gone. What's left kills him slow, and slow is the half I can beat." She glanced at Wick's face, at where his eyes were sitting. "You'll see that piece again tonight when you sleep. Everyone does, first time. It passes."

The corporal had gone quiet in the spent way — chest hitching, belt still between his teeth, the fight drained out through the hole in his leg. She smacked his cheek, twice, got a low cracked sound.

"Good. Still lying to me. Keep that up, corporal. Groaning counts."

She traded forceps for scalpel, dipped it, and laid her left hand flat on the thigh to steady it.

"Now the rot. You'll want the rules, because this part looks worse than it is. Dead meat doesn't bleed — I told you that. It also doesn't hurt. Nothing left in it that remembers how. So here's the whole science: I cut until it bleeds. Blood's the border. Red means I've found him again. Grey means I'm still in the dead part, and the dead part barely fights the blade — comes away like wet paper. Every cut that makes him curse me is a cut that's saving the leg. Every cut he doesn't feel is a cut that wouldn't have saved anything."

The scalpel went in at the upper edge of the grey. It came away in a curl, yellow and soft, and the smell doubled, thick enough to lean on.

"Breathe through your mouth. It gets worse before better — the stink lives in that stuff, and cutting lets it out."

She wiped the blade on her apron and set the next stroke.

"And your job changes. Before, I needed you against the bucking. Now I need you against the other thing. He's spent, and spent men go slack, and slack is what I watch for. His shoulders stay loose for ten seconds, you tell me — fast, don't wait to be sure. Bucking means fight. Slack means the body's settling its accounts, and I want to catch that at the door, not after it's sat down."

She looked up at the corporal without straightening.

"You've got a name and a home, and my assistant here doesn't know either one. Tell him. Talk through it — men who talk don't go slack."

Then she bent back to the work. Cut, curl, basin. Cut, curl. The lamp hissed.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my weight on his shoulders, but I lean down closer to his ear. "Hey, corporal. What's your name? Tell me." My voice is low, rough from holding him down.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The scalpel lifted another curl of grey and the corporal's scream came up through the belt, torn and muffled and real.

"That's the good noise," Sedge said. "Ugly, but ours."

The corporal's head rolled toward Wick's voice. What got out around the leather was half-swallowed, tried twice.

"Mullane." A breath like hauling wet rope. "Tom."

"Tom Mullane." She set the next stroke. "There. Now he's somebody instead of a leg. Names keep men in their bodies — cheapest medicine in this tent. Keep asking him things. Home, street, the dog. Doesn't matter what. Matters that he answers."

The blade walked down the tract. Cut, curl, basin. Cut, curl.

"You wanted all of it, so here's the manifest, and some men faint on the manifest alone. The tract runs a hand's length, top to bottom. I'm three fingers down from the top. Grey all the way so far, and shallow — that's mercy. The deep side is worse. That's where the metal sat for three days, and the rot kept house around its tenant. When I reach it, the stuff comes out in slabs and the stink will try to make you leave. Don't. Mouth-breathe and stay."

The corporal's jaw worked against the belt. "A farm," he got out. "South of—" and it died in his chest.

"South of's enough," Sedge said. "A direction's a home, for tonight." She glanced at his face — chest hitching, sweat standing on him, eyes tracking the lamp. "Still with us, Mullane. Keep lying to me like that."

She traded to a fresh blade and dipped it.

"After the cutting — twenty minutes yet, less if he keeps bleeding honestly — the wash. Carbolic, full strength, straight down the tract. The dead part won't feel a drop. The live part will feel all of it. Burns like a dropped coal and I won't pretend otherwise. That's fair — the living pay."

Cut. Curl. Basin.

"Then I pack it open. Wet gauze, floor of the wound up to the mouth. And here's where everyone argues with me: no stitches. None. A dirty wound sewn shut is a coffin with thread on it. It stays open, it drains, and tomorrow I unpack it and pack it again,

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hands shake. I wipe them on my trousers, but the shaking stays. "How long before he's out of the woods?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: S

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Out of the woods is a forest that doesn't exist here," I say, my voice sounding hollow. "Just tell me if he'll live the night."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content: "No

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Alright." I drop my head forward, arms propped on my knees. "So we wait."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lamp a fraction so the light lay along the thing instead of on the water, and the wrongness of the outline sharpened. Two shoulders, or what wanted to be two, and then a third rise where a neck should have been, folded the wrong way against the stones.

"There," she said. "You caught it. The head's set back on itself. Not broken. Set." She did not step in. The water around it had gone still, which she trusted less than movement. "Count the limbs before you decide it's a man. And if one of them twitches, you tell me before you do anything brave."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I count slowly, squinting. "Four limbs, I think. Two arms, two legs... but the way they're bent..." I swallow. "No twitching. It's too still."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady and let the silence sit a moment longer than comfort liked. Four limbs, no twitch. She filed both facts and did not spend them yet.

"Too still is a kind of answer," she said. "Not a good one." She tipped the light down the length of the left arm. The elbow bent once, as an elbow ought, and then again halfway to the wrist, the second joint sitting under the skin like a knuckle that had never been taught its place. "There. See the second bend? That's not drowning. Drowning doesn't rearrange the furniture."

She shifted her weight off the step and onto the stone lip, boots clear of the water. The surface did not so much as ring. "Head's set back. Arm's hinged twice. Legs look as if someone packed them for travel and forgot which way the knees face." A short breath, almost a laugh and not quite. "So. Not a man who fell in. Something that wore the idea of a man until the water disagreed with it."

She did not go closer. The lamp stayed high, the beam narrow. "We don't touch it from here. We watch the water for one full minute. If it stays flat, I go in to the knees and you stay on the step with the lamp. If it doesn't—" She glanced at Pike, grim and level. "—you say so, and we both get out of this hole before it remembers it has a mouth."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the question stand in the damp air long enough to take the heat out of it. She did not look away from the shape.

"Recently enough that the water hasn't finished with the skin," she said. "And not recently enough that I'd call what's left a person." She tipped the lamp a hair so the light caught the throat, or the place a throat had been folded shut against the stone. No pulse there. No rise. The second elbow under the left arm stayed where it was, knuckle-wrong and quiet. "A person drowns with the joints they were born with. This one came apart along lines a body doesn't own and then tried to remember how to be arranged. That's not a fall. That's a wearing-out."

She counted under her breath, not for Pike's sake. The water held flat. One minute, near enough.

"So yes. It was someone. Past tense. What's in the water now is the remainder, and remainders in cellars like this one have a habit of noticing when you start naming them." Her mouth went thin, not quite a smile. "We still don't touch it from the step. Lamp stays with you. I go to the knees, I look at the hands and the mouth, and I come back with an answer you can use. If the surface rings while I'm in it, you don't come after me. You get up the stair and you shut whatever will shut."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, gripping the lamp tighter. "Alright." I watch her step into the water, my throat dry. "I'm watching the surface. Be careful."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway went in without a splash, the way a person goes in when they have already decided the water is the smaller of two bad ideas. Cold climbed her boots and settled at the knees. She kept her weight on the back foot and her free hand clear of the surface, and she did not hurry the last two steps.

Up close the wrongness sorted itself into inventory. The left hand had five fingers and a sixth that had started under the wrist and given up halfway, a pale bud of bone sealed under skin like a mistake someone had tried to hide. The right hand was ordinary until the nails, which were too long and packed with cellar grit, not blood. She turned the lamp's spill with her chin and looked at the mouth.

It was closed. That was the part she did not like. The jaw sat where a jaw should, and the lips had drawn back just enough to show the teeth, and every tooth was a human tooth in a human row — except the set of them, which pointed a fraction inward, as if the mouth had been taught to keep hold of something rather than to speak. No tongue visible. No breath. The fold at the throat was only skin, pressed flat against the stone, no cord underneath it moving.

She counted one more breath of her own, then straightened.

"Hands first," she said, voice low, not looking back. "Left one's grown an extra start of a finger and then thought better of it. Right one's been scratching at stone, not at people. Mouth is shut and the teeth lean in. That's a keeper's mouth, not a biter's — not yet." A thin breath, almost the laugh again. "So it wore someone, and the wearing failed down here, and what's left isn't finished remembering how to be dead. Don't name it. Don't touch the water. I'm coming back to the step, and then we decide whether this cellar gets salt or fire."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not take the lamp. She stayed where the water met her knees and spoke to the shape, not to the question, so the answer would come out clean.

"It put a person on," she said. "Not all at once. The joints give the order. Head turned back and set, because the thing underneath wanted the eyes facing the wrong way for a while and the man didn't survive the turn. Arm hinged twice where an arm has one hinge. Legs folded for a shape that isn't ours. Left hand started a sixth finger and quit. That's not injury. That's a fit that failed."

She glanced once at the water between them, flat, and let the glance do the scolding for the step Pike had left.

"The nails say it lived long enough down here to scratch stone. The mouth says it was made to hold, not to bite — teeth tipped in, jaw shut, nothing moving under the throat. Then the water got into the wearing. Skin's still on it, so this is recent. The person's gone. What's left tried to keep the arrangement and couldn't, and it hasn't agreed to be a corpse yet." A short breath, dry as the lamp-smoke. "Plainly: something wore him until the cellar disagreed, and the disagreement is still in the water. Salt or fire. Your pick. Not our hands."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, looking at the thing's closed mouth. "Fire," I say quietly. "But I don't want to be the one who lights it." I step back towards the stair, offering her the lamp again. "What do we need to get?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not take the lamp. She came back up onto the lip with the water sliding off her boots in one sheet, and she put herself between Pike and the cellar until the step was under both of them again.

"Fire it is," she said. "And you don't light it. That's the sensible half of the choice." She wiped her hands on her coat, though they had never gone in. "We need three things from upstairs, and none of them is courage. A tin of lamp-oil, the coarse salt from the kitchen — the whole crock, not a pinch — and something that will burn when it's wet. Curtain, chair-leg, the rag pile by the scullery door. Dry, if the house has any dry left in it."

She tipped her chin at the shape without looking long. The surface behind her stayed flat. She trusted that less than she had a minute ago.

"Oil on the skin, salt in the water around it, then the rag. I strike the match. You stay on the stair with the lamp and you count. If the mouth opens before the flame takes, we leave the tin and we shut the cellar. If it takes, we don't stay to watch it remember." A thin breath, not quite a laugh. "Fetch the oil and the salt. I'll mind the step. And don't name it on the way up."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stayed on the lip of the step and did not spend the question on the shape. She spent it on the signs she already had, which was as far as she was willing to go with four feet of still water between them and anything that had not agreed to be dead.

"What's under the skin, I haven't opened," she said. "And I won't, not in that water. You want the wearing, not a dissection. Here it is."

She counted it off on her fingers, dry, the way she counted loads.

"It takes the arrangement first. Not the meat. The map of how a man is meant to bend. Head set back means it turned the eyes for its own looking and the neck locked where it left them. Second hinge in the arm means it tried to put a joint where it keeps one and the bone obliged halfway. Legs packed the wrong way is the same mistake, lower down. Sixth finger started and quit — it reached for a hand that isn't ours and ran out of person before the finger finished. That's how far it got. Far enough to rewrite the hinges. Not far enough to finish a shape of its own."

A short breath. The lamp-smoke didn't move.

"What it took is the use of him. Eyes, for a while. Hands, long enough to scratch stone instead of people. Mouth last, and the mouth it left is the tell you keep. Teeth tipped in. Jaw shut. Nothing under the throat. A keeper, not a biter. If you meet another and the teeth still point out and the jaw works like a man's, it hasn't finished the wearing. If the teeth have turned in and the skin's gone slack over joints that aren't in any book, you're late, and you don't stand in the water to be sure."

She glanced once at the flat surface and did not trust it.

"Plainly: the man is gone. What's under the skin is the argument that killed the fit — bone that started to follow a pattern and stopped when the cellar got in. You don't need the rest of the anatomy to know the next one. You need the hinges, the extra start of a finger, and a mouth that holds instead of speaks. Anything past that, we learn after it's salt and fire, not before." She tipped her chin toward the stair. "Oil. Salt. Rag. Then I strike the match. Detail's done."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, and start backing up the stairs. "What if it moves while you're down here alone?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stayed on the lip and did not turn her back on the water to watch him go.

"Then it gets one of us, not two," she said. "That's the whole of the plan, and it isn't a brave one." She set her heel against the stone so the step would tell her if she shifted. The surface behind her stayed flat. She counted that as a fact with a short life. "If it moves while you're gone, I don't fight it in four feet of its own water. I come up the stair as far as the door, and I shut what will shut, and I wait for the oil. If it comes faster than I do, you hear it. You don't come down to be sure. You salt the threshold from the kitchen side and you burn the stair if the door won't hold."

A short breath, dry as the wick.

"And if you come back and I'm not on this step, you don't call my name into the dark. You set the tin down, you strike nothing, and you leave. What's in that water already knows how to wear a voice. It doesn't get a second one tonight." She tipped her chin toward the climb without looking away from the cellar. "Oil. Salt. Rag. I'll mind the still. Go."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not put steel in it. She stayed on the lip, one boot still shedding water, and let the order die in the damp before it could become a fact.

"No," she said. "I'm not cutting. You don't open a remainder in four feet of its own water because the lamp is steady and the curiosity is worse." She tipped her chin at the shape and did not look long. The surface stayed flat. She trusted that the way she trusted a shut mouth. "What's underneath stays underneath until salt and fire have had their say. I've told you how far the wearing got. Hinges rewritten. A finger started and quit. A mouth taught to hold. That's the anatomy you can use. The rest is a story the water would like you to lean in for."

She drew a breath through her mouth, short, and gave him the smell because that much was already in the air and cost nothing.

"Wet stone. Lamp-smoke. Old cellar rot, the ordinary kind. Under it, hot iron and milk gone over — close, and only when the lamp dips. Not blood. Not a man's death. That's the fit failing, and it sits on the skin, not under it. Skin's still whole. I'm not the one who changes that tonight."

A thin breath, not quite a laugh.

"You want the inside, you get it after. From whatever the fire leaves on the stones, and only if I say the mouth stayed shut through the burning. Until then you don't narrate a knife into my hand." She set her heel against the step. "Oil. Salt. Rag. I'll mind the still. If it moves while you're gone, you already know the rest."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the shape for a moment longer, then turn and start up the stairs. My boots feel too loud on the old wood. "I'll be quick," I call back, my voice too tight. I don't look back.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer the tightness in that voice. Answering made people turn, and turned people came back down stairs they had already paid for.

She listened until the wood stopped complaining, then counted the quiet the way she counted a bad minute in standing water. The lamp-spill thinned as the climb took it, and the cellar took the dark back in strips. She kept her heel on the stone and her eyes on the surface, not on the shape.

The water stayed flat. That was the fact she had. Under the flat, the cold against her boots changed weight — the way silt shifts when a door opens upstairs. Not a limb. Not a mouth. She did not step off the lip to test it.

"Still," she said, to the stair and not to the thing. "Stay that way until the oil comes."

The mouth at the far end did not open. The second elbow did not unbend. She set that against the silt-shift and spent neither yet. Her hand found the match-tin in her coat and left it shut. Striking nothing in the dark was half the work.

A board answered a boot somewhere above, far enough to be the kitchen and not the landing. She let out the breath she had been keeping for the count.

"Quick is fine," she told the empty climb, dry as wick-smoke. "Correct is better. Whole crock. Don't talk to the cellar on the way."

The surface held. She did not trust it, and she did not leave the step.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stayed on the step below him, where the wood gave way to stone, and did not take the lamp out of his hands. The cellar behind her was dark again. The match-tin in her coat was lighter by one.

"Afterwards is the right time for it," she said. "Not before. You wanted it finished. Here it is, and I won't tidy it."

She set her heel where the lip still held a skin of water, so the telling would stay tied to the place.

"You came back with the tin, the crock, and a curtain that had already given up being dry. I took all three. You stayed where you are. I went in to the knees and no farther. Oil first, along the shoulders and the fold at the throat and both arms, heavier on the left where the second hinge sat under the skin. Not a soak. A line the flame could follow. The skin took it the way skin takes lamp-oil — slow, dull, no shine worth trusting."

She counted the next part on her fingers, same as before, because that was how she kept a job from turning into a story.

"Salt next. Whole crock, not a pinch, shaken out in a ring where the water met the stones around it, and then a handful on the chest and the shut mouth. It sat on the surface a moment and then went down. The water didn't ring. It thickened. Like silt deciding to be a floor. The extra start of a finger on the left wrist went the color of old wax where a grain stuck. Nothing moved."

A short breath. Lamp-smoke from his hands, and under it the ghost of hot iron, already fading.

"Rag on the near shoulder, oil-wet, one end in my hand. I struck the match on the tin, not on the stone. Flame took the rag before it took the skin. Yellow, then the blue you get when oil is thin and the cloth is mean. I laid it and stepped back to the lip. I did not stay in the water to watch it catch."

She glanced once toward the dark and did not give it her face for long.

"It caught at the shoulder and ran the line I'd made. Skin blackened and pulled. The head, set back the way it was, didn't turn. The fold at the throat opened because the skin shrank, not because anything under it decided to. No cord. No breath. The second bend in the left arm showed when the skin tightened — bone, ordinary bone, with a knuckle that had no business being there, and that knuckle split along the grain like green wood in a grate. The sixth finger didn't finish itself. It curled and went to char with the rest of the hand."

Her mouth thinned. Not quite a smile.

"The mouth stayed shut until the lips burned back. Then the teeth showed, still tipped in, still a keeper's set, and a sound came out of it that wasn't a word and wasn't a man's voice. Wet cloth on a hot stove. The jaw didn't work. The water around the ring of salt went flat-white and threw up a skin of scum, and the scum burned with a low blue that never climbed past the ankles of the shape. Legs packed wrong didn't unpack. They cracked where the knees weren't, and the smoke that came off them was the milk-gone-over smell, stronger, and then only wet stone and oil."

She wiped her palms on her coat, though they were dry.

"I waited until the rag was gone and the shoulders had fallen in and the surface inside the salt had stopped holding a flame. Nothing stood up. Nothing reached. The mouth, what was left of it, stayed a hole with the teeth leaning in, and no tongue, and no second voice trying on mine. I came up. I did not kick the remains apart. Fire had already had the argument. Salt held the water. That's the finish."

She looked at the lamp in his hands, not at his face, grim and level.

"What's on the stones down there now is char and a ring of spent salt and a shape that finally agreed to be dead. If you meet another, you already have the tells. You don't need this one's inside. It didn't get to keep one." A thin breath, dry as the wick. "We shut the cellar. We don't go back down tonight to be sure. Sure is how a remainder gets a second look at you."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the dark at the bottom of the stairs. "Could it have spoken?" I ask quietly. "If we'd been slower?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the dark at the foot of the stair and did not let the question pull her back down into it.

"Spoken, the way a man speaks — no," she said. "The jaw was shut and the teeth were tipped in to hold, not to shape a word. Nothing moved under the throat. I didn't see a tongue before the fire took the lips, and what came out of the mouth when they burned back wasn't speech. Wet cloth on a stove. A noise the fit made on the way out."

She set one hand on the match-tin and left it shut.

"A voice is a different theft. It doesn't need the mouth to work like ours. It wears one it's already heard — yours, mine, the man it put on — and it puts the sound in the water, or in the dark above the step, and it waits for someone to answer it as if a person were still in there." A short breath, dry as wick-smoke. "Slower, and it might have tried that. Not a conversation. A hook. You call a name, it gives the name back, and the fool who comes down to be sure walks into four feet of something that hasn't agreed to be dead."

Her mouth thinned, not quite a smile.

"That's why I told you not to call me if I wasn't on the step. It didn't get the chance. Fire took the mouth before it could borrow a second voice, and salt kept the water from carrying one up the stair." She tipped her chin toward the cellar door, grim and level. "We shut it. We don't stand here feeding it questions. Questions are a kind of leaning in."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I won't," I say, my voice low. I stand up, my legs stiff. "I just needed to know the shape of the silence it left." I turn toward the door, lamp held out. "Let's go shut it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway came up the last of the stone and put her shoulder to the cellar door before the dark at the foot of the stair could be mistaken for an answer. The wood was swollen with the damp. It met the frame a finger short of true, and she set her boot against the lower board and leaned until the latch found its seat with a dull click.

"The silence it left is a shut door and a smell of oil that'll be in the kitchen till morning," she said. Not to the dark. To the latch, which she tried once with her thumb and left alone when it held. "That's the shape. Not a voice. Not a name. If you start listening for the rest of it, you'll invent a mouth that isn't there."

She wiped her palm on her coat and stood a moment with her back to the wood, listening the way she listened to a bad minute — for boards, for water, for anything that wanted to be called a word. The house gave her the lamp-wick and Pike's boots and nothing from below. She spent that as a fact with a short life.

"Salt on the threshold before we sleep. Not a line for luck. A line so we know if something crosses it that isn't us." Her mouth thinned, not quite a smile. "And we don't open this again to be sure. Sure's a kind of knocking." She tipped her chin toward the kitchen, grim and level. "Lamp stays with you. I'll fetch the crock. If the door complains, you tell me. You don't answer it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, watching the door for a long moment before I turn away. "Alright," I say, my voice steadier now. "I'll put the lamp on the table. The silence feels... thicker than it did before." I start toward the kitchen, my footsteps too loud again. "Do you think there are more of them?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
She hooked the lamp a hand-span closer with one finger and left a smear on the glass. Didn't matter. The light would be bad no matter where it stood.

"Ball's out of the socket on the right," she said, taking his forearm and testing the give. "Front and below, the usual way. I pull down, swing out, and lever it back over the lip. It sounds like wet rope when it goes in. Don't flinch. Flinching travels down your arms."

She set her boot against the table leg and her heel into his armpit, and wrapped both hands around his wrist like she was arm-wrestling something much larger than him.

"He says he's ready," she observed, to the tent in general. "Nobody's ready. And I don't count to three — counting is a lie with a number on it. I just do it."

She did it. The man bucked, all of him at once, heels drumming the canvas under the table, and the shoulder made the sound she'd promised. His shout broke off into something smaller and worse, the sobbing that meant he'd stopped fighting it.

"In," she said, thumb pressing the joint. "Round. Sitting where it belongs." She flexed the arm once, gently. "The wall's a good thing to watch, by the way. Wall-watchers hold better than starers. Starers get curious at exactly the wrong moment."

She reached for the strapping, then stopped, eyeing the left shoulder. "That one's got ball in it. That one I dig. Worst part's over — for him. Yours is starting now."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, keeping my hands locked on his shoulders even though he's gone still. "Dig?" I ask, voice tight. My eyes dart from the wall to Sedge's hands, then back again. "What do you mean, dig?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Dig is the honest word for it," she said. "Ball went in low and front and stayed. If it had punched through and kept walking, I'd strap him and we'd all be asleep by now. It didn't. It's still in there, and in there happens to be a joint."

She set two fingers on the swelling below his collarbone and walked them across it, reading the meat the way she'd read a road. "Can't feel it from outside. Fine. Lead's heavy and bone's a liar — it'll be tucked against one or the other."

She strapped the right shoulder fast, while he was still limp enough to let her — two turns, pin, done. "Quiet minutes are for housekeeping." Then she folded a strap of leather and pushed it between his teeth. "Bite that. Not your tongue. I'd dose him, but the poppy went west with the last convoy and the whiskey died in spring. So he does this the old way."

She looked at Wick over the table. "He'll come awake for this part. They all do. Same job — weight down, eyes on the wall. If he comes up off the table, you go down with him. You're bigger. Win."

The probe was a hand's length of steel, thin as a knitting needle, tipped into a small question mark. She wiped it on her apron.

"For the record, I don't enjoy any of this. I don't take pleasure in it, and I won't pretend there's a trick that makes it kind. There's just my hand and however long it takes, and the alternative is him losing the arm to rot in a month. I like that less."

Two fingers held the wound open. She went in alongside them, slow, eyes half-shut, listening through her hand. "Ball makes a tidy corridor going in. I follow the corridor. If I meet gristle instead, I back out and try a new angle — I don't push. Pushing makes new holes, and new holes are how a man dies a week from now with a fever, and I look stupid at his funeral."

The probe stopped. A faint gritty scrape, like a coin dragged on slate.

"There you are." Almost fond. "Sitting on the blade of the scapula. Lazy lead. Didn't even have the manners to break." She drew the probe out and took up the blade instead, fitting it against the wound's lower lip.

"Now the part you asked about. The hole it made is exactly the size of the ball, and it has to come out through a hole the size of two of my fingers. So I make the door honest." Her thumb settled the edge in place. "When I cut, he's going to come up off that table like a fish.

Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Neither," Sedge said, thumb steady on the blade's edge. "It's a shoulder. The legs are a different tent, and tonight they can mind themselves. And no — this isn't the kind part. The kind part would have been poppy an hour ago. There wasn't any. So this is the other kind: the kind that works. He keeps the arm. That's already decided — nothing in there is arguing. The cut is just the toll on the road to keeping it."

She looked at Wick once. "Questions after. Now. Hold."

She cut.

He came up like she'd promised — one arc, the leather creaking between his teeth — and whatever weight was on his shoulders held, because the table stayed a table. Sedge leaned her ribs into his chest, pinning him with her whole side, and worked by feel. Blade in to the depth she'd measured on the probe. Out. Two fingers spreading the lips of it.

"Door's honest." Blood came slow and dark, welling rather than jumping. "Muscle bleeds politely when you cut with the grain. It's only the lying meat that sprays."

Her fingers went in to the second knuckle, curled, found the gritty knob of it tucked behind the scapula's blade, and levered. The ball came reluctant, then all at once, and her palm was under it before it could fall — a hazelnut of lead, shiny where her fingers had scrubbed it, dull everywhere else.

"There," she said, and dropped it in the tin dish, where it made its small unhurried clink. She felt once more with a fingertip, thorough. "No brothers. Good."

She packed the cut with lint, pressed until the ooze slowed, and bound it against the strapping on the far side, so he'd have to be symmetric whether he liked it or not. Then, to the man, while he still had the strap in his teeth: "You keep the arm. Whether it ever goes over your head again is between you and the next four weeks. Don't ask anything of it for a month. Joints hold grudges."

She peeled the strap from his teeth and wiped her hands on her apron, and only then looked at Wick properly.

"That was your answer, by the way. Bad like he keeps everything. A comfortable dead man and a sore live one — I know which one I'd rather sew up." She nodded at the man's shoulders. "Ease off when I say, not before. Now. Slowly. Letting go is a skill too, and it's the half most people do badly."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let go slowly, my hands trembling a little from the strain. "He kept the arm," I say, more to myself than anyone. I look at the man's face, pale but breathing steady. "He'll thank you later."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No, he won't." Sedge said it to the blade, not to Wick, wiping it down and folding the rag around the edge. "Some come back to thank. Most go home and never think of this tent again, and the ones who do come back mostly want a note for the pension board. It's just as well. Gratitude weighs nothing and I can't splint with it." She held the blade up to the bad lamp, checking the edge against the light. "You do it because the alternative is a man teaching himself to button his coat left-handed. That's the entire argument. It's short."

The man on the table had drifted into the grey country behind the pain — eyes open, breathing slow, following nothing. Sedge took his wrist, counted, let it go. "Can you stand?" He nodded. "Then stand." She looked at Wick. "Belt's the handle. Never the shoulders, not tonight. Third cot, slow, and if he goes grey, put him down where he is — don't negotiate with fainting. The ground is always closer than the cot."

While the man found his feet, she tipped the tin dish and let the ball roll into a clay jar on the shelf, where it settled among two dozen of its fellows with a dull rattle. "Lead's lead. The battery melts them down and shoots them back. Half the rounds in this war have already traveled through somebody."

She wrapped probe and blade together in the rag and held them out. "These want boiling. Firepit's behind the tent. And take the basin with them."

She glanced once at Wick's hands.

"You held through the cut, by the way. Most don't. The shaking now is fine — it means they still work, and it stops faster when they're carrying something." She was already turning to the second cot, where a boy sat with his forearm wrapped in a fielding that had given up its post an hour ago. "He could whistle when I triaged him, so he waited. He's stopped whistling. Instruments in the water, then come hold a basin."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the instruments and basin, my knuckles still white. "Right. Boiling water." I look at the boy on the cot, his silence suddenly loud. "What's waiting in the basin for him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Nothing yet," Sedge said over her shoulder, already kneeling at the second cot. "That basin's carrying the last man's evening, and he's done with it. Dump it on the coals — away from the tent, unless you want flies with opinions. Then scrub it, don't rinse it, scrub it. Fill it from the kettle and give the instruments a slow hundred at a proper boil. Less than that is theater, not medicine."

She turned the boy's forearm over in her lap.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Straight, then," Sedge said. "A ball is one traveler on one road. You watched that tonight — in, sit, dug out, done. Shrapnel is a shell that came apart before it arrived. It comes as a family. A dozen fragments, none of them pointed, none of them traveling straight. They don't drill. They tear."

She had

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
Sedge had the boy's arm in her lap. The fielding was dark and stuck. She cut the knot and let it fall.

"Shrapnel doesn't sit," she said, peeling back the last layer. "It ricochets. It finds a bone and decides to visit the marrow. It turns corners. It leaves a room full of doors open behind it, and infection walks right in." She looked up, her fingers already in the wreck of it. "A ball asks for a blade and a steady hand. Shrapnel asks for a prayer and a miracle. This one... is asking for both."

The boy's arm lay open in her hands. Wick saw red, white, and the glint of something that didn't belong. Not one something. Several.

"He was whistling an hour ago," Sedge said quietly. "Now he's not. That's your answer. It's worse." She reached for a fresh probe. "Your water's not boiling itself. Go. Then come back. You'll hold the basin while I fish."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge rolled a blanket into a bolster and laid the boy's forearm across it, hand up, elbow propped — a wound on display tells you more than a wound in a lap. Then she walked two fingertips down the torn channel, slow, watching the boy's face instead of her hand. Faces are honest; meat lies.

"Four that I can find," she said. "Four fragments and a pocket of grit. There may be a fifth hiding, but the door will tell me. The one that matters is here—" her fingertip stopped beside the ridge of the bone, a thumb's width from the wound mouth, "—because it's leaning on the artery. The artery doesn't know it's in trouble yet. That's the first tenant out. You always evict the one most likely to burn the building down."

She drew a grey curl out of the wreck with her forceps and held it up to the bad lamp. "Trouser wool. Every fragment brings a guest — cloth rides in with the steel and rots where the steel wouldn't. That's the whole difference. Balls are clean. Shrapnel packs you full of your own laundry." She flicked it into the dish. "Which is why we boil things and scrub basins, for those of you keeping score at home."

The boy's breathing had gone quick and shallow. Sedge put her hand flat on his sternum, once, and left it there.

"Talk to me instead. What were you whistling?" He mumbled something. "Good. Keep that. You'll lose the tune about four times before we're done and find it again five. That's how you'll know it's nearly over." She folded a fresh strap of leather and set it beside his hand, not in it. "Yours when you want it. You can shout all you like. Shouting's free. The only thing you can't do is pull."

Then she raised her voice toward the firepit, since instructions traveled further than questions.

"Slow hundred at a boil! Blade and probe come out first, forceps last — they want the hottest water, they're going the deepest. And wipe the basin again inside, your sleeve not your fingers."

She laid her instruments out in order of use, left to right, the way she'd done four thousand times, and looked at the boy's arm the way a locksmith looks at a stubborn door.

"When you're back, your job is counting," she said. "Every piece that drops in the basin, you say the number out loud. I'll be listening through my hands and I will lose count, because I always do at three and five. If we stop at two, we go back in next week with a saw, and nobody wants that arithmetic." She set the blade down last, nearest her hand. "The prayer's optional. The technique I've got. It's the luck we're short on, so hold still, all three of us."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "He's screaming again," I say, my voice low and steady despite the strain in my arms. "Tell me exactly what you're doing in there, and how much longer. All of it." I don't look away from the boy's face this time. He deserves that much.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Everything, then," Sedge said, and gave it to him while her fingers were already back in the wound. "What I'm doing right now is finding his pulse before I find the steel. The beat tells me where the walls are. The fragment's lying on the artery like a boot on a hose, so I go in alongside the beat, not across it, and I lift it straight up — you never lever a piece that's resting on a vessel. You take it off the way you'd take a blade off a friend. Vertical, or not at all."

It came, and the wound answered — dark blood welling fast, faster than the muscle had bled. Her thumb was flat on the artery before the clink reached the dish.

"One," she said. "Count's mine tonight; your mouth's busy keeping him on the table. And now we learn whether the wall holds. The fragment was leaning on the artery and the artery was leaning back." Her other hand stayed still on top. "Twenty heartbeats of pressure. If the arm goes grey, we have a different conversation."

She counted under her breath. The blood slowed.

"Wall holds. Second tenant." Forceps in, quick scrape. Clink. "Two. The coward — he was right under the door." The boy took the strap then, good teeth on leather, and screamed through it. "Three travels," she went on, fingers walking the bruise up the channel. "A fragment drags its bruise ahead of it like weather. Follow the weather, not the hole." Grit against steel, a coin dragged on slate. Clink. "Three. You're past the arithmetic, lad. Scream all you like, it's free."

She pulled the forceps and reached for a swab.

"Now the grit, and here's your answer about time: grit isn't measured in minutes. It's measured in swabs. I wipe, it comes back grey, I wipe again. We're done when it comes back clean three times running. Once is luck, twice is habit, three times is clean." She wiped. Grey. Wiped. Grey. Her thumb never left the artery. "The whole time, mind, I'm feeling the pulse through my fingertips. That's how I know nobody's dying on the table while we do housekeeping." Fourth swab, fifth — clean, clean. "Now I hunt the fifth, because I don't trust round numbers. I milk the arm from elbow to wound and see what the meat gives up."

Her hands ran the forearm's length, slow, wringing it like laundry. Halfway down, the meat produced it — a shard small as a grass seed, and her forceps went in after it along a path no wider than a hair.

"There. Hiding on the far face of the bone. The smart one — went deep and quiet and would've been the fever in a fortnight, and none of us the wiser." Clink. "Five. And that's why somebody counts, because I'd have sworn on the lamp there were four."

She packed the wound with lint, loose, and left the low end of it open.

"No stitches on this one. Balls get sewn. Families get windows — it drains or it rots, and it drains from the floor up. Ugly now is alive later." She bound a board along the forearm, two turns, pin. "Three weeks splinted. Bones and soldiers both do better with clear rules."

The boy was grey and soaked and breathing, and when she said, "The tune," he tried — three cracked notes, and it died.

"He'll have the whole thing by morning. That's how you'll know we got it all." She looked at

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
She looked at Wick on the floor and let him stay there. "Fair. The floor's the right place after a first one. But the rest is mostly quiet, and quiet carries, so listen while you sit."

She knelt at the cot and laid two fingers on each of the boy's wrists at once, counting both pulses against each other like a woman comparing coins.

"First item of the rest: the twins. Both wrists, same count, same beat, same push behind it. If the splinted arm ever lags its brother, the artery's closing down and I'm back in tonight with the blade." She counted. "Twins. We keep them."

Then she pressed the boy's thumbnail until it went white, and let go.

"Nail goes white, nail goes pink, and the time it takes is the truth. Pink inside a breath means the road's still open all the

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her press the thumbnail, holding my own breath until the pink comes back. "How many breaths is too many?" My voice sounds rough in the quiet.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"One breath," Sedge said, watching the nail flush. "Press, let go, and the pink should be home before you've finished letting the air out. One breath is the road open. Two is me pressing again to be sure. Three is me opening him back up on this table tonight — and three has never once gone well, so it remains a theory." She did the thumbnail twice more, satisfied herself, and stood, joints announcing it. "Now the rest. Item by item, since you're sitting comfortably."

"Second: temperature." She laid the back of her hand on the splinted forearm, then the good one, trading between them. "They should feel like brothers. Hotter means the fever's already found the wound. Colder means the road shut behind me. Same trick as bread — you can tell the bad loaf before you cut it." The arms agreed. She moved on.

"Third: the window." She tilted the cot's low end so the open drain showed beneath the binding. "Morning lint should come through straw-yellow — old blood and juice, leaving from the floor up, like I said. Grey-green, or if you smell it before you see it, the room's gone bad and somebody runs for me. Your nose is a better instrument than my lamp. Trust it over your optimism."

"Fourth: fever." Palm on the boy's forehead, then her own, comparing. "Count his pulse while he sleeps. Under ninety by morning is a boy. Over a hundred by tomorrow night is a message, and I want it before he's thought of sending it."

She crossed to the third cot, where the first man slept with his mouth open, and pressed two fingers into the strapping's edge, then felt his hand. "Fingers warm. Strapping's holding the joint, not strangling the blood — that's the whole art of a strap, and most people fail it." She came back to the stool and took up the tin dish, sorting with one finger. Lead pieces rattled into the clay jar. The grey curl of trouser wool she held up to the lamp. "Fifth, and smallest: the guests. Lead's lead. Wool goes to the fire, because rot rides on cloth and cloth rides on nothing once it's ash. That's tomorrow's coals, not tonight's."

She washed her own arms at the kettle, cold, to the elbow, and spoke over the sound of it.

"Sixth is the tent. Instruments off the boil onto the clean cloth — carry the cloth to them, never drag them to it. Basin upside down on the peg. Lamp can die now; it's earned it. That housekeeping is the reason the hundred men who came through here last month aren't buried behind it."

Then she crouched to Wick's level and set a cup of boiled water on the floor beside him.

"Seventh item is you. Off the floor before your legs vote for you, and drink — it tastes of the kettle and nothing else, which is the point of boiling it. You'll hear that dish clink in your sleep for a while. Everyone does. It goes quiet eventually, and what replaces it is worse, and I won't ruin tonight by naming it."

She stayed crouched, forearms on her knees, and gave him the ledger.

"Tonight's account: one shoulder returned to its socket, five pieces of steel and a pocket of grit out of a forearm, two arms kept, none lost. That's a good night by the arithmetic I use, and I don't describe the bad ones to men on the floor." She looked at him the way she'd looked at the blade earlier — checking the edge. "Last item. I've been the only hands in this tent since spring. You held through a cut and a fishing, you counted when it counted, and you didn't negotiate with fainting. That's not praise. It's inventory. Tomorrow you learn to wrap and to boil, and in a month you'll be holding the tray for my blade, because the war has run out of everyone who can do the rest. Sleep in the chair. The floor steals your back and gives nothing."

From the cot came a sound — the boy, asleep now, humming three cracked notes and then a fourth.

Sedge tilted her head at it. "Four. Ahead of schedule. That's how you'll know we got it all."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the cup and drink, the water hot and tasteless. "I'll sleep in the chair," I say, and my voice is steadier than I feel. "But tell me one thing straight — that clink in my sleep. What replaces it?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge took the empty cup back out of his hands and turned it over once, considering, the way she'd turned the blade to the lamp.

"You asked straight, so you get it straight. The answer's nothing. That's what replaces it. Nothing."

She set the cup on the shelf, next to the clay jar of lead.

"Not the faces, before you guess. Everyone guesses faces. The faces are just the clink dressed for church, and you can live with those — the dish rattles in your sleep and the faces file in behind it and it's all one sound, and sound means the work still costs you something. What comes after the clink goes quiet is that it stops costing. You'll stand at this table, do the whole night's work — probe, blade, five pieces, clean swabs — and feel exactly what you'd feel mending a boot. That's what replaces it. Not horror. Comfort."

She crouched back down to his level, forearms on her knees.

"And comfort is a symptom, same as a hot splint or a slow pulse. A medic who feels nothing starts cutting corners, because corners are where the cost was hiding. She doesn't boil the hundred. She stops counting at four because four's a round number and five was probably imagination. She wraps a strap snug instead of right. Her patients don't die of their wounds. They die of her ease, a week later, in another tent, and she never connects the two. That's the worse thing I wouldn't name, and now it's named, and look — the tent's still standing. Naming is the first tenth of treating anything."

She held up her own hand, pressing the thumbnail white with the other thumb, letting the pink come home.

"Mine went quiet in the third year. I caught myself whistling over the forceps. So now I run the trick on myself every night, same as the boy's nail. Does the work still cost? Yes — road's open, I'm still a medic. The day it comes back nothing, I hand the tray to whoever's nearest and go dig latrines, because a numb surgeon is only a tidy way of making widows."

From the cot, the boy hummed in his sleep — four cracked notes, and the start of a fifth that got away.

Sedge tilted her head at it. "Hear that. The opposite of nothing. First night's the best night for hearing it, so listen while you can." She stood, joints announcing it again. "Chair. Now. I've a ledger to write and a kettle to bank, and tomorrow you learn the boil, so I'll want your handwriting on the lint count. Bring your nothing with you if it comes. I know where it lives."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my legs protesting. "So you stay sharp by staying afraid," I say, watching her at the ledger. "That's the trick." I lower myself into the chair, the wood hard and unforgiving. "What's the lint count say about tonight?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway tilted the lamp. The light slid over the water and caught a pale back, a shoulder, then what might have been an elbow—except it bent the wrong way.

“Good,” she said. “Don’t make it fit a familiar shape just to be polite. What part’s wrong?” Her grip tightened on the lamp. “And keep your feet where they are. The water’s hiding the useful bits.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to see past the weird bend. "The... the elbow? But it's too high. And there's another one below it, I think." I point vaguely. "Like it's folded up wrong."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lamp a few inches, keeping her boots planted. The pale shape resolved, then lost itself again in the disturbed reflections.

“Could be another joint. Could be two limbs crossing. Water’s excellent at making a mess of anatomy.” Her mouth tightened. “Usually the anatomy has the decency to stay dead while we sort it out.”

She lowered the lamp beam toward the waterline, searching for where the pale shape joined the rest of the body. “Don’t decide it’s an arm yet. Look for where it attaches.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
“It might have been,” Halloway said. “I couldn’t tell you how recently from a back and a bad angle. Pale skin tells us very little in cold water.”

She kept the lamp trained on the shape. “We’d need to see the head, hands, and what’s attached where. Until then, it’s a body-shaped problem. Those are rarely improved by guessing.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, trying to settle my stomach. "I think... I see where it attaches. It's just... the shoulder looks wrong too."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp steady. The shoulder was half-submerged, its outline softened by the water and the angle.

“Wrong how?” she asked. “Higher than it should be? Pulled forward? Look for the collarbone, if you can see it. Don’t give it a name yet.”

She held her ground. “And don’t step in to get a better look. The cellar’s already made one mess of the evidence.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway studied the shoulder in the raised light. “Plainly? I couldn’t tell you what did it. The joint’s been forced up and inward. That lower bend looks like the same arm folded beneath the body, not another elbow.”

She kept her boots planted at the edge. “I can’t see a wound from here, and the water’s hiding too much to tell whether anything’s broken. I also can’t call it dead. It stopped moving a minute ago.”

Her eyes flicked to the water around the shape. “Hold the lamp there. Don’t take another step.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hold the lamp steady, my hand trembling a little. "Why can't you call it dead?" I ask, my voice low.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the body, not Pike. “Because ‘stopped moving’ isn’t the same as dead. Not underwater, not in a dark cellar, and not when we haven’t checked for breathing, a pulse, or a response.”

She angled the lamp toward the head, careful not to shift her footing. “It may be dead. It may be unconscious. It may be waiting for us to make a more useful mistake. I don’t promote a corpse to confirmed until it earns the title.”

Her gaze tracked the water around the pale shoulder. “Keep the light steady. I’ll look for movement.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s expression hardened. “I can tell you what I saw. The shoulder was displaced upward and inward. The lower bend was probably the same arm folded under the body. I saw no exposed bone, no open wound, and no missing flesh—but I also couldn’t see enough to rule any of those out.”

She kept the lamp trained on the pale shape. “I don’t know what did it. I don’t know what’s under the skin, what it took, or whether it did anything at all. The joint could’ve been crushed, dislocated, or distorted by the angle and the water. We haven’t seen a bite, a cut, or a clean sign of anything.”

Her voice stayed level. “So don’t take a guess from me as a field guide. Until we can examine the body, the only useful facts are that it’s badly bent, partly submerged, and stopped moving about a minute ago. That is not enough to know what you’ll meet next.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my knuckles white around the lantern handle. "Alright. Then let's not waste time. How do you want to approach it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp fixed on the pale shoulder. “We don’t walk straight up to it. First, you come back to the edge—slowly, without turning your back on the body. Keep the light on its head and hands.”

She watched the water around the shape for a fresh ripple. “Then we check for movement from here. If it stays still, I’ll look for a way to reach it without putting either of us in arm’s length. No grabbing, no rolling it over, and no hands in water we can’t see through.”

Her mouth tightened. “If it’s a person, we help them. If it isn’t, we avoid becoming the second body-shaped problem.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway cut through the sodden sleeve, keeping the blade shallow. The cloth parted; the skin beneath remained unbroken where she could see it. She stopped before the blade reached the displaced joint.

“Under the skin, I can’t tell you,” she said. “Not from this angle, and not without opening him. I see no bone, no wound, no missing flesh. The shoulder’s pushed up and inward. That’s all I can establish.”

The cellar smelled of wet stone, stagnant water, and something faintly sour. Nothing distinct enough to identify what had happened—or what had caused it.

“As for how far it got: I don’t know. The water hides most of him, and the clothes hide the rest. I haven’t found a bite or a cut.” She paused, watching the pale skin for movement. “I’m not going to invent one to make the report more useful.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes fixed on the blade. "That sour smell--is that him? Or something else?" I keep the lamp steady, but my heart's hammering.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway paused with the blade clear of the skin and leaned slightly away from the body, testing the air again.

“I can’t say. It’s faint, and the cellar’s full of things that go sour when left wet.” She kept her eyes on the exposed patch of shoulder. “The water, the clothes, the body—any of them could be responsible. It isn’t strong enough to tell me which, and it doesn’t prove the skin’s broken.”

She shifted the lamp’s beam across the waterline, looking for a trail or a change in its surface. “If it gets stronger as I work closer, I’ll note that. For now, it’s just a sour smell in a cellar. Not a diagnosis.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped with the blade above the cut sleeve.

For a moment, the only sound was water shifting against the cellar steps. She looked from the body to Pike on the stairs, then set the knife down on a dry patch of stone, edge turned away.

“Finish what?” she asked. Her voice stayed level. “The examination, or the thing?”

She watched the pale shape. No fresh ripple crossed the water around it. The exposed shoulder showed no movement; the rest of the body remained too submerged to judge.

“If you mean kill it, no. I won’t strike a body I can’t confirm is dead—or confirm isn’t a person—because the room’s frightening us.” She looked back at the water. “If you mean finish checking it, I can do that. Slowly, and without putting a hand where I can’t see it.”

Halloway leaned toward the body without stepping into the water. “I’ll call to it first. If it answers, we treat it as alive. If it doesn’t, that still won’t prove anything.” Her mouth tightened. “The dead are inconsiderate that way.”

She waited, eyes fixed on the waterline near the head, then spoke clearly into the cellar.

“Can you hear me? If you’re alive, move a hand.”

Nothing stirred. Halloway held her position and watched for another long moment before easing back from the edge.

“That’s all I can safely establish from here,” she said. “Still no movement. Still no proof.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the still water. My own voice comes out low, almost a whisper. "If we don't know what it is... how do we decide what to do next?" I grip the lamp tighter. "We can't just leave it here."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked once more at the waterline near the head. “We don’t decide what it is yet. We decide what we can safely do without knowing.”

She set the knife on the stone, well clear of the edge. “We keep it in sight and don’t leave it unattended. Then we get a rope, a long pole, and another pair of hands. No one goes into that water alone, and no one reaches in blind.”

Her gaze stayed on the pale shape. “If its airway’s under water, time matters. So does not making a second casualty. We’ll check the head from here as best we can, call to it again, and get help moving. If it answers, we treat it as a person in need of rescue. If it doesn’t, we still don’t call it dead.”

The sour smell hung faintly in the cellar. Halloway’s mouth tightened. “We’re not leaving it. We’re also not letting uncertainty do the thinking for us. It’s bad at the job.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I push myself off the steps, my boots scraping on the stone. "Then let's get the rope. I'll hold the light, you call." My eyes don't leave the water. "But if it moves... what's the plan?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the water. “If it moves, you don’t go toward it. You keep the light on its head and hands, and you tell me what moved.”

She picked up the knife, closed it, and put it away. “If it answers or reaches for help, we treat it as a person and get the rope to it. We secure the line to something solid before anyone takes the strain. Nobody wades in. If it comes toward us, we retreat up the steps together—slowly if it’s only shifting, quickly if it lunges. We don’t try to hold it off with our hands.”

Her gaze stayed fixed on the submerged shape. “And if it vanishes under the water, we don’t follow it. We mark where it went and get help.”

Halloway shifted back from the edge, leaving the body in view. “A rope is useful. A second person is better. Neither is improved by joining it in the cellar.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Alright. I'll keep the light steady." I force myself to take a slow breath. "Do you think it's still watching us?"
