dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned the clean blade so the witnesses could see its edge, then lowered its point to the floor.

“The killing wound was a thrust beneath the left arm. It entered between the ribs and pierced the heart.” She kept her voice level. “I delivered it. No other wound caused the death.”

She held her place until the words had settled. Then she sheathed the blade.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, making sure my voice is clear and steady. "I confirm the accounting. The cause of death was as stated." My hands are trembling slightly, so I press them flat against my sides.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head to the witnesses. “The account is complete. Let it be entered exactly as spoken.”

Only then did she look away from them, toward the still figure on the floor. Her hand rested on the sheathed blade, though she seemed to take no comfort from it.

“There is nothing further required of you,” she said. She paused, then added with the same care she had given the accounting, “Thank you for bearing witness.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned back to the witnesses. She did not look at the body again.

“The killing wound was a thrust beneath the left arm. It entered between the ribs and pierced the heart. I delivered it. No other wound caused the death.”

She let the silence hold for a moment. “That is the account.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I hear the account," I say, because that's the last of it. I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. My eyes drift toward the body for a second before I force them back to Auren.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave a single, measured nod. “The account has been heard. The obligation is discharged.”

She stepped away from the place of the duel, leaving a clear path to the body. Her hand fell from the hilt. “I will remain until the record is made,” she said. “After that, I will answer for anything else the code requires.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned toward Del. She did not reach for the blade.

“On the left side of the chest, beneath the arm,” she said. “The point passed between the ribs and into the heart. That is where it landed.”

She held her gaze steady. “The witnesses may enter those words as well.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow. "Between the ribs. Under the arm. Got it." I turn to the witnesses, but my voice falters. "You can... you can write that part, too."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited until there was room for her voice.

“Enter it as an addition to the account,” she said to the witnesses. “The point entered beneath the left arm, passed between the ribs, and pierced the heart.”

She did not look away from them. “Those are the words I gave. Del need not repeat them.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the correction without protest.

“The blade passed between the ribs and pierced the heart,” she said. “It cut the heart itself. That wound caused the death.”

She faced the witnesses. “Enter those words. I should have spoken them plainly the first time.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My shoulders relax a little, grateful she understood. "Then we've said it all," I say, turning to the witnesses. "Record it exactly. The account is closed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. “The account is closed.”

She remained beside the duelling place while the witnesses made their record. She did not amend what she had said, or offer an explanation for having needed the correction. When the pen stopped, she said, “I will sign it as spoken.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren faced Del, then the witnesses. “Yes. I left part of it unsaid.”

She held her hands still at her sides. “After the thrust, he remained standing for one breath. He fell before the next. I saw him breathe twice on the floor; I saw no third breath. I did not mark the time by a clock.”

Her voice stayed level. “He said nothing after the blade struck. His eyes were open at the end. There was blood beneath his left arm, and he did not move again.”

She looked to the record. “Enter all of that. Do not turn two breaths into a number of seconds, and do not give him words he did not speak.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Good. That's enough." I look at the witnesses. "He said nothing. That's part of it, too. Write it down."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren waited while the witnesses entered the last words. “He said nothing after the blade struck,” she repeated. “That belongs in the record.”

She read the account before signing it. Where the record matched what she had seen, she set her name beneath it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren left her signature beneath the record. She did not ask anyone to steady a voice or to look away. She faced the witnesses and spoke the account once more, entire.

“The killing wound was a thrust beneath the left arm, on the left side of the chest. The blade passed between the ribs and pierced the heart. It cut the heart itself. I delivered the thrust. No other wound caused his death.

“After the blade struck, he remained standing for one breath. He fell before the next. I saw him breathe twice on the floor; I saw no third breath. I did not mark the time by a clock.

“He said nothing after the blade struck. His eyes were open at the end. There was blood beneath his left arm, and I saw no further movement.”

Auren held her place. “That is what I saw. That is the account I signed.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the witnesses write her words. My own name goes at the bottom, a formality now. "It's done," I say, my voice low and rough. "I should go."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at the two names beneath the account. “Yes,” she said. “Your part is done.”

She stepped aside, leaving the way clear. “I will remain until they take him from the floor.” Her eyes went once to the body, then returned to the signed page. “The record will stay as we gave it.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I don't want to go home yet. Not alone. "You want me to wait with you?" The question comes out quieter than I meant it to.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked up from the signed page. For a moment she gave the question the same care she had given the account.

“Yes,” she said. “I would be grateful if you stayed.”

She moved away from the record, but not from the duelling place. “There is nothing more you are required to do. I would not have you mistake this for an obligation.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I know." I take a slow breath, folding my arms to stop the shaking. "Do you need me to say anything? About how he died?"

dialogue.name: Auren

“That is what I saw. I will not claim more than that.”

rung_labels.evidence: My blade entered beneath his left ribs.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren sheathed the blade before she began. The code did not require it, but she had never been able to give the account with steel still in her hand. It made the words sound like a continuation.

She turned to face the witnesses first, the three of them in their grey sashes along the rail, and then she turned to Del. The second was owed the account more than anyone. The witnesses only recorded it.

"Hear me," she said. Her voice did not rise. It never did. "I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing, and I give the accounting of the wound that ended the challenger."

She paused. Not for effect. The code set the pause there, a breath's length, so that anyone who wished to turn away could. Nobody did.

"He opened high, on the left line. It was a good opening. He had trained it well. I gave ground on it twice, and on the third pass he committed his weight forward to close the distance, and his guard came down from the shoulder by perhaps a hand's width." She held her own hand up, fingers together, to show it. That was also the code. *Show what you saw.* "I entered beneath it. The point went in below the fourth rib on the left side, angled upward. It passed through the lung and reached the heart. He did not feel the heart. He would have felt the rib, and then very little."

Her hand came down.

"He was dead before his knees reached the sand. I did not strike a second time. There was no need, and I would not have been permitted." She held Del's gaze. She didn't look away. Looking away was the one thing she had never allowed herself in eleven accountings. "The fault in his guard was small. It was not cowardice and it was not carelessness. It was the kind of error a man makes when he has fought well for a long time and is tired. I want that recorded as I have spoken it."

The eldest witness inclined his head and wrote.

Auren stood a moment longer. The wind moved the loose sand across the place where he had fallen, and she did not look there either.

"That is the whole of it," she said, more quietly, to Del alone. "If you have questions, the code allows you to ask them of me now, before the witnesses, and I am bound to answer truthfully." A pause. "And if you have none, that is also allowed."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat suddenly dry. My eyes sting, but I don't break our gaze. "I have only one," I say, my voice a little unsteady. "Would my brother have won, if he hadn't been tired?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. The code allowed the one answering a breath to consider, and she took it. She would not give Del a quick answer to a question like that. A quick answer would be a kind one, or a cruel one, and it would not be a true one.

"I will answer you in two parts," she said. "Both are true, and you should have both."

She did not glance at the witnesses. The eldest had lifted his pen and was waiting.

"The first part. He did not simply become tired. I made him tired. I gave ground on the left line twice because his opening was strong and I did not want to meet it while he was fresh. I drew the fight out. I made him chase. That was my intention from the second exchange onward." Her voice stayed level, but it did not hurry. "So when I say he tired, I do not mean it as a flaw in him that anyone might have exploited. It was a thing I did to him, deliberately, because I judged I could not beat his opening directly. Record that as well."

The pen moved.

"The second part." She held Del's eyes and did not let her own soften, because that would have been a lie told with the face instead of the mouth. "I believe that if he had come to me rested, and I had fought him the same way, I would still have killed him. I have done this for a long time, and he had not. That is what I believe." A pause, very small. "But I am not certain. His opening was better than I expected. There was a moment on the first pass when I was not where I meant to be. If he had seen it, it would have been my account being given, and he would be the one standing here speaking it to someone who loved me."

The wind lifted the sand again, and she let it pass.

"So. I think not. I cannot swear to it. And I will not tell you that he had no chance, because he did, and it would dishonour him to say otherwise before witnesses." She was quiet a moment. "He was good. He was not good enough on this day, against me. Those are not the same thing, and I will not let them be written as the same thing."

Then, more quietly, only to Del: "Is there anything else? You may ask as many as you need. The code does not limit it. I only said one because most people can only bear one."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Something shifted in Auren's face, very slightly. Not surprise, exactly. Recognition.

Most seconds did not know the closing words. They came to the sand with grief and nothing else, and when their questions ran out they simply stood there until the witnesses released them. Someone had taught Del the form. Perhaps the brother had, before he came here. Perhaps he had known it might be needed.

She turned again to the witnesses, as the code required, and then back to Del.

"The second has called for the account," she said. "I give it whole, and it will be written whole, and after this it is not spoken again by me."

The eldest witness set a fresh sheet beneath his pen.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing. The challenger was the brother of the one who stands second. He opened high on the left line, and his opening was stronger than mine. On the first pass I was not where I meant to be, and he did not see it. Had he seen it, he would be the one speaking." She did not hurry past that. She gave it the same weight as the rest. "Knowing I could not meet his opening directly, I gave ground twice and drew the fight long, with the intention of tiring him. This was done deliberately and it succeeded. On the third pass he committed forward, and his guard fell from the shoulder by a hand's width." Her hand rose again, fingers together, and held there. "I entered beneath it. The point went in below the fourth rib on the left, angled upward, through the lung and into the heart. He felt the rib and little after. He died before his knees reached the sand. There was one wound and no second."

Her hand lowered.

"His error was fatigue that I caused. It was not cowardice. It was not carelessness. He fought well, and he had a true chance, and he lost it on this day against me." A breath. "That is the account. I set nothing aside from it and I have added nothing to it that was not so."

The pen moved for some time after she stopped. Auren waited through all of it, standing exactly where she was, her eyes on Del and not on the place in the sand.

When the eldest witness finally lifted his pen, she spoke again, quietly, and the words had the plainness of something she had said ten times before and still did not say lightly.

"It is yours now to accept it or refuse it. If you refuse, the witnesses will record that the second found the account wanting, and they will hear from you where it failed. There is no shame in either answer." She paused. "Take what time you need. I am not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward, out of the spot for the second. I don't need time. The wind feels colder away from the sand. I meet her eyes and my voice doesn't shake. "I accept the account."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. It was not a bow. The code had no bow in it for this moment, and she had never invented one, because anything she added would have been hers, and nothing in the closing was meant to belong to her.

"The second accepts the account," she said, turning to the rail. "Let it be written."

The eldest witness wrote it. The two beside him, who had recorded nothing but kept the count of the passes, each set a thumb to the corner of the sheet in turn. Then the eldest rose, and the other two with him.

"The account is given and accepted," he said. His voice was thin and dry, an old man's voice, and he had said these words more times than Auren had heard them. "The matter between the Eleventh Standing and the challenger is closed. Neither house owes the other. Neither name is lessened." He looked at Del for a long moment, and something in his lined face might have been approval, or might only have been tiredness. "You spoke the form correctly. Not many do."

He rolled the sheet, tied it, and the three of them went down from the rail and across the far end of the yard without looking back. That was also the code. The witnesses did not linger over what they had witnessed.

Then it was only the two of them, and the wind, and the sand.

Auren did not move at once. She had noticed Del step out of the second's place before accepting. The code did not require it. It did not forbid it either. She had seen it done once before, by a woman whose husband Auren had killed in the sixth accounting, and that woman had meant something by it that Auren had not understood until much later. She did not know yet what Del meant by it. She did not presume.

"It is closed," she said. The formality was gone from her voice now, but not the care. She spoke the way a person speaks after setting down something heavy, when they are not yet sure their hands will stop shaking. "I will not speak of it again. That is not a courtesy. It is binding on me. If anyone asks me about this day, I will tell them to find the record."

She looked, for the first time, toward the place where he had fallen. Only briefly. Then back to Del.

"His blade is in the keeping-house, with his cloak and whatever he carried. They are yours by right. No one will question it." A pause. "He had written a name on a slip of paper and tucked it inside the hilt wrapping. I did not read it. I saw only that it was there when they carried him in. I thought you should know before you unwrap it, so it does not come to you as a surprise."

The wind pulled at her sleeve. She let it.

"I have no right to anything else from you," Auren said. "Not forgiveness, and not your company, and not your hatred either, if you would rather keep that for yourself. But you learned the closing form from someone, and I think it was him. If you ever want to know what he did well out there, not the wound, only the fighting, I will tell you that. It is not part of the account. It would only be the truth, and it would be his."

She stood where she was, and waited, and did not reach for her blade.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer. For a moment she did not move at all.

Then she looked toward the rail, where the three grey sashes had stood. It was empty. The far gate at the end of the yard still swung a little on its hinge.

"The witnesses are gone, Del," she said. She said it gently, the way she might have pointed out a step in the dark. "They have what they need. They took it with them."

She turned back. She did not let her eyes drift to the sand this time. She kept them on Del's face and saw what was in it, and did not pretend not to.

"And I cannot give it to you again." The words came slowly, but they did not waver. "I told you it was binding, and I did not say that to spare myself. You accepted the account. When a second accepts, it closes. If I speak the wound now, with no one at the rail and no pen moving, it stops being an accounting. It becomes a story. Stories get told again, and told differently, and one day someone tells it in a tavern with the angle wrong and a second blow added for colour." Her jaw tightened, very slightly. "The code closes it so that he is only killed once. I will not kill him a second time in the telling, not even for you. Not even when you ask it like that."

The wind came across the yard and she let it pass between them.

"But you are not refused. The record is at the witness-hall on Tallow Street. It is yours by right, as much as his blade is. Ask for the eldest by his sash. He will read it to you word for word, as many times as you ask. He will not tire of it and he will not change it. That is what he is for." A pause. "It will be the same account you heard. I gave it plainly. Below the fourth rib, on the left, rising. That much you already have, and no one can take it back from you."

She stopped there. It was the edge of what she could say, and she did not step past it.

"If the reason you are asking is that you did not hear it the first time, that is not a failing," Auren said, more quietly. "Most people do not. They hear the voice and the sand and the wind, and the words go somewhere they cannot reach until later. That is why it is written down. The code knew you would need it again. It only did not want the next telling to be mine."

She stood where she was, hands empty at her sides.

"I am still bound to answer anything else you ask truthfully. Anything that is not the wound."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a sharp, deep breath, pulling my eyes away from the sand. My hands are clenched at my sides. "Did he ever mention me? Here? Before the yard?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. She had been asked many things after many accountings, and she had learned that this kind of question deserved the most care of all, because it was the easiest to answer with something warm and false.

"Once," she said. "I will tell you exactly what he said, and nothing that he did not."

She drew a breath, and when she spoke again it was slower, the way she spoke when she was placing each word where it belonged.

"We met three days ago, at the naming. The challenger and the standing meet before the witnesses, and each names a second for the record. That is all it is meant to be. He said your name. He said it clearly, and the eldest wrote it down." A pause. "That part was the code. Anyone would have done it."

The wind moved across the yard. She did not look away from Del.

"The rest was not. When the naming was finished, he asked the eldest whether the second is made to stand near enough to hear the accounting, or whether they may stand back. The eldest told him near. He was quiet for a while. Then he turned to me. It is not usual for a challenger to speak to the standing at the naming, and I thought he meant to say something about the fight." Her jaw set, very slightly. "He did not. He said, *When you give it, give it plainly. Del will know if you soften it, and Del will never forgive either of us.*"

She let that stand in the air for a moment. She did not add to it.

"I told him I had never softened an accounting and would not begin with his. He nodded, and he left, and I did not see him again until this morning." Her voice lowered. "That is the whole of it. I have not dressed it. I do not know what he meant by it beyond the words themselves, and I will not guess for you, because a guess from me is worth nothing next to what you already know of him."

She was quiet for a breath, and then she said the last of it, because it was true and because the code bound her to truth whether or not it was comfortable to give.

"I gave it plainly because the code requires it. But I will not pretend I did not think of him asking. I thought of it when I held up my hand." She let her empty hands rest at her sides. "He was right about you. You did know. You asked for it plainly twice."

Then she waited, and did not fill the silence, and did not presume that it was hers to fill.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren was quiet for longer this time. The wind came and went twice before she spoke, and when she did, it was not a refusal. Not at first.

"You are right," she said. "The code says precisely."

She looked at Del steadily, and something in her face had gone very still, the stillness of someone who has found a flaw in a blade she has carried for years.

"And I was not precise. Not in all of it." She did not hurry the words. "I said he did not feel the heart. I said he felt the rib, and then very little. I said it twice, before the witnesses, and it was written twice." Her jaw tightened. "I do not know that. No one can know that but him. I have seen men struck that way before and I believe it is so, but belief is not what I saw. I put it into the account because it seemed a true thing, and because some part of me wanted it to be true. For you. For me. I do not know which." A breath. "That is tact. You named it correctly."

She did not look toward the sand. She did not let herself.

"So here is what I will do, and what I will not do. I will not give you the wound again, here, with no one at the rail. That has not changed. The account is closed, and if I open it in this yard with no pen moving, I make it mine to reshape, and I have just shown you how easily even I reshape it without meaning to." Her voice did not waver, but it had lost some of its evenness. "That is exactly why it must not be me, alone, telling it."

She drew herself up slightly, formally, as though the rail were still occupied.

"But a flaw in the account is a different matter from a retelling. The code allows the standing to go before the witnesses and name an error in what was spoken, so that it may be marked in the record. It is rarely done. I have never done it." A pause. "I will do it. Today, at the hall on Tallow Street, before the eldest, with you there if you wish to be. I will say that the words concerning what he felt were my belief and not my witness, and I will ask that they be marked so. The rest stands as I gave it. The blade, the rib, the line of it. That I saw, and that I will not take back."

She let her hands rest open at her sides.

"He told me you would know if I softened it. I told him I never had." The admission sat plainly in her voice, and she did not dress it. "I was wrong about that. You found it in the space of an hour. He knew you better than I knew myself."

Then she stopped, and waited, and did not ask Del to come with her. That was not hers to ask either.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look down at the sand for a long moment, my own breath coming sharp. Then I nod once. "I'll walk with you to Tallow Street."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head, once, the same small motion she had given the witnesses. Then she turned toward the far gate.

She did not walk ahead. She took the pace of someone who knew the way and did not intend to be followed so much as accompanied, and she kept to the left side, the side where the wound had been, though she did not think of that until they were already through the gate. Once she had thought of it, she did not change sides. Changing would have been a thing done for herself.

The yard gave onto a lane of packed earth, and the lane onto the lower market, where the stalls were still half-shuttered for the morning. A man selling lamp oil glanced at her grey-trimmed collar and then at the empty scabbard-loop at her hip where a second blade sometimes hung, and looked away. People in the lower market knew what it meant when the Eleventh Standing walked out of the yard before noon.

She said nothing through the market. There was nothing the code let her say about the morning, and nothing she would let herself say that was not about it.

At the corner where the lane met Candlewright's Row, she slowed.

"The keeping-house is there," she said, and lifted her chin a fraction toward a low stone building with a blue door. She did not point. "His things are inside. The hall is two streets further. I will not stop here unless you wish it. And if you wish to go in alone, I will wait at the corner, or I will go on to Tallow Street and you may come after, or not." A pause. "The correction does not need you present to be made. I only said you might be there, because it is yours more than it is mine."

She waited long enough for that to be an honest offer, then walked on when the moment came.

The witness-hall on Tallow Street was narrower than most people expected. It had been a chandler's shop once, and the old hooks still hung from the beams where the tapers had dried. The eldest was at the long table at the back, the rolled sheet from the yard still tied with its cord beside his elbow. He had not yet filed it. He looked up when the door opened, saw Auren, and then saw who was with her, and set his pen down very carefully.

"Standing," he said. "The matter is closed."

"It is," Auren said. "I have not come to open it. I have come to name an error in what I spoke."

The old man was still for a long moment. Then he rose, slowly, and went to the shelf behind him and took down a second sash, the formal one, and put it on over the grey. He did not ask her whether she was certain. He only untied the cord on the sheet and unrolled it flat, and weighted the corners with four smooth stones, and took up his pen.

"Speak it," he said.

Auren stood before the table exactly as she had stood before the rail. She did not look at the sheet. She knew what was written there.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing. In the account given this morning, and accepted, I said twice that the challenger did not feel the heart, that he felt the rib and very little after." Her voice was level. It was not easy, and she did not make it sound easy. "I did not witness that. I believed it. I have seen that wound before and I believe it still. But what a man feels is not a thing the standing can see, and I spoke it as though I had. I ask that those words be marked as my belief and not my witness. The rest stands. The line, the rib, the angle, the heart, the one wound and no second. Those I saw."

The pen moved. It moved for a long time, longer than the words seemed to need, and she understood that he was writing the reason as well as the correction, and she did not stop him.

When he finished, he looked up at her, and then past her.

"The second is present," he said. It was not quite a question. The code did not have a place for the second at a correction, because there had been so few corrections that no one had thought to make one. "Is there anything the second wishes set beside it?"

Auren did not turn around. She kept her eyes on the old man and her hands open at her sides, and she left the silence exactly as large as it needed to be.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned around.

She had not meant to. The correction was addressed to the table, and the code placed the standing facing the pen. But Del had spoken to her and not to the eldest, and she found she could not answer that with her back.

"The second asks for all of it," she said. She was looking at Del, but she pitched the words so they would carry to the table. "The code says the account is given whole. What I gave this morning was whole as to the wound. It was not whole as to the death. I left out what he said, and how long it took, and what I saw at the end, because I have always left those out. Eleven times." She stopped. "No one has ever asked. That is not the same as the code permitting it."

Behind her, the eldest's pen had not moved. Then it did: a short line, a word or two. She guessed it was *the standing concedes*, or something close.

"Is the record open?" she asked him, without turning.

"It is open while the correction is being made," the old man said. "The second has asked. You may make it longer."

Auren nodded once. She faced the table again, because this part belonged to the pen, and she held herself as she had at the rail.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing, and I add to the account what was left out of it.

"When the point went in, he did not cry out. He said *oh*. Quietly. The way a man says it when he has missed a step on a stair. I heard it clearly. I was close enough.

"I withdrew the blade. That took less than a breath. He stayed standing after it was out. I counted afterwards, in my head, the way I was trained, and I make it three heartbeats of my own, and my heart was going fast, so it was less time than that sounds. His sword arm dropped first. He did not let go of the hilt. Then his knees went, both together, and he went forward onto them, and then onto his left side, toward the wound."

Her hands stayed open at her sides. She did not raise one to show anything. There was nothing in this part that a hand could show.

"There was blood at his mouth when he was on his knees. Not a great deal. More at his side, into the sand, and it darkened the sand quickly because the sand was dry. His eyes were open. He breathed twice after he was down. I saw his chest move twice, and I heard it, and it was not a good sound. His right hand moved in the sand, a short way, toward nothing I could see. Then it stopped, and his breathing stopped, and I did not see him move again."

A breath. The pen moved, and she let it catch up.

"I said this morning that he was dead before his knees reached the sand. That was wrong, and I mark it now with the other. He was not. He breathed twice after. I do not know when he died, only when I stopped seeing him move. I ask that it be written so."

The old man's pen paused, then went on. He did not look up.

"I did not go to him. The standing does not approach until the witnesses call it, and they called it after he had been still for a count of ten. I stood where I was. I watched him the whole time. I did not look away from him, and I have not looked away from it since." She was quiet a moment. "That is all I saw. There is nothing else. I have kept nothing back that I know of, and if I find later that I have, I will come here again."

She stopped. The hooks overhead turned slightly in some draft from the door.

Then, without turning, more quietly, so that it was not quite part of what was written, though she knew the eldest would write it anyway: "You were standing where the second stands. You saw all of that. I know you did." A pause. "You wanted it said by the one who did it. I understand that. I should have understood it this morning."

She did not face Del again. The pen was still moving, and she would not turn from it while it moved.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I press my knuckles into the wooden table, hard enough to feel the grain bite into my skin. "Say it again," I manage, my voice raw. "Say the part about his hand in the sand."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. She looked at the eldest.

"The words are written," she said. "If I speak them again, I speak them as they stand. Nothing added."

The old man laid his pen down across the sheet, the nib clear of the ink. "Words spoken as written are a reading," he said. "Not a telling. The standing may read."

Auren nodded. She came around the end of the table, not close, but near enough that she was no longer speaking across the whole width of the room. She stopped a pace from Del's left side and stood as she had stood at the rail, hands open. She did not look at Del's knuckles on the wood. She had seen them. Looking would have been a kind of touching, and she had no right to that.

"His right hand moved in the sand," she said. Her voice was the same as before. She did not let it gentle, because gentling would have made it a different sentence. "A short way. Toward nothing I could see. Then it stopped."

She let it rest there, exactly that long and no longer.

"That is the whole of that part. There is no more of it than that. It was his right hand, the sword hand. He had let go of the hilt by then, though I did not see the moment he let go. It moved perhaps the length of a finger. The sand was dry and it left a mark, and the mark was still there when they carried him in."

She stopped. Then, because she could see the next question even if Del did not ask it, and because the code bound her to truth before it bound her to comfort:

"I do not know what he was reaching for. I have thought about it, since this morning. I will not tell you what I think, because I would be putting a meaning into his hand that he did not give me, and I have already put one thing into this account that was mine and not his. I will not do it twice in a day." A pause. "If you know what he would have reached for, you know it better than I do. That is not mine to take from you, and it is not mine to give you."

Behind her, the eldest had not picked up his pen. There was nothing new to write.

"I will say it again if you ask," Auren said, more quietly. "The same words. As many times as you ask, today, in this room, with the record open." She held herself very still. "And when the record closes, it will be his to read to you, and not mine. Not because I will not. Because I should not be the only voice you have for it."

She did not step closer, and she did not step away.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looked at the eldest. He understood before she asked. He turned the sheet on the table so that its head faced her, lifted two of the stones, and set them down again at the new corners. Then he took up his pen and waited, nib above the ink.

"A reading of the whole," Auren said. "As it now stands, with the corrections in their places. Nothing added. Nothing set aside."

"The standing may read," the old man said.

She did not look down at the sheet. She knew every line on it. But the code said a reading was a reading, and so she let her eyes rest on the ink as she spoke, so that nothing came from anywhere but the page.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing, and I give the accounting of the death of the challenger, whole.

"The challenger was the brother of the one who stands second. He came to the yard at first light. He was named at the rail and so was I. He opened high, on the left line. His opening was stronger than mine. He had trained it well, and trained it long.

"On the first pass I was not where I meant to be. My back foot was late by a half-step, and for the length of that half-step my right side was open to him. He did not see it. Had he seen it, he would be the one speaking this account, and I would be the one it was spoken of.

"Knowing that I could not meet his opening directly, I gave ground on the left line. Once on the first pass, and again on the second. I drew the fight long. I made him chase, and I meant to. My intention from the second exchange onward was to tire him, and it was done deliberately, and it succeeded.

"On the third pass he committed his weight forward to close the distance. His guard came down from the shoulder by a hand's width."

Her hand rose, fingers together, and held. She did not hurry it down.

"I entered beneath it. The point went in below the fourth rib on the left side, angled upward. It passed through the lung and reached the heart. There was one wound, and no second.

"It was said this morning that he did not feel the heart, and that he felt the rib and very little after. That is marked. It is the belief of the standing and not her witness. No one saw what he felt.

"When the point went in, he did not cry out. He said *oh*. Quietly. The way a man says it when he has missed a step on a stair.

"I withdrew the blade in less than a breath. He remained standing after it was out, for three beats of my heart, and my heart was fast. His sword arm dropped first. He did not let go of the hilt. Then his knees went, both together, and he came down onto them, and then forward, and onto his left side, toward the wound.

"There was blood at his mouth while he was on his knees. Not a great deal. There was more at his side, into the sand, and the sand was dry and darkened quickly.

"His eyes were open. He breathed twice after he was down. I saw his chest move twice and I heard it, and it was not a good sound.

"It was said this morning that he was dead before his knees reached the sand. That is marked. It was wrong. He breathed twice after. The standing does not know the moment of his death, only the moment she stopped seeing him move.

"His right hand moved in the sand. His sword hand. He had let go of the hilt by then, though I did not see him let go. It moved the length of a finger, toward nothing I could see. It left a mark in the dry sand, and the mark was still there when they carried him in. Then his hand stopped, and his breathing stopped, and I did not see him move again.

"I did not go to him. The standing does not approach until the witnesses call it. They called it when he had been still for a count of ten. For all of that time I stood where I was, and I watched him, and I did not look away.

"His error was fatigue, and the fatigue was caused by me. It was not cowardice. It was not carelessness. He fought well. He had a true chance, and he lost it on that day against me.

"That is the whole of the account. I have set nothing aside from it that I know of. What was mine and not his has been marked as mine."

Her hand had come down at some point. She did not remember when.

She lifted her eyes from the sheet. She did not turn fully to Del. The form did not place her so, and she would not borrow the moment. But she turned enough that Del was at the edge of her sight, the knuckles on the grain, the face above them.

The eldest had not written anything during the reading. Now he dipped his pen, and held it, and did not lower it to the page.

"The reading is ended," he said. "The record waits on the second."

Auren stood with her hands open and said nothing. It was not hers to say. She had given all of it, and what came after belonged to Del.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My knuckles ache from pressing into the wood. The blood is loud in my ears. "He was trying to roll over," I say, so softly I almost don't hear it myself. "That's why his hand moved. He hated being on his side."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move.

She had heard it. The room was small and the hooks overhead were still, and there was nothing else in it to hear. She kept her eyes where they were, on the sheet and not on Del. Watching a face at that moment would have been taking something from it.

For a breath no one spoke. The eldest's pen stayed where it was, lifted, the ink gathering slowly at the nib.

Then Auren turned, not to Del but to the table.

"The second has spoken," she said. Her voice was level, but it was lower than it had been for the reading. "I ask that it be written. Not as part of the account. The account is mine, and it holds only what I saw. This is not what I saw." A pause. "It is what the second knows. Set it beside the account, in the second's name, so that anyone who reads the one reads the other."

The old man looked at her for a long moment over the pen. There was no form for this. She had watched him discover that twice already today, and she watched him discover it a third time, and decide.

"The second's word, set beside," he said, and lowered the nib to the page.

He wrote slowly. Auren did not read it as it went down. She did not need to see how he phrased it, and she did not want to be the one who checked Del's words for accuracy. That had never been hers to do.

She stood where she was, a pace from Del's left side. She did not reach out. Her hands were open, as they had been all morning, and she left them so.

"I did not know that about him," she said, when the pen had gone quiet. She said it plainly, the way she had said everything else. "I could not have. I stood a sword's length from him and I saw his hand move, and I did not know what I was seeing." She was quiet a moment. "You did. From the rail, before I had even come to the end of it."

She stopped there. She did not say that it was right, or that it was surely so. She had not been inside his hand any more than she had been inside his heart, and she had spent the morning learning where the edge of her witness lay. She would not step past it now, not even to give Del something that would sound like comfort.

"That is not mine to confirm," she said. "It does not need me."

The eldest sanded the page, and tipped the grains back into their dish, and the small dry sound of it was very loud.

"It is set beside," he said.

Auren inclined her head to him. Then she stepped back, one pace, and then another, until she stood near the door with the width of the room between herself and the table. She did not leave. She had not been released, and she would not go until Del no longer needed anything that she was bound to give.

But the table, and the sheet, and whatever came next at it belonged to Del now, and to the brother, and she would not stand close enough to crowd that.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stare at the ink where my words have just gone into the record. My throat is too tight to speak. I press my palm flat over the sentence, the paper cool and slightly rough. Then I step away from the table, turn, and walk out of the hall. I don't look back at her.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not follow.

She heard the door open and the street come in for a moment, the cart wheels and a gull and someone calling a price for bread, and then the door closed and the street went out again. She did not turn her head to watch it. Del had not looked back. That was Del's to choose, and watching the choice made would have been a way of not honouring it.

The hooks overhead swung a little in the draft and slowly settled.

The eldest did not speak for some time. He looked at the sheet, at the place where the palm had lain. The ink there had been dry, but the warmth of a hand still showed on the paper as a faint difference in the grain. It would be gone in a moment. He did not touch it.

"The second has gone without releasing you," he said at last.

"Yes."

"There is no form for that either." He said it drily, without complaint. He was an old man, and he had seen a great deal of the code, and today had shown him more of its edges than he had expected to see. "By the letter, you are bound to answer until released."

"Then I am bound," Auren said.

He considered her over the table. "It could be a long time."

"It could." She did not shift her weight. "He asked me to give it plainly, and I did not, the first time. The second found every place where I had not. I will not argue with how the second chooses to end it." A pause. "If the second never comes back to release me, then any question the second ever asks me, I will answer truthfully, for as long as I live. I have made smaller promises and kept them."

The old man was quiet. Then he took off the formal sash, folded it with great care along creases it had held for decades, and laid it back on its shelf. He did not roll the sheet. He left it flat under its four stones so the ink could settle.

"I will file it tomorrow," he said. "Not today."

Auren understood that he was not speaking to her, and did not answer.

She went out a while later. The lane was full now, the market open, the lamp-oil seller shouting at a boy over a spilled measure. No one looked at her twice. She walked back the way she had come, past Candlewright's Row. She did not look at the blue door, because Del might be behind it, and she had no right to know either way. Then she went through the lower market and into the yard.

It was empty. The rail was bare. The sand had been raked, as it always was after, and the dark place was gone. The raking had turned it under.

She had not looked at that place all morning. She looked at it now.

She walked to where he had fallen and stood at a sword's length from it, where she had stood before, and looked down at the smooth, pale, ordinary sand. There was no mark of a hand. The rakers were thorough. They always were.

She did not kneel. She did not reach down to draw anything in the sand, a finger's length toward nothing, though for a moment she thought about it. It would have been hers and not his. She had marked enough of herself into this day.

So she only stood there, a long time, with her hands open at her sides, while the wind moved over the raked sand and left no mark on it either.

Eleven accountings, she thought. Eleven, and this was the first time anyone had made her give the whole of one.

She did not know yet whether she would ever give a twelfth. She knew that if she did, she would give all of it, from the first word, and would not wait to be asked.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I return to the yard an hour later. I'm carrying the blade now, and his cloak is over my arm. I see her standing there and I don't slow my steps. I stop a few paces away.

"You're released."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to the witnesses. She kept the cleaned blade lowered at her side and spoke without emphasis.

“The killing wound was a thrust to the left side of the chest. The point passed between the ribs and pierced the heart. That wound caused death.”

She fell silent, allowing the account to stand without ornament.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my voice steady despite the tightness in my chest. "I have witnessed the same. The account is true."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once. “Then it is witnessed.”

She turned the blade point-down and kept her silence. The account had been made; nothing more could make it cleaner.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned back to the witnesses. She held the blade point-down and repeated the account, unchanged.

“The killing wound was a thrust to the left side of the chest. The point passed between the ribs and pierced the heart. That wound caused death.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath I hadn't realized I was holding. "Truth witnessed. The account is clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head. “The record is complete.”

She lowered the blade and stood silent. There was nothing left to add without making the account less true.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren faced the witnesses, blade still lowered.

“The point entered the left side of the chest, passed between the ribs, and pierced the heart. That was where it landed, and that wound caused death.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my gaze shifting to the body on the ground. "And it was a clean pass," I add, for the record. "No deflection or hesitation in the blow."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave one measured nod.

“There was no deflection. The thrust did not hesitate. That is accurate.”

She kept her gaze on the witnesses. “Let it stand as an observation, not as part of the account of the wound.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to the witnesses, her voice level.

“The blade entered the left side of the chest, passed between the ribs, and pierced the heart. It pierced the heart; that wound caused death. There was no deflection or hesitation in the thrust.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my gaze settle on the body again. "The blade was clean when it entered. No prior contact with bone or leather?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren kept her gaze on the witnesses.

“No. The blade had made no prior contact with bone or leather. It entered cleanly and passed between the ribs.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to the witnesses. She kept the blade point-down.

“The exchange lasted only a few moments. I heard no words from him during it or after the thrust. The blade entered the left side of the chest, passed between the ribs, and pierced the heart. There was no deflection or hesitation, and the blade had made no prior contact with bone or leather. He fell. I saw no further movement or breath.”

She paused, making no attempt to dress the facts in gentler language.

“That is all I can state as observation. The rest would be invention.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I glance at the witnesses, then back to her.* "And the angle of entry?" I ask, because sometimes the blade tells a story of its own.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to the witnesses, keeping the blade point-down.

“The point entered the left side of the chest and traveled inward between the ribs to the heart. I did not establish a more exact angle of entry. To give one would be to claim what I did not observe.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

“The exchange lasted only a few moments. I heard no words from him during it or after the thrust. The blade had made no prior contact with bone or leather. It entered the left side of the chest, passed between the ribs, and pierced the heart. The thrust did not deflect or hesitate. He fell. I saw no further movement or breath.

“The point traveled inward between the ribs to the heart. I did not establish a more exact angle of entry. To state one would be to claim what I did not observe.

“That wound caused death. That is all I can state as observation.”

Auren fell silent and kept the blade lowered.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I wait a beat, letting the words settle in the cold air. "The account is complete and witnessed," I say, my voice carrying across the quiet space. "Truth stands."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once. “Then it is witnessed, and the record stands.”

She kept the blade lowered and said nothing more. The account had been given in full; anything beyond it would have been neither truth nor duty.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward and turn to face the witnesses. "You have heard the accounting. Do you dispute it?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren remained silent, the blade lowered at her side. The question belonged to the witnesses; she waited for their answer.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: A heavy silence hangs for a moment before one of them, a man with tired eyes, shakes his head. "No dispute," he says, and the others murmur agreement. I turn back to Auren. "It's done."

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not raise her voice. The yard was quiet enough that she did not need to.

She faced the witnesses, not the body, and set the cleaned blade point-down against the stone so both hands were empty. “The stroke was the third,” she said. “He opened on the high line and I answered low. The point entered beneath the left ribs and traveled upward. It opened the lung. He did not rise. That is the wound that killed him.”

She let the words stand as they were. No apology in them, and no ornament either. When the silence held, she added only what the code still required of her. “I name it before you so that it is known, and so that it is finished. Eleven. I take no pleasure in the count.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. My voice comes out steadier than I feel. "Witnessed. Eleven is confirmed." I meet Auren's gaze, my throat tight. "It's finished."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, the smallest acknowledgment the code allowed a second who had held the place and not looked away. She did not thank Del for the confirmation. Thanks would have made the accounting into a courtesy, and it was not one.

“Then it is closed,” she said. She lifted the blade from the stone, turned the point away from the witnesses, and slid it home until the guard met the mouth of the scabbard with a single clean sound. Her hands were steady. They always were, afterward. That was not the same thing as ease.

She faced the yard again, voice still level. “The body is to be covered and borne out before the light fails. No one touches the weapon but me. If any of you dispute the stroke, speak now, while the witnesses are still standing.” She waited through the length of three breaths. No one spoke. “Then you are released.”

Only when the first of them began to move did she look back at Del, and even then it was not a softening. “You kept your eyes open,” she said. “That was the duty. It is done.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not unsheathe the blade again, and she did not repeat what had already been set before the witnesses.

“The account has been spoken,” she said. Her voice did not lift to match the formality of the request; it stayed where it had been, level and spare. “You heard it. You named it witnessed. I closed it. The code does not ask me to say the wound twice so that the second may feel the shape of the rite in his own mouth.”

She met Del’s gaze and did not look past it toward the body, or toward the yard where the others had begun to move.

“If you were not ready when you said you were, that is yours to carry. It is not mine to mend by ornament. Eleven stands. The stroke stands. It is finished.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my hands clenching at my sides. "I know it's finished," I say, my voice dropping low. "I just... needed to hear you say it one more time."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move to meet the tightness in Del’s voice. She stood with the scabbard settled at her hip and let the request fall where the first one had fallen.

“No,” she said. The word was not sharp. It did not need to be. “You have heard the wound. You have confirmed the count. Hearing it again would not make it truer, and it would not make it lighter. The code keeps the account once, before witnesses, and then it is done with. I will not spend it a second time because the silence after it is hard to stand in.”

She looked at his clenched hands and did not comment on them. “If you need the words to live somewhere other than this yard, write them down from what you already heard. I will not speak them for you again. Eleven is closed. So is this.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer the question as if it were new.

“I have already said where it landed,” she said. “Beneath the left ribs. Upward. The lung. You heard the words when the witnesses were still standing to hear them, and you named them confirmed. Asking for them again does not make them plainer. It only asks me to break the close I have already set.”

She did not glance toward the body. Her hands stayed at her sides, empty of any gesture that might have been taken for a second telling.

“The witnesses have what the code owed them. So do you. If the place of it will not settle in you, that is not mended by dragging the account back out of the ground. Eleven is closed. I will not open it to point at the same wound a third time.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look away from her, my jaw working. "Fine. Then I'll write it down." My voice is rough. "I'll write it exactly as you said it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren gave that the smallest weight it could bear and no more.

“Then write what you heard,” she said. “Not what you wish had been said, and not a cleaner shape than the one that was spoken. If a word has already left you, leave the gap. Do not fill it from me. I will not read it back, and I will not correct it. The account was made once. Paper is your own burden.”

She set her hand once on the scabbard, not drawing, only settling it, and turned toward the gate as the yard began to empty.

“Do it away from the body. And do not bring it to me when it is done.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stopped with her shoulder already turned toward the gate, and she did not turn back all the way.

“The code says the account is spoken once, precisely, before witnesses,” she said. “It does not say the victor stands in the yard and answers until the second is satisfied with the shape of the words. You heard what the blade did. You heard what it opened. You confirmed it. I will not dress the same stroke in a second telling and call that precision.”

Her hand stayed on the scabbard. She did not draw.

“If the code is what you are invoking, then hear it all the way through. The close is part of it. I have set it. Paper may hold what you already heard. My mouth will not.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I am invoking it," I say, my voice low and tight. I step in front of her path, blocking the gate. "Because I am your second, and I am asking you for the account."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not step back from the body in the path, and she did not raise her hand from the scabbard. The gate stayed blocked. She let it.

“You are my second,” she said. “That is why you stood where the second stands, and why I accepted your witness when you gave it. It is not why the yard belongs to you, and it is not a claim on my mouth after the close.”

She met his eyes without heat. The line of her shoulder was still turned toward the gate, as if the obstruction were a fact and not a contest.

“A second keeps the place. A second does not bar the victor from leaving a finished accounting, and a second does not compel the wound to be spoken again by standing in the way. If that is the code you mean to invoke, you have it wrong. The duty ended when you said witnessed, and when I said it was finished.”

She waited one breath, no longer.

“Move,” she said. “Or do not. I will not draw on you for this, and I will not buy the gate with the account. Eleven is closed. The stroke has been named. You may stand there until the light fails. It will not open my mouth a second time.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not fill the silence the witnesses had left her. She stood with the gate still barred by Del’s body and did not treat the demand as unfinished business.

“The code does not say all of it,” she said. “It says the killing wound, spoken once, before those who are meant to hear it. I have done that. How long he took is not the wound. What he said is not the wound. What his face did at the end is not the wound, and it is not mine to spend so that the second may feel he has held the whole of a death in his hands.”

She looked past him only far enough to mark that the yard was not empty, then back.

“You are asking for a telling. The accounting is already made. I will not lengthen a man’s dying into a report because you have decided the close was too spare. The stroke was named. The lung was named. He did not rise. That is what killed him, and that is all the code takes from me.”

Her hand remained on the scabbard. She did not draw, and she did not step around him.

“Stand there if you must. The witnesses have heard what they were owed. I am finished. Eleven is closed.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let my shoulders slump, the fight draining out of me. "Fine," I mutter, stepping aside. I scrub a hand over my face. "Just... let me write it down before I forget."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not take the slump of his shoulders for a gift, and she did not fill the space he had left her with anything softer than the close already set.

“Then write it from what you heard,” she said, “and write it away from here. If a word has gone, leave the gap. I will not stand over the page and put it back.”

She passed him without looking at the body, the scabbard settled, her pace the same as it had been when the yard still held its witnesses. At the gate she stopped only long enough to set the last of it where it belonged.

“Do not bring it to me when it is done. Eleven is closed.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not take the demand as a reopening. She had already passed the place where the account could be spoken, and she did not turn back to spend it again for a confirmation that had already been given.

“There is nothing further to confirm,” she said, without looking at him. “You heard the stroke. You heard where it went. You named it witnessed. I will not stand in the gate and recite a man’s death a second time so the words can be made larger than the code allows.”

She went on through the gate. The scabbard did not shift. She did not give the time it took, or the face, or any word the dead man had or had not spoken. Those had never been part of the accounting, and she would not invent them to fill a silence.

“Eleven is closed,” she said, and did not stop.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I stand there for a long moment after she leaves, the silence of the yard pressing in. My hands are shaking. I take a breath, then another, and walk over to the small table at the edge of the yard where paper and ink are kept for the second. I sit down, dip the pen, and begin to write.

*The stroke was the third. He opened on the high line and she answered low. The point entered beneath the left ribs and traveled upward. It opened the lung. He did not rise. That is the wound that killed him.*

I stare at the words, my own handwriting stark against the page. It feels too small. Too clean. I put the pen down and don't look at the body.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not come back through the gate.

She heard the scratch of the pen start and let it stay behind her, where she had told him to keep it. The yard, the table, the page — none of it was hers anymore, and she did not turn to see whether the words on it were spare or too clean. Clean was not the point. Once was the point.

She walked until the stone under her boots gave way to the packed earth beyond the wall, and she did not stop to listen for whether he looked at the body. Her hand stayed on the scabbard. The blade stayed sheathed. Eleven remained what she had named it, and she did not spend another word on it for the silence he was sitting in.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I pick the pen up again, my knuckles white. I add one more line at the bottom, my script tight and angry.

*He made a sound when it went in. I didn’t close my eyes.*

dialogue.content:

She kept her hand on the scabbard and her pace even on the packed earth. The blade stayed sheathed. She did not look over her shoulder for the table, or for him, or for the body being covered before the light failed.

Eleven remained closed. She spent no further word on it.

dialogue.content:
"No," Halloway said. "It was never a person. But it's been studying to be one. 'Tried to' is exactly the word — remember you said it."

She raised the lamp a slow few inches, letting the light crawl up the shape instead of jumping at it. "Shoulders are right. Shoulders are the first thing they learn — it's all you see across a room, so it's all the reference they need to fool you. Then it falls apart. Left arm's got one elbow. Right one's got two. Left wrist is longer than its forearm. And before you ask — that's not the water. Water swells a thing even, like dough. This is lopsided. This was assembled wrong."

She kept her boots planted where they were.

"Now the part that matters. It stopped moving about a minute ago. That's when we came down the stairs. Corpses don't have timing, Pike. Dead is a thing you are. Stopping is a thing you do." A dry note came into her voice. "It's playing dead, and it's doing that badly too, which fits. They come out shaped like this when they're new, or starving, or hurt. And it didn't build this from imagination. It copied somebody. Somebody stood about where you're standing, long enough to be measured."

The water around the shape lay dead flat. Halloway watched the surface, not the thing.

"So watch the water. Four feet of still water is the most honest witness you'll ever get — if it's breathing, the surface shivers around it. Hasn't yet. And keep that offer to go round the side in your pocket. It's had an eye on you since the stairs. You flank it, you're not getting a better angle. You're giving it one."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong with the shape is most of my caseload," Halloway said. "Wrong *how*. Count. Ends, joints, whether the top half agrees with the bottom half. And is it standing on the bottom or riding the surface? A carcass bloats and floats after a few days. Floating fresh, it was built to."

She kept the lamp high and her boots where they were. The light lay flat across the water and stopped six feet short of the thing, and she let it stop there.

"Watch the surface while you count. Rings spreading out from it, it's either settling or breathing, and the difference matters more than your opinion of the smell. Nothing at all — then we've bought ourselves a minute. Minutes are the currency in this trade. Four feet of water is deep enough to hide half of it and shallow enough to introduce you to the other half."

A pipe somewhere overhead knocked twice and went quiet.

"So. Again, and slower. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore the way my heart's hammering. "Three... no, four limbs. Too many joints in the back ones. And it's not floating. It's standing on the bottom, but tilted." I swallow. "No rings in the water. It's still."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Four limbs, surplus joints, standing, tilted, and quiet." Halloway repeated it back like she was weighing each word. "First useful inventory anyone's given me down here. Now understand what you counted."

"Dead doesn't stand, and dead certainly doesn't *tilt*. It slumps flat or it floats flat — the only thing between those is wedged on something. And joints don't grow after death. Whatever grew those extras was born with plans for them." She paused. "Things with the right number of joints kill you with what they have. Things with too many have been saving up."

She lowered the lamp to waist height. Raking light came flat across the water, and the shape's outline changed — the extra joints stood out of the dark like knuckles on a fist.

"No rings bought us a minute. Sometimes still water is good news. Sometimes it's just practiced. Let's pretend we're rich." She kept her voice level. "Two more things, then I start spending. One: there's a tide line on the cellar walls — old watermark, scum, debris. Find the highest mark on the wall, then find where the water sits on *it*. If the two agree, it came in with the flood. If the thing's line sits lower, it moved after the water settled, and that's worth knowing before my boots are. Two — and don't go hunting for the head, you may not have found it yet — which way does the front of it face? Toward the stairs, or away?"

She shifted the lamp to her left hand and let the right hang loose.

"Things point at what they care about."

The smoke would choke us out, and the damp would just steam it, not cleanse it." *She wipes her knife on a clean rag.* "We salt it. Then we seal the cellar and let the river claim the rest."
