dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the cloth aside and turned from the body to face Del, because the account was owed to the second before it was owed to the room. She did not sit. Sitting came after, when it was finished. Not before.

"Given before witnesses, the twelfth account of my hand," she said. Her voice was level. Eleven previous accounts had taught her that a level voice was the only thing permitted her that resembled mercy, and even that was suspect. "The fallen is Tam Aris Vell, entered in the challenge under his own name and his own seal. He fought well. Hear it all the same.

"He fought with a high guard and quick feet, and he was better than the stories said. He drew first blood — a shallow cut inside my left forearm at the fourth pass. The mark is here for any witness who requires proof this was a contest.

"At the sixth pass I offered quarter. He declined it. I record that because it is true, and for no other reason. It does not lighten anything.

"At the ninth pass he came in on my left, where the cut had cost me some small measure he could not have seen but must have guessed. My blade entered beneath his right ribs, angled upward. It passed through the liver and stopped short of the spine. He was not killed instantly. He knew he was struck. I withdrew, and he stood perhaps two breaths, and he seemed to be trying to say something. If it was a word, I did not hear it, and I will not invent one for him.

"He fell. I remained beside him and counted, as the code requires. Death took him between ten and fifteen counts — nearer ten. I did not close his eyes. That right is yours."

She let the silence sit for a moment, exactly as long as the ritual demanded and no longer.

"His effects remain on his body. His horse is tied at the north rail. I owe his kin this same account, word for word. If you choose to carry it to them yourself, I will not refuse you, and I will not carry it in your place.

"The account is given. If any witness saw otherwise, speak, and I will enter the correction."

The witnesses were silent. Auren looked at Del then — properly looked, the way she had decided years ago the second deserved.

"You kept your eyes open," she said. "Most cannot, by the third sentence."

The first account had cost her a night's sleep. The eleventh had cost her the same. She saw no reason the twelfth should come cheaper. She had been hated for this honesty before. She had been thanked for it once, which had been worse. She stood very still and waited, having long ago given up expecting either.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "I heard it all." I step forward, past her, and kneel by the body. My hand shakes when I reach to close his eyes.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My fingers brush his eyelids closed. "The account is heard and confirmed," I say, my voice steadier than my hands. "You owe his kin nothing until dawn." I stand up, turning back to her. "And you're bleeding through your bandage."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned her left arm to the light and drew the bandage back with two fingers.

"Here. As it was given. Inside of the forearm, fourth pass — a draw-cut, his point finding me as I changed my line against his high guard. Four fingers long, deepest at the middle, the edges clean. He had first blood of me, and it was honestly taken."

She closed her hand slowly into a fist and opened it again, so the witnesses could see it was true. "Shallow. I kept my grip the whole duel through, and this is the proof of it. But shallow is not nothing — the forearm bleeds past its worth, which is why the bandage fails before the wound does. I will not make it larger than it is. I will not make it smaller."

She held the arm out toward Del, palm up, steady.

"The code gives the second the right to inspect the victor's marks before the account is closed. Look if you require it. If you decline, the witnesses stand in your place and the record will say so."

She kept the arm where it was and went on, because the rest was owed as well.

"At dawn I go to his kin with the account word for word, unless before dawn you tell me you carry it yourself. Until one of us says otherwise, dawn is mine to keep."

Her eyes went briefly to the body, to the closed eyes above Del's shoulder.

"And it is entered in my own record that you closed his eyes with your own hand. The code does not require that of me. I note it all the same."

The blood was welling again along the cut, slow and even. She did not move to stop it. Inspection first, binding after — that was the order of things, and she had long ago made a discipline of doing things in their order.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I lean in, careful not to touch the wound. "I see it. Clean." I step back. "And you'll need stitches before dawn if you're determined to ride out yourself." I keep my voice low, so only she can hear. "We should take care of that now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The blade cut you, through skin and part of the muscle. You bled. It cost you speed on your left side, which he used." I meet her eyes. "It's the truth, and the witnesses have heard it. Now come inside."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Aurin," I say softly, stepping closer and lowering my voice so only she can hear. "You've given the account. The witnesses have heard it. He's dead, and you're still bleeding. Come inside so I can stitch you up, *then* we can talk about what's left unsaid."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a sharp breath, my stomach twisting as she goes on. *He tried to call out. God.* But I keep my face still. When she finishes, I swallow and speak clearly for the witnesses. "The account is heard and confirmed. Aurin fought with honor, gave quarter where it was refused, and kept to the count." I look at her bloody arm. "Now come inside."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take her elbow, careful of the cut. "Inside. Now." I guide her toward the hall's side door, not letting go. "And you're getting the last of the good thread."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let the door shut behind us, the quiet of the hall a sharp contrast to the yard. "Sit," I say, nudging her toward a bench. "And take that jacket off before you ruin it."
